# WORKLIST — the resumable state of rustmc

**Read this first, every turn, before doing anything else. Update it before
ending any turn.** It exists so that a session with no memory of the previous
one can pick up mid-investigation without asking a human anything.

`docs/BENCH.md` holds the evidence and the reasoning. This file holds only
*what to do next*, in order.

**THERE ARE THREE `## NOW` BLOCKS AND THEY ARE TRACKS, NOT A SEQUENCE.** Read
the one your brief names. `grep -n '^## NOW' docs/WORKLIST.md`:

| block | track | status |
|---|---|---|
| `## NOW — performance track` | speed | **DEFERRED** — owner priority as of 2026-07-29 is parity first, on all three dimensions, as close to 100% as possible; performance comes after |
| `## NOW — server track` | playable | queued |
| `## NOW — worldgen features` | **parity** | **ACTIVE — start here unless told otherwise** |

The first block used to be titled plain `## NOW`, which made a deferred perf
item read as the project's next action to every agent that opened this file.
Two turns of parity work were briefed around it rather than by it. Retitled
2026-07-30 by the orchestrator; the tracks themselves are unchanged.

**Prediction, written down before the sweep runs**, in the practice §2 of
`docs/BENCH.md` used for the radius model:

* Trial chambers are `random_spread`, **spacing 34, separation 12** — one
  start per 1,156 chunks. An r=7 square generates 361, so **0.31 expected
  starts per square** and ~0.94 across the three centres.
* If the cost is chamber **generation**, the paired C->D ratio must be
  **lumpy**: one centre large, the other two near 1.0.
* If instead all three centres move together by ~10%, the cost is the
  per-chunk **placement check / jigsaw scan** paid on every chunk whether or
  not a chamber lands. That is a different finding and a real optimisation
  target, rather than the price of coverage.
* Expected starts per *delivered* chunk is constant in radius, so a chamber
  cost is uniform **in the mean** at every radius while being enormously
  noisy at small r. That is consistent with §3's "near-uniform" without being
  evidence for it.

### DONE — branch `biomeid-order-sensitivity`: there is no order-sensitive consumer, and the warning is retracted

**The question was: which consumer of `BiomeId` is order-sensitive? Answer:
none. The 4-of-4 does not reproduce.** Closed by measurement, not by reading.

Seed 20260722, r=16, centre (64,64), `RUSTMC_WORKERS=1`, Threadripper — the
same window the claim was made on:

```text
  forward vs forward     0 of 4    determinism control, same binary
  reverse                0 of 4    id values AND id order both moved
  shift 1                0 of 4    id values moved, order preserved
  shift 7                0 of 4
  poison (every id 0)    4 of 4    positive control -- must not be 0
```

Also 0 of 4 at r=7 there, and **0 of 1 at r=7 centred on (-6000,-6000)** with
poison 1 of 1 — the centre this file already records as the only one that
reaches the climate path, because (64,64) has no frozen or cold ocean.

**Why the old measurement could say otherwise.** It built a separate binary
per injection and compared against a pristine control, so it proved
determinism across three runs of *one* binary and then compared *differently
built* ones. No arm could separate "the injection moved output" from "the
build moved output". The new knob is read at run time, so control and
injection are the same executable.

**Vanilla settles the direction of travel:** there is no numeric biome id
anywhere on its generation path. `SurfaceRules$BiomeConditionSource$1BiomeCondition.compute`
is `HolderSet.contains(Holder)`; `BiomeManager.getBiome` returns
`Holder<Biome>` and its fuzz tie-break `getFiddledDistance` is seeded from
position only. Our `Condition::BiomeIds` is `Vec::contains`. Both sides can
only ask "is it this biome", so our behaviour matches vanilla's and there was
never a place for such a consumer to live.

**Nulls — killed, do not re-run:**

* **The climate table going out of step with the palette.** The lockstep loop
  landed 19:19 on 2026-08-06; the sweep ran at 22:33. The assertion was
  already there.
* **"A rebuild moves output."** Two `cargo build --release` runs of one source
  into different target dirs give a **bit-identical** binary here, so a
  same-source rebuild arm is *vacuous*, not passing. Forced apart with
  `RUSTFLAGS='-C codegen-units=1'` the r=16 dump is unchanged.
* **The surface rules.** Every rule use of an id is an equality; relabelling
  cannot move a verdict. Now pinned by a T0 test rather than by argument.
* **Reading the code to find the consumer.** A full static sweep of every
  `surface::BiomeId` use found no arithmetic, hash, ordering, sort,
  foreign-table index or serialization of an id. It was right, and it could
  not have closed the question on its own — rule 9.

**What guards it now:** `ci/biome-palette-order.sh` (dump-level, ~20 min at
r=16, exits 3 if the determinism/positive/digest controls fail) and
`eval::relabelling_is_undetectable` (three unit tests, microseconds, in the
**lib** so `--lib --bins` actually reaches them). Full write-up:
`docs/DETERMINISM.md` §13.

**Next item this leaves:** nothing. The `~10%` CPU-s/chunk regression above is
a different item with a different owner.

**For whoever merges this.** The branch is based on `9b4afd4` and every
number and every byte-compare in it is against *that* parent, stated so in
`docs/BENCH.md`. `main` moved 25 commits during the run; the rebase was
probed and applies cleanly, 14 of 14, no conflicts. **A rebase invalidates
the output-identical proof and nothing else** — re-run the byte-compare
against the new parent (both trees on the same `data/vanilla`,
`RUSTMC_WORKERS=1` and 12, all three dimensions) before the perf numbers are
quoted at the new base. The performance figures are ratios taken with both
arms on one commit, so they survive a rebase; the identity claim does not,
because it names a specific parent.

**The one thing this leaves open:** which consumer of `BiomeId` is
order-sensitive. Everything the surface rules do with an id is an equality,
so it is not them. Closed by finding the consumer, or by demonstrating the
renumbering result was an artefact — but the dumper was confirmed
deterministic across three runs, so it is not that.

Two separate things, and the second matters more than the first.

**1. The interning is written, type-checks workspace-clean, and is pushed.**
`BiomePalette` (u16, built eagerly from the datapack's whole biome directory,
so it never grows under the worker pool and needs no lock — an `Arc` per
answer was the other option and this project has already measured that shape
as a contention tax); `SurfaceBiomes` remapping every chunk container to
global ids once and indexing climate by id; a `Neighbourhood` resolving the
3x3 a chunk's fuzz can reach once per chunk instead of a `BTreeMap` walk over
up to 4,761 entries per query; `Rule::intern_biomes` rewriting
`Condition::Biome` to `Condition::BiomeIds` before the stage runs, returning
unresolved names so the caller can assert none; and `vertical_gradient`'s two
`BTreeMap` lookups on the hit path reduced to one.

**PROVED BYTE-IDENTICAL.** Against a pristine control built from the parent
commit, both trees on the same unified `data/vanilla`, `RUSTMC_WORKERS=1`
**and** 12, all three dimensions — overworld r=16 (1,089 chunks), nether r=8,
End r=8: **0 of 4 region files differ, on all six comparisons.** Every parity
number in `docs/BENCH.md` is therefore unchanged by construction, including
the End's 100.000000% and the overworld r=16 residual, because they are
functions of exactly these bytes.

**MEASURED, alternated arms, r=16, seed 20260722, Threadripper 1920X, zero
other harnesses live on every single run:**

```text

  12 workers  total  70.49    68.04   1.0360x   2.45 CPU-s   (n=3, spreads 0.33 / 0.19)
              surf   16.40    13.61   1.2053x   2.79 CPU-s
   1 worker   total  63.12    60.74   1.0392x   2.38 CPU-s   (n=4, spreads 1.15 / 1.06)
```

**The surface stage falls ~17%; the whole pipeline falls ~3.6%.** The
absolute saving is the same at both widths, which is what a width-independent

of the pipeline here, confirming the "a quarter" this file already used.

**An unpaired `bench-servers` before/after said the OPPOSITE, and the control
nobody had taken says why.** Two runs half an hour apart put the change at
**+5.6%** at r=7 and **+0.8%** at r=32 — wrong sign — with zero harnesses
witnessed either side of both. Alternated C A C A through the same harness it
is **-4.09%, every one of four pairs negative** (-2.05, -6.17, -4.56, -3.59).
The control: four `ctl` runs on the **same unchanged tree** spread **4.0%**
(21.47, 21.57, 20.82, 20.73) with a downward drift across rounds. So
`bench-servers`' run-to-run variance for a single three-square run is the
size of the effect. **Do not quote an unpaired `bench-servers` before/after
for anything smaller than ~8%** — the "CPU-seconds reproduce, rustmc -1.3%"
in `docs/BENCH.md` is six squares pooled within one session and does not
license it. Applying the paired figure: r=32 **0.0607 -> 0.0582, meets
`<=0.075`** — that is the square the target is stated over, and the only one
with a verdict. r=7 goes 0.0915 -> 0.0877 and gets **no verdict**: see result
2 below and the correction in `docs/BENCH.md`, which record that the honest
state of the target at r=7 is not comparable, therefore unresolved.

**The predicted third did not arrive, and the reason is in the profile that
predicted it.** The closing condition asked for the surface row to move "by
something like a third" on the strength of "44% of the stage is resolving a
biome id". But 14.1 of those 44 points are `quart_for_block` — the biome fuzz,
which vanilla computes too and which that same profile labels "not a defect".
It is still computed on every query here, because it must be. So the
*removable* share was never 44%, it was about 30%, and a bit over half of
that is now gone. Anyone re-reading that closing condition should read the
44% as an upper bound that included work nobody intended to remove.

**2. The `<=0.075 CPU-s/chunk` target is not radius-portable, and the failing
0.082364 is quoted against a target derived at a different radius.**

`ci/bench-servers.sh`'s own header states the denominator is the square
**asked for**, `(2r+1)^2`, while the numerator is the whole process — which
also pays for the `DECORATION_MARGIN` = 2 ring it had to generate,
`(2r+1+4)^2`. So the metric carries the margin ratio, and that ratio is a
property of the WINDOW, not of the generator:

```text
  r=32   4,761 generated / 4,225 delivered   = 1.127
  r=7      361 generated /   225 delivered   = 1.604
```

The target `<=0.075` was set as "1.5x better than Paper's 0.0614" and is
stated in BENCH.md **over the r=32 square**. The failing 0.082364 is an
**r=7** number. BENCH.md says in the same paragraph that "the two radii are
not comparable and must not be quoted as a trend" — and then declares the
target missed across exactly that gap.

Fitting `CPU_total(r) = F + c*(2r+5)^2` to the two published points
(0.082364 at r=7, 0.055041 at r=32) gives **F = 0.973 CPU-s fixed per
process, c = 0.048640 CPU-s per generated chunk**, and puts the crossing of
the fixed 0.075 number at **radius 8.7**. On that account the same generator
misses the target at r=7 and meets it at r=9 and above, with no change to
the code.

**That fit is a hypothesis, not a result: two points, two free parameters,
zero residuals by construction, and the points come from different commits a
week apart.** So it is pre-registered and being tested out-of-sample by a
seven-radius `ci/bench-servers.sh` sweep at HEAD. The predictions, written
down before the data:

```text
  r      4        7        9       12       16       24       32
  pred 0.1135   0.0824   0.0740   0.0670   0.0620   0.0573   0.0550
```

**MEASURED. The shape survived; only the constants moved.** Seven radii,
`BENCH_FLAVOURS=rustmc`, three centres each, seed 20260722, zero other
harnesses live before and after every run:

```text
  r  delivered generated margin   CPU_s  pred_s  resid%   CPU/chunk
   4        81       169  2.086   10.88   11.28   -3.67    0.134362
   7       225       361  1.604   20.58   21.54   -4.67    0.091481
   9       361       529  1.465   30.53   30.52   +0.03    0.084580
  12       625       841  1.346   48.70   47.20   +3.08    0.077920
  16      1089      1369  1.257   75.34   75.42   -0.11    0.069180
  24      2401      2809  1.170  152.61  152.39   +0.14    0.063560
  32      4225      4761  1.127  256.44  256.72   -0.11    0.060695
```

**`CPU_total(r) = 2.2493 + 0.053449 * (2r+5)^2`.** The four largest radii fit
to within **0.14%**. The two smallest come in *below* the line by 3.7% and
4.7%, so at tiny radii the generator is slightly cheaper than a uniform
per-generated-chunk cost — worth remembering before anyone quotes r=4.

Three results, in order of how much they matter:

1. **`<=0.075` is crossed at radius 12.25.** One unchanged generator sits
   above that threshold at every smaller radius and below it at every larger
   one — which is the finding: the quantity being compared to the target is a
   function of the radius, so the target has a verdict only over the square it
   was stated for. At r=32 — the radius it *is* stated over in
   `docs/BENCH.md` — we are at **0.0607, met with 19% margin.** At r=7 there
   is no verdict to give, in either direction.
2. **The generator's real cost is `c` = 0.0534 CPU-s per GENERATED chunk.**
   That is not the quantity `<=0.075` is stated in — the target is per
   *delivered* chunk — and the two converge only as the margin ring
   amortises, so this number must not be read as "the target is met with room
   to spare". The r=7 figure is that same `c` carrying a **1.604x margin
   ring** plus **2.25 CPU-s of fixed process cost** divided over only 225
   delivered chunks. Neither of those is the generator.
3. **A REGRESSION, and it is separate from all of the above.** r=7 measures
   0.0915 against the published 0.0824 (+11.1%) and r=32 measures 0.0607
   against 0.0550 (+10.3%) — near-uniform across the curve, so **the figures
   in `docs/BENCH.md` are stale and optimistic by about a tenth.** The
   published r=7 came from the four-flavour harness, which that file says
   charges rustmc ~7% extra for running last; this run was rustmc alone, the
   *more* favourable configuration, so the true drift is at least this large.
   Nobody has attributed it. **That is the next perf item, not the surface
   stage.**

**Caveat that must travel with these numbers:** the spread *between the three
centres* is 7-17% at every radius — real terrain variation, not noise. It
does not weaken the shape fit, because the same three centres are used at
every radius so the centre effect is common to all of them, but a 3-square
mean at one radius carries that variance and should not be quoted to four
figures as if it were repeatable to four figures.

**Do not quote either result yet.** The Threadripper has run merge gates
back to back for this whole session. One measurement did start alongside the
next gate — two `rustc` and somebody else's `worldgen-dump` at 316% — and was
discarded. The harness now waits for four consecutive clear polls, re-checks
**after** every run, and retakes rather than recording a number with a

matching names, because an abandoned vanilla server on that box matches
`java` and burns exactly zero.

**`oracle-work/bench-servers` is LIVE OUTPUT and AGENT-BRIEF links it as a
reference.** That file names three kinds of directory — shared references,
live per-run output, and generated tables — and its setup loop links every
`oracle-work/*` entry individually while skipping only `gameplay*`.
`bench-servers` is in the second kind: `ci/bench-servers.sh` writes `worlds/`,
`results.tsv` and its console fifos there on every run. **At least eight trees
on the box currently symlink it into `~/rustmc`**, so two benchmark runs write
each other's worlds — the same failure the brief documents for
`oracle-work/gameplay`, which cost a whole gate on 2026-08-03. It is a
*mixed* directory, which is presumably how it was missed: `jars/` inside it
really is a shared, sha256-verified asset worth linking.

Found because the sweep hung: `bench-servers.sh` sat in `pipe_read` with a
zero-byte log and no CPU. The fix in this branch's three trees is a real
directory with only `jars` linked back in (`~/fixlinks.sh` on the box). The

### CLOSED 2026-08-06 — server memory: 2,957 MB with one player, now 52 MB

Branch `tile-retirement`. Do not re-open any of the nulls below.

**What was measured.** Alternated arms, two checkouts, `ci/bench-boot.py`,
superflat, seed 0, `--radius 2`, n=3, Threadripper 1920X. The `before` arm
reproduces the published figures to the megabyte, which is what makes the
comparison honest rather than a straw man:

```text
                     with a player's view loaded     90 s after they leave
  vd=4   before              1,077 MB                      1,077 MB
  vd=4   after                   40 MB                         31 MB
  vd=10  before              2,957 MB                      2,957 MB
  vd=10  after                   52 MB                         30 MB
```

`probe_chunks` is identical across arms (81 and 441), so the fall is not a
server that stopped working. **Resident memory now falls on disconnect; it
previously did not fall at all.**

**The briefed cause was the smaller term, and this is the part to carry
forward.** The brief and `docs/BENCH.md` both named `crate::tiles` leaking
`&'static World`. That was real and is fixed, and it accounts for about 9 MB
of a 1,037 MB fall at vd=4. The dominant term was that `World::generate`
called `worldgen_assembly::block_props()`, which re-reads and re-parses
`data/vanilla/block_props.json` — **15.8 MB** — **once per tile**, on the
tile's own spawned thread, where glibc never returns the parse arena.
Twenty-five tiles at vd=10 meant twenty-five of those.

The published arithmetic would have caught it: it implied **4.7 MB per
superflat chunk**, and a superflat chunk contains four distinct block states.
A superflat `ChunkBlocks` allocates 192 KB through `alloc_zeroed` and touches
about 2 KB, so the rest was never resident. **A per-unit cost that is absurd
on its face is a measurement of something other than the unit.**

**What landed:** `WorldTables` loaded once and shared by every tile;
`Arc<World>` in place of `Box::leak`; `Tiles::retain_around` swept once a
second, retiring a tile unwanted by every connected player's view for
`RETIRE_AFTER_SECS` = 30, with `BlockEdits` held behind an `Arc` by `Tiles`
so a retired tile keeps what a player built and gets it back on
regeneration; `malloc_trim(0)` after every generation and every sweep;
`MAX_CONCURRENT_GENERATIONS` = 2; `WORLD_RADIUS` 2 → 10.

**Nulls — killed, do not re-run:**

* **Raising the tile radius as a MEMORY fix.** After the concurrency cap,
  resident memory is not a function of the radius: the sweep's RSS column
  reads 350, 392, 142, 464, 465, 527, 201 MB across r=2..10 and is a reading
  of how many generations were in flight when sampled. The radius was changed
  for the **discard** — 69% of generation work thrown away at r=2 against 29%
  at r=10 — not for memory.
* **Retiring tiles as the fix for a STANDING player.** A player standing
  still wants every tile in their view, so retirement cannot reduce their
  steady-state cost by construction. It bounds a session; it does not shrink
  a snapshot. The snapshot was fixed by the parse and the trim.
* **Superflat as a substrate for a canvas-memory measurement.** Its canvases
  are mostly untouched zero pages that never enter `VmRSS`. Use `--level
  normal`; `ci/bench-radius-sweep.sh` does.

**Next, and it is the one thing this run leaves open:** `serve_connection`
still calls `ItemIds::load`, `PlacementTable::load` and the shape / use /
`setPlacedBy` loads **inside the per-connection thread** rather than behind a
`OnceLock` — the same defect as the `block_props` one, one layer up, and
`docs/BENCH.md` measured it at about **8.5 MB per additional connection**.
Ten players is ~85 MB of duplicated immutable tables. Closed by the same
shape of fix (`WorldTables` is the pattern) and by `ci/t2-memory.sh`'s
measured peak dropping from 218 MB, with the corpus unchanged at 41/70.

### What closes it

`SurfaceOracle::biome` returns an owned `String` and every one of the ~28,864
biome answers a chunk is a `BTreeMap<(i32,i32)>` lookup over up to 4,761
entries followed by a 25-byte heap allocation, freed a few conditions later.
Vanilla's `SurfaceRules$Context.getBiome` memoises a `Holder<Biome>` per
y-update — which `SurfaceContext::biome` already does, one for one — so the
**counts match and the per-call cost does not**. Two changes, both
order-preserving by construction because no value moves, only its type:

1. **A `u16` id in place of the `String`**, interned against the stage's own
   palette, carried through `SurfaceOracle::biome`, `SurfaceContext::biome`
   and `Condition::Biome` (whose `wanted: Vec<String>` becomes a small sorted
   `Vec<u16>` resolved once per chunk). Kills the allocation *and* the
   `malloc`/`cfree`/string-compare block, which is another 10% of the stage.
2. **A 3x3 array of the neighbourhood's biome containers, resolved once per
   chunk** in `surface_one_chunk`, in place of `SurfaceShared::stored_biome_at`'s
   B-tree lookup per query. The fuzz reaches at most one chunk out — that is
   already the standing guard behind `RUSTMC_SURFACE_TIES=1`, whose interior
   fallback count must stay ZERO — so 3x3 covers every interior query, and the
   perimeter can keep the B-tree.

Closed by: `cmp` showing 0 of 9 region files differ against a pristine
`git archive` control of your parent commit, generated sequentially, at
`RUSTMC_WORKERS=1` **and** at 12; plus the surface row of
`RUSTMC_STAGE_CPU=1` at r=32 moving from **46.30 CPU-s** by something like a

### What was measured and killed this turn — do not re-run these

1. **The surface stage was NOT dropping a density marker.** `FlatCaches::none()`
   in that stage looks exactly like the biomes bug and is not one: vanilla's
   `NoiseChunk.preliminarySurfaceLevel` *is* the wrapped router (javap,
   offsets 388-413) but `Context.getMinSurfaceLevel` samples the four corners
   of a **16-block cell**, one cell is one chunk, and our `SurfaceLevels` memo
   is per worker and outlives the chunk. Wiring the caches in is worth ~0.1 s
   of 193. The other four markers — `cache_2d`, `cache_once`,
   `cache_all_in_cell`, `interpolated` — have no call site in this stage at
   all; the only density function it touches is `preliminary_surface_level`.
2. **`hole` never resamples.** `HoleCondition` is a `LazyXZCondition` reading
   vanilla's cached `surfaceDepth`; ours recomputed a `NormalNoise` **and**
   seeded a positional random at each of the rule's three `hole` sites, which
   read as a clean N-vs-1. `RUSTMC_SURFACE_NOISE=1` says `getSurfaceDepth` is
   asked **exactly 256 times a chunk** — `build_chunk`'s own once-per-column
   call and nothing else. No `hole` condition is reached anywhere on the r=8
   square. A memo is in place because it is free; it is worth zero.
3. **Named-noise resampling was real but small.** 42 `noise_threshold` sites
   over 8 noises, 19 of them naming `minecraft:surface`, each resampling a
   fresh `NormalNoise` where vanilla shares one memoised `DoubleSupplier`
   (`SurfaceRules$Context$1`/`$2`). The counter says **1.99x, not 61x**, and
   fixing it was **5.3% of the stage** — 48.90 -> 46.30 CPU-s. The count is now
   vanilla's by construction. Do not re-open it.
4. **The pipeline total did not move**, 193.03 -> 193.80 at one worker, which
   is inside the box's 1.5-2.5% spread. A 5% cut to a 25% stage is not visible
   in a total, and reading it as a regression would be reading noise.
5. **The counting question does not generalise as a free win.** It paid 10.3x
   on biomes and 5.3% here, on the same shape of defect. Take the differenced
   profile *first* next time; this turn took it after, and that is why a
   correct fix landed on the wrong tenth of the stage.

### The next lever inside biomes, if anyone returns to it

~1.6 CPU-s at r=16 remains: ~0.9 search, ~0.1 sampling, ~0.6 the `String`
clone per cell plus `Canvas::set_biome` plus the per-chunk `FlatCaches::fill`.
The search's remaining cost is **data layout, not algorithm** — `Node` is an
enum with `Vec<Node>` children, so each child visit is a pointer chase.
Flattening the tree into contiguous node spaces preserves the traversal order
and therefore the tie-break exactly, because the order *is* the child order.
Worth ~0.5 CPU-s at r=16 and it is not the biggest thing on the board.

**The persistent decoration pool.** Replace the decoration driver's per-level
`thread::scope` with ONE persistent pool and a ready-queue. Parallel
decoration is byte-identical over nine orders, but it rebuilds the pool at
every barrier — 2,604 thread spawns at r=16 — and that is most of its +22.3%
CPU and most of the gap between its 1.98x and its 6.3x critical-path bound.
The design and the closing conditions are below, verbatim from the turn that
wrote them.

### The one item, and the result that closes it

**One persistent pool, a ready-queue, no barrier.** A chunk becomes runnable
when its last blocking predecessor (earlier in the order, within
`2 * DECORATE_REACH`) finishes; a worker pops it, locks the master canvas long
enough to `detach` its footprint, decorates, locks again to `merge`. The
master canvas behind a `Mutex<&mut Canvas>` is enough — detach and merge are
~50 `BTreeMap` operations against ~9 ms of decoration per chunk.

Closed by:

1. `ci/stage-scale.sh` at r=16 showing the decoration row **above 3x** with
   its CPU-second column within a few points of the 1-worker 12.36 s. The
   arithmetic: at reach 2 the critical path is 217 levels over 1,369 chunks,
   so 6.3x is the bound; barrier stalls (mean level 6.3 chunks against 12
   workers) and 2,604 thread spawns are what stand between 1.98x and it.
2. `ci/decorate-order-sweep.sh` green — all nine orders, 0 of 4 differing.
3. `cmp` against a pristine parent-commit control at `RUSTMC_WORKERS=1` and
   at 12.

The measurement that names the target:

```text
  reach   levels   mean/level   decoration wall   decoration cpu-s
    1       145        9.4           5.39              14.73  (+19.1%)
    2       217        6.3           6.25              15.13  (+22.4%)
    3       361        3.8           7.13              15.86  (+28.3%)
```

CPU rises with the *level count* at ~436 us per level per worker, which is a
thread create-and-join.

### The thing a future turn must not assume — reads are unbounded

`Decoration::write` drops any write more than `write_radius` chunks out, so
writes are bounded. **Nothing bounds a read.** `RUSTMC_READ_REACH=1` records
the largest Chebyshev chunk distance any canvas access uses from the
decorating chunk. On the whole-canvas sequential run of the r=16 square it is
**39** — wider than the 37-chunk canvas. *Some call site inside decoration
reads right across the world and past its edge, and which one is unknown.*

So `DECORATE_REACH` is not a proof, it is a measured-safe constant, and it was
widened until the answer stopped changing (ORACLE rule 14): reach **1, 2, 3, 4,
6 and 8** all give byte-identical output to the sequential control.
`RUSTMC_OUTSIDE_READS=1` counts accesses naming a chunk the canvas lacks —
418,142 whole-canvas, rising to 429,361 / 433,589 / 442,021 / 458,789 at reach
1 / 2 / 4 / 8. It rises *with* the reach, which the naive model forbids, so it
is a flag rather than a margin.

### OWNER DECISION — parallel decoration is permitted, on one condition

Recorded 2026-07-29 at owner level. **Do not relitigate it.**

**Parallel decoration is PERMITTED, provided it preserves the order-invariant
core.** Item 1 of the definition of complete is explicitly *order-invariant*
parity, and vanilla does not itself have a stable decoration order (two
independently generated vanilla worlds of one seed differ by **3006 blocks**
on the r7 window).

* **Still forbidden:** any change to what a feature *computes* — float
  precision or operation order in noise (f32/f64, FMA, reassociation), RNG
  draw sequences within a feature, skipping or approximating work, fast-math.
* **Now permitted:** decorating independent chunks concurrently, if the
  order-invariant core is proved unchanged.
* **The proof is mandatory and is the gate** — the nine-order sweep, now
  `ci/decorate-order-sweep.sh`.

### Housekeeping a fresh agent needs

* **Never `git add -A`.** Other tracks share this tree. Commit explicit paths
  only, and **run `git status` and look for `MERGE_HEAD` first**.
* **`RUSTMC_REMOTE_DIR` must be unique to you.** This turn used `rustmc-i2b`.
  Two agents sharing one remote dir each deleted the other's files with
  `--delete`.
* **A worktree needs the gitignored data**: `cp -r ~/rustmc/data/vanilla
  data/` and `ln -s ~/rustmc/oracle-work oracle-work`, and on the remote,
  symlink both into your remote dir before the first build.
* **Take the control at your own HEAD**, from `git archive`, not from the
  working tree with the change backed out.
* **`Canvas` must stay `Sync`.** The server shares a `World` behind a
  `&'static`, so a `Cell` field on the canvas breaks 32 call sites in
  `rustmc-server` that `cargo build -p worldgen-dump` never touches.
* **A gate that skips is not a gate that passed.** `grep -c "skipping: no
  vanilla"` must be 0.
* **Measure with `perf stat`, not `time`.** Wall and CPU-s on the Threadripper
  vary ~1.5-2.5% run to run; instruction counts are stable to five digits.
* **Quote CPU-seconds, not cycles, across different core counts or
  placements.**
* **`ci/bench-servers.sh` clears `$WORK/worlds` on every run**, and `$WORK` is
  under the shared `oracle-work`. To re-time the rustmc row alone, run
  `worldgen-dump full` under `/usr/bin/time` directly.
* **A long benchmark run perturbs the row it runs last.** See the 7% above.
* The `NOW — server track` and `NOW — worldgen features` blocks belong to
  the other two tracks. This block is item 2 only.

when its own run carries a field the ensemble never had.** Worktree
`~/grit/work-vocab`, remote dir `~/rustmc-vocab`. Not merged — the orchestrator
gates. Full account in `docs/PARITY-ROADMAP.md` §50.

**WHAT CLOSED.** §15.4, both halves.

* **`ci/trace_vocabulary.py`** — the sorted union of `(kind, field)` over a
  recording. ONE implementation, imported by `ci/corpus-floor.py` and
  `ci/corpus-floor-report.py`. Refuses a comparison report, a non-trace, an
  **empty vocabulary**, and a `.` inside a kind or field.
* **The floor file records it**; `measure` refuses a run that carries none,
  `update` writes it one pair per line, `check_floor_file` prints
  `NO VOCABULARY` / `VOCABULARY STALE`.
* **`ci/corpus-floor-report.py` takes the run's own `vanilla.json`** as a
  fourth *positional* argument and prints `VOCABULARY DRIFT`, naming the pairs,
  withdrawing quotability. One direction only.
* **`oracle-runner recorder-id` → `rec:<16 hex>`**, in the `.prov` from both
  `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` and `ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh`, read out of the binary
  not the tree. §13's errand and §15.4's weaker half, both done.
* **`ci/corpus-floor-falsify.sh` cases 22-28**, in `ci/t0.sh`, 36/36.

**THE NUMBERS.** `ci/trace_vocabulary.py`, Threadripper, 2026-08-09.

```

  r1 of it                             87  — lacks take_item_entity.*
  ~/rustmc-{gate,look,blockage}        95  — the 91 plus add_entity.
                                             {y_rot,x_rot,y_head_rot,data}

```

22 (33/36); `-> symmetric difference` reds case 23 (35/36); reverted 36/36.

`ci/checks/gameplay-floor.toml` describes `twin-homog-20260809` (9 names) and
`ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` describes `yrot6-20260809` (7 names), because
`item-entity-tick` re-declared against the second and deliberately did not
re-base the first. **Two ensembles with different vocabularies, one declared
list** — §15.4's residual in the tracked artefacts rather than in an
annotation. Consequence: `ci/corpus-floor-falsify.sh` case 1 fails, and so does
`ci/t0.sh`, in any tree holding a saved measurement of the committed ensemble.
Measured on main's own `ci/corpus-floor.py` with main's own two files: the same
two `NEWLY UNSTABLE`, rc=1. A tree with no `oracle-work/corpus-floor` takes the
synthetic route and is green, which is why nobody has seen it — **case 1's
coverage of the committed declarations is a function of leftover working

Re-measured over `yrot6-20260809` (`~/rustmc-throw` r1-r3 + the corpus
`vanilla.json` of `~/rustmc-throw`, `~/rustmc-gate`, `~/rustmc-look`), so the


So the re-base is one command and the whole cost is recorder heterogeneity.
The choice is a **stale-vocabulary homogeneous** floor against a
**current-vocabulary heterogeneous** one, and it is a judgement, not a
measurement. Nobody has to re-derive that.

Refutations: **the `minecraft:chat_type` registry the client receives is KEY-SORTED, not bootstrap order** — `say_command` is 4 and `emote_command` is 1, refused by the capture on the first run; **`javap` strips trailing whitespace from a `Utf8` constant**, so `USAGE_REDIRECT` reads as `->` and produces `tell ->msg` where vanilla makes `tell -> msg`; **`BrigadierExceptions` SWAPS both arguments of every bound message** (bound first, `with: [0, -1]`); **`ListTag.write` wraps mismatched elements** and three call sites had been applying that by hand; **`resolution_matches_whole_tokens` asserted Brigadier tolerates extra whitespace and it does not**; **`ci/command-surface.py` silently dropped roots three times in one day**, all three now refusals plus a backstop. Refused by name with reasons: `/difficulty` (no `change_difficulty` in `ids.rs` at all), `/gamemode` (no per-player mode, no abilities model), `/give` (overflow drops an `ItemEntity` and plays an RNG-pitched sound), `/weather` and `/time` (state lives only on unmerged `player-systems`), `/setblock` (blocked on `block_state`, priced).
