### THE "NEIGHBOUR-AWARE SHAPE/PLACEMENT" FAMILY — DECOMPOSED, NOT BUILT (2026-08-05, same branch)

Briefed as "the largest remaining diverge family: 5 checks (180, 200, 240,
300, 450) that our placement path does not carry from neighbours", and asked
for the shared primitive. **There is a shared primitive and it is not the one
the framing implies, and it closes none of the five on its own.**

#### The criterion that actually splits them, which is mechanical

For each block, ask of `updateShape`: **does it read the level, or only the
neighbour state it was handed?** `javap -p -c -constants`, pinned 26.2 jar.
The signature is
`updateShape(BlockState, LevelReader, ScheduledTickAccess, BlockPos,
Direction, BlockPos, BlockState, RandomSource)`, so `aload_2` is the level and
`aload 7` is the neighbour state.

```text
  StairBlock       ignores aload 7 entirely; offset 49-53 calls
                   getStairsShape(state, BlockGetter, pos), which reads
                   pos.relative(FACING) and pos.relative(FACING.opposite)
                                                        -> NOT table-shaped
  RedStoneWireBlock reads aload_2 via getConnectionState(level, state, pos)
                   and getConnectingSide(level, pos, dir)
                                                        -> NOT table-shaped
  ChestBlock       uses aload 7 and only aload 7 -- chestCanConnectTo(
                   neighbourState) at 37, neighbourState.getValue at 59/100
                                                        -> TABLE-SHAPED
```

**This kills the obvious cheap fix.** It looks as though the 11,491
`connective` pairs `shapes.rs` refuses are an *extractor* limitation — the
sweep records one alternative `to` per `(state, dir)` and calls anything with
several `connective` — and that generalising `Row` to a partition would carry
them. For the chest that is true. For stairs and wire it is not, and not by a
detail: `ShapeGolden` varies **one** neighbour and holds the rest at the
probe world's value, so any partition it emitted for a stair would be valid
only in that context. A table keyed on `(state, direction, neighbour-state)`
cannot represent a function that does not have that signature. Anyone who
widens the extractor will produce rows that are wrong rather than missing,
which is strictly worse than refusing them.

#### AND THE EXTRACTION ALREADY NAMES THE ACCESS SHAPE THE PORT NEEDS (2026-08-05)

Stairs are **not in `connective` at all** — `140-fences-connect-to-each-other`
said they were and it was wrong. `data/vanilla/update_shape.json` has a
`refused` list carrying the extractor's own reason per bucket, and it is a
machine-readable record of **exactly which offsets each block reads**:

```text
  updateShape read -1,0,0    5,381 pairs   stairs, oak_fence_gate
  updateShape read  1,0,0    5,412         stairs, oak_fence_gate
  updateShape read  0,0,-1   6,976         stairs, oak_fence_gate, redstone_wire
  updateShape read  0,0,1    5,386         stairs, oak_fence_gate
  updateShape read  0,1,0   48,993         walls, redstone_wire
  updateShape read  0,-1,0   6,629         saplings and friends
  (plus getLightEngine 212, environmentAttributes 96, registryAccess 8)
```

**Every offset in that table is one of the six orthogonal neighbours. There is
not a single diagonal in it.** An audit this run proposed that stairs are
refused *because they read diagonals*; it was right that they are refused and
wrong about why, and the difference is the whole design input — a port built
for diagonal access would build the wrong thing.

**⚠ THE CONCLUSION I DREW FROM THIS TABLE WAS WRONG, AND IT IS CORRECTED HERE
BEFORE ANY CODE WAS WRITTEN ON IT (2026-08-05, same day).** I wrote: "a
`BlockGetter` over the six orthogonal neighbours is sufficient for every
refused block in this table". **It is not, and `450` is the counterexample.**

`ShapeGolden`'s probe **throws on the first read outside the two positions it
serves** — `ShapeGolden.java:403`, `"updateShape read " + relative(pos) + ",
not its own neighbour"`. So each bucket records *the first offending read for
that (state, direction) pair* and nothing the method would have gone on to
read. **The offsets in that table are a lower bound on the access shape, never
the shape itself**, and reading them as a specification is the same error as
reading a `blocks` list capped at eight as a census.

Measured directly instead, `javap -p -c -constants` on
`RedStoneWireBlock.getConnectingSide(BlockGetter, BlockPos, Direction,
boolean)`:

```text
    0-5    local5 = pos.relative(dir)
    7-15   getBlockState(local5)                      orthogonal
   57-63   getBlockState(local5.above())              DIAGONAL
  120-123  getBlockState(local5.below())              DIAGONAL
```

Two diagonals per horizontal direction, eight positions, plus `pos.above()`
from the three-argument overload. That is redstone wire climbing the block
beside it — **literally what `450-redstone-wire-climbs-the-block-beside-it` is
named for**, so the one check in the family whose whole subject is a diagonal
is the one the lower bound hid.

So the primitive is **arbitrary-position read access**, the same `blocks`
reader `shapes::set_block` already takes, and the per-block access shape is
documented from bytecode rather than inferred from the refusal table. A
six-neighbour window would have fitted stairs, ladder and chest and then
failed on wire, which is the worst possible order to discover it in.

The other caveat still stands: `ShapeGolden` caps each bucket's example list
at eight block names, so **absence from the lists above is not proof a block
is not refused** — presence is proof, absence is not. And `updateShape`'s own
reads are still a different question from how far the *cascade* propagates,
which for redstone is `updateIndirectNeighbourShapes`.

Row counts, for the five: stairs 0, rail 0, ladder 8, chest 16,
redstone_wire 1,296. Chest and wire are substantially carried by the table
already, which is a better starting position than "five ports" implies —
though see `260`'s correction for why **a row count is not coverage**: doors
have 32 rows and every one is the *lower* half, so the half that check breaks
has none.

#### The five, decomposed

```text
  180 stairs   placement AND updateShape, both via getStairsShape(level)
  200 ladder   placement only. LadderBlock.updateShape never touches FACING
  240 chest    placement needs the level (getChestType/candidatePartnerFacing);
               updateShape is table-shaped and is the ONLY one of the five
               our existing machinery could carry as data
  300 rail     NEITHER hook. getStateForPlacement reads no neighbour at all --
               only the player's horizontal facing and the fluid at the clicked
               pos -- and updateShape only schedules the waterlog tick. The
               connective logic is onPlace -> updateState -> updateDir ->
               RailState.place, a third hook with no port and no stub anywhere
               in this tree
  450 wire     placement AND updateShape via the level, PLUS
               updateIndirectNeighbourShapes, which is overridden to walk out
               to diagonal positions a six-face cascade never reaches. The
               check's own first difference is at power=0 on both sides, so no
               signal is involved and neighborChanged is not the blocker
```

#### So the shared primitive is real, and it is enabling rather than closing

**Every one of the five needs read access to the world from inside the
block-behaviour layer, and today neither entry point has it.**
`placement::state_for_placement` (`placement.rs:394`) takes
`(table, default, Click, into, known)` and `Click` (`placement.rs:117`) is
`{face, yaw, cursor_y}` — no level, no position. `shapes::update_shape`
(`shapes.rs:552`) is a table lookup. The world *is* in scope at the call site
(`world_send.rs:813`, which already calls `blocks.state_at(target)` four lines
later), so this is threading, not plumbing that does not exist.

But the primitive on its own moves nothing. After it, each of the five still
needs its own function transcribed from bytecode, and rail needs a hook that
does not exist. **This is five ports behind one enabling change, not one fix
for five checks.**

The module docs already anticipated exactly this from both sides and should be
read before anyone starts: `placement.rs:62-67` names the 195
neighbour-sensitive blocks that "get the isolated answer... it will matter
when connections do", and `shapes.rs:115-124` names the 11,491 connective
pairs as "the same gap seen from the other side". They were right.

#### Not implemented this run, deliberately

The cheapest single check is **200 (ladder)** — placement only, one
`isFaceSturdy` test on one neighbour, no `updateShape` half. It is the right
first port. It is not done here because the measurement budget for this branch
is spent on the rule-26 re-baselining, and `AGENT-BRIEF` is explicit that new
behaviour lands opt-in until it is measured; a placement change landing
unmeasured against a 35-check declared floor is the wrong trade.

**`LadderBlock.getStateForPlacement`, read out in full so the next agent does
not pay for it twice.** A survey commissioned this run summarised it as just
the `getNearestLookingDirections` loop; there is a refusal branch in front of
that loop which never appears in any summary of this method. All 88 lines of
`javap -p -c -constants`, offsets 0–176:

```java
if (!ctx.replacingClickedOnBlock()) {                        //   0, ifne 53
    BlockState behind = ctx.getLevel().getBlockState(        //   7-25
        ctx.getClickedPos().relative(ctx.getClickedFace().getOpposite()));
    if (behind.is(this)                                      //  31, ifeq 53
        && behind.getValue(FACING) == ctx.getClickedFace())  //  48, if_acmpne 53
        return null;                                         //  51-52
}
BlockState s = defaultBlockState();                          //  53
FluidState fluid = ctx.getLevel().getFluidState(ctx.getClickedPos());  // 77
for (Direction d : ctx.getNearestLookingDirections()) {      //  82-107
    if (!d.getAxis().isHorizontal()) continue;               // 115, ifeq 169
    s = s.setValue(FACING, d.getOpposite());                 // 121-133
    if (s.canSurvive(level, pos))                            // 141, ifeq 169
        return s.setValue(WATERLOGGED, fluid.is(Fluids.WATER));  // 147-168
}
return null;                                                 // 175-176
```

Four things fall out of it that change the estimate:

* **Two different world reads, at two different positions.** The refusal
  branch reads `clickedPos.relative(clickedFace.getOpposite())`; `canSurvive`
  reads `pos.relative(FACING.getOpposite())`, and `FACING` is the *loop's*
  direction, not the clicked face. A port that reuses one position for both is
  wrong whenever the click is not head-on.
* **The method can refuse.** Two `return null`s — the stacking guard and an
  exhausted loop. `state_for_placement` already returns `Option<String>`, so
  the shape fits, but "no state" has to mean "no block is placed" rather than
  "fall back to the default", and today's fallback is the default.
* **It needs the player's PITCH, which `Click` does not carry.**
  `getNearestLookingDirections()` is ordered by the look vector.
  `placement.rs` already knows pitch is a missing dimension — `PITCH_LEVEL`
  exists and the ten pitch-sensitive blocks are refused a table answer
  outright — so this is a known gap being met from the other side, and the
  ladder port needs `Click` widened before it needs anything else.
* **The waterlogged half is already done.** `placement.rs` computes
  `WATERLOGGED` from the fluid at the clicked position on top of whatever the
  table returned, which is exactly offsets 147–165. Nothing to port there.

### SERVER-SIDE PLAYER PHYSICS — SCOPED, NOT BUILT (2026-08-05, branch `rule26-movement-and-neighbour-shapes` off `15901ea`)

**The premise this was briefed on is refuted, and the correction makes the item
smaller to state and no cheaper to build.** The brief — and `540`'s own check
file, and the `THE MOTION COVERAGE HOLE` block below — say this server "treats
the client's on-ground flag as authoritative *where vanilla re-derives it*".
Vanilla does not re-derive it there. `javap -p -c -constants` on
`ServerGamePacketListenerImpl.handleMovePlayer`, pinned 26.2 jar:

```text
   689  ServerPlayer.move(MoverType, Vec3)          <- real collision runs
   961  ServerboundMovePlayerPacket.isOnGround()
   964  ServerPlayer.doCheckFallDamage(DDDZ)        <- fed the CLIENT's flag
  1151  ServerboundMovePlayerPacket.isOnGround()
  1160  ServerPlayer.setOnGroundWithMovement(ZZVec3) <- CLIENT's flag wins
```

`Entity.move` computes `onGround` from its own collision result — it is one of
the three methods in `Entity` that call `setOnGroundWithMovement` — and then
`handleMovePlayer` overwrites it, thirteen instructions later, with the boolean
the client sent. **Vanilla trusts the client's flag at exactly the point we do,
and fall damage is gated on the client's flag too.** Anyone who reads that as a
bug should note it is the documented NoFall vector and has been vanilla's
behaviour for years; it is not what `530` and `540` are seeing.

**What actually differs is that vanilla runs a player tick between move packets
and we run none.** `ServerPlayer.doTick` → `LivingEntity.aiStep` → `travel` →
`Entity.move` re-derives `onGround` from collision with no packet involved, so
vanilla's flag changes on ticks the client said nothing on. That is precisely
`540`'s observation — vanilla syncing twice inside step 0 — and it is why
`530`'s standing observer has a `lastSentMovement` that depends on which tick
its last motion packet went out on. The defect is **the absence of a tick**,
not misplaced trust.

#### What a faithful tick requires

Sizes are `javap -c` line counts as a cost proxy, from the survey this run
commissioned; the offsets and constants below I re-read myself.

```text
  LivingEntity.aiStep()                     398   the real mass
  LivingEntity.tick()                       333
  Entity.move(MoverType, Vec3)              327
  ServerPlayer.doTick()                     283
  Entity.collide(Vec3)                      180
  LivingEntity.travelInAir(Vec3)            131
  Player.aiStep() override                  ~120
  ServerPlayer.tick()                        99
  Entity.checkSupportingBlock                79
  LivingEntity.handleRelativeFrictionAnd...  49
  LivingEntity.travel(Vec3)                  26   dispatcher only
```

#### What it would MOVE — the subsystems it drags in, none of which exist

```text
  US   a VoxelShape engine. `Entity.collide` merges Level.getBlockCollisions,
       Level.getEntityCollisions and WorldBorder.getCollisionShape into one
       shape list and sweeps per axis. `grep -rn "aabb\|VoxelShape\|collision"
       crates/` finds exactly one thing: survival.rs's `collision_face_full_up`,
       a single-block "is this face solid" predicate. There is no sweep, no
       merge, no per-axis resolution. This is a new subsystem, not a
       half-finished one.
  US   auto-step: maxUpStep()/collectCandidateStepUpHeights inside collide().
  US   entity-vs-entity collision, plus Player.aiStep's inflated-AABB
       Level.getEntities query for touch().
  US   the ATTRIBUTE SYSTEM. LivingEntity.getDefaultGravity() is
       `getAttributeValue(Attributes.GRAVITY)` -- verified, it is not a bare
       0.08 -- and movement speed reaches travel() the same way. Hard-coding
       the default is an approximation, and approximations are the one-way
       door AGENT-BRIEF forbids.
  US   fluid interaction: 26.2 has refactored this into EntityFluidInteraction
       (applyCurrentTo/getFluidHeight/isInFluid); the old
       updateFluidHeightAndDoFluidPushing name is gone. travel() dispatches on
       it before anything else.
  US   block friction/speed factor via getBlockPosBelowThatAffectsMyMovement.
  US   applyEffectsFromBlocks over the tick's recorded Movement list.
  NOTE `Player extends Avatar` in 26.2, not LivingEntity directly. Any
       transcription that assumes the old hierarchy is reading the wrong
       override chain.
```

#### What it would RISK — three hazards read out of the bytecode

1. **The collision axis order is movement-dependent, not fixed.**
   `Direction.axisStepOrder(Vec3)` is `abs(x) < abs(z) ? YZX : YXZ` — Y always
   first, then the *~~smaller~~* **LARGER** horizontal magnitude.
   **Corrected 2026-08-06 on branch `entity-move-collision`**, which ported the
   method: `YZX_AXIS_ORDER` is `ImmutableList.of(Y, Z, X)`, so `|x| < |z|` —
   the branch this line describes — puts **Z** second, and Z is the bigger one.
   The `abs(x) < abs(z)` half was right and the reading of what `YZX` orders
   was not. A port that
   resolves X, then Z, then Y unconditionally is correct for axis-aligned
   movement and wrong diagonally into a corner, which is the single hardest
   class of bug to attribute later because it needs a diagonal scenario to
   show at all.
2. **A float epsilon widened to double.** `Mth.equal(double,double)` compares
   against `9.999999747378752E-6` — verified from the constant pool. That is
   `1.0E-5f` promoted, not `1.0E-5`. Rust typing `1e-5_f64` will not
   bit-match; it needs `1.0e-5_f32 as f64`. This is the same class as the
   `mul_add` trap already recorded in `tracker.rs`.
3. **The physics feeds the anti-cheat gates, so drift compounds.** "Moved
   wrongly" is `distSq(reported − lastGood) > 0.0625`; "moved too quickly"
   differences the reported delta against `getDeltaMovement().lengthSqr()`.
   Once the server computes its own delta movement, both gates start reading
   it, and a small divergence can turn into a teleport-back that the corpus
   sees as a completely different scenario. `Session::hop_to`'s header already
   records what that failure looks like from the rig's side.

#### What bounds the payoff

Two checks name it — `530` and `540` — and **`530` no longer does.** ORACLE
rule 26 removed the movement from the projection this run, so `530` is about
visibility again and needs no physics at all. That leaves `540` as the sole
check this subsystem would move, against a VoxelShape engine, the attribute
system and a fluid model.

It is, however, the gate on a whole class of *future* coverage that nothing
else unlocks: a check on a player's velocity is the only thing that can
re-claim the `add_entity` movement field this run just exempted, because
`EntityType.trackDeltas()` is false for only ten types and the corpus's one
observer of `set_entity_motion` watches an ITEM, for which vanilla
structurally never sends one. So the honest ordering is: physics is not on the
path to anything a player notices next — persistence, block entities and
`neighborChanged` all are — but it is the only route to closing a measurement
hole this corpus now carries knowingly.

**Do not start it to fix `540`.** `540`'s `diverge` floor is honest, it fails
loudly in both directions, and one check is not worth this.

### THE SAMPLING, THE UNGATED SUITE AND THE COMMAND (2026-08-05, branch `collapse-t1-list` off `dc95d7f`)

Three adjudicated items, one branch. Each closed a hole a previous run had
found and priced but not filled.

#### 1. `collapse_repeats` — and the coverage that replaced what it removed

A check may now declare `collapse_repeats = ["block_event"]`, and a run of
identical **consecutive** projected observations of a named kind compares as
one. Both chest checks declare it.

`ContainerOpenersCounter.recheckOpeners` re-arms every `CHECK_TICK_DELAY` = 5
ticks and calls `openerCountChanged` unconditionally at offset 167, so an open
chest emits the same `block_event(1, 1)` every 250 ms forever. How many land
inside `settle_ms` is decided by where the window edge falls against that
cadence, and `verdict_for` is exact sequence equality — so the count *was* the
check.

**THE MEASUREMENT IS PAIRED, NOT STATISTICAL, AND THAT IS WHY IT SETTLES.**
`ci/selfcheck-recompare.sh` is new: it re-compares the **saved** selfcheck
recordings under a chosen projection, in seconds instead of the five hours
N = 26 cost to record. The expensive half of `ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh` is
recording; the half a *projection* change moves is `compare`. Run twice, same
binary, same 26 recordings, one variable:

```text
  control (collapse stripped)   chest-opens-a-screen 1/25   a-bystander 3/25
  treatment (as committed)      chest-opens-a-screen 0/25   a-bystander 0/25
```

The control reproduces the declared rates **exactly**, which is what makes the
treatment number mean anything. And the per-run projections say what moved:
across all 26 recordings, uncollapsed, `chest-opens-a-screen` projected 8
observations in 25 runs and 7 in one (r19); `a-bystander-sees-a-chest-open` 10
in 23 and 9 in three (r16, r17, r18). Every flap's `first_difference` is the
**last** `block_event` — present in one run, absent in the other, byte
identical in every field it carries (`at [1,0,0]`, `b0 1`, `b1 1`, `block 201`,
digest `cbf29ce484222325`). **The only dimension that moved across twenty-six
cold-booted vanilla servers is the length of a trailing run of identical
observations.** Collapsed, both project to a constant on all 26.

That answers the power objection rather than waving at it.
`ci/selfcheck-aggregate.py` resolves the bystander check (25 comparisons miss a
3/25 event with p = 0.041, inside alpha) and reports `chest-opens-a-screen`
UNRESOLVED, because 25 comparisons miss a 1/25 event 36% of the time. That
model treats the two arms as independent samples and they are not: it is the
same 26 recordings, and the single comparison that diverged is one of the 25
that now matches. The flap was not missed, it was removed.

**The replacement coverage shipped in the same commit, which was the
condition.** Collapsing means the two checks stop testing the cadence, and an
exemption that removes a signal without something else claiming the mechanism
manufactures finding 16. The replacement measures the **gap**, not the count —
timing, which the corpus excludes from comparison on purpose — so it is a unit
test driving the real tick queue:
`the_wire_cadence_is_one_signal_every_check_tick_delay_ticks` asserts every gap
is exactly `CHECK_TICK_DELAY` and the first repeat is one delay after the open;
`the_cadence_stops_the_tick_the_opener_is_out_of_range` asserts
`[(5,1),(10,1),(15,0)]` and nothing left pending. **The wire cadence against
vanilla stays unmeasured** and is named as such on both check files and in the
test.

Declared only. `strict` ignores a check's own declarations on purpose, so the
cadence stays visible there — asserted by `strict_still_sees_every_repeat`, and
confirmed on the box: the chest pair reports `match` declared and `diverge`
strict in the same run.

#### 2. T1 in the gate, allowlisted by signature

`ci/t0.sh` is `--lib --bins` and reaches 17 test binaries. T1 reaches **95**. It
exits 101 on two honestly-red goldens, and a permanently-red stage gets
switched off within a day, so it had never been wired in — **78 test binaries,
every golden vector and every integration test under `tests/`, outside every
merge gate for the project's whole history.**

`ci/t1-gate.sh` runs it, `ci/t1-allowlist.py` adjudicates against
`ci/checks/t1-known-red.toml`. Measured 2026-08-05 in `~/rustmc-chain-0805`:
676 s, exit 101, 95 binaries, 1,112 passed, the two known reds and nothing
else. Every figure matches `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md`'s recorded signature, and the
two entries are **byte-identical to each other** — the "one defect, reported
twice" claim checked rather than repeated.

Behaviour proven on constructed logs before the real one existed, in five
directions: unchanged GREEN; 106 → 10,600 RED; same count with one confusion
row changed RED; declared-but-passing RED; suite dying after one binary RED on
the `min_binaries` floor. The real log then found a sixth thing the constructed
one could not — the panic line carries a thread id, `thread 'name' (1263378)
panicked at`, so an anchored `'.*' panicked at` misses it.

**WHERE IT GOES: a constraint, then a cost.** It must be **after** stage 3's
`gen-gameplay-tables.sh`, because four T1 binaries read `data/vanilla` tables
that script regenerates under the branch's own provenance — `block_props.json`
and `items.json` in `rustmc-server`'s `decorated_world`, `tiled_world` and
`margin_probe`, and `rustmc-behavior`'s `golden_survival` — and stage 1 seeds
that directory from a shared one with `cp -rn`. Running T1 earlier would gate
this branch's goldens against whichever branch last regenerated it, which is
the defect that reported a healthy branch as 12/55 on 2026-08-03. Given that,
cheap first: 676 s against ~50 minutes, so a golden regression surfaces in
eleven minutes instead of an hour. No argument runs the other way — a red T2
stops the loop anyway, so the expensive stage first buys nothing.

**A side effect worth more than it looks:** the `skipping: no vanilla` guard now
covers the worldgen integration tests, which were not in the loop at all. A gate
directory that has lost its `oracle-work` links can no longer report green.

#### 3. `server-answers-a-command` — and the arity nobody would have guessed

Closed the last self-contained `absent`. Three pieces, and the middle one is
the finding.

**`java_hash_set` moved down to `rustmc-data`.** `rustmc-worldgen` depends on
`rustmc-world`, so `nbt.rs` calling it was a cycle. `rustmc-data` is the bottom
of the graph, so the move adds no edge and needs none later; `rustmc-worldgen`
re-exports it, so nothing about the tree features changed. Not a second copy:
the module that moved is JVM-verified by `ci/hash-order-golden.sh`, and a
second one would be unverified and would agree with the first until it did not.

**`rustmc_world::nbt` writes `java.util.HashMap` bucket order.** Exact when a
compound's keys occupy distinct buckets; falls back to sorted order — legal
NBT, what it emitted before — when the table declines to order itself. It does
not touch the menu channel, which is one-key compounds, and 470 and 480 stayed
`match` across the change, measured rather than assumed.

**THE ARITY.** `RUSTMC_DUMP_PACKET=chat` (then `RUSTMC_DUMP_CHAT=1`) is a new env-gated instrument in
`trace::decode`'s chat arm: the projection digests the whole body, so a digest
cannot say which byte differs and `ascii_runs` shows the strings but not the
structure. Run through `ci/t2-gameplay-subset.sh 110-*.toml` it prints vanilla's
own 539 bytes, and decoding them shows

```text
  { with: [ {"": 2}, {"": 20}, {extra: [dn, {color:"gray", text:", "}, dn],
                                text: ""} ],
    translate: "commands.list.players" }
```

**`commands.list.players` takes THREE arguments in 26.2** — online, **max**,
and the joined names — and a primitive argument encodes as a compound whose
single key is the empty string. Reading `ListPlayersCommand` alone would have
produced two arguments and a wrong digest: `format` passes `list.size()` and
the joined component, and the maximum comes from the translation string's own
arity. This is the fifth or sixth time on this project that an hour of probing
beat an hour of reading, and the instrument is now in the tree.

The 539 bytes are `crate::commands`'s test vector verbatim, so the unit test is
the check rather than a restatement of the implementation.

### THE CONTAINER CHANNEL (2026-08-04, branch `menus-and-jump` off `faae26f`)

**The four menu checks were one item because a counter says so, and the
counter was read rather than assumed.** `ServerPlayer.containerCounter` has
exactly one `putfield` — `containerCounter % 100 + 1`, inside
`nextContainerCounter`, called from `openMenu`, `openHorseInventory` and
`openNautilusInventory` and nowhere else — and **nothing resets it**:
`doCloseContainer` touches `containerMenu`, and `restoreFrom` does not mention
it at all. The corpus plays all 62 scenarios down one actor connection, so it
runs for the whole corpus.

Confirmed against vanilla's own recording rather than inferred:

```text
  open_screen   window=1 menu=2   chest-opens-a-screen                    [idx  9]
                window=2 menu=14  a-furnace-opens-a-screen-a-chest-does-not [55]
                window=3 menu=12  a-crafting-table-opens-a-menu...          [56]
                window=4 menu=2   a-bystander-sees-a-chest-open             [57]
```

and **exactly four `open_screen` in the whole corpus**. The two
`open_sign_editor` at indices 34 and 54 sit between them and do *not* advance
the counter — `openTextEdit` never calls `nextContainerCounter` — which was a
prediction before it was a measurement.

#### What landed

* `crate::menu` — the counter, `incrementStateId`, the three menu specs and
  the bodies for `open_screen`, `container_set_content` and
  `container_set_data`.
* `crate::containers` — `ContainerOpenersCounter`, the block-event queue and
  `runBlockEvents`.
* `crate::protocol_ids` + `ci/dump-protocol-ids.sh` — the **tenth** generated
  table. `Registries.MENU` and `Registries.BLOCK` reach the wire as bare
  varints and neither is in `registries.bin`, because only datapack registries
  are synced to a client. `gen-gameplay-tables.sh` picked it up from the
  source `open` with no further wiring, which is the derived-list design
  working as intended.

#### Numbers derived twice and then confirmed by vanilla's bytes

Every one of these was derived from the jar, cross-checked a second way, and
only then seen on the wire:

```text
  menu type ids       generic_9x3 2, crafting 12, furnace 14
  block registry id   minecraft:chest 201  (NOT a state id — five figures)
  slot counts         chest 63, furnace 39 + 4 data slots, crafting 46
  state id            1 on every fresh menu — (0 + 1) & 32767, not a choice
```

The block id was derived independently of the registry report as the
**first-appearance ordinal** in `block_props.json`'s 32,366-state table
(1,196 blocks; air 0, stone 1, chest 201), because `Block.BLOCK_STATE_REGISTRY`
is filled by walking `BuiltInRegistries.BLOCK` in order. Both derivations
agree and vanilla's `block_event` then carries 201.

#### The mechanism behind both container entries in `gameplay-unstable.toml`

`CHECK_TICK_DELAY` is 5, `recheckOpeners` re-arms whenever the count is above
zero, and — the part that surprises — it calls `openerCountChanged`
**unconditionally**, at offset 167, on the path where the count did not change
as well as the path where it did. `ChestBlockEntity.signalOpenCount` is
`level.blockEvent(pos, block, 1, openCount)`.

So an open chest emits the same `block_event(1, 1)` every 250 ms forever.
Vanilla's own recording:

```text
  chest-opens-a-screen    settle 1000 ms   6 events   66 261 511 777 994 1244
  a-bystander-sees...     settle 2000 ms  10 events    7 206 ... 1956 2221
```

and `verdict_for` is **exact sequence equality**, so the count is the check.
That is why the pair flaps in vanilla against itself at 1/25 and 3/25: same
mechanism, two window lengths, and the rates are in the ratio the lengths
predict. **A `diverge` on either is not automatically a defect and a `match`
is not proof the cadence is right — read the cadence out of the recording.**

#### The three-way split the checks exist to separate

`ChestBlockEntity` overrides `startOpen`/`stopOpen` and owns an openers
counter. `AbstractFurnaceBlockEntity` declares **neither**, so a furnace has
no lid and no block event. `CraftingTableBlock` has no block entity at all —
its provider is a `SimpleMenuProvider` built in `getMenuProvider`. Getting
this wrong in the tidy direction — one code path for "a container opened" —
passes 090 and fails 470 and 480. `has_openers_counter` is therefore kept a
**separate predicate** from `trigger_event` even though the two answer alike
today; a piston answers yes to the second and no to the first.

Also measured: `block_entity_data` appears **only** for signs (indices 34 and
54), so 470's and 480's projections see none on either side — which is what
480's `about` claims and is now checked rather than asserted.

#### The counter hazard, which is the thing to watch

Twenty-one block classes reach `Player.openMenu` and **three are
implemented**. That is recorded in `menu_for_state` as a hazard, not a
feature gap: a scenario that right-clicks a barrel advances vanilla's counter
and not ours, and *every* later menu check then reports a window id one too
low — four healthy checks accused instead of the one missing block. **Before
reading a wall of window-id divergences as four bugs, check whether some
scenario earlier in corpus order clicks a container that is not in that
list.**

#### Nulls and traps, so nobody pays for them twice

* **`AbstractContainerMenu.stillValid` is not implemented, and it is safe.**
  `ServerPlayer.tick` closes a menu whose `stillValid` has gone false, and a
  container's is `distanceToSqr(pos + 0.5) <= 64.0` — eight blocks — so on
  vanilla the actor's chest menu closes by itself as the corpus walks to the
  next workspace. It **cannot shift the counter**: neither `closeContainer`
  nor `doCloseContainer` touches `containerCounter`. And the packet it emits
  is one nothing observes — `container_close` (0x11) appears **zero times**
  across all 62 scenarios of vanilla's recording, because every one of those
  closes lands in the un-measured settle between scenarios.
* **`chat`'s declared projection digests the whole packet body.** The chat arm
  of `trace::decode` consumes zero bytes, so `rest` is `digest(body)`. Any
  check on that channel needs byte-identical NBT; there is no partial credit.
* **No block entity ever sends `block_entity_data` for a chest or a furnace.**
  Neither overrides `getUpdatePacket`, the base returns null, and
  `ChunkHolder.broadcastBlockEntity` returns without sending on null.
* **The block-event queue is a set.** `ObjectLinkedOpenHashSet.add` on an
  equal element does not re-add, so two identical events *in one tick*
  collapse to one. Per-tick only: `runBlockEvents` empties it every tick, and
  the 5-tick chest repeat therefore never collides with itself.
* **`AABB(BlockPos).inflate(n)` is not symmetric** — `−n` on the low side and
  `+n + 1` on the high side, because the base box is the unit cube from the
  corner rather than the point. A test asserted otherwise and failed.
* **`ClientboundBlockEventPacket`'s constructor order is not its wire order.**
  Constructor `(pos, block, b0, b1)`, wire `pos, b0, b1, block`.
* **The three container packets do not agree about field widths.**
  `containerId` is a varint in all of them, `container_set_content`'s
  `stateId` is a varint, and `container_set_data`'s `id` and `value` are
  **shorts**.

#### Measured, and the arithmetic closes

`./ci/t2-gameplay.sh` on the Threadripper in `~/rustmc-menus`, corpus 62,
against a baseline **re-derived on the same rig at `faae26f`** rather than
taken from the previous run's report — the ratchet only ratchets if the floor
is current:

```text
  before (faae26f, re-derived)   declared 30/62   23 diverge, 9 absent
  after  (cd20f78)               declared 34/62   23 diverge, 5 absent
```

0 vacuous, 0 inert, 0 error on both. Attributed check by check by
`verdicts.py` against the gate's own per-check output: **the only four
verdicts that changed are the four menu checks**, all `absent -> match`, and
nothing fell. 30 + 4 = 34, and 34 + 23 + 5 = 62.

`strict` was 16 -> 18. One run, not ratcheted, not quoted as a parity claim.

Both chest checks are baselined at `match` knowing they flap 1/25 and 3/25 in
vanilla against itself, with the reading instructions on the lines. A softer
floor would hide a real fall to `diverge`, which is the failure this file was
tightened for two runs ago.

#### THE RATCHET AND THE UNSTABLE FILE — proposed, not built

> **BUILT 2026-08-05 on `collapse-t1-list`, and the option taken is the one
> recommended below.** Everything from here to the end of this subsection is
> the reasoning as it stood before the measurement; it is kept because the
> three rejected alternatives are still the right rejections. What actually
> landed, and the paired N = 26 measurement that justified it, is in **THE
> SAMPLING, THE UNGATED SUITE AND THE COMMAND** at the top of this block.

**This stopped being a proposal and became a defect on 2026-08-04**, when
`chest-opens-a-screen` was locked at `match` with its 1-in-25 flap disclosed
beside it and the next gate run went red on it. The measurement is on the
baseline line: identical mechanism, identical `b0`/`b1`, identical start, mean
gap 235.6 ms against 237.5 ms, and a **27 ms band** at the window edge
deciding the verdict.

`ci/t2-gameplay.sh` **never reads `gameplay-unstable.toml`.** Only
`ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh` does. So the ratchet has no notion of a
known-unstable check, and a check recorded — with a measured rate — as
irreproducible in *vanilla against vanilla* can still be pinned to a hard
`match`. The gate then goes red at random. **That is a false alarm by
construction**, and false alarms get silenced, which is how a real regression
eventually walks through.

The selfcheck's problem was power: absence is not evidence at an N too small
to resolve the rate. **The gate's problem is different and worse.** It has
exactly one run, so it has *no* power for a 1-in-25 event, and it must not
assert a verdict it cannot support.

##### The option I would take: remove the randomness from the projection

Let a check declare that a run of **identical consecutive observations
collapses to one** — `collapse_repeats = ["block_event"]` — with the
mechanism and the measured cadence written in the file beside it.

* the reference becomes **deterministic** under that projection, so `match`
  becomes a floor the instrument can actually support;
* every field assertion stays sharp: the collapsed observation still carries
  `at`, `b0`, `b1` and `block`, so a wrong viewer count or a lid at the wrong
  position still fails;
* both entries leave `gameplay-unstable.toml` **for the right reason** — the
  instability was in this harness's sampling, not in vanilla's behaviour —
  rather than by exemption.

**It is not a loosening, and the precedent is already in the tree.**
`trace::decode` decodes `ClientboundSoundPacket` specifically so it can throw
the `long seed` away, because `Level.playSound` fills it from
`soundSeedGenerator.nextLong()` and digesting it made every check naming
`sound` unmatchable for everybody, vanilla included. That is the same move:
a dimension no check claims to test, removed from the comparison instead of
declared unstable. Neither chest check's `about` mentions repeats — 090 is
"right-clicking a chest opens it", 490 is "the player who opened it gets a
screen and everyone else gets a lid" — and the repeat count is an artefact of
`settle_ms`.

**Its failure mode, stated rather than discovered later:** the cadence stops
being tested by these two checks, so a server that emitted the lid once and
never repeated would pass. `CHECK_TICK_DELAY = 5` is a real mechanism and
that coverage must be replaced deliberately. The replacement measures the
**gap**, not the count — and gap measurement is timing, which this corpus
deliberately excludes from strict comparison, so its honest home is a unit
test over `Openers::recheck` (which already asserts one signal per recheck)
plus an explicit note that the *wire* cadence is unmeasured.

##### The three I would not take, and why

* **Verdict sets in the baseline** (`= ["match", "diverge"]`). A
  hand-maintained widening with no link to any measured rate: nothing stops a
  set being widened to make a red go away, and the file cannot tell a declared
  instability from a convenient one. It also cannot say *why* both are
  acceptable, so a wrong `b1` — which also lands on `diverge` — is
  indistinguishable from the cadence flap.
* **Suppress a regression when the difference falls on the declared
  `field`.** For both chest checks the declared field is `block_event`, which
  is the *entire* projection. Suppressing on it suppresses everything the
  check tests. That converts a check into a no-op precisely for the checks it
  was added to protect — the sixteenth member of the "check that could not
  fail" family, invented on purpose.
* **Re-run a declared-unstable check N times and take the modal verdict.**
  Two failure modes and the second is fatal here. Cost, first. Then **state**:
  the corpus is one connection through one world, and re-running a menu
  scenario advances `ServerPlayer.containerCounter`, so every later menu check
  shifts by one — the mechanism would corrupt exactly the checks it was added
  to stabilise.

##### The fallback, if the projection change proves fiddly

A **floor/ceiling split**: the baseline stores the floor the measured rate can
support *and* the recorded ceiling; below floor is red, between them is green
with a note, above prompts an update. It is honest bookkeeping and it removes
the false alarm — but it does not remove the non-determinism, so the hole
named on today's baseline line stays open. Second choice, not the answer.

##### THE DECLARED RATE IS A VANILLA-vs-VANILLA RATE AND IT IS NOT OURS

Three runs of the same tree now exist and they settle something the proposal
above was assuming wrongly:

```text
                                    run A      run B      run C
                                    62 checks  63 (red)   63 (green)
  chest-opens-a-screen              match      diverge    diverge
  a-bystander-sees-a-chest-open     match      match      diverge
  a-furnace-opens-a-screen...       match      match      match
  a-crafting-table-opens-a-menu...  match      match      match
  declared                          34/62      33/63      32/63
```

**Three of six check-runs of the chest pair diverged.** `gameplay-unstable.toml`
records 1/25 and 3/25, and those are *vanilla against vanilla* — two runs of
one jittery implementation, whose errors are drawn from the same
distribution. Ours is a different comparison: this server's cadence is
**exactly 250 ms** and vanilla's jitters 195-265, so the two disagree at a
window edge more often than vanilla disagrees with itself, not less. Being
*more* regular than the reference costs us here.

N = 3 per check is far too small to state a rate and none is stated. What it
is large enough to do is refute "our flap rate will be comparable to
vanilla's", which is what the `match` floor was silently resting on.

**This strengthens the recommendation rather than changing it.** A ratchet
cannot borrow the selfcheck's numbers, because the selfcheck measures a
different comparison; and a per-check rate for *our* comparison would need
its own N = 25-ish campaign per check per branch, which nothing can afford.
Removing the random dimension from the projection needs no rate at all.

**Either way it is a rig change, and a rig change needs its own re-derived
baseline before any green from it is trusted.**

#### T1 IS NOT IN ANY MERGE GATE, AND 78 TEST BINARIES LIVE ONLY THERE

> **CLOSED 2026-08-05.** `ci/handoff.sh` stage 4 runs `ci/t1-gate.sh`, which
> adjudicates the two standing reds by signature against
> `ci/checks/t1-known-red.toml`. The measurement below was reproduced
> exactly on the branch that closed it — 676 s, 95 binaries, the same two
> reds at the same 106 — and where the stage sits, and why, is recorded in
> the stage's own comment and in the section at the top of this block.

Run for the first time in a handoff on 2026-08-04, because nothing had ever
required it. Measured on the Threadripper in `~/rustmc-menus`, tree
`82ebd66`:

```text
  ./ci/t1.sh    exit 101    wall 676 s   (incl. rsync and rebuild)
                95 test binaries, 1,104 tests passed
                2 binaries FAILED: carved_chunks_match_vanilla
                                   surface_chunks_match_vanilla
```

**Both failures are the documented standing reds and neither moved.** Every
figure matches the signature in `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md` exactly — 106 of
7,077,888 (99.998502%), y 32..63: 54, y 128..159: 52, `calcite -> dirt` 27,
`calcite -> grass_block` 18, `sandstone -> stone` 22, seed 0, first example
chunk (80, 153). So this branch moved nothing there, which is the only claim
that was owed.

**The finding is the coverage, not the number.** `ci/handoff.sh` has three
stages and runs `ci/t0-remote.sh` and `ci/t2-gameplay.sh`; it does not run
T1, and `ci/t0.sh:16` says outright that the golden-vector gates live in T1.
`ci/t0.sh` selects `--lib --bins`, which reached **17** binaries on this
tree. T1 reaches **95**. So **78 test binaries — every golden vector and
every integration test under `tests/` — are outside every merge gate this
project runs.**

That is the same family as `--lib` never reaching `tools/oracle-runner`'s
nineteen tests, except one level up: not a gate that cannot fail, but a gate
nobody runs. It is why `crates/rustmc-worldgen/tests/golden_hash_order.rs`
— the JVM-verified check on the module this branch touched — had to be
confirmed by hand here rather than by a gate.

**Why it cannot simply be added, and what to do about it.** T1 exits 101 on
two *known* reds, so wiring it into `handoff.sh` as-is makes every handoff
fail and it would be switched off within a day. It needs the two standing
reds allowlisted so that a *third* failure is what turns it red — the same
shape as `gameplay-baseline.toml`, and for the same reason: a ratchet over an
honestly-red suite, rather than a pass list. 676 s is affordable next to
`ci/t2-gameplay.sh`'s ~50 minutes; the blocker is the allowlist, not the cost.

**ADJUDICATED BY THE ORCHESTRATOR, 2026-08-04: approved, and allowlist by
SIGNATURE rather than by name.** A name-only allowlist lets a known failure
get quietly *worse* — 106 mismatches becoming 10,600 would still read as "the
known red", which is the stale-baseline defect transplanted into a new file.
The entry must record the **count, the y-bands, and the seed/chunk**, so that
a change in the *nature* of a known failure is as red as a third failure
appearing:

```text
  carved_chunks_match_vanilla / surface_chunks_match_vanilla
    106 of 7,077,888        y 32..63: 54    y 128..159: 52
    seed 0                  first example chunk (80, 153)
```

**Not to be implemented on the `menus-and-jump` branch** — it is its own
change, and that branch is finished.

#### Item 2 — the NBT order question, answered the other way

The brief asked whether vanilla's `HashMap` key order is *stably*
reproducible or only accidentally deterministic, and said that if it were the
latter the check needed its claim narrowed. **It is the former, and the
instrument already existed.**

`crates/rustmc-worldgen/src/java_hash_set.rs` reproduces `HashMap`'s spread,
bucket index, resize and treeification and is checked against real JVM output
by `ci/hash-order-golden.sh`. It is generic over a `JavaHash` trait; NBT keys
needed only `String.hashCode`, which — unlike the rest of that module — is
specified in the JLS rather than being one JDK's implementation detail. The
test added there now predicts, without being told them, both key orders the
previous run measured off vanilla's own bytes:

```text
  ["translate","with"]                            -> with, translate
  ["text","click_event","hover_event","insertion"] -> click_event, insertion,
                                                      text, hover_event
```

Four keys in the default sixteen buckets collide nowhere, so **insertion order
does not enter at all** and nothing has to model how the codec built the tag.

Two things that change the shape of the remaining work:

* **`chat`'s declared projection digests the whole body.** The chat arm of
  `trace::decode` consumes zero bytes, so `rest` is `digest(body)`. Byte-
  identical NBT is not a nicety for `server-answers-a-command`, it *is* the
  check — there is no partial credit and no narrowing needed.
* **The obstacle is placement, not derivation.** `rustmc-worldgen` depends on
  `rustmc-world`, so `nbt.rs` cannot call `java_hash_set` without a cycle.
  Closing this means lifting that module down into `rustmc-world` or
  `rustmc-data`, **not writing a second one**. A pointer to that now sits on
  `write_payload`'s compound branch, which is the file anyone chasing this
  reads first.

The command tree and the `commands.list.players` component are still
unbuilt; that is the whole of what remains for the check.

#### Item 3 — the on-ground bit, and a premise that needed correcting

`Step::Walk` now carries `on_ground`, defaulted true so every existing check
sends what it sent, threaded into `Session::hop_to`. One bit and not a physics
model: `handleMovePlayer` skips its 0.0625 "moved wrongly" comparison outright
for a creative player (offset 808) and this corpus is creative by
construction.

**The brief priced this as a fix and it is coverage.** The arm it reaches —
`ServerEntity.sendChanges`' `wasOnGround != entity.onGround()`, offsets
680..691 — is *already ported* in `crate::tracker` and *already unit tested*
by `a_change_of_ground_flag_forces_a_position_sync`. What was missing was any
scenario that could exercise it, because `hop_to` wrote a literal 1 into every
movement packet. So `540-a-player-that-leaves-the-ground-is-resynced` was
predicted `match` in its own file, which is an unusual thing to write here,
and the red-first discipline had to be inverted: the check was **falsified
deliberately** by deleting the disjunct and re-running, rather than assumed
falsifiable.

Its first `observe` list named the three *packets* — `entity_position_sync`,
`move_entity_pos`, `move_entity_pos_rot` — and `trace::decode` emits none of
those, folding them into `entity_position` and `move_entity`. That projection
would have filtered every observation away and scored `absent` for ever on
both servers whatever they did. **The fifteenth "check that could not fail"
in this corpus, and the first caught before its first run rather than after.**

##### AND THE PREDICTION WAS WRONG, WHICH IS THE BETTER OUTCOME

The file predicted `match` and said in writing what a `diverge` would mean:
"the port is wrong in a way no unit test reached, which is a better outcome
than the prediction being right". **It came back `diverge`**, on
`ci/t2-gameplay-subset.sh`, 2026-08-04, in `~/rustmc-menus`. Both projections
whole, from `oracle-runner explain`:

```text
  vanilla 3 observations, ours 2

  [0] van entity_position at [0,0,3] step 0  rest e3e08e2b2ee20519
      our entity_position at [0,0,3] step 0  rest 7cf1ac6bc31f675f
  [1] van entity_position at [0,0,3] step 0  rest e3e07e2b2ee20366
      our entity_position at [0,0,0] step 1  rest 7cf19c6bc31f65ac
  [2] van move_entity     d=[0,0,-12288] step 1
      our (nothing)
```

**Vanilla syncs TWICE inside step 0 and then sends the return walk as a
delta. This server syncs once and sends the return walk as a sync.** Read
straight off that, and it is one cause rather than three:

* vanilla's sync #1 is the flag going false, exactly as designed. Its sync #2
  is the flag going **back true inside the same step, without any packet
  saying so** — the player is standing on a superflat block, so vanilla's own
  physics restores `onGround` and `wasOnGround != entity.onGround()` fires a
  second time;
* which is why step 1 is a *delta* on vanilla: `wasOnGround` is already true
  when the walk back claims true, so the forced-sync disjunct is false and
  `sendChanges` takes the `move_entity` branch — 3 blocks x 4096 = 12288, on
  the nose;
* and it is a *sync* here, because this server's `onGround` is whatever the
  last packet claimed and nothing ever re-derives it, so the flag is still
  false when the walk back says true.

**So this server treats the client's ground flag as authoritative and vanilla
treats it as a claim.** `handleMovePlayer` never calls `setDeltaMovement`; it
calls `player.move(MoverType.PLAYER, vec)` and
`setOnGroundWithMovement(onGround, horizontalCollision, vec)`, and the
server's own tick is what puts the player back on the floor.

The `rest` digests differ even at `[0]`, where both sides are structurally
the same packet, so there is a second and smaller gap underneath:
`ClientboundEntityPositionSyncPacket.of` builds its `PositionMoveRotation`
from `trackingPosition()`, **`getDeltaMovement()`**, `getYRot()`, `getXRot()`
— note *not* `PositionMoveRotation.of(entity)`, which would use
`getKnownMovement()` — and this server leaves a player's `movement` at its
initial value forever, because `world_send.rs` updates position, rotations
and the ground flag and nothing else.

**Both are the same missing thing: there is no server-side player physics.**
That is a named item with a size, and it is emphatically not the one bit item
3 was priced at. The bit was the whole cost of the *rig*, exactly as
forecast; what the rig then measured is a second defect that the forecast had
no way to see, and that is the check earning its keep on its first run.

**The falsification control was run anyway and it is what makes the check
trustworthy.** With `|| self.was_on_ground != e.on_ground` deleted from
`crate::tracker`, the verdict moves `diverge -> absent` — this server then
emits nothing at all on that projection. So the check has three
distinguishable states, it is driven by exactly the arm it names, and the
`diverge` is a real defect rather than a dead projection. The tree was
restored and `git diff` on `tracker.rs` is empty.

The check is therefore **left red and baselined at `diverge`**, which is the
honest floor: above `absent`, reproducible, and it hands the next agent a
named defect with a measured signature instead of a green tick over an
unfixed one.

#### The `absent` column is down to five, and three of them are ceilings

> **Down to four on 2026-08-05**: `server-answers-a-command` reached `match`,
> declared and strict. The remaining reachable one is
> `swapping-to-the-offhand-shows-on-both-channels`; the other three are the
> 25/25 ceilings below and reading a `diverge` on any of them as a defect is
> a mistake three previous runs have now made.

```text
  a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory   25/25 flaps — `diverge` at best
  spawn-egg-makes-a-mob                     25/25 flaps — `diverge` at best
  water-spreads                             25/25 flaps — `diverge` at best
  server-answers-a-command                  reachable
  swapping-to-the-offhand-shows-on-both-channels   reachable
```

**Only two `absent` checks in the corpus can still reach `match`.** The other

cannot reproduce them against itself — and reading a `diverge` on any of them

#### Next item, and what closes it

> **DONE 2026-08-05.** Both halves landed: `java_hash_set` moved down to
> `rustmc-data` and `rustmc_world::nbt` writes bucket order, and
> `crate::commands` answers `/list`. The red observation was written first —
> `absent`, on a subset run, before the commit — exactly as this section asks.
> **The one thing this plan had wrong**: `commands.list.players` takes *three*
> arguments in 26.2, online, max and names, which no reading of
> `ListPlayersCommand` would have given and which `RUSTMC_DUMP_PACKET=chat` settled
> in one run.

**`server-answers-a-command`**, and it is now de-risked rather than merely
recommended. What is left is two separable pieces, neither of which is a
research question any more:

1. **The command tree and the `/list` reply.** One packet, `system_chat`,
   carrying `Component.translatable("commands.list.players", n, names)`. No
   counters, no block entities, nothing shared with anything else in the
   corpus.
2. **Byte-identical NBT**, because `chat`'s projection digests the whole body.
   The order is `java.util.HashMap` bucket order, it is reproducible, and
   `rustmc_worldgen::java_hash_set` already does it and is JVM-verified. The
   work is **moving that module down** into `rustmc-world` or `rustmc-data` —
   `rustmc-worldgen` depends on `rustmc-world`, so `nbt.rs` cannot call it
   today — and then writing compounds in bucket order instead of `BTreeMap`
   order.

It closes when the full gate reports `server-answers-a-command` as `match`
with every other verdict unchanged. **Write the red observation first**: it
is `absent` now, so a subset run after step 1 and before step 2 should show
`diverge` on the body digest alone, which is the cheapest possible proof that
step 2 is the remaining half rather than a guess.

The other named item, and the larger one, is what `540` found: **there is no
server-side player physics**, so this server echoes the client's ground flag
instead of re-deriving it and never sets a player's delta-movement. That is
the root of `540`'s `diverge` and it is not a bit.

### THE MOTION COVERAGE HOLE (2026-08-04, branch `entities-motion` off `3b80d0d`)

**Why this run existed.** Three fixes on the parent — the `movedPlayers` sweep
at the foot of `ChunkMap.tick`, the `entity_position_sync` body, and the IEEE
form of the two distance predicates — were covered by unit tests and by
nothing on the wire, because **no scenario in the corpus had ever changed
anybody's visibility.** Every check that moves anything moves the actor, and
the only other entity in almost every scenario is the other player, which
moves too and is therefore covered by the entity loop rather than by the
sweep. The sweep could have been deleted and the corpus would have stayed
green.

**What landed.**

* `530-walking-away-drops-a-standing-player-from-view` — corpus 61 -> 62. The
  actor walks away from the standing observer and back **twice**, once to a
  separation vanilla still tracks at (47 blocks) and once past it (75). One
  trip would only prove the sweep runs; two pin the limit, which is the
  difference between a check and a constant.
* `Session::hop_to` walks at four blocks a packet instead of eight — and the
  first repair took one block, which broke `080-other-player-is-an-entity`.
  See below: inside a legal window the hop wants to be **large**.
* A server view distance: `--view-distance`, defaulting to
  `server.properties`' own 10, feeding the login packet's chunk radius, the
  chunk sender and `ChunkMap.getPlayerViewDistance`'s clamp. The gate passes
  4 on both sides.

**Measured, and the arithmetic closes.** `./ci/t2-gameplay.sh` on the
Threadripper in `~/rustmc-entities-motion`, tree at `b202955`, corpus 62
(`find ci/checks/gameplay -type f | sort | xargs md5sum | md5sum` =
`dcfb9e16c66c2f8e634b0883dc0b7bb9` at the tip, which differs from the gated
tree by two comment-only commits and no verdict line):

```text
  before (61 checks, 3b80d0d)   declared 29/61   23 diverge, 9 absent
  after  (62 checks)            declared 30/62   23 diverge, 9 absent
```

0 vacuous, 0 inert, 0 error on both. Attributed check by check against the
baseline run's own verdict list: **every one of the 61 carried-over checks has
an identical verdict**, and the whole of the +1 is the new check. 29 + 1 = 30
and 30 + 23 + 9 = 62.

`strict` was 16 on both runs. It is not ratcheted, it is one run, and it is
not quoted here as a parity claim.

**The `absent` column did not move and no check reached `match` from it.**
That was the run's first item and it is not done; the section below on
per-player counters is why the two candidates that looked cheapest are not,
and it is worth more than a rushed half-built menu channel would have been.

#### The red observation that agreed with its prediction and measured nothing

Read this one before writing another moving check. 530 was committed alone
with `absent`/then `diverge` predicted in the file **and** in the baseline,
and its first run came back `diverge` with the extra `remove_entities` at
step 0 — exactly as written. It was still worthless: **vanilla had emitted
nothing at all**, on that run and the one after it.

`Session::hop_to` moved 8 blocks a packet. Packets leave every 30 ms and a
tick is 50, so two reach the server against one `lastGood` and
`handleMovePlayer` tests their sum against `100.0f * i`:

```text
  [Server thread/WARN]: oracle moved too quickly! 0.0,0.0,16.0
```

Three teleports; the actor never got further than 24 blocks from the
observer; and because a measured step deliberately never reads the socket,
the `accept_teleportation` never went out, so the first refusal pinned it for
the rest of the walk. **`Session::goto` next door had already been through
exactly this and fixed it at 0.5 blocks a packet**, with the whole story
written above its own `HOP`. The correction lived in the function it
corrected and did not travel — the same shape as the gamerule ids.

**And the repair overshot.** At one block a packet the walk was legal and
080 fell `match -> diverge` on the full gate — vanilla's first `move_entity`
delta 12288 against our 8192, three blocks against two. 080 walks four blocks:
one packet at the old pace, four at the new one, and the two servers'
`sendChanges` divided the four differently. Neither server changed. **More
packets for the same walk buy no fidelity and make every observation of it
phase-sensitive.** Four blocks a packet is legal at every routine fold and
leaves 080 at the single hop it was measured `match` in.

**The cheap guard, for any scenario that walks:**
`grep -c 'moved too quickly' <vanilla-dir>/logs/latest.log` must be 0. It is
one line and it is the difference between measuring a server and measuring a
rig.

#### The defect it found once the rig was real

`TrackedEntity.updatePlayer` bounds visibility by
`min(getEffectiveRange(), getPlayerViewDistance(player) * 16)` and
`getPlayerViewDistance` is `Mth.clamp(requested, 2, serverViewDistance)`.
**This server had no `serverViewDistance`.** `status.rs` set the join
packet's chunk radius to the radius of the generated **spawn tile** and
handed the same number to `PlayerIdentity.view_distance` — so how much world
had been generated decided how far a player could see another player: 2 under
`--radius 2`, a 32-block limit against vanilla's 64.

    server unfixed  diverge  vanilla removes at step 2, we remove at step 0
    server fixed    match

That difference *is* 64 blocks against 32, and it is the only thing between
the two runs.

**Three doc comments in our own source were wrong about this and one of them
wrote a prediction.** `JoinInfo::chunk_radius` says — said — "the client's
own view distance, echoed back", which matched neither the code beside it nor
vanilla, and 530's first prediction was built on it: it said this server
would track at 160 blocks. It tracked at 32.

#### What the rig cannot express, scoped and deliberately not built

**It can walk.** It could not walk further than about 16 blocks and now can;
nothing else was missing.

**`entity_position_sync` is reached by nothing in this corpus, and this run
settled that rather than causing it.** Measured from 530's own recordings:
with `hop_to` at 8 blocks a packet the trace carries `entity_position`, at one
block it carries none, because the `i16` arm needs more than 8 blocks between
two `sendChanges` body runs and a player's `updateInterval` is 2 ticks — 26
blocks per body run at the old pace, 3.3 at the new one. The old pace's
"coverage" was fiction anyway: vanilla was refusing those packets, so the
recording carried ours and not vanilla's. Nothing else moves fast enough —
`goto` is 0.5 blocks a packet and 080 covers four blocks in one hop.

**It cannot jump, and the cost is one bit — not a physics model.** The
`entity_position_sync` arm `wasOnGround != entity.onGround()` has never been
reachable, because `hop_to` writes a literal `1` for the on-ground byte of
every `MOVE_PLAYER_POS`. The expensive answer is
the plausible one: it *looks* like the client must model the jump arc (0.42,
gravity 0.08, drag 0.98, one packet per tick) because `handleMovePlayer` runs
the claimed delta through `player.move` and rejects a disagreement over
0.0625. **It does not, in this substrate** — that comparison is skipped
outright for a creative player, and the corpus is creative by construction:

```text
  handleMovePlayer, offsets 785..837
    787: ldc2_w 0.0625d / 791: ifle 855
    798: isSleeping  : ifne 855
    808: isCreative  : ifne 855      <-- the corpus substrate
    818: isSpectator : ifne 855
    837: LOGGER "{} moved wrongly!"
```

and vanilla's own jump detector sits immediately above it:

```text
  offsets 631..657
    if (player.onGround() && !packet.isOnGround() && <upward-movement flag>)
        player.jumpFromGround();
```

So: an `on_ground` field on `Step::Walk`, or a `Step::Jump`, threaded into
`hop_to`. No physics, no tick alignment, no new packet type. **Read from the
jar, not measured** — no probe has yet sent the flag clear, and that
measurement belongs with the change.

**Both uncovered arms want the same rig item**, so do them together: a
`Step::Walk` that chooses its pace *and* its on-ground bit. The pace is a
window, not a point — `100 * i` allows a claimed 10 blocks between ticks and
the `i16` arm needs more than 8 between body runs — and a window that narrow
is exactly what must be measured against vanilla rather than reasoned into a
constant. One recording settles it; this run has already paid for finding out
what happens when it is not.

#### Two things a new check inherits from the checks before it

Both measured from the gate's own vanilla recording, and both change **which
`absent` check is cheap** — the previous block's table is wrong about this.

**Container ids and menu state ids are per-player counters that run for the
whole corpus.** One actor plays every scenario and
`ServerPlayer.nextContainerCounter` is `containerCounter % 100 + 1` on a
field that lives as long as the player:

```text
  open_screen         window=1  chest-opens-a-screen
                      window=2  a-furnace-opens-a-screen-a-chest-does-not
                      window=3  a-crafting-table-opens-a-menu-with-no-block-entity
                      window=4  a-bystander-sees-a-chest-open

  container_set_slot  window=0 state=2  torch-falls-with-its-support
                      window=0 state=3  swapping-to-the-offhand (slot 36)
                      window=0 state=4  swapping-to-the-offhand (slot 45)
```

So **the four menu checks are one indivisible item, in corpus order.** A
server that implements only the crafting table sends `window=1` where vanilla
sends `window=3` and diverges on a field that has nothing to do with crafting
tables. `a-crafting-table-opens-a-menu-with-no-block-entity` looks like the
cheapest of the four — no block entity, a one-key title, `stateId` always 1
on a fresh menu — and is not separately closable. Same for the offhand swap:
its states 3 and 4 require a server that also produced state 2 where
`torch-falls-with-its-support` did.

**Vanilla's NBT compounds are not written in sorted key order and ours are.**
`CompoundTag` wraps a `java.util.HashMap` and `write` iterates `keySet()`;
`rustmc_world::nbt::Nbt::Compound` is a `BTreeMap`. Visible in vanilla's own
bytes without decoding anything, because `trace::ascii_runs` scans the packet
in wire order: the reply to `/list` carries `with` before `translate`, and
inside a display name `click_event, insertion, text, hover_event`. Neither is
alphabetical. Nothing in the corpus compares a multi-key compound today, so
it has cost nothing yet — but it is the whole difficulty of
`server-answers-a-command` and it will bite `placing-a-sign-opens-its-editor`
the same way. It does **not** bite the menu channel: `container.crafting` is
one key and one key has no order.

#### The `absent` column, re-ranked by what it actually costs

Nine `absent`, of which **three can never reach `match`** (in
`gameplay-unstable.toml` at 25 flaps / 25) and are `absent -> diverge` at
best: `spawn-egg-makes-a-mob`, `a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory`,
`water-spreads`. Of the six that remain:

| check | needs | self-contained? |
|---|---|---|
| `server-answers-a-command` | command dispatch + a `commands.list.players` component | **yes** — the only one |
| `chest-opens-a-screen` | block entity + `block_event` + menu | no — window id 1 of 4 |
| `a-furnace-opens-a-screen-a-chest-does-not` | block entity + a second menu type | no — window id 2 of 4 |
| `a-crafting-table-opens-a-menu-with-no-block-entity` | menu only, no block entity | no — window id 3 of 4 |
| `a-bystander-sees-a-chest-open` | the chest lid `block_event` | no — window id 4 of 4 |
| `swapping-to-the-offhand-shows-on-both-channels` | offhand + `ItemStack` on the wire | no — inventory state id |

`server-answers-a-command` is one packet and no counters; its cost is
entirely the NBT key order above. The menu channel is four checks at once and
its cost is block entities plus two menu types — the crafting table's own
sequence is fully read (`open_screen` **before** `container_set_content`,
`MenuType.CRAFTING` protocol id 12, 46 slots, `stateId` 1, title
`container.crafting` with no style or args, no block entity anywhere on the
path) and the insertion point is the `Used::Consumed` arm of
`handle_use_item_on` in `world_send.rs`.

#### Nulls and traps, so nobody pays for them twice

* **`data/vanilla/registries.bin` does not contain `minecraft:entity_type`
  and never will.** Only datapack-driven registries are synced to a client;
  built-in ones are compiled into it. Resolving kind ids against the capture
  produced a fully-written tracker that sent absolutely nothing. Ids now come
  from `ci/dump-entity-types.sh` out of vanilla's registry report.
* **`minecraft:move_entity_rot` is 56, not 55.**
  `move_minecart_along_track` sits between it and `pos_rot`.
* **`add_entity` writes `xRot` before `yRot`; `move_entity_pos_rot` writes
  `yRot` before `xRot`.** The wire is not self-consistent; neither order can
  be inferred from the other.
* **`Entity.getEyeY()` widens a `float`.** `PLAYER_EYE_HEIGHT` is
  `1.6200000047683716`, not `1.62`; the difference put a thrown item 4.8e-9
  of a block out. Caught only because `gameplay-unstable.toml` had written
  vanilla's exact recorded position down.
* **`ServerEntity.tickCount++` is outside the `updateInterval` gate.** Inside
  it, a player's heartbeat halves to one per 120 ticks and looks fine.
* **`updatePlayer`'s range test is horizontal, `<=`, and clamped by the
  *player's* view distance**, not the entity type's.
* **`Level.addFreshEntity` announces synchronously.**
  `ServerLevel$EntityCallbacks.onTrackingStart` opens with
  `getChunkSource().addEntity(entity)` and `ChunkMap.addEntity` calls
  `updatePlayers` before returning. Unlike `ChunkHolder.blockChanged`, there
  is no deferral. I guessed the opposite by analogy and the bytecode refuted
  it.
* **A thrown item does not fall.** `ItemEntity.tick` is not ported —
  deliberately an absence, not an approximation, because faking the fall needs
  a collision system and forecloses `Entity.move`'s swept AABB.

#### Next item, and what closes it

**`070-sand-falls-when-unsupported`: the falling-block entity.** It is
`diverge` today with `we never sent: add_entity` against vanilla's
`kind_id 51`, it is not declared unstable, and the tracker it needs now
exists — so it is the one remaining check whose `match` is both reachable and
entity-shaped. `FallingBlockEntity` needs `Block.tick` -> `checkFallable`,
the entity's own gravity tick, and the landing that turns it back into a
block, so it also drags in the first real `Entity.move`.

It closes when the full gate reports `sand-falls-when-unsupported` as `match`
with the declared count at 30 and every other verdict unchanged.

##### The spawn half, read from the jar 2026-08-04 — do not re-derive it

    javap -p -c -constants ... net.minecraft.world.level.block.FallingBlock \
                               net.minecraft.world.entity.item.FallingBlockEntity

**`FallingBlock.updateShape` is the trigger, and it is why the extraction is
blind here.** It schedules a tick and then delegates to `Block.updateShape`,
which returns the state *unchanged*:

    scheduleTick(pos, this, getDelayAfterPlace());   // getDelayAfterPlace() == 2
    return super.updateShape(...);                   // same state

So `ShapeGolden` sees no state change and emits no row — `update_shape.json`
has zero sand rows — while the entire behaviour is the **side effect**. This
is the same shape as `ObserverBlock`, exactly as the diverge map said, and it
means 070 needs a hole in the extraction filled, not a new mechanism. This
server already has scheduled ticks (`crate::ticks`), so both halves of the
trigger are within reach of existing machinery.

    FallingBlock.tick(state, level, pos, random):
        if (!isFree(level.getBlockState(pos.below())) || pos.getY() < level.getMinY())
            return;
        FallingBlockEntity.fall(level, pos, state);

    FallingBlock.isFree(state) =
        state.isAir() || state.is(BlockTags.FIRE) || state.liquid()
        || state.canBeReplaced()

    FallingBlockEntity.fall(level, pos, state):
        pos'  = (pos.getX() + 0.5, pos.getY(), pos.getZ() + 0.5)
        state' = state.hasProperty(WATERLOGGED) ? state.setValue(WATERLOGGED, false) : state
        level.setBlock(pos, state.getFluidState().createLegacyBlock(), 3)
        ... addFreshEntity

`x + 0.5, y, z + 0.5` is confirmed against the gate's own recording of
vanilla: `add_entity at [1.5, 1.0, 0.5]` for a sand block at (1, 1, 0).

**`add_entity`'s `data` field is NOT zero for a falling block.**
`FallingBlockEntity.getAddEntityPacket` uses the *three*-argument
`ClientboundAddEntityPacket` constructor with `data = Block.getId(blockState)`
— the block state id. Every other entity this server creates reaches the
two-argument form and gets 0. `crate::entities::Entity` already carries `data`
for exactly this, and `Arrival` already writes it.

**The landing needs `Entity.move` and that is the real cost of this item.**
`FallingBlockEntity.tick` is gravity, a `move(MoverType.SELF, ...)`, and a
landing that writes the block back. `move` resolves a swept AABB against every
intersecting block shape. Do it properly — a floor-finder is a one-way door
and is the reason `ItemEntity.tick` was left out of `crate::dropitem` rather
than approximated.

After that, the menu channel (the table above), which is not entity work and
wants a fresh agent at the area boundary.

**The headline: `neighborChanged` is the top lever and its number is 3 to 5,
not 9. Two of the nine checks a source-only audit put on that path are not on
it at all, and the jar says so.** Do not brief a `neighborChanged` build on 9.

`~/rustmc-heartbeat`, tree at `9911560` plus this branch's doc-only edits,

`5c61672527c08de4236d28da43438fba` at launch). Result **declared 27/61 (22
