#### Group 1 — `neighborChanged` is not ported: SEVEN checks, not nine

Confirmed against the pinned jar, `javap -p` on
`oracle-work/vanilla-26.2/versions/26.2/server-26.2.jar`: the block that has to
react overrides `neighborChanged` in every one of these seven.
`RedStoneWireBlock`, `RedstoneLampBlock`, `RedstoneTorchBlock` (which
`RedstoneWallTorchBlock` extends), `DiodeBlock` (which `RepeaterBlock`
extends), `PistonBaseBlock`.

| check | first differing observation | what it needs beyond `neighborChanged` |
|---|---|---|
| `100` redstone-torch-powers-wire | vanilla `section_blocks_update` carries wire `power=15`/`power=14` **and** the torch; ours a bare `block_update` for the torch at `[3,0,0]` | nothing — wire strength calculation is part of the same build |
| `360` a-lever-lights-a-lamp | vanilla `section_blocks_update` carries `redstone_lamp[lit=true]` + `lever[powered=true]`; ours a bare `block_update` for the lever | nothing; lamp-on is immediate, only lamp-*off* schedules |
| `370` wire-power-falls-off-with-distance | vanilla `section_blocks_update` carries wire 14/13/15 + the redstone block; ours a bare `block_update` for the redstone block | nothing |
| `400` a-redstone-torch-turns-off | observations 0–3 identical; vanilla's 5th is `redstone_wall_torch[facing=east,lit=false]`, **ours said nothing more** | a `RedstoneTorchBlock.tick` port — see below |
| `410` a-repeater-delays-the-signal | observations 0–7 identical, `DELAY` cycling already matches; vanilla's 9th is a `section_blocks_update` with `repeater[powered=true]` + wire `power=15`, **ours said nothing more** | a `DiodeBlock.tick` port |
| `380` a-piston-extends-when-powered | observations 0–2 identical; vanilla's 4th is `block_event(at=[1,0,0], b0=0, b1=2, block=138)`, ours is the ack | **a `block_event` producer** — a kind this server has never sent |
| `390` a-piston-pushes-the-block-in-front | same `block_event` as 380 | `block_event` **plus** `MovingPistonBlock` and a `PistonMovingBlockEntity` — and there are no block entities at all |

**So the lever's real number.** `100`, `360` and `370` are cleared by the
`neighborChanged` build itself: the entire remaining gap is a redstone state
change arriving in a `section_blocks_update`, a packet this server already
produces (140 sends one). `400` and `410` are each **one observation** from
green and need a hand-ported `tick` on top: `crates/rustmc-server/src/ticks.rs`
already runs vanilla's `DRAIN_ORDER` queue off the clock, but only `CoralBlock`
and `ButtonBlock` have behaviours, because `Block.tick` takes a `ServerLevel`
(a class, not an interface) and the `Proxy` trick that made
`getStateForPlacement` and `updateShape` extractable does not work on it.
`380`/`390` are not reachable from this build at all.

**3 certain, 5 with two `tick` ports, never 9.**

#### The two that fell out of Group 1, and why the doc comment made them look alike

Neither `ObserverBlock` nor `FallingBlock` overrides `neighborChanged`. Read
with `javap -c` from the pinned jar:

```text
  ObserverBlock.updateShape:  if (FACING == direction && !POWERED) startSignal(...)
                              return super.updateShape(...)
  FallingBlock.updateShape:   scheduleTick(pos, this, getDelayAfterPlace())
                              return super.updateShape(...)
```

Both hang their behaviour off `updateShape` — **the path this server does
implement** — as a side effect that returns the block's own state. So
`ShapeGolden`'s discovery pass, which drops "a pair whose answer is never
anything but itself", cannot see them: `data/vanilla/update_shape.json` has
**0 `minecraft:observer` rows and 0 `minecraft:sand` rows**.

* `440` an-observer-pulses — observations 0–3 identical, then vanilla sends
  `observer[powered=true]` and `observer[powered=false]` and ours sends
  nothing. Needs the shape-side-effect schedule plus an `ObserverBlock.tick`.
  **`neighborChanged` clears nothing here**, and this check was one of the
  three called "closest to green" on the redstone path.
* `070` sand-falls-when-unsupported — ours emits the support's removal and
  **nothing else**: 2 observations against vanilla's 10. Needs the same
  schedule, plus `add_entity`, which no code in this server sends.

#### `140-fences-connect-to-each-other` is not a check that could not fail

The open question was whether it is finding 15 — a check too weak to fail —
since it cited the same "connective, not carried" comment as four diverging
checks and no fence-specific code exists. **It is not.** Its four projected
observations are the clicked-block resync, the place-target resync, the ack,
and **one informative observation**, which is exactly the connective one:

```text
  section_blocks_update at [2,0,0] carrying
    [2,0,0] oak_fence[...,west=true]     the fence just placed
    [1,0,0] oak_fence[east=true,...]     the fence nobody clicked
  identical on both servers, byte for byte
```

Had the existing fence not been rewritten, that observation would carry one
block instead of two. The check discriminates and this server passes it.

The mechanism the sweep missed is not code, it is the **extraction**:
`update_shape.json` carries **all 128 `oak_fence` (state, direction) pairs and
zero `oak_stairs` pairs**. A fence's join is one boolean per direction, so a
pair answers with the block's own state and exactly one other — which is
`ShapeGolden`'s *emission* rule, not its refusal rule. A stair's corner has
four alternatives and lands in `connective` (11,491 pairs) and is dropped. The
doc comment offering "a fence choosing which way to join" as an example of what
is not carried was **wrong by its own stated rule**, and it cost an audit a
whole group. Corrected on `ShapeTable`; `ShapeGolden.java`'s identical wrong
example is deliberately left for the next regeneration, because its digest is
part of the table's provenance stamp and editing it marks the table STALE.

#### `450` is Group 2, resolved — it was left as a tie

`redstone-wire-climbs-the-block-beside-it` was placed in Group 2 "at low
confidence" with Group 1 flagged as the alternative. The trace settles it: the
first difference is the placed dust's own connection shape at **`power=0` on
both sides**, so no signal exists yet to propagate.

```text
  vanilla  redstone_wire[east=side,north=none,power=0,south=none,west=side]
  ours     redstone_wire[east=side,north=side,power=0,south=side,west=side]
```

Vanilla then also rewrites the neighbouring dust to `east=up` — the climb — in
a `section_blocks_update` we never send. `placement.rs:62-67` names redstone by
name in its 195 neighbour-sensitive blocks; the table also holds 1,296
`redstone_wire` rows. I have **not** separated which of the two produced the
wrong answer, and say so rather than picking. Either way it is Group 2.

#### `270`'s `about` misdescribed its own failure, and the correction is bigger than the old map said

`sign-takes-a-sixteenth-of-a-turn` matches on the sixteenth of a turn:
`rotation=9` on both sides at yaw 22.5, and `460`'s yaw 0 gives `rotation=8` on
both — the rule verified at two different yaws. The old note said the residue
was `block_entity_data` + `open_sign_editor`. **The trace shows a third
difference and it is an ordinary one:** vanilla sends an extra `block_update`
at the sign's position *ahead of* `handleUseItemOn`'s two forced resyncs, which
a plain stone placement does not (`020-place-block` matches at four
observations; the sign is 7 against our 4). So deleting the two sign-specific
kinds from `observe` would **not** make this check match. Both `about` fields
are rewritten to say what the check measures rather than what it is named for.

#### Groups 3 to 6 stand, now with trace evidence rather than inference

| check | first differing observation |
|---|---|
| `170` slab-stacks-into-a-double-slab | vanilla `oak_slab[type=double]`, ours `oak_slab[type=bottom]` |
| `250` snow-layers-stack | vanilla `snow[layers=2]`, ours `snow[layers=1]` |
| `310` hoe-turns-grass-into-farmland | vanilla `farmland[moisture=0]`, ours `grass_block` — at the same position, in the forced resync |
| `320` flint-and-steel-lights-a-fire | vanilla `fire[age=0,...]` at `[2,1,0]`, ours `air` |
| `420` a-comparator-switches-to-subtract-mode | `MODE` matches; vanilla's 5th is a `sound`, ours is the next `block_update` — one kind, as recorded |
| `430` a-note-block-retunes-when-right-clicked | **content, not just missing kinds**: vanilla `note_block[instrument=harp,...]`, ours `note_block[instrument=basedrum,...]` at observation 0, *plus* the missing `block_event` and `sound` |
| `180` stairs-make-a-corner-when-two-meet | vanilla `section_blocks_update` rewrites the first stair to `shape=outer_left`; ours a bare `block_update` for the new stair |
| `240` chest-pairs-with-its-neighbour | vanilla `chest[type=right]`, ours `chest[type=single]` — the *placed* chest, so the placement half fails first |
| `300` rail-curves-towards-its-neighbour | vanilla `section_blocks_update` bends the old rail to `shape=south_west`; ours a bare `block_update` |
| `200` ladder-hangs-off-the-wall-behind-it | vanilla `ladder[facing=west]`, ours `air` — we place nothing at all |
| `460` placing-a-sign-opens-its-editor | same as `270` |

**`430` is a new finding and was not in the old map.** It was recorded as
"missing `block_event` and `sound`". The trace's *first* difference is neither
— it is at observation 0, in the measured step's own forced resync at
`[1,0,0]`, which carries the note block's state:

```text
  vanilla  note_block[instrument=harp,note=1,powered=false]
  ours     note_block[instrument=basedrum,note=1,powered=false]
```

`NoteBlock.setInstrument`, `javap -c` from the pinned jar:

```text
  above = getBlockState(pos.above()).instrument()
  if (above.worksAboveNoteBlock()) return setValue(INSTRUMENT, above)
  below = getBlockState(pos.below()).instrument()
  return setValue(INSTRUMENT, below.worksAboveNoteBlock() ? HARP : below)
```

The rig places the note block on the superflat floor, which is
`grass_block` — the trace's own `[1,-1,0]` resync says so. Grass's instrument
takes the `worksAboveNoteBlock` branch, so vanilla answers `HARP`. Ours answers
`BASEDRUM`, the instrument of **stone**, which is not present anywhere in this
scenario. So our placement answer for `note_block` encodes a block from
somewhere other than this world — most likely the extraction grid's own floor,
which `placement.rs:62-67` describes only as "the isolated answer". That is a
sharper defect than the comment admits: the isolated answer is not the block's
default, it is whatever the *dumper's* world had underneath. Not confirmed
against the grid; flagged rather than asserted. Fixing the two missing kinds
alone would leave this check diverging either way.

**`240` likewise refines**: the old map could not tell which half of the
double-chest gap fires first. The trace says the *placed* chest's own `type` is
already wrong, so the placement-time half is what a fix must start with.

### The `gameplay-unstable.toml` churn fix — IMPLEMENTED 2026-08-04

Shipped exactly as the proposal below specified it, point estimate first.
Every entry carries `flaps` and `comparisons`; when a declared entry is not
seen, `ci/selfcheck-aggregate.py` computes `(1 - flaps/comparisons) ** C` and
above alpha = 0.05 prints `UNRESOLVED AT THIS N` **with the arithmetic** and
does not fail. `NEWLY UNSTABLE` is untouched. A missing or nonsensical rate
**fails closed** — `NO POWER TEST POSSIBLE`, exit 1.

Replayed against the saved N = 26 reports of 2026-08-04:

```text
  committed file, reports 2..26   26 runs, declared 7, measured 7,
                                  54/61 reproduced, strict 34/61      exit 0
  committed file, reports 2..12   UNRESOLVED chest-opens-a-screen
                                    (1 - 1/25)^11 = 0.96^11 = 0.638
                                  UNRESOLVED a-bystander-sees-a-chest-open
                                    (1 - 3/25)^11 = 0.88^11 = 0.245   exit 0
                                  (before: two NO LONGER UNSTABLE,    exit 1)
  break-block declared 24/25      NO LONGER UNSTABLE, 0.04^11 = 4e-16 exit 1
  water-spreads removed           NEWLY UNSTABLE (diverge, 10/11)     exit 1
  chest-opens-a-screen rate gone  NO POWER TEST POSSIBLE              exit 1
```

The full replay table lives in the script's header, next to the code it
describes. **The proposal is kept below verbatim** — it named the Clopper–Pearson
caveat in advance and said to ship the point estimate first, and a proposal
whose stated reasoning survived contact is worth keeping legible.

**The problem, stated as a defect rather than an annoyance.** The chest pair has
gone in and out of that file **four times**. Every one of those readings was
honest and every one was correctly reported. N = 26 settled it: both entries are
real, `chest-opens-a-screen` at 1/25 and `a-bystander-sees-a-chest-open` at
3/25. Nothing about the world was changing — twelve runs could not resolve
either rate, and the instrument reported that inability as a fact about the
file.

**A 1-in-25 event goes unseen in eleven comparisons about 64% of the time**
(`0.96^11 = 0.64`). So the *next* routine N = 12 run is more likely than not to
print `NO LONGER UNSTABLE chest-opens-a-screen` and exit 1 against a file that
is correct. That is a false alarm, it fires on the default configuration, and
**false alarms get silenced** — the failure mode is not a wrong number, it is
somebody deleting a true entry, or worse, learning to ignore this gate.

Note the shape: this is the same defect class as a check that cannot fail,
inverted. A check that cannot fail proves nothing by passing; **a gate that
fires when it has no power to distinguish proves nothing by failing.**

#### The option I would take

**Make "absence is not evidence" mechanical, which is a rule this project
already applies everywhere else.** `Verdict::Vacuous` exists because a negative
result is only evidence if the mechanism was demonstrably live. The same
sentence applies here and is currently enforced by nobody.

1. Give each entry a **machine-readable rate** beside the prose — `flaps = 1`,
   `comparisons = 25` — rather than regexing it back out of `measured`. This is
   the only migration, and it is mechanical across seven entries.
2. In `ci/selfcheck-aggregate.py`, when a declared entry is **not** observed in
   this run, compute the chance of that happening if the declared rate were
   true: `(1 - flaps/comparisons) ** C`, where `C` is this run's comparison
   count.
   * Above a threshold (α = 0.05 to start): print
     `UNRESOLVED AT THIS N — declared 1/25, this run had 11 comparisons, a true
     rate would be missed 64% of the time` and **do not fail**.
   * At or below it: print `NO LONGER UNSTABLE` and fail, exactly as now.
3. **The `NEWLY UNSTABLE` direction is unchanged.** Seeing a flap is positive
   evidence at any N; only absence needs a power test.

What this buys: N = 12 becomes a usable default again — it still catches every
high-rate regression, which is what it has power for — while a rare entry
survives a run too small to see it, and the message says *why* rather than
leaving a reader to infer it. The gate keeps failing wherever it can actually
discriminate.

#### What I would not do, and why

* **Always run N = 26.** Four and a half hours per run makes the selfcheck
  something nobody runs, which is a worse silencing than the one being fixed.
* **Drop set-equality in the `NO LONGER` direction.** That removes the
  staleness catch entirely, including where it has full power — a 25/25 entry
  that stops reproducing is exactly the instrument regression this file was
  written to surface.
* **Widen `settle_ms` on the two chest checks to dodge the boundary.** It
  treats the symptom, and the 250 ms repeat is a real vanilla mechanism the
  corpus should be able to observe.

**One caveat to adjudicate.** `flaps/comparisons` is a point estimate from a
small sample and is itself uncertain — 1/25 could be a true rate anywhere from
about 0.1% to 17%. The conservative version uses the upper Clopper–Pearson
bound, which makes the script slower to declare staleness. I would ship the
point estimate first because it is one line and already removes the observed
failure, and revisit only if a real stale entry survives it.

### Branch `vacuous-and-motion`, off `adb7cee` — MERGED 2026-08-04 as `92f1658`

**The vacuous and the `set_entity_motion` residual are ONE fact, and the
second exemption is dead without being measured. It would have removed a real
signal to hide a bound this harness does not apply.**

#### The vacuous is `520-a-standing-player-is-rebroadcast-on-a-timer`

Two corpus runs on the same tree at `adb7cee`, declared byte-identical:

```text
  08:11  ~/rustmc-heartbeat  strict 17/61  (39 diverge, 5 absent, 0 vacuous)
  08:42  ~/rustmc-gate       strict 16/61  (40 diverge, 4 absent, 1 vacuous)
```

Exactly two checks moved and **one cause moved both**:

```text
  coral-dries-out-unprompted                    strict  match  -> diverge
  a-standing-player-is-rebroadcast-on-a-timer   strict  absent -> vacuous
```

Scenario 520, observer stream, straight out of the two recordings:

```text
  08:11  4 heartbeats + 12 set_entity_motion  -> strict ref non-empty -> absent
  08:42  2 heartbeats +  0 set_entity_motion  -> strict ref EMPTY     -> vacuous
  rustmc                                   0  in both
```

`project` drops `move_entity_heartbeat` whenever `kinds` is `None`, and strict
passes `None`. **The exemption did not create instability. It removed the
packet that was silently guaranteeing every strict window was non-empty**, and
what was underneath became visible in a bucket nothing had reached before.

#### Those 12 packets are a dropped item from check 500, twenty checks earlier

`add_entity kind_id 71` in `500-dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor`. The
item is still alive during 520 and supplies **12 of 520's 12** non-heartbeat
observations. In the other run it supplies **34 of coral's 42**. That is the
"0 or 34, half the runs each" signature: not a flapping predicate — the
lifetime of a leftover entity.

`ci/t2-gameplay-subset.sh 500-… 520-…` reproduces it deterministically in two
checks and one minute.

#### The mechanism, from bytecode, and it is not the one the brief expected

`ServerEntity.sendChanges`, offset 873, is
`needsSync || trackDelta || (entity instanceof LivingEntity && isFallFlying())`
around the `distanceToSqr(lastSentMovement) > 1.0E-7 ||
(d > 0 && lengthSqr == 0)` predicate. Both terms were checked:

* `EntityType.trackDeltas()` is an **exclusion** list and `PLAYER` is on it,
  with `LLAMA_SPIT`, `WITHER`, `BAT`, both item frames, `LEASH_KNOT`,
  `PAINTING`, `END_CRYSTAL`, `EVOKER_FANGS`. So `trackDelta` is **false for a
  player** and true for a dropped item.
* `Entity.needsSync` is written `true` in exactly five places —
  `Entity.push(DDD)`, `Entity.load`, `LivingEntity.knockback`,
  `LivingEntity.jumpFromGround`, `LivingEntity.startSleeping` — and cleared at
  the end of every gated `sendChanges` (offset 1189), so it is a one-tick
  pulse, not a latch.

**A standing harness player therefore cannot emit `set_entity_motion` at all**,
and measurement agrees: a clean 520 recording contains zero. Every one of these
packets is about an *item*, where `trackDelta` is true and the predicate alone
decides. Decoded, the item alternates
`v = (0, -0.12000244155527073, 0)` with `v = (0, 0, 0)` once a second forever —
one tick of gravity, then the stop packet through the `d > 0 && lengthSqr == 0`
clause.

#### The actual defect: `near()` cannot bound an entity observation

`compare::near` keeps **any observation with no `at` field**. Twenty recorded
kinds never carry one:

```text
  block_changed_ack  chat  container_set_content  container_set_slot
  entity_event  move_entity  move_entity_heartbeat  open_screen
  remove_entities  set_entity_data  set_entity_motion  set_equipment
  take_item_entity  + the six still-undecoded packet:0x.. kinds
```

Workspaces are 32 blocks apart and `within` defaults to 16 — and
`scenario::within`'s own docstring says 16 is *"tight enough to exclude the
neighbouring workspace 32 blocks away"*. That is the intent. It cannot be
delivered for entity packets, because an entity's position is not on them,
while an item's client tracking range easily covers the neighbour. So a
neighbouring scenario's entity lands in every later scenario's strict
projection, unbounded, and its lifetime is a race.

**This is why an entity-tracking kind is the measured differing kind in so
many unrelated checks.** It is one bound that does not apply, not ten separate
mechanisms.

#### Why the second exemption must not ship

Filtering `set_entity_motion` the way the heartbeat was filtered would delete a
real signal — item and mob physics, a mechanism this server has to reproduce —
to paper over a projection bound. There is no "vanilla already said no" tell
here: `sendChanges` sent the packet *because* the velocity really changed. It
would be the fifteenth check that cannot fail, and this branch would have
authored it.

#### MEASURED — the registered floor was missed and prediction 7 was refuted

Quantity A, N = 12, re-aggregated from the twelve recordings already on disk in
`~/rustmc-heartbeat/oracle-work/gameplay-selfcheck/`. **No server time**: the
same bytes the 35/60 came from.

```text
  baseline  (adb7cee reports, same aggregator)  declared 53/60   strict 35/60
  treatment (same recordings, new binary)       declared 54/60   strict 37/60
```

**Prediction 5 FAILED.** Floor was >= 42 of 60; measured **37**. The refutation
line of <= 36 was not crossed, so the mechanism is real and is *not* the
dominant cause of strict irreproducibility. Name by name:

```text
  FIXED     coral-dries-out-unprompted                      11/11 -> 0
  FIXED     a-lever-lights-a-lamp                            7/11 -> 0
  IMPROVED  swapping-to-the-offhand-shows-on-both-channels    9/11 -> 4/11
  BROKEN    (none)
```

**Prediction 6 half refuted.** Coral yes. `520` no — and the reason is not
instability: with the leak gone its strict projection is **legitimately
empty**, because its only content is heartbeats and strict drops those by
design. It is `vacuous` in every run. A permanently-vacuous check can never be
strict-reproducible, so it is a **fixed −1 on the strict score forever**, not a
flap. `selfcheck-aggregate.py` counts any non-`match` as unstable and cannot
tell those apart.

**Prediction 7 REFUTED, twice, in opposite directions — and it is the result
that mattered.**

1. The first version seeded the position table from **any** positioned packet.
   Measured: `520`'s *declared* verdict went `vacuous`, which is gate-red. The
   two clients get an `entity_position` inside a window, and then
   `record::run_one` walks them 32 blocks to the next workspace **outside any
   measured window** — the trace holds no packet saying they moved. Their
   placement went stale by exactly one spacing and they were bounded out of
   the following scenario. Corrected: **only `add_entity` may seed the
   table.** A player is never announced by `add_entity` inside a window
   because it joined at login, so every client stays unplaced and unbounded.
2. The corrected version then moves declared the *other* way: `520` becomes
   declared-**stable**, 10/11 -> 0/11, so the declared-unstable set goes 7 -> 6
   and `ci/checks/gameplay-unstable.toml` is stale.

**`520`'s declared instability was the leak too.** The flapping count was the
leaked *item's* heartbeats, not the players'. The argument written on that
check — "a count over a fixed window holds floor(L/P) or ceil(L/P), so it is
structurally unstable rather than mistuned" — is true in general and was about
the wrong entity. Left standing beside its refutation, as its own file already
does with the previous one.

**`gameplay-unstable.toml` is NOT edited on this branch.** Dropping 520 from it
is a declared movement and the owner reserved those; the selfcheck exits 1
until it is done, and that is the decision to take, not to take quietly.

#### SUPERSEDED — quantity A is 34 of 61 at N = 26, and that is not a regression

The figures below are all **N = 12**. The published ceiling is now
**34 of 61 at N = 26**, measured once on merged `main` `92f1658`.

A check counts as reproduced only if it matched in *every* comparison, so
quantity A is **monotonically non-increasing in N by construction** — 25
comparisons give a flaky check more than twice the opportunity to flap that 11
do. **37 of 60 at N = 12 was optimistic by construction; 34 of 61 supersedes
it because it is better sampled, not because anything got worse.** A quoted
without its N is meaningless. `docs/SERVER.md` carries the sequence and the
60/61 ceiling.

#### WHAT THIS SHIPS ON — and it is not the number

**The hypothesis "the leak is the dominant cause of strict irreproducibility"
is dead and stays dead: 35 -> 37 against a registered floor of 42.** Nothing
here may be read as a strict-recovery win, and a future reader finding 37/60
beside a floor of 42 should be able to see immediately which claim failed.

It ships as **a correctness fix against a documented contract**. `near()` kept
every observation with no `at` field while twenty recorded kinds never carry
one, and `scenario::within`'s own docstring promises exclusion of "the
neighbouring workspace 32 blocks away". That is a plain bug against what the
projection says it does, and it would be one if quantity A had not moved at
all. The 35 -> 37, and `coral-dries-out-unprompted` and `a-lever-lights-a-lamp`

```text

  RECORDED  61 scenario(s), 0 could not be run  (both sides)
```

#### The surviving strict vacuous is the legitimate kind

`a-standing-player-is-rebroadcast-on-a-timer`, and it is **both sides empty**,

only observations are heartbeats, which strict drops by design, and the twelve

#### Can 520 still fail? Yes, on the axis that is gated

Written onto the check itself, where the next person will find it.

```text
  declared  absent    vanilla 2, this server 0   — CAN fail, IS failing
  strict    vacuous   both projections empty     — can never be scored
```

Declared is the gated axis and is where the exemption's guard lives. It moves
to `match` when `ServerEntity`'s 60-tick re-broadcast lands and sends the same
count, to `diverge` on the wrong payload or count, and stays `absent` while we
send nothing. **And it is stronger than the earlier "presence, never
correctness" reading**: the 10/11 declared instability was the leaked item's
heartbeats, not the players', so at 0/11 it now discriminates the *count*.
Held at arm's length as one N = 12 sample, on this file's own standing caveat.

Strict can never score it, and `selfcheck-aggregate.py` cannot tell a
permanently vacuous check from a flapping one, so it costs quantity A a fixed
1. Strict is a diagnostic and is not gated, so the guard does not depend on it.

#### Rule 7, immediately: a denominator that moved

The first re-aggregation read **37/61** with a spurious
`NEWLY UNSTABLE clicking-the-top-of-a-door-opens-the-bottom (error, 11/11)`.
The recordings hold **60** scenarios; the 61st check was added to the tree
after they were taken, so comparing with the current check list scores a
scenario that is not in the traces as `error`. Only the 60 the recordings
contain are comparable to 35/60. Both figures above use exactly those 60.

#### `Vacuous` had the `Inert` hole, in one direction only — closed

`verdict_for` chose `Vacuous` from `reference.is_empty()` alone, which is the
shape of finding 13. It pre-empted a one-sided `Diverge`: **a subject that
spoke where the reference was silent** was reported as a broken check. Narrower
than `Inert`'s, which overwrote two-sided divergences after the fact — an
empty reference can never coexist with a two-sided `Diverge`, and never with

Measured inert on this corpus before landing: no declared projection has an

### Branch `move-entity-heartbeat`, off `4b14811` — IN PROGRESS 2026-08-04

Four items. **Two of the four briefs' premises were refuted by measurement**,
which is the usual rate here and both refutations are the useful part.

**Item 1 — the `move_entity` exemption. MEASURED: strict self-reproduction
0 of 55 -> 35 of 60.**

```text
  ./ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh          # ends in ci/selfcheck-aggregate.py
  12 runs, declared 7, measured 7, 53/60 reproduced
  12 runs, strict reproduced 35/60       (quantity A, was 0 of 55)
```

**Quantity A is vanilla against ITSELF**, matching under strict in all eleven
comparisons. It is not a parity claim and nothing published may cite it as
one. Predicted >= 30 of 60 with a refutation line at 9 of 60, both registered
in `d08cdab` before the run.

Predictions: **1 confirmed (A), 3 confirmed (A), 4 REFUTED (A)**, 2 is a
different quantity and is settled by the corpus run below. Prediction 4 said
`520` would not be unstable; it measured **10 of 11, declared**. The argument
that failed was "a window of exactly two periods holds two events for every
phase", which is true only of an exactly periodic source — measured
inter-arrivals were 2930 and 3006 ms. A count over a fixed window holds
floor(L/P) or ceil(L/P) with P(ceil) = frac(L/P), so it is structurally
unstable rather than mistuned and no retuning was attempted. It is declared at
its rate. It still meets its condition: a server sending no heartbeat scores
`absent`, never `match`, so presence stays detectable — the check discriminates
PRESENCE and not CORRECTNESS, and that is written on it.

**`chest-opens-a-screen` also left the unstable file and that is NOT ours** —
it names no entity kind, so the exemption cannot reach it. Third consecutive
swap of the chest pair on one 250 ms `block_event` cadence.

**The mechanism, unchanged from what was written before the run.** The mechanism
is confirmed from bytecode: `ServerEntity.sendChanges` computes
`moved = positionCodec.delta(trackingPosition()).lengthSqr() >= 7.62939453125E-6`
(`ldc2_w; dcmpl; iflt`, so `>=`, and the constant is exactly 2⁻¹⁷) and
`sendPos = moved || tickCount % 60 == 0`. Wire deltas are `encodeX/Y/Z`, the
position in 1/4096 of a block truncated to `short`, so vanilla's own movement
test in wire units is the integer predicate `dx² + dy² + dz² >= 128`.
`trace::decode` files a sub-threshold packet as `move_entity_heartbeat`;
`compare::project` drops that kind unless a check names it in `observe`.

Two things measured before the big run, on the Threadripper in
`~/rustmc-heartbeat`, `ci/t2-gameplay-subset.sh 520-… 080-…`:

```text
  vanilla's heartbeat carries  d = [0, 0, 0]        exactly zero movement
  a real 4-block walk carries  d = [16384, 0, 0]    4 * 4096, 181x the boundary
```

The boundary is √128 = 11.31 wire units = **0.00276 of a block**. Real
movement is not near it and cannot be, because vanilla would not have sent the
packet.

**The exemption does not ship alone, and `520-a-standing-player-is-rebroadcast-on-a-timer`
is the reason it is allowed to.** Dropping the heartbeat everywhere would make
a server that never sends it indistinguishable from vanilla under every check
— a check that cannot fail, manufactured by our own fix. 520 names the kind,
waits 6000 ms and expects two heartbeats. **The window is two periods because
the count of multiples of P in a half-open window of length exactly 2P is two
for every phase** — that, and not "long enough to see one", is what makes it
stable. Confirmed live and red on first observation: `absent`, vanilla two,
ours nothing, because this tree has no `MOVE_ENTITY_POS` sender at all.

The registered prediction is in commit `d08cdab` and is not repeated here.
Its refutation threshold is **strict below 9 of 60**, at which point the
exemption is wrong and does not ship.

**Item 2 — the door's `dir=UP` row. The brief's reason it was unreachable is
refuted, and it is reachable today.** `DoorBlock.playerWillDestroy` calls
`preventDropFromBottomPart` only under
`preventsBlockDrops() || !hasCorrectToolForDrops(state)`; `preventsBlockDrops`
is `abilities.instabuild` and an oak door does not
`requiresCorrectToolForDrops`, so **that routing is creative-only** and a
survival dig skips it. And `preventDropFromBottomPart` does not bypass the
shape update anyway — it writes `pos.below()` at flag **35**, bit 16 clear, so
`updateNeighbourShapes` runs. That is how 132 reaches the typed rule.

So `half=upper, dir=DOWN` is covered three times over (260 at flag 3, 132 at
flag 35, 280 at flag 10) and the single untested arm is `half=lower, dir=UP`.
`DoorBlock.setOpen` is `Level.setBlock(pos, …, 10)` — one position, verified
`bipush 10` — so right-clicking the UPPER half leaves the lower half only
`updateShape` to learn from. That is check 280 with the click moved one block
up, and it needs no new step kind, no survival mode and no operator:
`281-clicking-the-top-of-a-door-opens-the-bottom`.

**Nulls, from bytecode, so nobody re-runs them.** A **piston** cannot reach it
(a door is `PushReaction.DESTROY`, removed via `getToDestroy()` at flag 18,
bit 16 SET). A **fluid** cannot (`canHoldAnyFluid` carries an explicit
`instanceof DoorBlock` exclusion, so a fluid never replaces a door). An
**explosion** reaches it but draws from `level.random` and would flap.
**`/setblock` and `/fill`** reach it at flags 258 and 256 — but `strict` sets
816, bit 16 SET, and neither is usable because the harness ops nobody.

**Item 3 — DATA_ITEM. The cost argument is empty on both sides; the real
question is different.** `set_entity_data` is already decoded and its whole
payload already sits in the `rest` digest, compared bit-exactly, so covering
it costs one string in one `observe` list. But adding it to 350 buys nothing:
350 is declared unstable because `popResource` scatters the drop by
`Mth.nextDouble(random, -0.25, 0.25)` per axis and that rides `add_entity`,
which 350 observes — **a check that cannot pass cannot be made to cover
more.** Covering DATA_ITEM therefore needs a new check observing
`set_entity_data` *without* `add_entity` or `set_entity_motion`, and whether
that could be stable is a question about the kind, which the selfcheck's own
reports cannot answer because they are scoped to each check's `observe` list.
`ci/selfcheck-kind-stability.py` answers it from the twelve recordings already
being paid for, and the answer is a **confirmed positive: cover it.**

```text
  ci/selfcheck-kind-stability.py set_entity_data \
      oracle-work/gameplay-selfcheck/r[0-9]*.json

  IDENTICAL IN ALL 12   torch-falls-with-its-support             4 obs each
  IDENTICAL IN ALL 12   sand-falls-when-unsupported              4 obs each
  IDENTICAL IN ALL 12   a-dropped-item-goes-into-your-inventory  4 obs each
  IDENTICAL IN ALL 12   dropping-an-item-throws-it-on-the-floor  4 obs each
  DIFFERS               spawn-egg-makes-a-mob   (counts {4: 12}, payload)
```

Every scenario carrying an **item or falling-block** entity reproduces
`set_entity_data` bit for bit across twelve cold vanilla servers, digest
included. The single exception is a **mob**, at an identical count, so it is
the mob's synched data and not an item's. So a new check observing
`set_entity_data` and not `add_entity`/`set_entity_motion` would be stable, and
it costs one string in one `observe` list. **Not built here** — it is a new
check and this branch is already carrying two.



There is a real coupling with item 1 here and it should be stated rather than
discovered later: **`strict` already covers DATA_ITEM bit-exactly**, because
strict passes no kind filter. That coverage was worth nothing while vanilla
reproduced itself under strict on 0 of 55. If item 1 makes strict a usable
diagnostic, this blind spot is closed by construction and a new declared check
buys only readability.

**Item 4 — survival mining. SCOPED, NOT BUILT. The premise is confirmed and
the blocker is not the one the brief names.**

Confirmed: `ServerPlayerGameMode.handleBlockBreakAction` START does
`if (abilities.instabuild) { destroyAndAck(pos, seq, "creative destroy");
return; }` at offset 171–194, and `isDestroyingBlock = true` /
`destroyPos = pos` are assigned at offsets 429–439 — **after** that return. So
in creative `destroyPos` is never set, STOP's `pos.equals(destroyPos)` is
false, and a `finish_dig` check is `inert` by construction. Exactly as briefed.

The STOP path, read out in full because it changes the cost estimate:

```text
  elapsed  = gameTicks - destroyProgressStart
  progress = state.getDestroyProgress(player, level, pos) * (elapsed + 1)
  if (progress >= 0.7f)  -> destroyBlockProgress(id, pos, -1); destroyAndAck
  else if (!hasDelayedDestroy) -> hasDelayedDestroy = true, finish later in tick()
```

**The threshold is 0.7, not 1.0**, and a client that finishes early is
*delayed*, not rejected. So the rig needs no tick-accurate timing — a `wait`
step of a couple of seconds is enough, and `Step::Wait` already exists. Timing
is not the blocker.

**The blocker is that the corpus cannot put an item in a survival player's
hand.** `Step::Hold` sends `SET_CREATIVE_MODE_SLOT` (`client.rs:677`), and
`handleSetCreativeModeSlot` opens with `if (player.hasInfiniteMaterials())`
and jumps the entire body when false. In survival it is a **silent no-op** —
the same shape as the `gamerule` that was refused for a week without anyone
reading the reply. Every check in the corpus uses `hold`, so this is a
rig-wide dependency and not a per-scenario flag. `status.rs` already says so
in its own comment: `GAME_TYPE == CREATIVE` is hard-coded partly because
creative is the only way a client can hold a block to place.

What it would cost, cheapest ordering, harness first:

```text
  RIG   a second vanilla instance booted survival, or ops.json + a
        `/gamemode` step; setup steps stay creative (their observations are
        discarded) and the measured step runs survival. Small, but it is a
        SUBSTRATE change — done globally it re-baselines all 61 checks.
  US    survival gamemode at all: abilities.instabuild off, blockActionRestricted
  US    a NEW generated table — no `destroySpeed`/`requiresCorrectToolForDrops`
        exists anywhere in `data/vanilla` today; `block_props.json`'s generator
        already walks every state and is the natural home
  US    tool speeds: 26.2 carries them in the `minecraft:tool` data component
        as per-block-set rules, so an item-component dump as well
  US    `getDestroyProgress` and every modifier on it — correct tool, efficiency,
        haste/mining fatigue, in-water without aqua affinity (/5), airborne (/5)
  US    `ServerPlayerGameMode.tick`, `incrementDestroyProgress`,
        `destroyProgressStart`, `gameTicks`, `lastSentState`, the
        `hasDelayedDestroy`/`delayedDestroyPos`/`delayedTickStart` triple
  US    `ClientboundBlockDestructionPacket` (id 5), the 0..9 crack stages
  US    LOOT TABLES, if any check watches what the break drops — the largest
        single piece here by a wide margin
```

**Two things bound the payoff and both argue for deferring it.** A survival
break drops an item through `popResource`, which is randomised, so any
survival check that watches the drop is unstable in principle exactly like 350
and 500 — the only stable survival checks observe `block_update`,
`block_changed_ack` and `block_destruction`, which means **loot tables buy no
checkable coverage** and can be cut from the estimate entirely. And nothing
above is on the path to anything a player notices sooner: it buys `finish_dig`
and the crack animation, against `neighborChanged`, block entities and
persistence still being absent.

### Prediction 2 settled (quantity C) — verified check by check, not by totals

`./ci/t2-gameplay.sh` on the branch, Threadripper `~/rustmc-heartbeat`,
2026-08-04, log `corpus-gate.log`:

```text
  RECORDED  61 scenario(s), 0 could not be run   (vanilla and rustmc)
  CORPUS  declared  27/61 match  (22 diverge, 12 absent, 0 vacuous, 0 inert, 0 error)
  CORPUS  strict    17/61 match  (39 diverge,  5 absent, 0 vacuous, 0 inert, 0 error)
  T2-GAMEPLAY GREEN
```

**Totals being consistent is not the same as the claim being true**, so the
verdicts were diffed against `gameplay-baseline.toml` name by name rather than
counted:

```text
  61 outcomes, 61 baseline entries
  disagreements baseline-vs-measured   0
  unlisted   []        in-baseline-but-not-run   []
  clicking-the-top-of-a-door-opens-the-bottom   -> match
  a-standing-player-is-rebroadcast-on-a-timer   -> absent
  pre-existing matches                          26
```

That argument is circular unless no pre-existing baseline entry was edited, so
that was checked too: `git diff 4b14811..HEAD -- ci/checks/gameplay-baseline.toml`
removes **no** non-comment line and adds exactly two `expect` keys. So each of
the 26 pre-existing `match` entries measured `match`, nothing that was
non-match became match, and **the 26 are the same 26 by name** — not merely
the same count. Prediction 2 confirmed.

**Quantity B moved 9/59 -> 17/61 and is not evidence for anything.** It is a
one-run number against a reference that reproduces itself on 35 of 60; the
exemption is tested by A, not by B. Recorded as a floor holding.

**`0 vacuous, 0 inert, 0 error` survived both new checks**, which is the
property that must not regress.

### The instrument trap that nearly cost the N=26 run — Rule 7, again

`pgrep -f 't2-gameplay-selfcheck'` run over ssh **matches its own command
line**, so it reports RUNNING forever. Two waiters and one chained launcher
were built on it; the launcher's `until` loop therefore never exited and
**N = 26 was never started**, while a verification step printed
`N26 RUNNING` and confirmed it. The instrument was matching itself, exactly
like the `pgrep` already listed under Rule 7 in `docs/AGENT-BRIEF.md`.

Caught by asking for the log file rather than the exit status: no
`selfcheck-n26.log` existed. **Use `pgrep -f '[t]2-gameplay-selfcheck'`** — the
bracket makes the pattern match the process without matching the literal text
in the checking command — and confirm from process ids AND log content, never
from a boolean.

### What the remaining 25 strict-unstable checks actually are — MEASURED

Not theorised. `ci/selfcheck-kind-stability.py` over the twelve recordings,
per kind, naming the scenarios each kind fails to reproduce in. **Read the
caveat first:** that script is *unbounded*, while `strict` applies each
scenario's `within` and `observe_from`, so it can name a scenario whose
difference falls outside the box strict looks at. It attributes; it does not
score.

Two undecoded packet ids had to be resolved first, by counting `addPacket`
order in `GameProtocols` and anchoring on three known ids
(`MOVE_ENTITY_POS` 53, `REMOVE_ENTITIES` 77, `SECTION_BLOCKS_UPDATE` 84, all
consistent at `id = n - 2`):

```text
  packet:0x53  =  83   ClientboundRotateHeadPacket
  packet:0x8A  = 138   ClientboundWaypointPacket
```

Both are entity/player tracking. `rotate_head` is sent from
**`ServerEntity.sendChanges`** — the same method as the heartbeat.

```text
  KIND                  scenarios it fails to reproduce in
  set_entity_motion     10   (0 identical)   <- the largest single residual
  rotate_head            6   (0 identical)
  sound                  8   (37 identical)
  add_entity             4   (1 identical)
  block_update           3   (45 identical)
  block_event            2   (3 identical)
  waypoint               2   (1 identical)
  section_blocks_update  1   (24 identical)
  level_event            0   (9 identical)   <- fully reproducible
  set_entity_data        1   (4 identical)   <- see item 3
```

**The brief's grouping of the eleven 11/11 checks as "the tick-packaging
family, not entities" is refuted by the attribution, and in two different
directions.**

* **The pistons are not tick packaging. They are a random sound pitch.**
  `a-piston-extends-when-powered` and `a-piston-pushes-the-block-in-front`
  both differ on `sound` at an *identical* count, `{3: 12}` — three sounds in
  all twelve runs, payload different. Same signature on
  `door-opens-when-right-clicked` `{1: 12}`,
  `flint-and-steel-lights-a-fire` `{1: 12}` and both chest checks. That is
  `playSound`'s pitch argument, drawn from `level.getRandom()`. It is
  unmatchable by anybody, exactly like the spawn yaw — **not** a packaging
  artefact and **not** exemptable.
* **`coral-dries-out-unprompted`, `torch-falls-with-its-support` and
  `redstone-torch-powers-wire` ARE entities**, via `set_entity_motion`, which
  is the opposite of what the grouping assumed.

**Counted: at least 10 of the 25, and 6 of the 11 sitting at 11/11, have an
entity-tracking kind as a measured differing kind.** So the honest answer to
"is there a second exemption to find" is **yes, probably, and it is in the
same method** — but it is not the same shape and must not be assumed to be.

**The reason it cannot be waved through on the heartbeat's argument.** The
heartbeat was exemptable because vanilla's *own* predicate had already
declared the entity did not move; the packet existed only because a counter
wrapped. `set_entity_motion` has no such tell — its gate is
`motion.distanceToSqr(lastSentMovement) > 1.0E-7`, which is a real change to a
real field. Anything done here needs the same bytecode-first treatment the
heartbeat got, and guessing would be the opposite of the method that produced
this result.

What the data does say, and it is a strong hint for whoever takes it:
the failures are **burst-or-nothing**, not off-by-one.

```text
  coral-dries-out-unprompted          counts {0: 6,  34: 6}
  a-lever-lights-a-lamp               counts {0: 5,  10: 1, 12: 6}
  redstone-torch-powers-wire          counts {0: 11, 20: 1}
  a-standing-player-is-rebroadcast    counts {0: 10, 12: 1, 26: 1}
```

Half the runs emit **no** motion packet and half emit thirty-four. A predicate
on a continuously varying quantity does not do that. Something is switching
the whole stream on and off — the first thing to read is the guard at offsets
873–918, `needsSync || trackDelta || (LivingEntity && isFallFlying)`, which
gates the motion block entirely.

**The seven checks at 1 of 11 are not characterisable at this N and should
not be theorised about.** `ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh`'s own header gives the
arithmetic: a 1-in-11 flap is missed by twelve runs about one time in nine.
The chest pair has now swapped membership three runs running to prove it.
**N = 26 is the instrument for that band**, and it is running.

### Cold start: one branch, `oracle-hardening-stack`, off `9098a0b`

Everything here is measured on the Threadripper 2026-08-03. Where a brief's
premise was refuted it says so, and there are four.

Four branches were cut from `9098a0b` **independently** and each gated green on
its own tree. Four greens on four trees is not a green on the thing that
becomes `main`, so they are stacked into one branch and gated once as a unit,
in the order below and for these reasons: the guard first, because it is what
makes every later reading trustworthy; the reduced count last, so the final
baseline lands with its reason attached to it.

```text
  1  ci-gate-hardening    8 commits   the handoff loop; stage 1 had never run
  2  selfcheck-sampling   8           2 runs -> 12, and five undeclared unstables
  3  inert-precedence     7           inert could overwrite a real diverge
  4  timing-and-damage   11           the three duration checks, and a decoder trap
```

**The baseline was not the conflict the stacking was expected to hit.** Only
one of the four touches `ci/checks/gameplay-baseline.toml`, so there was
nothing to reconcile and nothing to regenerate: the tip's baseline is
`timing-and-damage`'s, which is the one carrying the reduced count and its
reason. Four files overlap at all, and exactly one conflicted —
`tools/oracle-runner/src/compare.rs`, where `inert-precedence` and
`timing-and-damage` each appended a test to the same point in the test module.
Both tests kept, in order; the functional hunks (the `Verdict::Match` guard on
the inert override, and `Timing::Bucket` rounding to the nearest multiple) both
auto-merged and are both live at the tip.

**Gated as a unit**, `./ci/handoff.sh oracle-hardening-stack --dry-run` into a
fresh `~/rustmc-stack`, 2026-08-03 19:08–19:34, log
`~/rustmc-private/gates/gate-oracle-hardening-stack-20260803-190807.log`:

```text
  T0 GREEN
  CORPUS  declared  22/55 match   (22 diverge, 11 absent, 0 vacuous, 0 inert, 0 error)
  CORPUS  strict     7/55 match   (44 diverge,  4 absent, 0 vacuous, 0 inert, 0 error)
  T2-GAMEPLAY GREEN
  grep -c "skipping: no vanilla"  ->  0
  GREEN  oracle-hardening-stack — 34 commits, T0+T2 green, 0 skips (dry run, not merged)
```

23 -> **22** is 410 and nothing else: it drops `match` -> `diverge` because the
check now runs the experiment its `about` describes, and 330 and 335 still
`match` with their new 500 ms buckets. **55/55 live in both directions.**

The baseline is **exact**, not merely un-regressed: replaying the run's
`report.json` against `gameplay-baseline.toml` by verdict rank gives 55
entries, 55 outcomes, **none ahead, none behind, none unlisted.** Worth
separating from "green", because a ratchet passes a check that has quietly
improved and would go on passing it — so "nothing regressed" and "the file
describes the server" are two different statements and only the second one is
being made here.

**The guard has now refused the exact artefact that caused the incident.**
`ci/t2-gameplay.sh`'s preflight had never once been pointed at a bad set — it
was proven on constructed cases. Four cases against the real one, in the gated
tree, log `~/rustmc-private/guard-refusal-proof-2026-08-03.log`:

```text
  A  the stale seed exactly as found, unstamped        exit 4   8 of 8 refused
  B  the stale seed wearing this tree's own stamps     exit 4   2 of 8: "changed since it was stamped"
  C  b4613ce9 use_without_item.json dropped into an    exit 4   1 of 8 — the 12/55
     otherwise current, correctly stamped set                   artefact, exact position
  D  the shared seed: current, correct, stamped        exit 4   8 of 8 FOREIGN
  E  control — this tree's own set                     exit 0   8 ok
```

B is the one that matters most and is the least obvious: the same eight
filenames, the same directory layout, **six of the eight byte-identical**, and
the guard names the two that are not. A file-presence check passes all eight of
A's files and all eight of B's. **"Is the file there" was never the question** —
one file was there and wrong, which is how the 12/55 happened.

**The loop had never run its own stage 1.** `ci/handoff.sh`'s `remote()` is
`ssh -n`, which points the remote process's stdin at `/dev/null`, and stage 1
is `remote "bash -s" <<EOF`. The script went into a closed pipe, `bash -s`
read EOF, and the stage exited **0** having done nothing — so the stage
written to stop the gate reading another tree's `data/vanilla` has not run
since it was written. Found by pointing it at a fresh gate directory for the
first time: after a "successful" stage 1 the directory had no `oracle-work`
and no `data/vanilla` at all. It now has `remote_script()` without `-n`, prints
`STAGE1 OK`, and the caller greps for it — an exit code proves the ssh
returned, only output proves the stage ran.

Isolated to one line, so nobody has to take the story on trust:

```text
  $ ssh -n threadripper "bash -s" <<< 'echo STAGE_RAN'   ->  (nothing), rc=0
  $ ssh    threadripper "bash -s" <<< 'echo STAGE_RAN'   ->  STAGE_RAN, rc=0
```

Two more from the same file: it could not prepare a directory that did not
already exist (`cd` before `mkdir`), and `$SKIPS` is nearly a dead guard —
T0 is `--lib --bins` so the worldgen tests that print `skipping: no vanilla`
are not in the loop, and `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` refuses rather than skipping. The
one live emitter reachable from the loop is `ci/dump-flat-preset.sh` under
stage 3. Said so in the comment rather than leaving the number to imply more.

**The canonical shared `data/vanilla` has been regenerated from main's own
generators, and two of eight tables were wrong — but only one of them was
stale.** The earlier note here predicted three (`set_placed_by.json` absent,
`use_without_item.json` and `registries.bin` differing). Regenerating the whole
set with `ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh --force` and digesting every artefact
against what came out refuted two thirds of that:

```text
  block_props   flat_preset   items   placement   set_placed_by   update_shape
      identical, all six, byte for byte

  use_without_item.json  b4613ce9 -> e5933ec1   STALE. 1,659,485 -> 1,792,307
                         bytes: the setBlock flags and tick delays the merged
                         branch added to UseGolden.java. Real, and the last
                         live half of the 12/55 fault.

  registries.bin         NOT stale — NOT REPRODUCIBLE. Four dumps, four
                         digests, all exactly 121,847 bytes.
```

`set_placed_by.json` had already been repaired and the repaired copy is
correct: a fresh generation reproduces its digest exactly.

`registries.bin` is the one worth carrying forward. `cmp -l` between two dumps
is 1,235 bytes in one region from offset 2092, and the region is text: two
entries of a biome's `attributes` — `minecraft:visual/water_fog_color` and
`minecraft:visual/sky_color` — swap places. An unordered collection being
serialised, inside **vanilla's own** registry encoding; `ci/dump-registries.sh`
writes each body verbatim, so there is nothing on our side to pin. Three
consequences: "verify against a freshly generated copy" is structurally
impossible for that one table and a difference there must not be read as
staleness; the provenance stamp is still self-consistent, because `md5=` pins
a file to *its own* stamp rather than to what the generator produces; and it is
**armed** — we replay those bytes to a client while a live vanilla server
re-derives the order every boot, so the first check ever written over the
configuration phase is unmatchable for a reason with nothing to do with this
server. That is the `DAMAGE_EVENT` shape again, in data rather than in a
decoder.

**And the tree that seed lives in was never a checkout.** `~/rustmc/.git` on
the box is a 54-byte file reading
`gitdir: /home/sayer/rustmc/.git/worktrees/rustmc-gate`, which cannot resolve,
because `.git` **is** that file. The source there was a **file snapshot dated
2026-07-28**. So the seed was never generated by "main's generators" at any
point — it was generated by whatever scripts sat in a six-day-old snapshot, and
`cp -rn` propagated that forward into every gate directory ever created. That
is the entire mechanism, and it also explains why every provenance stamp on the
box records `commit=unknown`: none of these trees can answer `git rev-parse`.
Repaired with `git archive 9098a0b | tar -x`; the tracked file list now matches
`9098a0b` exactly.

Census of the 17 trees on the box that have a `data/vanilla`, taken before the
regeneration: **11 were wrong.** Seven are still symlinks into the shared copy
and so were wrong by construction rather than by accident; two have no
`set_placed_by.json` at all; one was seeded from the stale copy and never
regenerated; one holds a third pair of digests that main's generators do not
produce. Six were already correct, every one of them because it had
regenerated for itself. The laptop's copy was a fourth variant — 51 entries,
`registries.bin` and `flat_preset.json` absent entirely — and has been synced.

The fix is not the copying. It is `ci/gen-gameplay-tables.sh` plus the
provenance stamps, which make a tree generate its own and refuse anything else,
and the census is the measurement that says so: **the six correct trees are
exactly the six that had stopped sharing.**

**The new N had never run, and the reason is the transport again.** Two
independent attempts on 2026-08-03 to run `ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh` at its
configured N both died in **run 6 at `recorded 25/55`** — same run, same
scenario, to the line. That reads as a poisoned scenario and is not one: runs 1
through 5 each walked past that same scenario without incident, **five clean
traversals in the run's own log**, so the content is exonerated by the
measurement itself. Both deaths were at about **65 minutes of wall clock**, in
whichever run happened to be in flight, and both were launched over a plain
`ssh` tethered to a caller with a ceiling under an hour. N = 12 needs about two
and a half hours.

The failure mode is the bad kind: recordings stop mid-run, so the pairwise
comparisons and the aggregation never execute, and what is left is a log full
of successful `recorded n/55` lines and **no verdict at all**. Progress, no
failure, nothing to grep for.

So, stated plainly: **the designed sample count had never once executed**, the
eight names in `gameplay-unstable.toml` were assembled by hand from the five
traces that survived, and the N-run aggregation had never run on live data at
any N — only replayed against saved reports. That is the same shape as the
`ssh -n` that ate stage 1 for its whole existence, in the same turn, in a
different file: **the transport killed the stage and the exit code said
nothing.** The header now says to launch it `setsid nohup`, detached, and why.

**The selfcheck was a coin flip on the flaps it exists to catch.** Two runs
flagged unstable on disagreement catches a two-outcome check at `2p(1-p)` —
50% at best. Check 235's measured 4:2 split had a 44% chance of ever being
seen. Now 12 runs, run 1 against each of 2..12, detection
`1 - p^12 - (1-p)^12`: 99.95% on an even flap, 99.23% on 4:2, and **88.78% on
a one-in-six** — the honest limit, written into the script with the
arithmetic, along with the N = 26 it would take to get that last line to 99%.

**Run at its configured N for the first time, the selfcheck FAILED — and both
directions moved.** Twelve cold vanilla servers, run to completion detached,
2026-08-03 20:44–22:55, log
`~/rustmc-private/selfcheck-N12-2026-08-03.log`:

```text
  SELFCHECK FAILED: the reference's own reproducibility moved
    NEWLY UNSTABLE  sand-falls-when-unsupported  (diverge, 1/11 comparisons)
```

Two of those should end as decoders, not declarations, and the entries say so.
**Recorded and not hidden:** 500 has a *second* cause that is ours, and it has
two halves rather than one. Both are now written into `Normalizer`'s own doc
comment, because the comment previously claimed it discarded "the thing it must
not depend on" and it discards one of three:

* **Scope.** `Normalizer::entity` is called from `decode`, which runs on every
  non-housekeeping packet — and `is_housekeeping` is thirteen chunk/time/tab
  packets, none of which carry an entity id. A scenario's `observe` list is not
  applied until `compare::project`. So a packet a check filters away has
  **already consumed an index**, and one extra unobserved entity packet from
  either server shifts every later index by one. The check then diverges on the
  one axis its `observe` list exists to say it does not watch.
* **Socket order.** `record::pump_both` alternates the two sessions in 25 ms
  slices through **one shared** `Normalizer` — shared deliberately, so one
  entity gets one number on both streams — which makes the index a function of
  which socket delivered first. Forty lines further down the same file sorts
  observations by `who` with the comment that "interleaving two sockets read in
  turn is a property of the harness's scheduling and not of the server". **The
  sort takes the interleaving out of the order while the numbering has already
  put it into the value.** One file, two opposite treatments of one quantity.

Vanilla's side, counted rather than recalled: `ServerLevel.ENTITY_COUNTER` is a
`static AtomicInteger` and `getNextEntityId` loops `incrementAndGet` until
`hasEntityWithId` is false — so the raw id depends on everything the process has
ever spawned and is **reused** once an entity is removed. Renumbering is
mandatory; where it happens is the bug.

Measured, so the severity is not argued: **6 of 55** checks name any
entity-bearing kind, every one is a single-entity scenario, and the substrate
runs `spawn-monsters=false` with `spawn_mobs false`, so index 0 is the only
value any of them can produce today. All three protections are properties of
the *substrate*, not of the harness, and the first two-entity check removes
them together.

And the priority is higher than "armed but harmless" suggests, for a reason
that only shows up when the two lists are put side by side:

```text
  080-other-player-is-an-entity                       declared UNSTABLE

  510-swapping-to-the-offhand-shows-on-both-channels  declared UNSTABLE
```

**Six of the six checks that observe an entity kind are reference-unstable;
three of the other forty-nine are.** 100% against 6%.

The rest of that argument stands and is sharper for it. The other five have
declared causes that are not this one and are not being reattributed. The point

`NEWLY UNSTABLE sand-falls-when-unsupported`, in the same shape and the same

Fix it before entities are built.

**No check in the corpus set `timing`, so three whose claim is a duration
could not fail.** 330 and 335 now carry `timing = { bucket = { ms = 500 } }`,
which is the difference `ticksToStayPressed` 20 vs 30 makes. Measured un-press
arrivals: stone 956/972/986/1002, oak 1495/1500/1511/1516. `Timing::Bucket`
now rounds to the **nearest** multiple rather than flooring, because the
arrivals cluster *on* multiples of the delay and a floor bucket of 250, 500 or
1000 ms puts a boundary on top of the stone cluster and splits those four
samples. Its own doc comment already said "rounded".

**410's premise was refuted and its rig was inverted.** The claim was that it
sees the propagation untimed. It does not see it at all: vanilla kept the
repeater `powered=false` for the whole scenario and never sent a
`block_update` at the wire, in either run. `DiodeBlock.getStateForPlacement`
points FACING back at the placer and `getInputSignal` reads

the power into the output side. That is also the real reason the baseline
recorded this check as having "falsified the prediction" that it needed
redstone propagation: it never ran it. Rig corrected; the baseline note too.

**440 is not testable on this wire, and its `about` no longer claims to be.**
The pulse is **two** game ticks, 100 ms — this paragraph said one until
2026-08-03 and was contradicted by the paragraph four below it in its own
block, which is what a stale caveat looks like from the inside. The measured
gap between its two updates is 132/68/68/132 ms: spread 64 ms, against a
one-tick 50 ms difference that a check would have to resolve. No bucket is
both wider than the jitter and narrower than one tick, and an interval
projection does not help because the quantum *is* the tick.

The instrument was already honest; the **check** was not. Its `about` opened
"an observer emits a TWO-tick pulse", so the corpus stated a duration claim
that nothing in the run could refute — a server pulsing for one tick or three
still emits two updates, in this order, at this position, and still comes back
`match`. Rewritten to claim only the count, the order and the position, with
the two-tick figure kept as derivation. **A note explaining why a claim is
untestable does not retract the claim; only editing the claim does.**

**Two figures in the corpus's own `about` fields were wrong, counted rather
than recalled.** 335 said "the eleven wooden ones": `Blocks` declares 14
`_BUTTON` fields and the `ButtonBlock` constructor takes `bipush 20` twice and
`bipush 30` **twelve** times — the old count predates pale oak. And 440 said "a
one-tick pulse": `ObserverBlock.startSignal` schedules with `iconst_2` and so
does the `scheduleTick` inside `ObserverBlock.tick`, so the pulse is **two**
ticks, 100 ms — which is what the measured 132/68/68/132 ms gaps average to,

**`DAMAGE_EVENT` was an armed trap.** It decoded `entity` and the damage type
and stopped, so `sourceCauseId` and `sourceDirectId` fell into the trailing

handled so wire-0 is "absent" rather than entity 0.

**Finding 13: `inert` was assigned by vanilla alone and overwrote `Diverge`.**
`informative()` reads the reference projection and nothing else, and the line
using it overwrote every verdict but `Vacuous`. The forced resync carries the
*actual block state*, so a server that placed the wrong block differs only
there — and was relabelled "dead check". Constructed end to end on real
recorded vanilla bytes with the real binary: declared said `1 inert`, and
**`strict` said `1 diverge` in the same run**, because strict never applies
the override. Now only a `Match` may be relabelled.

Severity is bounded, and by measurement rather than argument: `informative(pr)
== 0` *is* the inert condition, so the inert count is the count of checks with
an uninformative reference, and both directions report **0 inert** across all
55 (vanilla vs vanilla, and vanilla vs rustmc at the 17:09 gate). No check is
in that position today. And `Inert` is not baselineable, so even when it fires
the gate reds — what was lost was the diagnosis, not the failure.

**290, 310, 320, 500 are SOUND, measured.** A second audit left them UNCLEAR on

does: the allowance is consumed at most once per (step, position), so the

**First thing to do: `./ci/t2-gameplay.sh`.** If anything comes back `WORSE`
it is a flaky check rather than a regression, and the trace is the place to
look before the code.

**Four checks are new, and two of them exist because the check they shadow
could not fail** on the thing being claimed: 230 pins one bed facing, so a
hard-coded `[1,0,1]` passes it for ever; 330 pins one button delay, so a
hard-coded 20 passes it for ever. Both came back `match` on their first run,
which is the only evidence that the offset and the delay are really read. The
pattern is written up in `ci/checks/gameplay/README.md`: **a check that
exercises one input cannot tell a mechanism that reads that input from a
constant.** Ask it of any check you add.

**What to distrust first.** Three separate "checks that could not fail" were
found *in the extractors* this run, not in the corpus — a water probe that
could not detect water, a randomness detector that was a coin flip, and a
class map that answered nothing. `docs/SERVER.md` has all three written up
under "Three more, and none of them were in the harness". The pattern that
found each: **ask what the instrument would report if the thing it measures
were absent.** All three answered "the same clean number".

**The instruments now in the tree, and what each refuses.**

* `ci/placed-golden.sh` + `tools/goldengen/vanilla/PlacedGolden.java` ->
  `data/vanilla/set_placed_by.json`. Shares `UseGolden`'s `TableLevel` rather
  than growing a second one. Refuses to write a table unless: the four bed
  facings give four *distinct* head offsets; every `oak_door` state writes one
  upper half at `[0,1,0]`; `small_dripleaf` comes back `worldSensitive` (which
  is how a blind water probe is caught); the class map covers >1,000 blocks
  and names `DoorBlock`, `ButtonBlock` and `BedBlock`; and the superclass
  chain exists, contains `DoorBlock` for `WeatheringCopperDoorBlock`, and
  resolves 21 blocks to `DoorBlock`.
* `ci/use-golden.sh` additionally refuses a table where `dragon_egg` is not
  flagged random. It had been **flaky since it was written** — twice in six
  runs it called the egg deterministic — and that is fixed rather than
  worked around.
* Both tables now carry **`flags` per write** and
  `tickDelay`/`tickPriority`/`tickAt`/**`tickKind`** per scheduled tick. All
  are load-bearing and all were previously hard-coded or absent on the
  consumer side.

**A tick has a queue, and the use table is mostly the wrong one.** 34 blocks
schedule something from `useWithoutItem` and **22 of them are trapdoors** —
`TrapDoorBlock` has no `tick` override at all. `toggle` ends with
`if (WATERLOGGED) scheduleTick(pos, Fluids.WATER, ...)`, so those 640 rows are
**fluid** ticks, and the row count confirms it: exactly 32 of each trapdoor's
64 states schedule, which is precisely the `waterlogged=true` half. Reading
the delay without the queue puts a block tick for `oak_trapdoor` into a queue
that has no rule for it — and `UNIQUE_TICK_HASH` then makes that entry *block*
a real block tick at the same position until it drains. `tickKind` is recorded
now and `crate::ticks::on_used` refuses fluid ticks.

That fix cannot move the corpus and the reason is checked rather than assumed:
no check right-clicks a trapdoor (`210` clicks the *stone* beside it twice),
and the substrate is superflat with no water, so no trapdoor in the corpus is
waterlogged in the first place.

**The single class map is the thing to reuse.** `set_placed_by.json` carries
`classes` and `superclasses` for the **whole registry**, and
`PlacedByTable::is_a` is the project's only answer to "what kind of block is
this". Two rules key on it already (`ButtonBlock` in `crate::ticks`,
`DoorBlock` in `crate::shapes`). Three things it cost to get right, in the
order they bit:

  1. **Never key a rule on a block id.** "Ends in `_button`" holds until one
     block breaks it and the break is silent.
  2. **The map must cover the registry, not the rows.** A rule asks what class
     a block's *neighbour* is, and a neighbour can be anything; a partial map
     answers "not that class" for everything it omits. That is how the button
     check failed to move on its first run with no error anywhere — `class`
     had been added to the use table and the table not regenerated, so every
     lookup returned nothing.
  3. **`is_a`, not a string compare.** The bytecode tests `instanceof`.
     **21 blocks answer `instanceof DoorBlock` and only 17 are called
     `DoorBlock`** — the four unwaxed copper doors are
     `WeatheringCopperDoorBlock`. Comparing simple names gave those four no
     door rule at all, and **no corpus check would ever have caught it**,
     because every door check places an oak door. Found by reading the class
     map after extracting it, not by a test.

**Nulls, so nobody re-runs them.**

* *"Flag any rule that touched the RNG"* — exact, cannot flake, and far too
  coarse. `DoorBlock.playSound` draws a sound **pitch**, which no table here
  carries, so 55 blocks including every door, trapdoor and fence gate came
  back random and lost every cell. Killed.
* *RNG seeds `0..5`* — `RandomSource.create` is `java.util.Random`, whose
  scramble leaves small consecutive seeds correlated; the dragon egg's
  teleport failed under all six and the classification looked stable while
  being blind. The seeds are eight well-spread constants now. Killed.
* *A generalised "double block" `updateShape` rule* — the family disagrees.
  `DoorBlock` copies the whole neighbour state, `BedBlock` copies only
  `OCCUPIED` onto its *own* state along a horizontal axis and matches the
  same **block** rather than `instanceof`, `DoublePlantBlock` returns AIR or
  nothing. One rule would be right about one of three. Killed by reading,
  before writing any; both the door and the bed are now written out
  separately and `DoublePlantBlock` is not ported.
* *Extending `update_shape.json` to carry the door* — not attempted and not
  recommended lightly: a row is one `to` per neighbour class by construction,
  so this needs a schema change plus a regeneration of the *expensive* table.
  The typed rule is 40 lines and consulted only where the table is silent.

**The first ten minutes, if you are picking this up.**

  1. `./ci/t2-gameplay.sh` — the ratchet is one run short, see above. Nothing
     else should be started until it is green.
  2. Read `crate::placedby`'s module docs. The class map and `is_a` are the
     part of this branch most likely to be reused wrongly, and both failures
     it already cost are written there.
  3. Then the repeater. `DiodeBlock`'s bytecode is transcribed below so the
     first move is writing code, not reading a jar.

**Nothing is stubbed and nothing is half-done.** Every mechanism named above
is ported, gated and measured; the deliberate omissions are listed as nulls
and gaps, not as work in progress. The one *deliberately unwired* thing is
`setPlacedBy`'s scheduled tick (`DiodeBlock`, `CrafterBlock`): the data is
loaded and `PlacedByTable::scheduled_tick` exposes it, but nothing consumes
it, because a repeater that began scheduling on placement would change
behaviour this branch never measured.

**The next item, and what closes it.** `block_event` is still the largest
untouched packet, and its four checks still all need a producer first — that
ranking has not changed. The cheapest real progress is the three checks that
miss **no observation kinds at all** and differ only in content: the
redstone-torch inverter, the observer pulse, and the repeater delay. Those are
`neighborChanged` — the *other* half of a block update, gated on
`UPDATE_NEIGHBORS`, which `crate::shapes` carries the flag for and does not
implement.

Read ahead so the next run starts from bytecode rather than from a name.
`DiodeBlock`, which is the repeater and the comparator:

```text
  neighborChanged: if (!level.getBlockState(pos).is(this)) return;
                   if (state.canSurvive(level, pos)):
                       checkTickOnNeighbor(level, pos, state); return;
                   dropResources(...); level.removeBlock(pos, false);
                   for (Direction d : Direction.values()):
                       level.updateNeighborsAt(pos.relative(d), this);

  tick:            if (isLocked(level, pos, state)) return;
                   wasPowered = state.getValue(POWERED);
                   on = shouldTurnOn(level, pos, state);
                   if (wasPowered && !on):
                       setBlock(pos, state.setValue(POWERED, false), 2);
                   else if (!wasPowered):
                       setBlock(pos, state.setValue(POWERED, true), 2);
                       if (!on):
                           scheduleTick(pos, this, getDelay(state),
                                        TickPriority.VERY_HIGH);
```

Two things in there a plausible version gets wrong. The flags are **2**,
`UPDATE_CLIENTS` alone — not `UPDATE_ALL` — and the priority is
**`VERY_HIGH`**, ordinal 1, not `NORMAL`. `crate::ticks`'s drain order already
sorts on priority, so a repeater scheduled at `NORMAL` runs in the wrong order
against anything sharing its tick. `set_placed_by.json` already carries
`DiodeBlock`'s placement-time tick (delay and priority, loaded and
deliberately unwired), so the schedule side starts from data.

### The four-check price, measured

The previous run priced `setPlacedBy` at four checks as a *hypothesis*.
Measured against the recorded traces and the tables, **the count is right and
the price is not**: two of the four need a second mechanism that no existing
table can hold, and that was invisible from the trace alone.

All five candidate checks observe **only** `block_update`,
`section_blocks_update` and `block_changed_ack`, from the **actor** — so
vanilla's `sound`, `level_event` and `move_entity` lines drop out of every
comparison below and neither `sound` nor `level_event` is on the path. Read
out of the check files, not the summary.

Filtering the last run's traces to that projection:

```text
                               R 2  block_update air, ack
  button-unpresses-itself      V 5  ..., ack, then block_update powered=false
                               R 4  (no un-press)
```

So the two *placement* checks close on `setPlacedBy` alone. The other two do
not, and this is the finding:

**`update_shape.json` structurally cannot carry a door's upper half, and it
does not — 0 rows.** All 32 `oak_door` rows are `half=lower, dir=0`
(support lost -> air). A table row is **one `to` per neighbour class**, and
`DoorBlock.updateShape` for the upper half asked from `DOWN` returns
`neighborState.setValue(HALF, half)` — the *whole neighbour state* with
`HALF` put back, which varies with the neighbour. One row cannot express it,
so the sweep carried nothing. It is **not** in the `refused` list either
(11 buckets, none naming a door), so nothing in the dump's own diagnostics
says it is missing: a gap that reports as silence.

Read from the bytecode rather than recalled — and the recall was wrong, which
is why it is quoted:

```text
  DoorBlock.setPlacedBy   level.setBlockAndUpdate(pos.above(),
                                                  state.setValue(HALF, UPPER))
  BedBlock.setPlacedBy    level.setBlockAndUpdate(pos.relative(FACING),
                                                  state.setValue(PART, HEAD))
  DoorBlock.updateShape   if (dir.getAxis() == Y && (half == LOWER) == (dir == UP))
                              return nb.getBlock() instanceof DoorBlock
                                     && nb.getValue(HALF) != half
                                   ? nb.setValue(HALF, half)   // WHOLE state
                                   : AIR;
```

I had written that branch from memory as a four-property copy of
`FACING/OPEN/HINGE/POWERED`. It is not; it is the neighbour state entire.

`setPlacedBy` has **16 overrides** in 26.2 (`javap -p` over
`net/minecraft/world/level/block/*.class`). Four write a second block from a
fixed offset and a property override — `DoorBlock`, `BedBlock`,
`DoublePlantBlock`, `SmallDripleafBlock` — which is a table. The rest are
random (`MossyCarpetBlock`), schedule a tick (`DiodeBlock`, `CrafterBlock`),
or want a block entity, and a table must refuse them by name.
