### The use-vs-place gate, derived 2026-08-03 — and we have it backwards

**This server places first and never consults the block.** Vanilla gives the
block first refusal, and the difference is not "a missing feature", it is an
inversion: right-clicking a lever with a block in hand *flips the lever* on
vanilla and *places the block* here.

`ServerPlayerGameMode.useItemOn`, from the bytecode, in order:

```text
  state = level.getBlockState(hit.getBlockPos())
  if !state.getBlock().isEnabled(level.enabledFeatures())     -> FAIL

  if gameModeForPlayer == SPECTATOR:
      mp = state.getMenuProvider(level, pos)
      if mp != null: player.openMenu(mp)                      -> CONSUME
      else                                                    -> PASS

  holdingSomething = !mainHand.isEmpty() || !offhand.isEmpty()
  skipBlock        = player.isSecondaryUseActive() && holdingSomething
  if skipBlock: goto PLACEMENT

  r = state.useItemOn(getItemInHand(hand), level, player, hand, hit)
  if r.consumesAction():  trigger ITEM_USED_ON_BLOCK          -> r
  if r instanceof InteractionResult.TryEmptyHandInteraction
     && hand == MAIN_HAND:
      r2 = state.useWithoutItem(level, player, hit)
      if r2.consumesAction(): trigger DEFAULT_BLOCK_USE       -> r2

  PLACEMENT:
  if stack.isEmpty() || player.getCooldowns().isOnCooldown(stack) -> PASS
  ctx = new UseOnContext(player, hand, hit); ... item places ...
```

Four things a plausible version gets wrong, all of them read rather than
recalled:

  * **`useWithoutItem` is not gated on an empty hand.** It runs when the
    item-aware `useItemOn` returns the marker `TryEmptyHandInteraction`,
    which is the default, **and** the hand is `MAIN_HAND`. Every corpus
    check that right-clicks a block holds a *stick* and still gets the block
    behaviour, which is why they work at all.
  * **Sneaking only skips the block if you are holding something.**
    `skipBlock` is the conjunction; sneaking with both hands empty still
    runs the block interaction.
  * `holdingSomething` reads **both** hands, not the one being used.
  * The empty-stack test sits *after* the block interaction, so an empty
    hand still reaches `useWithoutItem` and only then falls out at `PASS`.

**51 classes override `useWithoutItem`** in 26.2 (counted from the jar:
`javap -p` over `net/minecraft/world/level/block/*.class`). That is the same
order of magnitude as `placement.json`'s extraction and wants the same
treatment rather than 51 special cases — and one generator can serve
`setPlacedBy` too, since both questions are "what `setBlock` calls does this
make". The set splits into pure state changes (Button, Comparator, Door,
FenceGate, Lever, NoteBlock, Repeater, TrapDoor, DaylightDetector) and
things a table cannot hold (menus, cake, bells, jukeboxes); the first group
is what the corpus is currently waiting on.

This is the substrate for the biggest cluster of divergences in the corpus:
`lever-flips-when-right-clicked`, `door-opens-when-right-clicked`,
`button-unpresses-itself`, `a-repeater-delays-the-signal-it-passes-on`,
`a-comparator-switches-to-subtract-mode`,
`a-note-block-retunes-when-right-clicked`, and indirectly the two that need
a lever to flip before any redstone can run. Six to eight checks on one
mechanism, against `block_event`'s four.

**Evidence that it is exactly this, not something near it.** Three of those
checks are missing no observation kinds at all and differ only in content,
and the content is the un-cycled property:

```text
  a-redstone-torch-...    vanilla lever[powered=true]   ours powered=false
  a-repeater-delays-...   vanilla repeater[delay=2]     ours delay=1
  an-observer-pulses-...  vanilla observer[powered=true] ours said nothing
```

**What was measured and closed.** The gameplay oracle's intermittent
broadcast channel is understood, and it was never a race in either server:
the harness never sent `chunk_batch_received`, so vanilla delivered nine
chunks and stopped, and `ChunkMap.isChunkTracked` withheld every broadcast
and every entity from both clients. 9 chunks against 117 with the

**What that falsified, and it had been written into this server's code.**
"Vanilla never sends the acting player a broadcast `block_update`" is false;
`ChunkHolder.broadcast` excludes nobody. `Players::broadcast_except` is gone.

**What fixing the instrument then exposed**, which is the larger result: this
server broadcast at the wrong moment and in the wrong shape. Vanilla only
*records* a change and sends at a tick boundary, coalescing more than one
change per section into a `section_blocks_update`. 13 divergences and 8
`inert` verdicts across 23 scenarios were those two facts. `crate::broadcast`
and `crate::shortset` are the fix.

**The substrate was not what the script said it was, and that was the last
thing standing.** All four gamerules `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` sets had been silent
no-ops since the corpus was written — 26.2 made game rules a registry with
snake_case ids, so `gamerule randomTickSpeed 0` answers `Incorrect argument
for command` and the server carries on. Random ticks ran through every number
this project has quoted about gameplay. Fixed, with `gamerule_or_die` so a
refused console command can never be silent again, and **exactly one check
moved when it landed**: `trapdoor-half-follows-the-cursor`, whose divergence
was the grass under its rig block dying on a random tick.

### 2026-08-03, later — the tick loop body, and two errors of my own

**The blocker named yesterday was not one.** `checkDespawn` was called out as
"not a filter, it *mutates*", which is true and is why it cannot be reordered
— but `Entity.checkDespawn()` is a **bare `return`**. The only classes in the
jar that override it are `Mob`, `ShulkerBullet`, `WitherBoss` and
`EnderDragon`, and this server has no mobs, so the mutation is unreachable and
the loop body is **complete rather than approximate**.
`crates/rustmc-entity/src/tick.rs` is that body, gate for gate, with every
gate a trait method so a gate this server cannot evaluate has to be answered
rather than quietly omitted.

Four details a plausible version gets wrong, and **two more that I got wrong
myself** by writing the passenger path from memory before reading it — worth
recording because it is exactly the failure mode this project exists to
avoid, committed by the person warning about it:

  * `checkDespawn` runs **before** the range gate. Testing the cheap gate
    first is the obvious optimisation and would keep mobs alive that vanilla
    deletes.
  * A player is exempt from the range gate, by `instanceof ServerPlayer`.
  * **A passenger gets `rideTick()`, not `tick()`.** Different methods.
  * **A non-player passenger absent from the `EntityTickList` is skipped**
    entirely; a player passenger is exempt from that check.
  * `setOldPosAndRot` precedes `tick`, and `tickCount` is incremented **by the
    loop** in both paths, not by `tick`.
  * `guardEntityTick` rethrows as `ReportedException` — a throwing entity
    stops the server rather than being skipped.

`MobCategory` is recorded with it: despawn distance is a per-category field
(128, or **64** for `water_ambient`) and the no-despawn distance is a
**constant 32** on the enum, not a second field.

**Corpus 34 -> 37**, into the three areas with no coverage: an inventory
check that works without survival (a cascade drops an item the player picks
up — a creative dig drops nothing, but the cascade is not a player break so
`dropResources` runs), a lever lighting a lamp (`neighborChanged`, the half
of a block update we carry a flag for and do not fill in), and wire power
falling off with distance. Two packets that were being recorded as
`packet:0x..` are decoded now — `block_entity_data` and `open_sign_editor` —
so block-entity checks can see what vanilla actually sends.

**Still open, in the order it is worth doing:**

*(The first two entries of this list — confirming the fastutil ordering
prediction and rewriting the baseline — were done on 2026-08-03. The
prediction held on both servers and the baseline is
`ci/checks/gameplay-baseline.toml` at 12/30, `T2-GAMEPLAY GREEN`.)*

1. **Run `ci/t2-gameplay-selfcheck.sh` once.** It was written today and has
   never been executed. It records the corpus against vanilla **twice** and
   diffs vanilla against itself, and the expected answer is that every
   scenario matches. Three withdrawn conclusions on this project were all a
   reference disagreeing with itself between runs, and until today the
   substrate could not have supported the check anyway — random ticks were
   running and the spawn moved on every join. Both are fixed, so this is now
   a question that can be answered. Anything but all-match is an instrument
   fault and outranks everything below it.

2. **`setPlacedBy`, which is the best value in the corpus: one mechanism
   closes three checks.** `door-places-both-halves`,
   `bed-places-two-blocks` and `digging-a-door-takes-both-halves` are all the
   same gap — a block whose placement writes a *second* block that
   `getStateForPlacement` does not describe. `DoorBlock.setPlacedBy` writes
   `pos.above()` with `half=upper`; `BedBlock.setPlacedBy` writes
   `pos.relative(facing)` with `part=head`. Breaking either half then takes
   both, which is why the dig check is the same item.
   It wants an extraction in the established shape — `placement.json` and
   `update_shape.json` are the precedents — rather than a per-block special
   case, because the set of blocks with a writing `setPlacedBy` is not
   guessable from names.

   **Concretely**, and modelled on `ci/placement-golden.sh` plus
   `tools/goldengen/vanilla/PlacementGolden.java`, which is the closest
   precedent because it also needs no generated chunk: put each block's
   default state into a recording level, call
   `Block.setPlacedBy(level, pos, state, placer, stack)` with a null placer
   where the block tolerates one, and write down **every `setBlock` the call
   makes** — offset from `pos`, and the state written. Blocks that write
   nothing fall out on their own, which is the answer for the ~1,000 that do
   not need this. `ShapeGolden.java` already demonstrates the recording-level
   trick, including the correction that made it work: hand back
   `EntityBlock.newBlockEntity`, or a shulker box as the candidate ground
   makes the whole thing unanswerable.

   Expect the placer to be the hard part — `BedBlock` reads
   `placer.getDirection()` and `DoorBlock` does not — so a null placer will
   throw for some blocks and those need the `Proxy` treatment or a real
   `Player`. Record which blocks refuse rather than dropping them, exactly as
   the shape table records its 79,111 refusals.
3. **`canBeReplaced` is item-aware, and ours is not.** `slab-stacks-into-a-
   double-slab` and `snow-layers-stack` are both this. `handle_use_item_on`
   picks its target with `blocks.replaceable(pos)`, a static per-block
   property; vanilla's `BlockPlaceContext` sets `replaceClicked` from
   `state.canBeReplaced(context)`, which takes the **held item** and the
   click. The default is the surprise:

   ```java
   state.canBeReplaced() && (ctx.getItemInHand().isEmpty()
                             || !ctx.getItemInHand().is(this.asItem()))
   ```

   — a replaceable block refuses to be replaced by *its own* item. `SlabBlock`
   and `SnowLayerBlock` then override it in the opposite direction, which is
   how a second slab merges into a double and a second snow deepens the
   layer instead of stacking above it. Another extraction in the
   `placement.json` shape; the overriding classes are few but not guessable.
4. **`Players::broadcast` still tells every connected player about every
   change.** Vanilla filters on `isChunkTracked`. The `contains` half is read
   and written out below — Euclidean with a two-chunk pad, not the Chebyshev
   test the name suggests — and since this server sends chunks synchronously
   it is the *whole* predicate here.
5. **Entity *behaviour*, now that the loop that would run it exists.**
   `crates/rustmc-entity/src/tick.rs` is the body; what it has no
   implementation to call is `Entity.tick()` itself — `baseTick`, movement
   integration, gravity. `sand-falls-when-unsupported` and
   `spawn-egg-makes-a-mob` are the two checks that go green when it lands,
   and both are live and failing now. Note the corpus needs entity
   *broadcasting* as much as ticking: `add_entity` and `set_entity_data`
   reach a client through `ChunkMap.TrackedEntity`, which this server does
   not have either.
6. **The smallest divergence in the corpus, already derived.** A standing
   sign's `rotation` is
   `RotationSegment.convertToSegment(context.getRotation() + 180.0f)`, and
   `convertToSegment` is `SEGMENTED_ANGLE16.fromDegrees`, which is

   ```java
   Math.round(degrees * (16f / 360f)) & 15
   ```

   Note **Java's** `Math.round`, which is `floor(x + 0.5)` — not Rust's
   `f32::round`, which is half-away-from-zero and disagrees on every negative
   half. The `+ 180.0f` is not a guess: the corpus set yaw `22.5` and vanilla
   answered `rotation=9`, and `round(202.5 * 16 / 360) = 9` while
   `round(22.5 * 16 / 360) = 1`. This is the one placement rule in the game
   with more than eight values, so `placement.json` cannot hold it and it
   needs a rule rather than a table entry.
7. **A gate the corpus cannot exercise, said plainly rather than left to
   imply coverage.** `SectionPos.asLong` gives `z` 22 bits and this server had
   it at 20, which is wrong for every negative section `z`. Workspaces sit at
   absolute `z = 0`, so section `z` is never negative and **no check can see
   the fix or a regression of it**; only the unit test in
   `crate::broadcast` can. Moving the workspaces to a negative `z` would buy
   the coverage for the price of one more baseline.
8. **SOLVED — the `grass_block` -> `dirt` was random ticks, because the
   gamerules never applied.** Kept here in full because it was chased twice
   and both chases were reasonable.

   `gamerule randomTickSpeed 0` answers **"Incorrect argument for command"**
   in 26.2 and the server carries on. Game rules became a registry —
   `minecraft:game_rule`, 59 entries — with snake_case namespaced ids, so all
   four rules this harness sets had been silent no-ops since the corpus was
   written, while `ci/t2-gameplay.sh` and `docs/SERVER.md` both asserted they
   were in force:

   ```text
     doDaylightCycle -> advance_time        doMobSpawning   -> spawn_mobs
     doWeatherCycle  -> advance_weather     randomTickSpeed -> random_tick_speed
   ```

   Random ticks were running through every measurement either document has
   quoted. The grass under a freshly placed rig block was dying on a random
   tick, at unpredictable moments, which is why it looked like far-away noise
   the first time and like an impossible `SpreadingSnowyBlock` bug the
   second. **The bytecode was right both times** — `randomTick` is the only
   method in that class that writes a block, and `ServerLevel.tickChunk`
   really does gate on `randomTickSpeed <= 0`. The world simply was not the
   one the script described.

   Fixed with the 26.2 ids plus `gamerule_or_die`, which greps the server log
   after each rule and exits on `Incorrect argument` or `Unknown or
   incomplete`. Confirmed: `Gamerule random_tick_speed is now set to: 0`,
   zero refusals.

   **The general lesson, and it is the second instance of it on the same
   day:** a command that fails must not be able to fail quietly, exactly as
   `ci/t0.sh` running `--lib` against a binary crate could not fail. Ask of
   any green substrate what would have had to happen for it to come back red.

### 2026-08-03 — the broadcast channel was a stalled chunk sender

**Closed. The gameplay oracle's "intermittent broadcast" was one
non-conformance in the harness, not a race in either server.**

`PlayerChunkSender` is constructed with `maxUnacknowledgedBatches = 1`. The
`MAX_UNACKNOWLEDGED_BATCHES = 10` constant is only ever assigned inside
`onChunkBatchReceivedByClient`. `sendNextChunks` returns immediately while
`unacknowledgedBatches >= maxUnacknowledgedBatches`, so a client that never
sends serverbound `chunk_batch_received` (id 11, one big-endian `f32`) gets
**one batch and then nothing, for the rest of the session** — and the first
batch is `floor(START_CHUNKS_PER_TICK)` = 9 chunks.

It reaches far past chunk loading because of one predicate:

```java
ChunkMap.isChunkTracked(player, x, z)
    = player.getChunkTrackingView().contains(x, z)
      && !player.connection.chunkSender.isPending(ChunkPos.pack(x, z))
```

`ChunkHolder.broadcastChanges` sends to `getPlayers(pos, false)`, which
filters on exactly that, and so does entity pairing in
`ChunkMap.TrackedEntity.updatePlayer`. **A chunk still queued for delivery is
a chunk whose block changes and entities are withheld.** Direct sends — the
two `handleUseItemOn` resyncs and `block_changed_ack` — go to
`connection.send` with no such gate. That is the reliable/unreliable split,
mechanised, and it was never actor-versus-observer.

Measured, `ci/chunk-batch-probe.sh`, vanilla 26.2 superflat, view-distance 4,
8 s after login, Threadripper:

```text
  without the acknowledgement    chunks=9    batches=1
  with the acknowledgement       chunks=117  batches=4
```

Every scenario walks 32(n+1) blocks to a workspace **outside** those 9
chunks, so at the workspace every chunk in the tracking view had been
re-marked pending and no broadcast could reach either client. The residual
run-to-run variation is the narrow window after `ChunkMap.move` widens the
tracking view and before the new chunks are marked pending: `contains` is
already true and `isPending` is not yet, so a change in that window *is*
broadcast. That is why it was intermittent rather than simply absent.

**What this falsifies, and it was stated as a finding twice:** "vanilla never
sends the acting player a broadcast block update; its actor-facing protocol
only ever corrects a wrong prediction". Wrong. `ChunkHolder.broadcast` is
`list.forEach(p -> p.connection.send(packet))` with **no exclusion of
anyone**, and the list is `getPlayers(pos, false)`. The actor was missing
from that list because the actor's own chunk was pending, not because vanilla
excludes it.

**Nulls, so nobody re-runs them:** it is not a decoder bug, not a dropped
packet, not a wrong packet id, not a socket-read race, and not
`player_loaded` (that was a different, real bug, already fixed). The three
unexplained results in `ci/checks/gameplay/open/README.md` — a pig five
blocks away never announced, two players five blocks apart never told the
other moved, `add_entity` arriving only after a 24-block round trip — are all
the same predicate and need no probe of their own.

**Left open by this, and both are real parity gaps in our server:**

1. We do not implement `PlayerChunkSender` at all — no per-tick quota, no
   batch acknowledgement, no `pendingChunks`, and **no gating of broadcasts
   or entity pairing on chunk delivery**. A client that never acknowledges a
   batch gets 9 chunks from vanilla and the whole world from us.
   `Players::broadcast` still sends to every connected player regardless of
   what chunks they hold.

   **The `contains` half is read and is not what a plausible implementation
   writes.** `ChunkTrackingView.Positioned.contains(x, z)` is
   `contains(x, z, true)`, which is
   `ChunkTrackingView.isWithinDistance(centerX, centerZ, viewDistance, x, z, true)`:

   ```java
   int pad = includeEdge ? 2 : 1;
   long dx = Math.max(0, Math.abs(x - cx) - pad);
   long dz = Math.max(0, Math.abs(z - cz) - pad);
   return dx * dx + dz * dz < (long) (viewDistance * viewDistance);
   ```

   **Euclidean, with a two-chunk pad, and strictly less than.** Not
   `max(|dx|, |dz|) <= viewDistance`, which is what the name suggests and
   what any reasonable guess produces — and which differs at the corners and
   again within two chunks of the centre. Since this server sends chunks
   synchronously, `isPending` is always false for us, so `contains` alone is
   the *whole* predicate here and closing this gap is one filter, not two.
2. `ChunkHolder.broadcastChanges` coalesces: >1 change in one section in one
   tick becomes a `section_blocks_update`, not several `block_update`s.
   **Done 2026-08-03** — `crate::broadcast` plus `crate::shortset`.

### 2026-08-03 — the entity tick loop, read out of the bytecode

`crates/rustmc-entity/src/store.rs` deliberately had **no tick loop** on the
grounds that vanilla's order is observable and must come from the bytecode
rather than from a plausible guess. This is that reading, and the *order*
half of it now exists as `crates/rustmc-entity/src/tick_list.rs`. The loop
**body** does not, because none of the gates it consults — `isRemoved`,
`checkDespawn`, `inEntityTickingRange` — exists in that crate yet, and a body
written before them would be a guess exactly where the order is not.

**`ServerLevel.tick(BooleanSupplier)`, in order** — the phase list, with the
profiler and the debug plumbing stripped out:

```text
  EnvironmentAttributeSystem.invalidateTickCache
  WorldBorder.tick
  the sleep / time advance   (SleepStatus, ServerClockManager.moveToTimeMarker)
  LevelTicks.tick            block ticks
  LevelTicks.tick            fluid ticks
  Raids.tick
  ServerChunkCache.tick      chunk loading, random ticks, and the broadcasts
  EnderDragonFight.tick
  EntityTickList.forEach     <- the entity loop
  PersistentEntitySectionManager.tick
```

Two consequences worth having before writing any of it. Block and fluid
ticks run **before** the chunk source, so a scheduled tick's change is
broadcast in the same tick that fired it. The entity loop runs **after** it,
so a block change an entity causes is not broadcast until the next tick. And
`ServerGamePacketListenerImpl.tick` — which is what actually sends
`block_changed_ack` — runs after all of this, which is why the measured
actor-side order for a placement is resync, resync, broadcast, **then** ack.

**`EntityTickList` is the order, and it is not entity-id order.** Both
`active` and `passive` are `Int2ObjectLinkedOpenHashMap`, so iteration is
**insertion order**, keyed by entity id. `forEach` walks `active.values()`.

`add` and `remove` both call `ensureActiveIsNotIterated` first: if a
`forEach` is in progress over `active`, it copies every entry into `passive`
in the current order and swaps the two maps, so the mutation lands on a fresh
map and the in-flight iteration keeps walking the old one. **An entity added
or removed during a tick therefore cannot change that tick's iteration.**

**Per entity**, `ServerLevel`'s `forEach` body, in order:

```text
  if (entity.isRemoved()) return;
  if (tickRateManager.isEntityFrozen(entity)) return;
  entity.checkDespawn();
  if (<gated>) if (!distanceManager.inEntityTickingRange(entity.chunkPosition())) return;
  Entity vehicle = entity.getVehicle();
  if (vehicle != null) {
      if (!vehicle.isRemoved() && vehicle.hasPassenger(entity)) return;  // its vehicle ticks it
      entity.stopRiding();
  }
  guardEntityTick(this::tickNonPassenger, entity);
```

and `tickNonPassenger` is `setOldPosAndRot()`, **then** `tick()`, **then**
`tickPassenger(vehicle, p)` for each `getPassengers()` in list order,
recursively. So a passenger ticks after its vehicle and never on its own.

Not yet read: `guardEntityTick`'s crash handling, `Entity.tick` itself, and
`inEntityTickingRange`'s gate condition at offset 40.

**Blocks cascade and something ticks.** Both measured over a socket by
`ci/dig-probe.py` against a running server:

```text
  rig:        block_update minecraft:stone at (9, 62, 8), ack 12
  torch:      block_update minecraft:torch at (9, 63, 8), ack 13
  cascade:    block_update minecraft:air at (9, 62, 8) took the torch
              at (9, 63, 8), ack 14
  coral:      block_update minecraft:fire_coral_block at (9, 63, 8), ack 17
  tick:       minecraft:dead_fire_coral_block at (9, 63, 8) 3.2s later,
              unprompted
```

"Unprompted" is the claim in that last line: between the placement and the
death the probe sends nothing but keep-alive replies. It is the first
`block_update` this server has ever emitted that no packet asked for.

**`updateShape` is a table, extracted** (`cc4e92f`).
`tools/goldengen/vanilla/ShapeGolden.java` puts each of the 32,366 states in
a level that answers **two** positions and throws for a third, then sweeps
the neighbour over every state in the game — 84 s on the Threadripper, run
twice, byte-identical.

```text
  32366 states, 103318 sensitive (state, direction) pairs
  12716 carried, 11491 connective, 79111 refused
  119 distinct neighbour sets        # 3.4 MB, loaded once per process
```

Carried is the destruction family. Connective is fences and stairs choosing
how to join — the same gap `placement.json` names as its 195
neighbour-sensitive blocks. Refused is a rule that read more of the world
than its own neighbour; 48,993 read the block **above**. The correction worth
remembering: the harness first refused 10,563 pairs for reading
`getBlockEntity`, which made the *torch* unanswerable — a **shulker box** as
the candidate ground was the cause, and handing back
`EntityBlock.newBlockEntity` took the carried set from 2,510 to 12,716.

**Ticks are the machinery plus one behaviour, and the limit is an oracle.**
`Block.tick` takes a **`ServerLevel`** — a class, not an interface — so the
`Proxy` trick that made `getStateForPlacement` and `updateShape` extractable
does not work on it. `crate::ticks` is therefore `LevelTicks` done properly
(`DRAIN_ORDER` = trigger, priority, then a sub-tick counter; one tick per
`(pos, type)`; the state re-read at fire time) plus `CoralBlock`, whose whole
rule is three lines of bytecode and whose `deadBlock` was read by reflection
rather than derived from the name.

**Three bytecode details a plausible reimplementation gets wrong:**
`UPDATE_SHAPE_ORDER` is `WEST, EAST, NORTH, SOUTH, DOWN, UP` and not
`Direction.values()`; the direction handed to `updateShape` points **back**
at the block that changed, so passing `d` instead of `d.getOpposite()`
inverts every wall torch; and a dig writes
`getFluidState(pos).createLegacyBlock()`, not air, so breaking water is a
no-op instead of draining the ocean a block at a time.

**`RUSTMC_TRACE_TICKS=1` earned itself on its first run.** The coral was
placed and nothing happened; the trace said `water true — North=water[level=0]
East=water[level=0]`. The seed-0 spawn is a **shoreline** and the probe's rig
square is in it, so the server was right and the probe was standing in the
sea. The check puts the coral one block up now. Note also that the first
version of the trace sat *after* the early return it needed to explain and
printed nothing at all — an instrument has to be placed before the branch it
is there to decide.

**Also fixed, out of order because it gated all three tracks** (`21166de`):
`player::tests` failed **21 runs in 40**. Four tests shared one temp path —
`temp_dir()/rustmc-items-<pid>/items.json` — `cargo test` runs a module's
tests on parallel threads in one process, `fs::write` truncates before it
writes, and a read landing inside another test's truncate got an empty file.
`ItemIds::parse(&Value)` split from `load(&Path)` takes the filesystem out.
**60 consecutive runs, 0 failures.**

**For the worldgen track, because it is not mine to fix:**
`DECORATION_MARGIN` does not converge at seed 0. `tests/margin_probe.rs`
regenerates chunk (0,0) inside areas of 2 to 7 rings and the column at (8,8)
reads **74, 74, 62, 74, 62, 62**, with 24 to 334 blocks moving between one
context and the next. It **oscillates** rather than converging. At seed
20260722 the same comparison is **0 differences over 196,608 blocks**
(`tests/tiled_world.rs`), so it is seed-dependent. Reproduce with
`RUSTMC_MARGIN_PROBE=1 RUSTMC_MARGIN_SEED=<seed> cargo test --release -p
rustmc-server --test margin_probe -- --nocapture`. Write-up in
`docs/SERVER.md`, "The finding".

> **Taken up and closed by the worldgen track, 2026-08-12, branch
> `worldgen-decoration-margin` — and the seed-0 numbers above no longer
> reproduce.** Re-run at `d049ef5a`: seed 0's column at (8,8) is **74 at every
> context** and moves 2, 0, 0, 0, 0. The generator has moved since. What is
> real is worse: **no margin width converges at all**, at any seed, because a
> tile's rim sits at depth `DECORATION_MARGIN` below the outermost ring it
> decorated whatever the margin is. Seed 12345 moves 40, 56, 41, 29, 33 on the
> same rungs. `docs/DETERMINISM.md` §31.

What is left, in the order it matters to a player standing in the world:

1. **No inventory.** One hotbar slot is remembered from
   `set_creative_mode_slot` and nothing else: no container, no counts,
   nothing consumed, and a **survival** player has nothing to place at all.
   The client is never told what it is holding, which needs the `ItemStack`
   stream codec — count, item id, then the added/removed component lists —
   and that wants a capture rather than a reading, like every other packet
   here.
2. **Random ticks.** Vanilla picks positions per section per tick under
   `randomTickSpeed`; the *selection* is portable and the behaviours behind
   it (crops, fire, ice, leaf decay) are the same `ServerLevel` oracle
   problem as `Block.tick`. Worth doing selection-first and saying what it
   cannot yet serve.
3. **No `neighborChanged`.** The redstone half of a block update. Its flag is
   carried and honoured through every level of `crate::shapes`, so this is
   filling in one branch rather than finding where it goes.
4. **No block entities**, so a generated chest is empty and a door places only
   its lower half — `DoorBlock.setPlacedBy` writes the upper one with a second
   `setBlockAndUpdate` that `getStateForPlacement` does not describe. Every
   multi-block block is also in the shape table's *refused* set, so breaking
   the bottom of a door leaves the top.
5. **A second player is never *seen*.** No `player_info_update`, no
   `add_entity`. The list entry has to precede the entity, and the entity
   needs metadata and a movement relay.
6. ~~**Nothing is saved**~~ — closed 2026-08-05, branch `chunk-persistence`:
   `--world <dir>` saves edited chunks as real Anvil and loads them back, and
   vanilla can open the result (`ci/t2-vanilla-loads-ours.sh`). **Nothing
   retires a tile** still holds, so a long walk still grows memory without
   bound.

**The command that demonstrates the current state:**

```text
  ./ci/shape-golden.sh                       # once, ~84s, Threadripper
  ./target/release/rustmc-server run --port 25619 --radius 2
  ./ci/dig-probe.py 127.0.0.1 25619 Walker
```

**What it prints now**, measured 2026-07-28 on the Threadripper:

```text

    break:      block_update minecraft:air at (8, 62, 8), ack 1
    place:      block_update minecraft:stone at (8, 62, 8), ack 2
    axis:       block_update minecraft:oak_log[axis=x] at (9, 62, 8), ack 4
    oak_stairs: block_update minecraft:oak_stairs[facing=east,...] ack 6
    furnace:    block_update minecraft:furnace[facing=west,lit=false] ack 8
    redstone:   block_update minecraft:redstone_wire[east=side,...] ack 10
    rig:        block_update minecraft:stone at (9, 62, 8), ack 12
    torch:      block_update minecraft:torch at (9, 63, 8), ack 13
    cascade:    block_update minecraft:air at (9, 62, 8) took the torch
                at (9, 63, 8), ack 14
    coral:      block_update minecraft:fire_coral_block at (9, 63, 8), ack 17
    tick:       minecraft:dead_fire_coral_block at (9, 63, 8) 3.2s later,
                unprompted
    grew:       chunk (3, -2) arrived 0.0s after walking out
```

**The next increment closes when** a survival player places a block out of a
stack that runs out — an inventory with counts, and a client that is told
what is in it.

**Gate:** `RUSTMC_REMOTE_DIR=rustmc-server ./ci/t0-remote.sh`. The
`RUSTMC_REMOTE_DIR` is not optional while two agents share the machine — both
default to `threadripper:rustmc` and rsync `--delete` into it, which cost one
run here. `docs/SERVER.md` has the one-time command that gives a private
remote directory the extract it needs; `data/vanilla/placement.json` and
`data/vanilla/update_shape.json` are two more files that have to be there, or
every placement silently takes the block's default state and nothing
cascades.

### The plugin API is 0.3.0 as of 2026-08-09 — what that costs a server branch

*(Appended by the `api-0.3-seal` agent. Self-contained; nothing above is
mine and nothing above was edited.)*

`grit-plugin-api` landed its irreversibility seal on the plugins repo's `main`
(`f31a805`). It is a **path dependency with no version resolution between the
repos**, so there is nothing to absorb a mismatch: every server tree builds
against whatever `../plugins` currently is.

**What this means for a branch: rebase onto `main` before you gate, or T0 dies
at six `E0639 cannot create non-exhaustive struct using struct expression`.**
`Manifest` is `#[non_exhaustive]` now, and the six struct literals it breaks
were migrated to `Manifest::new(..).requires(..)` on `main` in `8146d510`.
Measured 2026-08-09: **69 of the 75 branches on `origin` did not contain
`8146d510`** at the moment the seal landed. That is not a queue of 69 breakages
— `ci/handoff.sh` already refuses a branch behind `main` with `exit 3` and the
remedy in the message — but it does mean "rebase before gating" stopped being
advice and became a compile error, and a branch that fails this way is not
broken.

Nothing else in the seal touches this repo, and that was surveyed before it
landed rather than after: over the five files here that name `grit_plugin_api`
at all, the server uses **none** of `PluginScope`, `Ctx::enter_plugin`,
`Ctx::leave_plugin`, `Refused`, `RegisterError`, `IdError`, `LoadError`,
`ApiVersion` or `Pose`; its `Priority::Normal` and `BatchSummary::default()`
uses stay legal under `#[non_exhaustive]`; and all five `setup.events()` call
sites are `.on::<E, _>(..)`, which the new `Registrar` provides. The
item-by-item inventory is in the plugins repo's `docs/CONTRACT.md` §4b.

**One thing here is still open, and it is a gate hole rather than a defect.**
The plugins repo's `host-proof/` is the only crate that compiles against both
repos, and on 2026-08-09 it was found **already broken** — the server's
`a5dcc7b1` changed `shapes::set_block`'s last argument from
`&mut Vec<(BlockPos, i32)>` to `&mut shapes::Effects`, and `host-proof` is the
only caller of that function outside this repo. It went red in both repos'
green, because `ci/t0.sh` builds this workspace and `host-proof` is not in it,
while the plugins repo's own `cargo test --workspace` deliberately excludes it.
Repaired on the plugins side. **Nothing yet gates it**, so the next signature
change to a `pub` server function that `host-proof` names will do this again,
silently. The cheap fix is a stage that builds `../plugins/host-proof` after
T0 — the sibling is already on the box, and the build is seconds once the
server workspace is warm. Not done here because adding a stage to `ci/t0.sh`
makes every agent's gate depend on it and that is the orchestrator's call, not
a passing agent's.

### 2026-08-12 (branch `worldgen-sulfur-r18`, off `main` d049ef5a) — THE 35 SURVIVE A SECOND GENERATION: ADJUDICATED AT r=18 AGAINST A FLOOR OF 0 THE TWINS MEASURED THEMSELVES

**BASE SHA `d049ef5a9c504ce61af44b939c7b19b0d9fe4b65`**, and it is the first
line because the result depends on it. `worldgen-decoration-margin` is live on
whether `DECORATION_MARGIN = 2` converges; **at this sha that branch points at
exactly `d049ef5a` and `DECORATION_MARGIN` is still 2**, so nothing of its has
landed and this was measured against a generator that still exists. A
behavioural change from it landing *later* voids every number below.

**The question `sulfur-cinnabar-r19` left open, answered.** All forty r=16
references complete chunks 46..82 only, so chunk (77,47) sat **one ring inside
the completed edge** and its 35 `sulfur -> cinnabar` could have been the
references measuring their own truncation — a blind spot the pool cannot see,
because all forty are truncated identically. Two independent r=18 vanilla runs
(`gen-wide-12345-r18-ow-x1`, `-x2`, harvested 2026-08-11, identical in every
`HARVEST-ORDER` parameter) complete **44..84**, which puts the chunk **three
rings in**.

**The answer: 35, to the block, against a floor of 0.** `docs/DETERMINISM.md`
§34. The chunk's total charge moves 49 -> 51 and both new positions are
`gold_ore -> deepslate_gold_ore`, which is the pool falling N=40 -> N=2 (the
charge is monotone decreasing in N) and not the radius. The row itself does not
move.

**The floor is the twins' own, never inherited and never subtracted.** Over
`44 44 84 84` (1,681 chunks, the widest square both twins are `minecraft:full`
across, and exactly what `worldgen-dump full 12345 20` writes) the twins
disagree by **28,668** of 165,249,024. **On chunk (77,47) they disagree by 0 of
98,304** — they reproduce it block for block. Our charge on the window is
47,237 / 47,851, which is 1.65x the floor, so **the window carries no exactness
level**; it is registered `quotable = false`.

**The coverage refusal FIRED, watched rather than asserted** — three paths, all
rc=3: `ref-chunk-extent.py --window 43 43 85 85` on the twins (168 of 1,849 at
`initialize_light`), `--window 44 44 84 84` on our r=16 dump (592 of 1,681
absent), and `refs-12345-widen2.sh charge` end to end. **And the silent failure
it prevents was measured:** `region-differ diff x1 <our r=16 dump>` reports
`chunks=1089 blocks=107053056 mismatches=10650` on `48 48 80 80` **and the
identical numbers on `44 44 84 84`**. A window 54% larger scored not one extra
chunk and said nothing about it.

**Nulls and controls — do not re-run these.**

* **Extending the dumper is not a code change.** `worldgen-dump full 12345 R`
  already writes `[64-R, 64+R]`; r=20 covers the twins' completed extent. 95 s
  at `RUSTMC_WORKERS=1`.
* **The tip did not move the generator.** Our r=20 dump at `d049ef5a` is
  byte-identical in every region file to the `31e4615f` one, and
  `git diff 31e4615f d049ef5a -- crates/rustmc-worldgen/ tools/` is empty.

### 2026-08-10 (branch `worldgen-sulfur-cluster-bounds`, off `worldgen-sulfur-cinnabar-order` a17daf5d) — THE SCAN BOUNDS ARE CLEAN, SO THE MINESHAFT LEAD IS DEAD AND THE CENSUS THAT FOUND IT WAS STRUCTURALLY BLIND

**Read the block below this one first for the baseline; it is unchanged and
still the figure to beat. 312 charged against a binding floor of 3 (104x),
measured on tip 8c7e024c.**

**Null, paid for and written up — do not re-run it.** A `javap` read of
`net/minecraft/world/level/levelgen/Column.class` settles the arithmetic
question §21 left open. `Column.scan` anchors on the column's own `getY()`,
hands that same integer to both `scanDirection` calls, and `scanDirection`
re-anchors with `setY(startY)` and walks `i = 1; while (i < range && ...)`.
**No clamp, no offset, no alternate anchor anywhere in the method.** Our
`scan`/`scan_direction` at `speleothem_cluster.rs:252-284` are identical, and
so are `place` and `placeColumn` throughout — including the unconditional
`nextBoolean()` before the merge conjunction.

So a cluster with origins at y 13..24 and `floor_to_ceiling_search_range: 12`
sees **y 2..35 and nothing else, in vanilla exactly as in ours**. The
`oak_planks`/`rail` at y −44..−43 are 57 blocks outside that and **cannot be
the mechanism**. §21's first branch — "the scan is reaching further than its
own range says" — is dead.

**And the reason the census could not find the real cause is structural, which
is the more useful half.** That census diffed *our own two chunk orders*.
Chunk (78,47) decorates identically in both — only its *timing* moves — so
anything our code writes there is present in both arms and cancels. **An
ours-vs-ours order diff can only ever show the downstream damage, never the
interfering write.** The planks showed up because they were the only thing
left in the part of the column a whole-column census printed.

**THE MECHANISM, MEASURED END TO END — `docs/DETERMINISM.md` §21 has the
working.** Diffing the (77,48) cluster's read *positions* (not states) across
the two orders, the arms fork at column **(1247,24,766)**: `zx` does two reads
and abandons, `default` scans fully. Two reads is `is_empty_or_water`
answering false. The block is a
`sulfur_spike[thickness=tip,vertical_direction=down]` written by
**`minecraft:sulfur_spike` from chunk (78,47)** — legal in principle, its
`random_offset` `xz_spread` is `clamped_normal(0, 3, −10..10)` — and under
`zx` it lands *before* (77,48) decorates. `Column.scan`'s guard fails, the
column is abandoned **before a single draw**, and every column deleted that
way costs the cluster its draws. That is the 1,081-vs-2,721 shift.

**The row is a covering failure, not a misplacement.** Nothing in decoration
writes `cinnabar` at all — 0 of 624 in-box writes under `zx`, 0 of 757 under
`default`. Cinnabar is laid down in the noise stage. So `sulfur -> cinnabar`
can only mean vanilla covered the block and our reshaped cluster did not, and
no reading of cinnabar-writing code could ever have explained it.

**Second defect, unrelated to the row and fixed here.**
`LevelReader#isWaterAt` is `getFluidState(pos).is(FluidTags.WATER)` and
`data/minecraft/tags/fluid/water.json` holds **`water` and `flowing_water`**.
We had that predicate written twice and the copies disagreed:
`speleothem_cluster`'s `canPlacePool` accepted both, the
`SpeleothemWorld::is_water_at` impl in `stage/decorate.rs` accepted only
`minecraft:water`. A speleothem crossing *flowing* water was left
un-waterlogged while a pool two blocks away was refused correctly, in the same
feature, from the same fluid. Now one `pub(crate) fn is_water_fluid` in
`feature/speleothem.rs` with both call sites pointed at it, and a unit test on
both tag members. **Block output only — no draw on either path — so it cannot
move a stream and it is NOT the cause of the 312.**

**The instrument.** `RUSTMC_TRACE_READS=x0,x1,y0,y1,z0,z1`
(`canvas.rs`, new) logs every canvas read in a box with the feature that
asked — the tree had instruments for "who wrote this block" and none for
"what did this feature see", and the second is the question when a feature's
*decision* diverged. `ci/sulfur-read-trace.sh` runs the same four chunks
(`RUSTMC_DECORATE_PREFIX=78,48,1`) under `zx` and `default` and diffs the read
logs; the first differing line is the interfering block by construction. It
needs **no vanilla reference**, which matters because (78,47) is at z=47 and
is outside the r=16 reference set entirely.

**THE DELTA IS 0 FOR THE WHOLE BRANCH, AND THE ROW IS UNCHANGED.** The branch
point `a17daf5d` was dumped and compared against both the instrument-only tip
and the final tip: `diff -rq` exit 0 both times, 4 region files each side. So
nothing on this branch moves a block on this window — **and in particular
`RUSTMC_TRACE_READS`, which is inserted into `Canvas::block_at` and
restructures its control flow, is output-inert as a measurement rather than as
an argument.** Had it not been, today's read-position trace would have been
measuring the instrument rather than the world.

Per-commit, `ci/waterlog-poison-control.sh`,
two dumps of ours differing only by a revert of the fix commit — seed 12345,
r=16, centre (64,64), `RUSTMC_DECORATE_ORDER=zx`, `RUSTMC_WORKERS=1`, 4 region
files each — compare **IDENTICAL**. So the `isWaterAt` fix is **byte-inert on
this window, 0 in either direction over the identical position set**, and
`sulfur -> cinnabar` still stands at **312 against a binding floor of 3**.
That baseline is the previous agent's on tip `8c7e024c` and was **not**
re-taken here. A gate a window cannot exercise proves nothing; this window
cannot exercise this fix, and that is the honest reading of the 0.

The control fires correctly rather than vacuously: each arm must produce
region files, `diff`'s exit code decides rather than its output length, and

— so IDENTICAL is a real tie, not two failures agreeing. **Its first version

```text

    charge          1,279 of 107,053,056      99.998805%
    innocent floor  0 .. 362   median 1       N = 39, forty rows references
    margin          3.53x on the max, 1,279x on the median
    quotable        TRUE
```

**No code moved.** It is the *same dump* as the 1,329 — `dump-zx`, stamped
`decorate-order: zx`, reused unchanged — so this is **not** a fidelity
improvement and must never be read as one. The ensemble is the only thing that
changed: the floor fell 141..2,241 -> 0..362 and the charge fell 1,329 -> 1,279
because adding references can only remove positions from an intersection.

**The control, which is the reason to believe it.** Restricted to the original
sixteen references the *same* `.pos` directory reproduces **141 / 590 / 2,241
and 1,329 to the block**, wired as a refusal. All forty carry `HARVEST-ORDER`
naming `gen_order=rows`/`dump_order=zx`, verified twice — by the harvest
script's gate and by hand.

**§24.9's registered prediction, scored — wrong in the expensive direction.**

```text
                  predicted        measured at n=40      miss
    max floor   1,135 / 1,262            362        3.1x / 3.5x too high
    median          102                    1           ~100x too high
    charge      ~1,329, falling         1,279            right
    n to convict at all  33-37            ~20
    n for a 2x margin    85-113          ~28-32
```

**Why the fit failed:** the floor is `sum_p (1-q_p)^N`, a sum of *exponentials*
in N. Over `n = 8..16` its heavy tail makes it look like a power law; past
`n ~ 25` every term collapses geometrically and it falls off a cliff. §24.2's
`rho = +0.826` still governs the **max** — which is why the max is 362 while the
median is 1 — but it does not stop the exponential. **Rule: a floor ladder
fitted on `n <= 16` and extrapolated past `n ~ 25` overstates the cost, in the
direction that stops a project buying something it can afford. Measure two
rungs past the crossing before quoting a price.**

**What it cost.** 24 references at min 58 / median 63 / max 72 s (~25 min of
exclusive corpus lock) + 48 anchor diffs in 137 s (2.85 s/diff). **77 diffs
total where the pair matrix would have been 1,560** — §24.7's anchor
construction, verified candidate-by-candidate before being trusted. Disk 528 MB.
The *wall* clock bore no relation: the first attempt sat 60 min in the lock
queue behind a 2-hour corpus run with a gate blocked 97 min, and generated
nothing.

**NULLS — do not re-run any of these.** y band (§24.4, every band worse on the
max); unanimous-only (§24.5, innocent runs score up to 2,169 unanimous — it
refuted a claim in two of our own docstrings, both corrected); a new nether
window (§24.8, floor 48 vs 95,240 one seed apart, so it is a biome artefact and
not a dimension fact; 31x worse per block at r=16); a new End r=16 window; a
fresh overworld seed. **What makes a good window is the BIOME** — feature
classes that read the world before they write — not the dimension, seed or
radius.

**One bug worth knowing about (§25.5):** `list(combinations(refs, n))` is fine
at 16 references and OOM-kills at 40 (`C(40,20)` = 1.4e11). Fixed. It is
invisible until the pool is big enough to matter.

**The cross-border `sulfur_spike` at (1247,24,766) — §24.11.** Chunk (77,47),
one south of the window. **The block is measured, not inferred: 18 of 18

r=16 references cannot fix it; the geometry excludes it. Costed: **r=19 centre

comparable — 2 refs (~3 min) for rule 6 with margin, 16 refs ~21 min + ~2 min
of diffs, **floor measured fresh, never carried from r=16**.

**The single next item.** The window adjudicates again, so the worklist is no

|---|---|---|---|

**What it was.** `IcebergFeature#generateIcebergBlock` and `#carve` each guard
their body with Java's `if (d1 < 0.0)`. The port inverted each into an early
`if (d1 >= 0.0) { return; }`. The two agree on every value except **NaN**,
which fails `<` and `>=` alike, so Java skips the body and the inverted guard
falls into it. `signedDistanceEllipse` divides by its major and minor axes; the
keel's major is `Mth.ceil(half * (1 - y^2 / (depth * 8)))`, which passes through
**zero** on the slice where `y^2` crosses `depth * 8`, and at the berg's own
centre column `dx == dz == 0` — so that slice evaluates `0.0 / 0.0`.

**The cost is the rest of the feature, not one block.** Falling into the body
spends a `nextDouble` vanilla never draws. Against vanilla's own execution the
two draw sequences agree for **6,865 draws** and part at draw **6,866**. That is
why a 912-block confusion pair was worth 1,788: `packed_ice -> air` (400) and
`air -> packed_ice` (310), killed last turn as unadjudicable because `air`
carries floors of 406 and 579, were the same defect. **Inside its floor means
the window cannot convict a row, not that the row is innocent.**

**Two defects, and two poison controls to separate them.**

| poison | charge | poison-not-base | base-not-poison |
|---|---|---|---|
| revert `generate_iceberg_block` only | 3,038 | 0 | 75 |
| revert `carve` only | 1,398 | 4 | 1,719 |
| revert **both** | **3,113** | **0** | **0** |
| revert **both**, on the restacked tip | **3,117** | **0** | **0** |

Reverting one arm cannot return to 3,113, and the attempt is what proved there
are two: the first line recovers 3,038 as a **strict subset** of the base and
the `carve` guard is worth the other 75. The both-arms line fires byte-exact
over the identical position set and re-derives the 3,113 on **this** tree, so
the delta is between two measurements taken the same way rather than against an
inherited number.

**The linter pushes towards the wrong spelling**, which is probably how it was
born: `clippy::neg_cmp_op_on_partial_ord` rejects the faithful
`!(d < 0.0)` under `-D warnings`, and the obvious fix is `>= 0.0`. The repair
is not an `#[allow]` — the body is nested inside a positive `if d < 0.0`,
vanilla's own shape, which satisfies the lint with no suppression and leaves
nothing negated for the next reader to be advised to rewrite. **Port any Java

#### DEFECT 1 — a mushroom is not a `VegetationBlock` (33 blocks, commit 5041a85b)

```text
  air         -> brown_mushroom   30 -> 0
  short_grass -> brown_mushroom    2 -> 0
  air         -> red_mushroom      1 -> 0

  brown_mushroom in the window   vanilla 0   ours 32 -> 0
  red_mushroom   in the window   vanilla 28  ours 29 -> 28
```

**Not a displacement — there is no reciprocal row anywhere in the charge.**
Vanilla holds zero brown mushrooms in 1,089 chunks; we held 32 in four
patches, at the rate `brown_mushroom_normal`'s `rarity_filter` of 256
predicts.

`family_of` filed both mushrooms under `Family::Vegetation`
(`belowState.is(#supports_vegetation)`), and the doc beside it said the
mushrooms' own light check "only widens the answer". Both halves are false:

```text
  MushroomBlock#canSurvive
    belowState.is(#overrides_mushroom_light_requirement)   -> true
    else getRawBrightness(pos, 0) < 13 && mayPlaceOn(belowState, ..)
  MushroomBlock#mayPlaceOn  =  belowState.isSolidRender()
```

The light term is a **conjunction**, so it narrows; and `mayPlaceOn` is
*overridden* away from the vegetation tag. The two errors do not cancel.

**During decoration that light term can never pass, and that is read out of
the jar rather than assumed.** `ChunkPyramid`'s generation pyramid runs
`FEATURES` before `INITIALIZE_LIGHT` and `LIGHT`, so the chunk has no sky
data; `SkyLightSectionStorage.getLightValue` returns **15** for a column whose
`topSections.get(..) == currentLowestY` — `bipush 15; ireturn`, never reaching
a data layer — and `LevelLightEngine.getRawBrightness` is
`max(block 0, sky 15)`. So the four-block tag decides every worldgen mushroom.
Corroborated: **all 28 mushrooms vanilla places in this window stand on
podzol.**

`SurvivalWorld::raw_brightness` is new, defaults to `None`, and is answered
only by a decorating world (`decorate::WORLDGEN_RAW_BRIGHTNESS`). A runtime
placer answers `None` and gets `Survival::Unknown` rather than a guess —
`rustmc-behavior` is shared with the server, where light is real.

**THE GATE THAT COULD NOT FAIL.** `data/vanilla/survival.json` had recorded
the truth since it was generated: `brown_mushroom` on `grass_block` is
`survives: null, reads: canSurvive read LevelReader.getRawBrightness/2`.
`golden_survival` **skipped** every such row on the stated grounds that
"nothing can be learned there" — so a port that *answered* an unanswerable row
was never checked. It is now an assertion in the other direction: where the
oracle could not be shown enough of the world, the port must decline too.

```text
  SURVIVAL: 991 answered and 100.000000% correct, 117 unported,
            65 the oracle could not show and this port correctly declines
```

#### DEFECT 2 — `getRandomFacingStairs` draws HALF too (14 blocks, commit 97532e8f)

The ruined portal at (768..776, 42..50, 1032..1039). **The census named it
before any code was read:** every stair we emitted inside it was
`facing=north, half=bottom` — the blockstate default — against vanilla's
north/south/east and top/bottom.

`BlockAgeProcessor.getRandomFacingStairs` sets `StairBlock.FACING` from
`Direction$Plane.HORIZONTAL.getRandomDirection(random)` **and then**
`StairBlock.HALF` from `Util.getRandom(Half.values(), random)`, which is
`array[nextInt(2)]`; `Half.values()` is `[TOP, BOTTOM]`, so index 0 is `top`
and `bottom` is the default. We drew only the facing, so every such stair
carried the default half **and** the stream ran one draw short —
and `maybeReplaceFullStoneBlock` calls it twice while building both candidate
arrays, so a qualifying stone block ran **two** draws short and the
`getRandomBlock` after it was desynchronised. That is why the symptom was not
only wrong stair halves but `mossy_stone_bricks` where vanilla has
`cracked_stone_bricks`.

**This is the defect the earlier one hid.** The two eager
`getRandomFacingStairs` calls were already found and fixed; making the array
building eager settled the draw *count per call* and made it look deliberate.
The doc comment said "five draws, two of them on the array that loses" and two
unit tests asserted that five-draw tape — code, comment and tests all saying
the same wrong thing, so nothing could disagree. It is **seven** draws, four
of them on the losing array, and `the_half_draw_indexes_top_first` now pins
the enum order.

#### DEFECT 3 — a crossing pillar asks `isAir()`, we asked for a name (6 blocks, same commit)

Two 3-tall `oak_planks` pillars at (1158, -38..-36, 894) and (1160, …), in
open cave, where both references hold `cave_air`.

`MineShaftCrossing.placeSupportPillar` places a corner pillar only when
`getBlock(level, x, height + 1, z, box).isAir()` is **false**. Ours read
`w.get_block(..) != "minecraft:air"`. A crossing sits in a corridor system the
carvers have usually opened, so the block over its corners is `cave_air` —
air to vanilla, not to a name test.

`writer::is_air` already existed and already covered `cave_air` and
`void_air`, and **`place_chest` thirty lines above it in the same file carries
a comment about being caught by exactly this, on exactly this block, for
exactly this reason.** The correction did not travel the length of one file.
Third time this project has paid for a state-or-name comparison standing in
for a vanilla predicate (`has_grass`, the chest, this).

#### POISON CONTROLS — and the mushroom item's coverage is thinner than it looks

**A. Mushrooms in `Family::Vegetation` with the light gate merely conjoined** —
no tag short-circuit, `#supports_vegetation` as the support test. The
prediction written down before running it was that this convicts, because
`podzol` is in `#supports_vegetation` and a light of 15 would then kill the 28
mushrooms vanilla *does* place.

```text
  N=8 admissible charge   13,509      IDENTICAL to the correct fix
    no longer charged           53      the same 53
    NEWLY charged                0
```

**The prediction was wrong and the reason is worth more than the control.**
`RUSTMC_TRACE_PATCH=1` over chunk (71,53), which holds five of them, emits
**1,070 `SIMPLE` lines and not one names `red_mushroom`** — while the same
trace does name `brown_mushroom`, so the instrument is live. Every underground
mushroom in this window is placed by something that never calls
`SimpleBlockFeature`, and therefore never asks `canSurvive` at all. **Nothing
in this window routes a mushroom over a tag block through the rule**, so the
tag short-circuit is unexercised and this control cannot fail here.

**B. The tag short-circuit and no light term at all.**

```text
  diff -rq against the correct fix, 1,089 chunks: BYTE-IDENTICAL
```

**A2. The light comparison inverted** (`light < 13 -> No`), which ought to be
the crudest possible way to get this wrong.

```text
  N=8 admissible charge   13,509      IDENTICAL to the correct fix
```

Identical because 15 fails the inverted test and falls through to the
`Some(_) => Survival::Unknown` arm, and an `Unknown` refuses just as a `No`
does.

**So state it plainly rather than banking a green delta: this window
adjudicates exactly one bit of `MushroomBlock#canSurvive` — that a mushroom
must not survive at a lit surface over `grass_block`.** It cannot distinguish
the real rule from "tag or refuse", from "light only", or from an inverted
comparison; every variant that declines produces the same 1,089 chunks. The
33 blocks are closed and the *old* rule is convicted by 33, but the shape of
the new one rests on the bytecode, not on this measurement. A window holding a
mushroom over a non-tag block in genuine darkness would test the rest; there
is no such case here, and the `isSolidRender()` half of `mayPlaceOn` is
reached by nothing at all.

**C. Stairs: spend the HALF draw but discard its value** (always `bottom`) —
separating "the stream ran short" from "the value was wrong". This one could
fail, and did.

```text
  N=8 admissible charge   13,515      (correct fix 13,509, baseline 13,562)
    no longer charged           47      NEWLY charged 0
    still charged                6      of the ruined portal's 14
```

**It splits the defect exactly.** The missing *draw* accounts for 8 of the 14
and the discarded *value* for the other 6 — and those 6 are precisely the
cells where vanilla's stair is `half=top`:

```text
  2  stone_brick_stairs[north,top]        -> stone_brick_stairs[north,bottom]
  2  mossy_stone_brick_stairs[south,top]  -> cracked_stone_bricks
  1  stone_brick_stairs[south,top]        -> cracked_stone_bricks
  1  stone_brick_stairs[east,top]         -> cracked_stone_bricks
```

So the window adjudicates both halves of that fix independently, which is more
than it does for the mushroom.

**D. Neither structure fix is a disablement**, which a green delta would not
show:

```text

  stone_brick_stairs          7         4        7
```

#### THE 5, ATTRIBUTED BUT NOT CLOSED

At (790,64,950), (791,64,950), (792,64,948), (792,64,950) — one patch in chunk

Measured, not reasoned: `RUSTMC_TRACE_PATCH=1` shows

empty when the patch ran. It then becomes `acacia_leaves` in all three worlds,

**That ordering is correct, and it is the point.** Savanna's
`VEGETAL_DECORATION` list is `glow_lichen, patch_tall_grass, trees_savanna,
flower_warm, patch_grass_savanna, …` — `patch_tall_grass` genuinely runs

ordering defect. Vanilla holds `air` at two of the cells and `short_grass` at
the other two, the latter from `patch_grass_savanna` at index 4, which could
only land because vanilla's `patch_tall_grass` left those cells empty.

So the divergence is **inside `patch_tall_grass`** — its `rarity_filter` 5 /
`count` 96 / trapezoid `random_offset` chain, or the stream feeding it.

**It is invisible to `ci/order-stability.sh` by construction and that is a
limitation of the instrument, stated here rather than left to be re-derived:**
both features are in the same chunk, so chunk-visitation order can never
separate them. The order-stable filter certifies nothing about intra-chunk
feature order or intra-feature stream position.

### 2026-08-10 (branch `worldgen-spruce-leaves`, off `worldgen-12345-residual-census` 1979b091) — THE SPRUCE CANOPY WAS ONE OR TWO ROWS SHORT ON TWO THIRDS OF EVERY SPRUCE TREE, AND THE FLOOR IT WAS BRIEFED AGAINST WAS NOT ZERO

**Two things, and the first one changes how the second should be read.**

#### 1. THE BRIEFED PREMISE WAS WRONG — `spruce_leaves` is 1,293 against 262, not 1,422 against 0

The brief opened "1,422 blocks against a per-block floor of exactly zero — a
floor of zero means every one of the sixteen vanilla references agrees,
position for position, so all 1,422 are defects, not noise." **The floor is not
zero and that sentence was never true of `spruce_leaves`.**

`ci/floor-tables/ow-r16-12345-rows-n15.toml` keys every row on the full block
STATE. The script that produced the published ranking pooled the CHARGE to the
bare block name with `s.split("[")[0]` and looked that up in the state-keyed
table, so every stateful block missed its key and `dict.get(name, 0)` returned
the table's documented "never charged" default of **zero**. Fourteen of the
twenty-eight published rows were affected, all in the same direction, because a
missing floor always reads as a clean one. The rows that were right are exactly
the single-state blocks, which is why the table looked plausible.

Re-taken with charge and floor under one key function
(`ci/rank-block-floor.py`, charge 7,490 at N=16, floor leave-one-out N=15,
pool c..r):

```text
  MISS     spruce_leaves 1,293 / 262   4.9x     snow        443 / 182  2.4x
           water           617 /  39  15.8x     grass_block 350 / 134  2.6x
           deepslate       453 /  23  19.7x     air       1,553 / 579  2.7x
  SURPLUS  spruce_leaves 1,021 / 426   2.4x     spruce_log  120 /  54  2.2x
  GENUINE ZEROS, unaffected: blue_ice 67 / 0, sulfur_spike 116 / 0
```

**The item survives** — 4.9x is still the largest adjudicating named item on
this window — but it is a MOVED tree, not a missing one, and it was never the
unambiguous thing the brief described.

**Positionally, before any bytecode** (`ci/residual-census.py`, N=6, charge
7,606 reproduced): the spruce charge is 1,422 miss and 1,024 surplus, of which
**322 positions hold `spruce_leaves` on BOTH sides and differ only in
`distance`** — and those differences are symmetric (2->1 67, 1->2 56, 2->3 55,
3->2 46), so nothing is systematically off by one. All 1,422 sit at y 64..79
in 21 chunks, 92.8% of them in the two outermost rings, clustered at (49,48)
274, (50,48) 185, (48,48) 156, (48,50) 105. `spruce_log` moves both ways too
(air -> spruce_log 88, spruce_log -> air 45).

#### 2. THE DEFECT — `SpruceFoliagePlacer` stops at `-foliageHeight`, and we stopped at `offset - foliageHeight`

From `javap -p -c -constants` on the pinned 26.2 jar. Spruce is the odd one
out and the whole difference is one instruction:

```text
  BlobFoliagePlacer     6: iload 9 (offset)   8: iload 7   10: isub
  PineFoliagePlacer     9: iload 9 (offset)  11: iload 7   [isub]
  SpruceFoliagePlacer                        28: iload 7   30: ineg
```

There is no `offset` load at all in the spruce comparison. Blob, pine and bush
move a fixed-height canopy up and down by `offset`; spruce anchors its bottom
row at `-foliageHeight` and lets a nonzero offset make the canopy **taller**.
`spruce.json` samples `offset` from `uniform 0..2`, so this was wrong on about
two thirds of every spruce tree in the world, short by one or two rows each.
And because `place_leaves_row` draws for the corner cut, the missing rows also
shifted the RNG stream for every feature decorated after the tree in the same
chunk — which is why logs move and why 322 leaves differ only in `distance`.

**CHECKED AND NOT DEFECTIVE — do not re-run these.** `foliageHeight` is
`max(4, treeHeight - trunkHeight.sample(random))` and matches;
`shouldSkipLocation` is `x == range && z == range && range > 0`, takes no
draw, and matches; `shouldSkipLocationSigned`'s double-trunk
`min(abs(x), abs(x-1))` matches; `placeLeavesRow`'s `-range..=range+extra`
bounds match; the base `FoliagePlacer.createFoliage` samples `offset` last,
immediately before dispatch, which is where our arm samples it; and
`TreeFeature.doPlace`'s draw order is `getTreeHeight -> foliageHeight ->
foliageRadius -> getMaxFreeTreeHeight -> placeTrunk -> forEach(createFoliage)`,
which is ours exactly. **`giant_trunk_placer` and `mega_pine_foliage_placer`
are still unimplemented so mega spruce does not generate** — a separate gap,
and both configs carry `offset: 0` so this defect would not have bitten them.

**The gate that did not exist.** `a_spruce_foliage_height_draws_and_a_blobs_does_not`
and `a_conifer_corner_costs_no_draw` both cover this placer and both passed
throughout, because neither looks at how many rows there are.
`a_spruce_canopy_reaches_below_its_attachment_by_the_offset` pins the lowest
row at offsets 0, 1 and 2, pins it again at a second foliage height so it
cannot pass by the bound being hard-wired, and asserts the blob contrast.
Falsified by reverting the one instruction on the box: **offset 0 still passes
— the two forms agree there, which is exactly why this hid — and offset 1
reads -3 against -4.**

#### What was actually missing — three things, and only one of them was a feature

1. **The piece stream stood still.** `place_piece` already modelled
   `StructureTemplate.placeInWorld`'s one draw — `LootTableSeed =
   random.nextLong()` for each placed `RandomizableContainer` — and every
   village call site handed it `None`. Read out of the bytecode: that
   `nextLong` is the **only** `RandomSource` call on the whole
   single-pool-element placement path. `getRandomPalette` and
   `RuleProcessor.processBlock` build their own from `Mth.getSeed(pos)`,
   `processBlockInfos` takes no random at all, and all three savanna
   processor lists are `minecraft:rule` only.
2. **`minecraft:block_pile` was unimplemented**, along with
   `rotated_block_provider`. Commit 73a03d6f.
3. **The invocation.** `FeaturePoolElement.place` is one call. The comment in
   `place_village_in_chunk` said the blocker was an unmeasured stream index —
   and that had already stopped being true: `structure_step_indices()` derives
   it, and the ruined portals four screens above were already seeding off it.
   **A caveat that outlived its own fix, reading as authoritative.**

#### The controls, and the one that fired

* **Stream change alone: byte-identical, 0 positions moved either way.** The
  drawn `LootTableSeed` is discarded, so this had to be block-neutral, and it
  is — `diff -rq` over 1,089 chunks. It is a confirmed prediction, not a
  poison control, and it is not banked as one.
* **The coupling control fired, which is the finding.** The acacia at idx58
  and a hay pile at idx45 are **in the same chunk (80,74)**, and 45 sorts
  before 58, so the tree's stream position depends on the pile having spent
  its draws first. Placing the acacia *without* the pile was predicted not to
  close its 65 — and it does not:

  ```text
    acacia only   13,548 -> 13,601     -4 closed, +57 NEWLY charged, net +53
    hay only      13,548 -> 13,514    -34 closed,   0 newly charged
    both          13,548 -> 13,449    -99 closed,   0 newly charged
  ```

  The 57 are **55 `air -> acacia_leaves` and 2 `air -> acacia_log`, at
  x 1287..1293, y 66..68** — a whole tree, standing where vanilla has air. A
  tree on the wrong stream position is **worse than no tree**: it costs two
  mismatches per block instead of one. This is why the elements were ported
  cheapest-per-block but *measured* in stream order, and it is a control that
  could have come back clean and did not.
* **`RUSTMC_VILLAGE_FEATURE_SKIP` is what makes those three states one
  binary.** A per-element before/after taken across three builds is a delta
  with a rebuild in it; this knob declines a named feature and consumes none
  of its draws, exactly as an unported one does.

>

> (`block_pile`, `rotated_block_provider`, in `rustmc-worldgen` with their own

#### Defect 1 — the water source-conversion game rule (34 blocks)

`WaterFluid#canConvertToSource` is nothing but
`getGameRules().get(WATER_SOURCE_CONVERSION)`. `GameRules`'s static
initialiser gives both the id and the default:

```text
  ldc "water_source_conversion" … iconst_1 … registerBoolean   -> default TRUE
  ldc "lava_source_conversion"  … iconst_0 … registerBoolean   -> default FALSE
```

`ci/gen-vanilla-region.sh` sends `gamerule water_source_conversion false` to
every reference server before the window is forceloaded. `stage/fluid.rs`
hardcoded the arm true and said so in a doc comment: *"It is not overridden by
the harness that produced the references."* **It is overridden.** The comment
was written while the script still used the pre-26.2 camelCase ids and the
console was answering `Incorrect argument for command`, so it recorded a
property of that week's references as a property of the harness.

All 30 of the directly-charged cells had ≥2 horizontal water-source
neighbours and a solid-or-source block below **in our own world** — measured
by extracting the neighbourhood of all 34 water positions in both worlds
before the fix, not inferred from the rule.

`FluidRules` is now a value the caller has to name: `VANILLA_DEFAULT` carries
the registration defaults, `REFERENCE_HARNESS` what `oracle-work` was
generated under. It is a property of the world, not of the port.

#### Defect 2 — lava was never ticked (24 blocks)

The scope note said lava was left out because *"the r=7 reference has zero
non-source lava"*. True of r=7, false of r=16.

**The decline was live code, and that was checked before it was relied on** —
the previous turn lost time to a `has_grass` predicate comparing a *state*
against a *block* name, which made the path behind it unreachable and its
gate's zero meaningless:

```text
  RUSTMC_POST_PROCESS_STATS=1, r=16 window
                      before  after
  fluid_ticked       160,701  160,700
  fluid_writes         1,057    1,094
  skipped_other_fluid  5,736        -      the arm the scope note describes
  ticked_lava              -    5,736      the same marks, now ticked
  merged_face_branch       0        0      the one approximation, never used
```

**5,736 before and 5,736 after is the load-bearing pair.** It says the marked
set did not move and only the behaviour did. `merged_face_branch` is 0 on both
sides, so `canPassThroughWall`'s approximation is not part of any figure here.

Everything the two fluids disagree about now lives on `Kind`, read from the
jar. `isFastLava` is the dimension's `FAST_LAVA` environment attribute, false
outside the nether:

```text
  getDropOff            water iconst_1   lava isFastLava ? 1 : 2  -> 2
  getSlopeFindDistance  water iconst_4   lava isFastLava ? 4 : 2  -> 2
  getTickDelay          -                lava isFastLava ? 10 : 30    (no tick queue)
  canConvertToSource    WATER_SOURCE_CONVERSION / LAVA_SOURCE_CONVERSION
```

**`drop_off = 2` is the whole of `level=2`, and it was pinned before the fix
ran.** `getLegacyLevel` writes `8 - amount`, a source is amount 8, one
overworld step is `8 - 2 = 6`, and `8 - 6 = 2` — which is the state all 24 of
vanilla's flowing lava blocks carry. The constant and the census agreed before
a line was changed.

Two overrides the old single-fluid code had **silently wrong**, both found by
reading the jar rather than by the measurement:

* `FluidState#canBeReplacedWith`. Lava's is
  `getHeight(..) >= 0.44444445f && incoming.is(FluidTags.WATER)` — there is no
  direction in it at all — and the old code gave lava water's
  `direction == DOWN`. `getHeight` is `getOwnHeight` (`amount / 9.0F`) unless
  the block above holds the same fluid, in which case `1.0F`.
* `LiquidBlockContainer#canPlaceLiquid` ends in `fluid == Fluids.WATER`, so
  lava can never enter a waterloggable block. The old signature had no fluid
  argument at all and would have let a lava flow waterlog a fence.

`LavaFluid#spreadTo` is implemented: lava spreading DOWN into water sets stone
instead of placing lava, and only when the target is a `LiquidBlock` — a
waterlogged block below lava is not one, so it fizzes and is left alone.

`is_water` became `is_same(kind)`, and the rename is the point: every caller
asks whether a neighbour is the same fluid as the one *spreading*.

#### The result that closes it

```text
  vanilla A  44,643 lava = 44,619 level=0 + 24 level=2
  vanilla B  44,643 lava = 44,619 level=0 + 24 level=2
  ours       44,643 lava = 44,619 level=0 + 24 level=2
  diff -q against A: identical.  against B: identical.
```

Not equal in count — **identical position for position and state for state**,
over the whole 1,089-chunk window, against both twins.

#### POISON CONTROLS — three, and all three could have failed

**A. `sources >= 3` instead of modelling the rule** — the off-by-one somebody


Convicted, **but only by 2 blocks**. Say that plainly rather than banking it:
on this window the right predicate and that off-by-one are 2 blocks apart, and
a cascade does most of the work for the wrong answer. This control is thin and
the next one is why the item is still closed.

**B. The same code with `FluidRules::VANILLA_DEFAULT`.** The prediction was
that it reproduces the baseline exactly, because the game rule is the only
thing the commit changed.

```text
  diff -rq against the pre-change dump, 1,089 chunks: BYTE-IDENTICAL
```

So the 34 are attributable to that one bit and to nothing else that rode along
in the commit — and the knob is load-bearing rather than decorative.

**C. Lava enabled with WATER's constants** (`drop_off` 1,
`slope_find_distance` 4) — the port somebody writes who adds the fluid without
reading `LavaFluid`.

```text
  N=8 admissible charge   13,586      (correct fix 13,562)
  no longer charged           34      the water 34 only; none of the 24 close
  NEWLY charged                0
  our flowing lava:       24 blocks of lava[level=1]
  at vanilla's own 24 level=2 positions: 24 of 24
```

**So the window adjudicates the constant and not merely the trigger.** The
wrong drop-off finds exactly the right 24 cells and writes the wrong state in

**What poison C does NOT cover, stated so a green number is not read as
coverage:** it moved `slope_find_distance` from 2 to 4 as well, and that
changed nothing — 0 newly charged. So **only the drop-off half of `Kind` is
adjudicated by this window; the slope-find distance is not.** The geometry
here bounds the flow before four steps matter. A window with a long open shelf
of lava would test it; this one does not.
