### THE ANOMALY IS SOLVED: THE BEARDIFIER IS ACTIVE AND WE HAVE NONE

**And the claim that it was inert was mine, verified twice with the wrong
test.** Withdrawn here in full.

The reasoning was: `NoiseChunk` swaps the real beardifier in wherever
`DensityFunctions$BeardifierMarker.INSTANCE` appears in the density tree, so
the beard reaches terrain only through a marker in the router — and
`grep -rl beardifier` over the whole datapack matches nothing. I checked that
grep twice and called it "the linchpin of that elimination".

**The marker is never in the datapack, in any version.** `NoiseChunk`'s own
constructor puts it there, offsets 495-506:

```text
  noiseRouter.finalDensity()
  getstatic DensityFunctions$BeardifierMarker.INSTANCE
  invokestatic DensityFunctions.add
  invokestatic DensityFunctions.cacheAllInCell
  invokeinterface DensityFunction.mapAll(this::wrap)
```

and `wrap` (offsets 295-306) substitutes the `beardifier` field for it. The
grep tested a thing that is never true.

### THE MEASUREMENT

`ci/nether-real-fill-probe.sh` now takes structure pieces and builds a **real**
`Beardifier` — `Beardifier(List<Rigid>, List<JigsawJunction>, BoundingBox)` is
public, so no `StructureManager` is needed. The piece box is read out of the
reference chunk's own `structures.starts.<id>.Children[].BB`, so the input is
vanilla's and not invented.

Nether chunk (58,67), seed 20260722, against vanilla's finished world:

```text
  beardless fill   19,078 non-air    699 blocks of vanilla's are missing
  bearded  fill    19,691 non-air     75 blocks of vanilla's are missing
```

**The beard is 624 blocks in one chunk**, and it is 90% of what was missing.
Across the r=7 nether window, `soul_sand`/`soul_soil` where the beardless fill
leaves air is **4,852 blocks — 22% of the dimension's 22,014 residual**, with
another 4,556 in the reverse direction. Twenty chunks carry 50 or more.

### WHY EVERY INSTRUMENT AGREED, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING

Three independent-looking checks all passed while all three were blind:

* `ci/nether-fill-probe.sh` passed the marker, so it computed the beardless
  fill;
* `ci/nether-real-fill-probe.sh` **seeded the chunk's `NoiseChunk` with the
  marker on purpose**, to avoid needing a `StructureManager` — so vanilla's own
  `doFill` was run on a beardless density and agreed, line for line;
* our port has no beardifier at all, so it agreed too.

"Two controls on different code paths, both green" was true and worthless: the
paths differed and the *assumption* did not. **An instrument's blind spot is
not tested by another instrument that shares it** — and the way to have caught
this was to ask "what would make all three agree while all three are wrong",
which is a different question from "do they agree".

The residual itself was the evidence, and it was there the whole time: 4,852
one way and 4,556 the other is a *positional* signature, and I read it as a
mechanism that adds blocks rather than as terrain that sits somewhere else.

### WHAT IT DOES NOT TOUCH

**The overworld's order-invariant core of zero is unaffected**, and this was
checked rather than hoped: the r=7 overworld window's only structure starts are
`shipwreck` (1) and `mineshaft` (2), and neither declares
`terrain_adaptation` at all. No beard, no gap. `docs/PARITY.md`'s overworld
numbers stand as written.

**The End and the second overworld seed are checked too, and both are clear.**
The rule that prompted it is the one this finding taught: *a term that is zero
on every window you have looked at is not a term that is zero.*

```text
  End,  van-end-20260722-c8362   1,681 chunks   end_city x1        no adaptation
  s2,   vanilla-s2-r7            2,210 chunks   mineshaft x15      no adaptation
                                                shipwreck, buried_treasure,
                                                ocean_ruin_warm,
                                                ruined_portal_ocean    all none
                                                trial_chambers x3  ENCAPSULATE
```

The three trial chambers are the only bearding structures anywhere in the
seed-31415926 reference, and all three are far outside the measured window —
starts at chunks (5,10), (45,76) and (82,45) against a window of 59..69, with
pieces at x 60..98, 673..720 and 1294..1312. The window is blocks 944..1119.
Nothing bridges that at a beard radius of 12.

**So all three published parity claims survive**: overworld seed 20260722 core
0, overworld seed 31415926 core 0, and the End at 100.000000%. They survive by
inspection of the references rather than by luck, and the inspection is one
command that should be run for every new window before its number is quoted.

### NEXT: NETHER FOSSIL, THEN THE BEARDIFIER — IN THAT ORDER

The beard needs structure **starts before the noise stage**, which is where
vanilla computes them (`STRUCTURE_STARTS` precedes `NOISE`). So it is blocked
behind porting a structure that beards, and in the nether the only one with a
start anywhere in the window is `nether_fossil` — `terrain_adaptation:
beard_thin`, `step: underground_decoration`, a single template piece, 12 starts
in 120 chunks sampled.

1. **Move structure starts ahead of the noise stage — and the blocker is
   named.** Vanilla's `STRUCTURE_STARTS` precedes `NOISE`. Ours is
   `setup -> noise -> biomes -> surface -> carvers -> structures -> decoration`,
   with structures already its own stage
   (`generate.rs` 2247-2491, `times.mark("structures")`), so the stage graph
   is not the hard part.

   **The hard part is that the stage reads the canvas.** It takes
   `WORLD_SURFACE_WG` and `OCEAN_FLOOR_WG` off `pipeline.canvas()` in five
   places — the shipwreck's height, two `ocean_floor_wg - 1` reads, a
   `world_surface_wg - 1`, and one more before `freeze_wg()`. Those are the
   **noise stage's own heightmap fossils**, so the stage cannot move above the
   thing that produces them.

   **The unblock is already written down in that code.** The comment beside the
   second read says reading `OCEAN_FLOOR_WG` off the canvas "is exactly
   `getBaseHeight`" — and vanilla's `ChunkGenerator.getBaseHeight` does **not**
   read a chunk. It walks a noise column against the density router
   (`iterateNoiseColumn`), which is available before any chunk is filled. So
   the work is:

   * ~~prove the canvas heightmap equal to `getBaseHeight`~~ **DONE, see
     below** — the equality now has a vanilla-side oracle;
   * ~~implement `getBaseHeight`/`iterateNoiseColumn` against the router~~
     **DONE** — `stage::noise::base_height(router, seeding, settings, x, z, Wg)`,
     gated below;
   * ~~swap the five canvas reads for router samples~~ **DONE**, byte-neutral;
   * ~~move the stage~~ **DONE**, byte-identical — see below.

### THE FIVE READS ARE SWAPPED, AND THE OUTPUT DID NOT MOVE

`grep -c 'canvas().world_surface_wg\|canvas().ocean_floor_wg'` over
`generate.rs` is now **0**. The structures stage reads no heightmap off the
canvas at all; it calls `stage::noise::base_height` against the router.

**Both rectangles were kept exactly as they were.** Two of the five bound
against `area` and three against `pipeline.generated()`, and each still
answers `None` outside its own bound. The router walk could answer anywhere —
vanilla's `getBaseHeight` has no bounds at all — so *removing* them is a real
and possibly more faithful change, and it is deliberately **not** part of this
commit. It would alter which structures refuse, which is a behaviour change
that needs its own measurement, and folding it in here would have hidden it
inside a refactor that is otherwise provably neutral.

```text
  seed 20260722, twin-masked, vanilla first
    overworld  chunks 57..71          1,079  unchanged
    nether     chunks 57..71 y 0..127 22,014 unchanged
```

Exactly the numbers from before the swap, to the block.

### THE STRUCTURES STAGE NOW RUNS BEFORE THE NOISE STAGE

Where vanilla runs it: `ChunkPyramid` orders `STRUCTURE_STARTS` ahead of
`NOISE`, and the reason it matters is `Beardifier` — a structure raises terrain
around itself through a density term, so its pieces must exist before the fill.

The three couplings resolved exactly as enumerated:

* **`sampler`** (`ClimateSampler::from_router`) and **`biomes`**
  (`Mutex<ParameterList>` from `biome_table()`) hoisted above the block. Both
  are pure constructions from the router and registry data — neither touches
  the canvas or the pipeline.
* **`pipeline.canvas_mut().freeze_wg()` stayed behind**, after the carvers,
  where it belongs. It is the "the `_WG` maps are frozen after CARVERS"
  mechanism and hoisting it would have frozen the maps before anything wrote
  them.
* `times.mark("structures")` moved with the block, so it still measures the
  block rather than a gap.

### WHAT WAS CHECKED BESIDES THE BYTES

A green diff proves no behavioural regression on one window; it does not prove
the ordering is sound. So, separately:

* **Dependency analysis, comments stripped.** Every `let` binding created
  between the biomes stage and the structures block was tested against the
  block's text. Four apparent hits, all false: `climate` and `list` occur only
  inside the string `"the climate list lock"`, `generated` only in comments and
  as the method `pipeline.generated()`, and `props` is redefined by the block
  itself. **The block has no data dependency on noise, biomes, surface or
  carvers.**
* **The block does not mutate the pipeline.** Its only `pipeline.` use is
  `generated()`, a rectangle read.
* **`through` gating is position-independent.** All four structure kinds sit
  behind `if through >= Through::Decoration`, so a run stopped earlier does the
  same nothing before and after the move — which answers the caution recorded
  last turn, and is confirmed empirically below rather than by reading the
  gate.

### AND THE GATE IS BYTES, NOT COUNTS

A matching mismatch count is not proof two worlds are the same world. A
control was built from the parent commit and the region files compared
directly:

```text
  full generation, seed 20260722 r=7      4 of 4 region files IDENTICAL
  RUSTMC_THROUGH=carvers, same window     4 of 4 region files IDENTICAL
```

and the residuals are unchanged to the block — overworld **1,079**, nether
**22,014**, twin-masked, vanilla first. The second row is the probe caution
settled: the `RUSTMC_THROUGH` output did not move.

### THE NETHER IS 99.885%, AND ONE STRUCTURE DID IT

Seed 20260722, chunks 57..71, y 0..127, vanilla first, twin-masked against
`oracle-work/van-nether-20260722-r7-b`:

```text
  no nether structures     22,014 / 7,372,752   99.701%
  fossil placed, beard fed  8,756               99.881%    -13,258
  fossil bones written      8,472               99.885%       -284
                                                 total  -13,542  -61.5%
```

Decomposed over nine orders, and it is still almost entirely order-invariant,
which is the opposite of the overworld:

```text
  default 8472  diag 8472  spawn 8825  zx 8837  spiral 8913
  zx_rev 13364  spiral_in 15605  reverse 15959  zx_zrev 16535
  intersection 8459
```

Thirteen blocks of order noise, the same thirteen as at 22,014.

**It reproduces on a second window**, centre (100,100), chunks 93..107, with
its own independently generated vanilla pair:

```text
  window 1, chunks 57..71     22,014 -> 8,472     -13,542   -61.5%
  window 2, chunks 93..107    25,641 -> 10,038    -15,603   -60.9%
```

and the placement oracle holds on both — **30 of 30 and 33 of 33** starts
identical to vanilla's saved `Children[]`. Two windows a third of the
dimension apart agreeing to within half a percent is what separates a ported
rule from a fitted one, and it is the check the fossil work would otherwise
have lacked: it was developed against window 1's reference.

### AND THE SECOND SEED, WHICH REPRODUCED THE PORT AND BROKE THE PERCENTAGE

Seed **31415926**, chunks 57..71, its own vanilla pair:

```text
  before  46,146 / 7,277,560   99.366%
  after   39,941 / 7,277,560   99.451%    -6,205   -13.4%
```

**13.4% against 61.5% and 60.9%**, and the placement is nonetheless perfect:
**14 of 14** starts identical to vanilla's saved `Children[]`, on a seed the
port had never seen.

The percentage is the wrong normalisation. The beard is a function of how many
structures there are, not of what else is broken:

```text
  window                          closed   fossils   per fossil
  20260722, chunks 57..71         13,542        30        451.4
  20260722, chunks 93..107        15,603        33        472.8
  31415926, chunks 57..71          6,205        14        443.2
                                        mean 455.8, spread +/-3.7%
```

Three windows, two seeds, within 4%. **Quote blocks per fossil, not the
percentage.**

### THE BIOME CAVEAT, WHICH IS THE REAL FINDING OF THAT SEED

The 31415926 window is **basalt deltas** — 904,491 `basalt` and 167,026
`blackstone`, against **zero of either** in both 20260722 windows, which are
100% `soul_sand_valley`.

**And then the order decomposition inverted that conclusion**, which is why
the standing rule says decompose *before* investigating a residual:

```text
  window                       residual    core   order share   core exactness
  20260722 soul sand valley        8,472   8,459         0.2%      99.8853%
  31415926 basalt deltas          39,941   6,127        84.7%      99.9158%

  31415926 by order:
    default 39941  diag 39941  spawn 51235  zx 51319  spiral_in 108668
    spiral 129498  zx_zrev 155949  zx_rev 173073  reverse 213864
```

**Basalt deltas is not worse. By the order-invariant measure it is BETTER** —
6,127 against 8,459. 84.7% of its residual is chunk-visitation order, the
overworld's pattern; soul sand valley's residual is 99.8% order-invariant and
therefore nearly all real.

This section said "in basalt deltas this port is at 99.451%, worse" before the
decomposition was run. **Withdrawn.** The rule was on the page and was not
followed: a raw residual is not a defect count until it has been decomposed,
and 5.4x between the cheapest and dearest order was the tell.

**So `the nether is 99.885%` is still a soul-sand-valley claim** — but because
soul sand valley is the *harder* biome, not the easier one. Three of the five
nether biomes remain unmeasured.

And vanilla's own run-to-run variance follows the biome by three orders of
magnitude. The twin mask drops **95,240** positions here — 1.3% of the window
— against 48 and 20 in soul sand valley. Diffing the two vanilla runs directly:

```text
  22,083  basalt -> netherrack    20,761  netherrack -> basalt
  16,772  basalt -> blackstone
```

`basalt_deltas` decoration is enormously order-sensitive **in vanilla**. That
makes this window a much weaker instrument — a real defect of ours on any of
those 95,240 positions is invisible — and it is the strongest case in the
project for why the twin mask is not optional:

```text
  unmasked   102,727
  masked      39,941     the mask removes 62,786, or 61%
```

**Measured, after being asserted wrongly once.** The first version of this
said 135,181, which is the masked count plus the mask size — arithmetic, not a
measurement, and wrong by 32,454, because we agree with reference A at that
many of the positions the two vanilla runs disagree about. The mask's *size*
is not the number of our mismatches it removes.

`RUSTMC_TRACE_BEARD=1` reads `starts=14 pieces=14 chunks_with_a_beard=18`
here, so the mechanism is demonstrably live at this seed too.

**The beard is worth forty-six times the bones.** 13,258 against 284. The
terrain a structure raises around itself is a far larger fact about a world
than the structure is, and this is the number to quote when anyone asks why
`Beardifier` was worth a week.

**The brief predicted 4,852 and the measurement is 13,258.** That estimate
counted `soul_sand`/`soul_soil` written where the beardless fill leaves air —
one direction of a positional disagreement, with 4,556 more in the other, and
it still undercounts because moving terrain moves which surface rule fires on
it. It was a lower bound and was not labelled as one.

### `nether_fossil` HAD A COMPLETE ORACLE, WHICH IS RARE — USE THE TRICK AGAIN

Vanilla **saves its own decision** into
`structures.starts.minecraft:nether_fossil.Children[]`, and
`worldgen-dump jigsaw-starts <ref> nether_fossil` reads it back. Against
`oracle-work/van-nether-20260722-r7`:

```text
  vanilla 30 starts    ours 30 starts
  MISSING 0   EXTRA 0   piece mismatches 0
```

exact on the chunk, the template name, the rotation, the template position
and the bounding box. `ci/nether-fossil-golden.sh` freezes it into
`golden/nether_fossil_starts.json` and `tests/golden_nether_fossil.rs` gates
it. That single comparison covers the `random_spread` placement, the biome
tag, `getBaseColumn`, the ledge walk, the height provider, the fossil choice
and the rotation draw — every step at once, separately from the blocks.

**This generalises and it is the highest-value instrument on this project.**
Any structure vanilla saves pieces for can be gated the same way, before a
single block is written. The nether reference also carries one
`bastion_remnant` with 105 pieces already listed with `gld` and `proj` — a
bastion port has its layout oracle waiting.

### WHAT THE REMAINING 8,472 IS NOT

**Not missing structures**, and that is measured. `structures.starts` in the
reference holds 30 `nether_fossil` and one `bastion_remnant`, and the
bastion's pieces span x 833..880 — chunks 52..55, outside the measured 57..71.
There is **no fortress and no ruined portal start in the reference at all**.
Porting them will not move this number.

What it is: the same positional signature as before at a third the amplitude —
`soul_soil -> netherrack` 1,225, `soul_sand -> netherrack` 1,086,
`air -> soul_soil` 994, `air -> soul_sand` 900, `soul_sand -> air` 862,
`soul_soil -> air` 704 — plus `air -> netherrack` 608 and
`air -> cave_air` 513. Terrain still sitting a few blocks off in places the
beard did not reach, and two `canSurvive` rules.

The window is 100% `soul_sand_valley`, all 57,344 biome cells, so it says
nothing about the other four nether biomes.

### THREE THINGS THE BYTECODE SAID AND A GUESS WOULD NOT

* **The rotation is drawn before the template.** `NetherFossilPieces.addPieces`
  calls `Rotation.getRandom(random)` at offset 0 and
  `Util.getRandom(FOSSILS, random)` at offset 16. Swapped, every site gets a
  different fossil in a different rotation and the world still looks right.
* **`FOSSILS` is in declaration order.** `fossil_10` is index 9, after
  `fossil_9`. Sorting the filenames puts it at index 1.
* **The `SOUL_SAND` arm of the ledge test is unreachable.** `getBaseColumn` is
  the noise stage — default block, default fluid, air — so there is no soul
  sand in any column; surface rules have not run. The test reduces to
  `isFaceSturdy`, which on a nether base column reduces again to "is
  netherrack". Both reductions are properties of *this dimension's settings*,
  not of the method, and are recorded as such.

### THE INSTRUMENT THAT MUST OUTLIVE THIS TURN

`RUSTMC_TRACE_BEARD=1` prints `starts=`, `pieces=` and
`chunks_with_a_beard=`. It exists because the beard's overworld regression
gate once reported all three dimensions unchanged and **proved nothing** —
`starts=0`, no village in the area, so the term could not have fired however
wrong it was.

**"The world did not move" reads identically when a term correctly declines
and when it is wired to nothing.** Before believing any null about the beard,
run the trace. On the nether it reads `starts=30 pieces=30
chunks_with_a_beard=35`.

### A CONSEQUENCE WORTH KNOWING BEFORE IT SURPRISES SOMEONE

The nether structures stage is **not** gated on `Through::Decoration`, because
it changes the noise stage's own output rather than only writing blocks in
decoration. So `ci/nether-fill-probe.sh` — which drives vanilla's `doFill`
with `BeardifierMarker.INSTANCE` and is therefore beardless by construction —
will now differ from our noise stage in the 35 chunks a fossil reaches. That
is the probe being right about a beardless fill, not a regression.

### SOUL SAND VALLEY'S 8,459, DECOMPOSED — IT IS THE CAVE CARVERS

The order sweep is already exhausted on this one (8,472 raw, 8,459 core, 99.8%
invariant), so it was decomposed three other ways instead. All three agree and
none of them is the beard.

**1. It is not where the beard acts. The beard's chunks are 16x BETTER.**

```text
  bearded chunks in window     23    mismatches    60    mean  2.6
  unbearded chunks            202    mismatches 8,412    mean 41.6
```

None of the ten worst chunks is bearded. Whatever is wrong, the beard is not
it — and where a fossil flattens the ground we are very nearly exact.

**2. It is half shape and half material, and the shape half is carving.**

```text
  MASK differs (solid/air class changed)   4,462   52.7%
  MATERIAL only                            4,010   47.3%
```

Tracked across our own stages against vanilla's finished world:

```text
  ours THROUGH=noise    vs vanilla   mask differs  254,368
  ours THROUGH=carvers  vs vanilla   mask differs    7,691
  ours FULL             vs vanilla   mask differs    4,462
```

254,368 at the noise stage is every cave vanilla carved and we had not yet.
Our carvers take that to 7,691 and decoration to 4,462. **The fill under them
is exact — two whole chunks, 65,536 blocks, zero, against vanilla's own
`doFill` — so the shape that is left is the carvers, not the terrain.**

**3. The material half is the soul surface rule, and it is asymmetric.**

```text
  1,225  soul_soil  -> netherrack      407  netherrack -> soul_soil
  1,086  soul_sand  -> netherrack      259  netherrack -> soul_sand
```

Vanilla puts soul material on netherrack 2,311 times where we do not; we do it
666 times where vanilla does not. **3.5:1** — we systematically leave
netherrack where vanilla converts. A `stone_depth` / surface-scan question,
not a noise one.

**4. And 914 blocks are carving placement with no shape change at all.**

```text
  513  air -> cave_air      401  cave_air -> air
```

Balanced within 25%, which is *misplaced* rather than *too much* or *too
little* — the same signature the whole residual had before the beard, one
stage further down.

So the remaining defect is **the cave carvers (~5,376 across the mask and the
cave_air split), then the soul sand valley surface rule (~2,977)**. Terrain,
structures, the density function and the beard are all excluded by
measurement.


### THE CARVERS: HALF THE CHUNKS ARE PERFECT, AND IT IS NOT A THRESHOLD

The 4,462 mask blocks, taken apart three ways. The order sweep is already
exhausted here — the whole 8,459 is 99.8% order-invariant — so these are
structural decompositions, not traversal ones.

**1. It is concentrated, and half the window is exact.**

```text
  mask-differing blocks 4,462 over 116 of 225 chunks
    top  1 chunk    849   19.0%
    top  3 chunks 1,462   32.8%
    top 20 chunks 3,578   80.2%
    top 40 chunks 4,206   94.3%
  chunks with ZERO mask disagreement: 109 of 225
```

**109 chunks are byte-perfect in shape.** A wrong tunnel radius, a wrong
threshold or a wrong y-range would be thin and universal — every cave slightly
off, no chunk clean. This is the opposite: a per-chunk defect that fires in
about forty chunks and not at all in half of them.

**2. It is whole features, not edges.**

```text
  540 connected components, mean size 8.3
  singletons          431 blocks    9.7%
  components >= 20  3,725 blocks   83.5%
  largest: 619 339 315 266 240 213 208 143 129 128 119 90
```

Edge error from a slightly-wrong radius is singletons and pairs. 83.5% of
these blocks sit in components of twenty or more.

**3. The volume is balanced to 0.7%. The GRANULARITY is 3:1.**

```text
  vanilla carved, we did not    137 components   2,223 blocks   mean 16.2
  we carved, vanilla did not    403 components   2,239 blocks   mean  5.6
```

**This corrects the reading the brief for this item carried.** At block level
the two directions look balanced within 25% — 2,504 against 1,958 — and that
was read as "misplaced, not too much or too little". The volume half of that
is right and stronger than stated: 2,223 against 2,239 is balanced to **0.7%**,
so we carve almost exactly the right amount of rock.

But the *shape* of the error is not balanced at all. Vanilla's missing volume
arrives as a few large blobs; ours as three times as many small ones. A rigid
displacement would pair components off at matching sizes, and these do not
pair. So it is misplacement, but not a translation.

**Where to start: chunk (57,64), 849 mask blocks — 19% of the total in one
chunk — and it is one of the two chunks whose FILL was proved byte-identical
to vanilla's own `doFill`.** Exact terrain, wrong caves, same chunk. That is
as clean an isolation as this dimension is going to offer.


### THE CARVER DRIVER IS EXCLUDED — AND THAT CORRECTS MY OWN LAST CONCLUSION

**First, the question that gets asked before anything else now: is there a
savable vanilla-side artefact, the way `Children[]` was for structures? No,
and it was checked rather than assumed.** A finished nether chunk carries
`sections`, `structures`, `Heightmaps`, `PostProcessing`, `block_ticks`,
`fluid_ticks`, `Status`, `isLightOn`, `InhabitedTime`, `LastUpdate` — and no
carving field of any kind. `CarvingMask` is a `ProtoChunk` member created by
`getOrCreateCarvingMask()` and dropped when the chunk is written as a full
chunk. **The trick that has paid out three times does not extend to carvers.**
Do not go looking again.

**Second, the driver is not the defect.** `NoiseBasedChunkGenerator.applyCarvers`:

```text
  for j in -8..=8:  for k in -8..=8:              289 source chunks
      setLargeFeatureSeed(seed + l, src.x, src.z)  l = carver index
      if isStartChunk(random): carve(..)
```

Ours matches all of it — `SWEEP_RADIUS = 8`, the same seed expression, the
same one `nextFloat` per offer whether or not it carves. Three further things
collapse in this dimension specifically:

* **every nether biome has exactly one carver**, `minecraft:nether_cave` —
  soul sand valley, basalt deltas, nether wastes, crimson and warped forest
  alike. So the index `l` is always 0 and `seed + l` is just `seed`; the
  carver list's order cannot matter; and **which biome the source chunk holds
  cannot matter either**, because all five answer the same.
* the sweep is **not truncated by our own generated area**.
  `RUSTMC_TRACE_CARVER=57,64` shows that chunk drawing from sources at x=49,
  eight chunks outside the 57..71 window, because `carvers_at` samples the
  climate router rather than the canvas.
* `set_large_feature_seed` itself is validated independently — it is the same
  function the `nether_fossil` placement uses, and that reproduces vanilla
  exactly at 30/30, 33/33 and 14/14 across two seeds.

**Third, and this is a correction.** Last turn this file concluded the carver
residual was "a per-chunk draw or coordinate defect, not a radius, threshold
or y-range". The draw half is now excluded above.

The reconciliation is arithmetic. `nether_cave` has `probability: 0.2` over
289 sources, so **roughly 58 carves touch every single chunk**. 109 chunks
being byte-perfect in shape therefore means the overwhelming majority of
carves are exactly right. What is left is a **rare, data-dependent divergence
inside the carve itself** — and one wrong carve contaminates the ten to twenty
chunks it crosses, which is what produced the appearance that particular
chunks are special.

So "about forty chunks are wrong" is not forty defects. It is a handful of
carves, and the next instrument has to be **per carve**, not per chunk.

### THE MARK SET: 11 MISSING OF 4,034, AND THE ORACLE IS NEW

`ci/mark-oracle.py` replaced the chunk-column-55 comparison that produced the
"2,261 missing marks" figure. **That figure was wrong and is withdrawn** —
see `docs/ORACLE.md` §24. Column 55's blocks differ from vanilla's by 6,688
while vanilla's own twin differs by 444, so the two mark sets belonged to two
different worlds.

```text
  ci/mark-oracle.py oracle-work/vanilla-r7 oracle-work/vanilla-r7-b \
                    <our-region-dir> <our-mark-dump>

  oracle chunks   24 clean, 47 rejected for 11,410 marks in blocks we
                  do not reproduce
  vanilla         4,034 positions BOTH vanilla runs mark
  MISSING 85 -> 11        EXTRA 0
```

Generate ours with `RUSTMC_DUMP_POST_MARKS=<path>` at r=12 so the ring is
inside our decoration margin. `EXTRA 0` is what makes the other direction
usable: nothing we mark is wrong, so every missing one is a missing call.

**The 11 that are left**, and none of them moves a block in either window:

```text
   993 -12 1181  cinnabar     1006 -4 1168  sulfur    1007 -4 1170  sulfur
   994 -12 1181  cinnabar     1006 -4 1169  sulfur    1008 -4 1170  sulfur
  1172  39 1023  andesite     1006 -4 1170  sulfur    1008 -3 1169  sulfur
  1173  39 1022  stone        1007 -4 1169  sulfur
```

All eight `markPosForPostProcessing` call sites in the jar are now ported, so
these are **not** a missing call site. The six sulfur positions are a diagonal
run through a `sulfur_pool` barrier shell, which is `markAboveForPostProcessing`
— and that walk reads the world **during** decoration, so it can differ even
where the finished blocks agree. Suspect the timing, not the call.

### DONE THIS TURN (1): `LakeFeature` MARKS ABOVE WHAT IT LAYS

under `flag = k >= 4`) and **every barrier block** (offsets 1207-1211). The

`sulfur_pool` is a `minecraft:lake` whose barrier is `minecraft:sulfur`, which

```text
  marks at r=12          120,498 -> 181,783
```

### DONE THIS TURN (2): MULTIFACE GROWTH MARKS WHAT IT PLACES

`MultifaceGrowthFeature.placeGrowthIfPossible` marks **after** its `setBlock`
(offsets 95-103); `MultifaceSpreader$SpreadConfig.placeBlock` marks **before**
its own (offsets 23-42) when the caller's `markForPostprocessing` flag is set.
The feature passes `iconst_1`. The two orders differ and both are reproduced,
because the list is replayed in insertion order.

```text
  ci/mark-oracle.py   MISSING 85 -> 11    all 74 glow_lichen marks
  twin-masked residual UNCHANGED at 1081
```

That last line killed the brief's prediction that closing the marks would
close cluster E as a side effect. **A mark is not a placement.** It was
*necessary* — see (3) — and it was not sufficient.

### DONE THIS TURN (3): A MULTIFACE BLOCK THAT LOSES ITS LAST FACE BECOMES AIR

Cluster E, and it is the shape half of the pass. Both positions hold a plain
`minecraft:air` in a field of `cave_air`, in **both** vanilla references —
which is what a `MultifaceBlock` looks like after `postProcessGeneration` has
taken its final face away. Vanilla places the lichen exactly where we do and
then removes it.

`MultifaceBlock#updateShape`, offsets 34-81:

```text
  if (!hasAnyFace(state)) return AIR
  if (!hasFace(state, dir)) return state
  if (canAttachTo(level, dir, npos, nstate)) return state
  return removeFace(state, getFaceProperty(dir))    AIR if that was the last
```

`canAttachTo` is the **OR** of `isFaceFull(getBlockSupportShape, opposite)`
and `isFaceFull(getCollisionShape, opposite)` — two different questions, so
`ShapeFacts` gained `face_is_collision_full` beside `face_is_sturdy`. Leaves
have no sturdy face and a full collision face on all six, which is why glow
lichen grows on them at all.

**The family is exactly three blocks, read off the jar.** `BlockTypes`
registers `glow_lichen` and `sculk_vein` with their own codecs and a plain
`multiface` type with `MultifaceBlock.CODEC`; those two classes are the only
subclasses of `MultifaceBlock` and neither overrides `updateShape`; and
`resin_clump` is the only other block in the generated report carrying the six
face properties **and** `waterlogged`. `brown_mushroom_block`,
`red_mushroom_block`, `mushroom_stem` and `chorus_plant` have the six faces
and no `waterlogged` and are `HugeMushroomBlock`/`ChorusPlantBlock` — a test
on the six properties alone sweeps in all four.

```text
  twin-masked residual   1081 -> 1079    core 2 -> 0
  POST-PROCESS shapes     223 -> 225     exactly the two blocks
```

### THE HYPOTHESES THIS TURN KILLED

* **"There are 2,261 missing marks."** No. There were 85, on a box that had
  been validated. The 2,261 was measured on a chunk column where vanilla
  builds a trial chamber and we build a sulfur cave. `docs/ORACLE.md` §24.
* **"Closing the mark gap will close clusters E and F as a side effect."**
  Half true, and the half that is false is the instructive one. F closed with
  the marks. E's marks closed and E did not move a block until the fold rule
  was added; the mark and the rule are both necessary and neither is
  sufficient. This is `docs/ORACLE.md` §22's pattern for the third time.
* **"E is a predicate, so read `canSpreadInto` before assuming the feature is
  wrong."** Neither. We place the lichen exactly where vanilla does; vanilla
  removes it afterwards.
* **"Generate ours at the reference's own radius so the extents match, and
  the border-ring comparison becomes valid."** No — r=7 gives missing 979 and
  extra 332 against r=12's 2,261 and 28. The ring is not one world seen twice
  and no radius makes it one.
* **"Nothing we mark is wrong (EXTRA 0), so the mark oracle is sound."** It
  was sound about blocks and unmasked about marks. Two of its own extras were
  positions vanilla disagrees with itself about. Rule 6 applies to every
  channel, not to the one it was first written for.

## Item 2 at r=32 — the margin was hiding a bigger gap (2026-07-28)

The r=7 table below is superseded. Re-run at **4,225 chunks a square**, same
three centres, same seed, same heap, warmed on the same 225-chunk square:

```text
  flavour   wall s   CPU s   CPU s/chunk   vs vanilla CPU   vs vanilla wall
  folia     119.33  245.25   0.0580        0.56x            1.14x
  paper      34.58  259.43   0.0614        0.60x            0.33x
  vanilla   104.97  435.92   0.1032        1.00x            1.00x
  rustmc    738.80  746.59   0.1767        1.71x            7.04x
```

**The r=7 reading flattered rustmc.** 1.38x -> **1.71x** vanilla's CPU,
2.35x -> **2.88x** Paper's, 4.58x -> **7.04x** vanilla's wall, 13.8x ->
21.4x Paper's. Per centre 1.89x / 1.68x / 1.60x CPU and 6.63x / 6.73x /
7.86x wall. Folia also passes Paper on CPU at this size, which it did not at
r=7.

**Why, and it is the opposite of what the r=7 section predicted.** Both sides
amortise a skirt; vanilla's is ~3x ours, so a bigger square helps vanilla
more. And the r=7 claim that vanilla's skirt "cannot be separated from
outside the process" is **wrong** — it can, by measuring one centre at four
radii and fitting `c * ((2r+1+2m)/(2r+1))^2`:

```text
  vanilla (64,64):  r=7  0.21138   r=8  0.18481   r=16 0.11666   r=32 0.08743
  best fit: m = 6.5 chunks of skirt, c = 0.0602 CPU-s per GENERATED chunk
            spread in c across a 19x range in delivered chunks: 2.3%
            (m=2 spreads 51%, m=4 26%, m=5 15%, m=6 4.6%, m=7 6.3%, m=8 14%)
```

**The control that makes it skirt and not terrain:** rustmc's skirt is known
exactly (2), so its cost per *generated* chunk is the same quantity at every
radius. At the same centre it drifts **-2.3%** from r=7 to r=32 (0.15039 ->
0.14694) while vanilla's delivered cost falls **-58.6%**. Terrain is a
rounding error. Paper and Folia two-point solves land at m=5.7 and m=6.7 —
corroboration, not measurement (two points, two unknowns), but three JVM
servers between 5.7 and 6.7 is what a shared chunk-status radius looks like.

> **Like-for-like, skirt removed on both sides: rustmc 0.147 CPU-s per
> generated chunk against vanilla's 0.060 — 2.44x; against Paper's 0.041,
> 3.6x.** That independently reproduces the 2.25x this repo has carried since
> 2026-07-26 from a completely different method.

**Memory.** rustmc needed **14.4 GB resident** for the r=32 square — 4,761
generated chunks at ~3.0 MB each — because `Pipeline` holds the whole
square's `Canvas` *and* every chunk's retained aquifer/flat-cache/surface
state until the carver stage. The three JVMs did the same square in `-Xmx4G`.
The harness records `%M` now.

**Parity at r=32**, 4,225 chunks / 415,334,400 blocks, vanilla first:

```text
  vanilla vs paper     156,351 blocks   99.962355%
  vanilla vs folia     395,968 blocks   99.904663%
  vanilla vs rustmc    747,518 blocks   99.820020%
```

At r=7 rustmc had the best of these; at r=32 the worst. Not a ranking — the
two radii are not comparable (row-batching changes promotion order) and
Paper's and Folia's worst chunks are all on the square boundary while
rustmc's are interior, (40,32) at 13,598 blocks and (51,72) at 11,203. That
interior residual is **item 1's**, over a sample 19x bigger than item 1 has
been using.

**Where rustmc's CPU actually goes** — `RUSTMC_STAGE_TIMES=1`, Threadripper,
1,369 generated chunks at (64,64), seed 20260722:

```text
  noise       23.6%   36.2 ms/chunk
  biomes       7.8%   12.0 ms
  surface     15.8%   24.3 ms
  carvers      2.5%    3.9 ms
  structures   0.1%    0.1 ms
  decoration  50.1%   76.8 ms      <- half the pipeline
  TOTAL      209.85s  153.3 ms/chunk
```

**The order has inverted since the laptop table** (surface 44%, decoration
24%): the stored-biome-container change gutted the surface stage's biome
query, which is now `5.03s = 4.84s climate sample + 0.19s parameter search`
out of 209.85 s — **2.4% of the total**. BENCH.md's "the profile is flat,
there is no single row left to attack" is no longer true. r=8 agrees with
r=16 to within 3% on every row, and 153.3 ms/chunk reproduces the server
benchmark's 0.147 CPU-s per generated chunk at the same centre.

Two consequences:

1. **Threads are capped at 1.8x.** Everything but decoration is per-chunk
   independent given a per-thread router (`worldgen-dump scale` already gets
   8.26x on 12 threads for the noise stage) — but that is only 49.9% of the
   pipeline, so Amdahl caps a noise+biomes+surface+carvers parallel pipeline
   at 1.8x wall. Decoration resists for the reason `DECORATION_MARGIN`
   exists, and parallelising it is a parity risk, not a refactor.
2. **The noise stage costs 53% more inside the pipeline than outside it.**
   `worldgen-dump bench 20260722 64` is 23.67 ms/chunk on this machine
   (1.72 graph clone + 7.92 setup + 14.03 fill); the pipeline's `noise` row
   is 36.2. The two differ in where the blocks go, and `Canvas::set_block`
   does a `BTreeMap` lookup **and** a linear `Vec<String>` palette scan
   **per block** — 98,304 of each per chunk, on a key that does not change
   for the whole chunk. Not yet measured; the terrain differs too (origin
   against (64,64)) and is worth some of the 12.5 ms, not most of it.

**Harness changes this needed:** `BENCH_PROBE_TIMEOUT` (the 1,200 s deadline
was chosen when the slowest square was 18.6 s), `BENCH_WARMUP_RADIUS` (warm
on 225 chunks at any radius, which is both cheaper and more comparable), and
`settle()` — the gap between squares was a `sleep 3`, but `forceload remove
all` makes the server unload and *write* the square just timed, which at
4,225 chunks can be charged to the next square. It is the same CPU probe
with no commands sent, and it prints what it cost. The r=32 numbers above
predate it; the bound is that rustmc runs a **fresh process per square** and
so cannot carry anything, and its ordering (700/780/760) matches vanilla's
(369/464/474) and Paper's (241/261/277) — cheapest square first on both
sides, which contamination would not produce.

## Item 2, first optimisation pass — 1.79x, byte-identical (2026-07-28)

**Profile first.** `perf record` on the Threadripper, r=6 at (64,64), and it
**killed the hypothesis it was taken to test**:

```text
  8.58%  ImprovedNoise::noise_with_fudge        <- noise total ~17%, NOT 54%
  6.40%  malloc
  4.81%  cfree
  4.30%  Pipeline::prime_heightmaps
  3.79%  DensityFunction::compute
  3.42%  libc, unresolved
  3.40%  drop_in_place<BTreeMap<String, BTreeSet<String>>>
  3.24%  BTreeMap::clone::clone_subtree
  2.60%  PerlinNoise::get_value_with_fudge
  2.20%  ChunkSampler::evaluate
  2.17%  getenv
  1.74%  biome::manager::quart_for_block
  1.67%  std::env::__var
  1.64%  Canvas::set_block
```

> **Noise is ~17% in this tree, not the 54% the sibling project measured.**
> SIMD over the noise lattice is worth **~13% of a chunk even at 4x on the
> whole of it**, and it is the change most likely to break bit-exactness
> because reassociating float adds changes results. **It is not the lever.**

What the profile named instead — three symbols nobody had costed:

1. **`getenv` + `std::env::var` = 3.8%**, spent asking whether tracing is on
   with every switch off. Every `RUSTMC_TRACE_*` gate is read at its point of
   use, inside feature inner loops; `vegetation_patch.rs` reads one 10 times.
   Fixed: `crate::trace_switch`, one `OnceLock` per switch. A `OnceLock`
   rather than the `thread_local!` `canvas.rs` uses, because a worker pool
   would pay that init check per thread.
2. **`BlockTags` clone + drop = 6.6%** — every block tag in the game,
   deep-copied *per placement attempt*. `EnvironmentScan` and
   `BlockPredicateFilter` both do `world.block_tags().clone()`, not because
   they want a copy but because `predicate.test` needs `&mut world` and
   `&tags` at once. A borrow-checker workaround nobody re-costed. Fixed: the
   resolved map lives behind an `Arc`, so the same `.clone()` is a refcount
   bump. **No call site changed.**
3. **`prime_heightmaps` 4.3%** — a string-keyed `props.matches` per *block*,
   asked about `minecraft:air` a few hundred times per column on the way down
   to the surface. Fixed: memoised per `(palette id, map)`, lazily and per
   slot so the set of pairs asked about is exactly the old set, never a
   superset.

**Measured, Threadripper, seed 20260722, per generated chunk:**

```text
  r=16 (64,64), 1369 chunks   209.85s -> 138.41s -> 117.43s    1.79x total
  r=8  (64,64),  441 chunks    69.29s ->  41.94s ->  38.86s    1.78x
  r=6  (64,64),  289 chunks         -  ->  29.64s ->  23.57s
  r=4  (0,0),    169 chunks    17.76s ->  15.09s ->  13.63s    1.30x
  pipeline    153.3 ms/chunk -> 101.1 -> 85.8      decoration 76.8 -> 23.0
```

**A 10.4% profile share bought 34% of the runtime**, so the flat profile
**under**-attributed the winner — several unresolved libc frames (9.5%
together) sit in `getenv`'s address range. Next round: a symbol at 3% is
worth probing rather than dismissing.

**OUTPUT-IDENTICAL, PROVED, both commits.** Four windows, two centres,
regenerated and `cmp`ed against the previous binary's dumps: **16 of 16
region files byte-identical, 0 differ**, twice. `cmp` rather than
`region-differ diff` deliberately — it also covers palettes, heightmaps and
biomes, which a block differ does not look at.

**The four-server table, re-measured at r=32** (JVM rows unchanged, and the
parity rows unchanged too, because the output is byte-identical):

```text
  flavour          wall s   CPU s   CPU/chunk  vs vanilla CPU  vs paper CPU
  folia            119.33  245.25   0.0580     0.56x           0.95x
  paper             34.58  259.43   0.0614     0.60x           1.00x
  vanilla          104.97  435.92   0.1032     1.00x           1.68x
  rustmc  before   738.80  746.59   0.1767     1.71x           2.88x
  rustmc  AFTER    506.90  517.03   0.1224     1.19x           1.99x
```

Per centre against vanilla: **1.31x / 1.23x / 1.05x**, from 1.89/1.68/1.60.

### What the goal requires, and why the two targets are one target

Targets: **<=0.075 CPU-s/chunk** (1.5x Paper), stretch **<=0.056**, and
**1.5-2x Paper on wall** — Paper is 34.58 s a square, so 1.5x is 23.05 s.

```text
  CPU s/chunk   0.1224 -> <=0.075    a further 1.63x
  wall/square   506.90s -> <=23.05s  a further 22.0x
```

**Multicore alone does not reach the wall goal.** `worldgen-dump scale`
measures this box at 8.26x on 12 threads and 9.39x on 24, and that is the
*optimistic* end because the noise stage is the most parallel one there is.
At 9.6x, 506.90 / 9.6 = **52.8 s — 2.3x short of 23.05 s.**

> So the wall goal needs multicore **and** ~2.3x more single-core efficiency,
> i.e. **0.053 CPU-s/chunk**, which is the stretch target almost exactly.
> **The stretch efficiency target is a precondition for the wall target, not
> an alternative to it.** 0.053 x 9.6 = 22.1x against a 22.0x requirement —
> no headroom, so anything past the stretch target buys margin on both.

Two things that make it less tight than it reads: the margin is still 11.3%
of our work at r=32 while vanilla's fitted skirt is 6.5 chunks against our 2,
so at a server's real radius ours amortises to nearly nothing; and a player
experiences a streaming rate, not a square-completion one.

## Item 2, measured for the first time — 2026-07-28

Everything below is in `docs/BENCH.md` with the method; this is the summary
and the two things the measurement got wrong before it got them right.
**Superseded by the r=32 section above** — the numbers here are correct for
225-chunk squares and that size flatters rustmc.

**Workload.** Producing a finished 15x15 chunk square (225 chunks asked for)
through every stage, seed 20260722, three separated centres, every server
asked for the same three, one boot each, JVM warmed on a fourth throwaway
square first, same `-Xms4G -Xmx4G` on all three JVMs. Threadripper 1920X
(12c/24t), JDK 25.0.3, Paper build 84, Folia build 1.

It is the only workload the four share. rustmc has no entities, no block
updates and no random ticks, so a TPS or MSPT comparison would time an empty
loop against a full one.

```text
  flavour   wall s   CPU s   CPU s/chunk   vs vanilla CPU   vs vanilla wall
  paper       4.28   25.28   0.112         0.58x            0.33x
  folia      13.42   27.37   0.122         0.63x            1.04x
  vanilla    12.89   43.23   0.192         1.00x            1.00x
  rustmc     59.03   59.48   0.264         1.38x            4.58x
```

Per centre, because the terrain spread is large: rustmc is 1.14x / 1.43x /
1.60x vanilla's CPU and 3.02x / 5.55x / 6.31x its wall. Against Paper,
2.35x the CPU and 13.8x the wall. Vanilla's 0.192 CPU-s/chunk independently
reproduces the 0.211 this project already carried.

**Parity, same square, vanilla first, 225 chunks / 22,118,400 blocks:**

```text
  vanilla vs rustmc    4,395 blocks   99.980130%
  vanilla vs paper     7,436 blocks   99.966380%
  vanilla vs folia    29,922 blocks   99.864719%
```

**This is not "we beat Paper on parity."** One square, one driver, ONE
vanilla reference, and rule 6 says a residual is a defect only when two
independently generated vanilla worlds agree on it. Cross-chunk decoration
order alone is worth 4,885 blocks between two vanilla extents; Paper runs
Moonrise and Folia a regionised scheduler, so both promote chunks in a
different order. What it does establish: **"vanilla parity" is a live
variable for the forks too**, and a benchmark assuming the three Java
servers produce the same world assumes something false.

**Two findings the measurement produced on the way:**

1. **Folia implements neither `/save-all` nor `/tick`.** The first probe
   froze ticks and polled `save-all flush` + `region-differ scan` until the
   square was on disk; against Folia every command was rejected and the run
   measured Folia's five-minute autosave interval — 303 s of wall for 33 s
   of CPU — in a table that looked fine. The probe is now CPU-only
   (`ci/bench-probe.py`), nothing is sent inside the timed window, and the
   same code runs against all three. Folia also rejects `tick freeze`, so
   its square ticks live: its CPU column is an over-estimate and its parity
   row carries whatever ticked.
2. **`gamerule randomTickSpeed 0` has never worked, in any script here.**
   26.2's rule ids are snake_case and several are not renamings:
   `doMobSpawning` is `spawn_mobs`, `doWeatherCycle` is `advance_weather`,
   `doFireTick` is now the integer `fire_spread_radius_around_player`. Read
   out of the constant pool of
   `net/minecraft/world/level/gamerules/GameRules.class`.
   **`ci/gen-vanilla-region.sh` generates every vanilla reference world this
   project measures against**, and its five gamerules have been rejected on
   every run since it was written — `tick freeze` has carried it alone,
   exactly as its own comment claims. Both scripts now send 26.2's ids.
   Nothing already generated is invalidated: freeze stops the tick loop and
   the gamerules only mattered if freeze failed.

**Instruments added:** `ci/bench-servers.sh` (the harness, method in its
header), `ci/bench-probe.py` (the CPU probe, commands on stdin).
Both radii are supported: r<=7 goes as one `forceload add`, anything larger
row by row. `$WORK/worlds` is cleared at the start of every run — a short
run left an earlier run's worlds in place once and the parity pass diffed
this run's vanilla against last run's Paper without complaining. Paper and Folia jars are
fetched from `fill.papermc.io/v3` and sha256-verified into
`oracle-work/bench-servers/jars/`, which is gitignored like every other
third-party jar.

## Where item 1 actually stands — measured 2026-07-28

Main window, seed 31415926, chunks 62..66 (25 chunks, 2,457,600 blocks),
against **three independently generated vanilla worlds of the same seed**:

```text
  ./target/release/worldgen-dump full 31415926 2 oracle-work/rustmc-31415926-c64 64 64
  ./target/release/region-differ diff <vanilla> \
      oracle-work/rustmc-31415926-c64/region --bbox 62 62 66 66 --positions

  van-s2-c62         mismatches=14   99.999430%
  van-gen34/region   mismatches=14   99.999430%
  van-gen17/region   mismatches= 1   99.999959%
```

(Vanilla **first**, always. The references were rsynced to the Threadripper so
both worlds and the tools live on one machine. `van-gen17` and `van-gen34` are
`oracle-work/gen-31415926-25717` and `-25734`, whose region directories are
buried at `world/dimensions/minecraft/overworld/region`.)

**The three vanilla worlds do not agree with each other.**

```text
  van-s2-c62  vs  van-gen34    mismatches=0
  van-s2-c62  vs  van-gen17    mismatches=13   <- 11 gravel, 2 diorite
```

and those 13 are *exactly* the 13 this port was being charged with. Vanilla
generated the same seed twice and produced two different answers on those
blocks; `van-gen17` produces **ours**. So the honest figure for this window is
the **order-invariant** one — blocks where every vanilla reference agrees and
this port differs:

```text
  ORDER-INVARIANT RESIDUAL: 1 block   99.999959%
```

and it is a single mineshaft fence at (993,-5,1062), `east=true` here against
`east=false` in all three.

### Why the 13 move, and why that is vanilla's variation rather than ours

Established before the second reference was found, and it explains the
variation exactly:

  * The 11 gravel are **`ore_gravel`** from chunk (63,65) —
    `RUSTMC_TRACE_WRITE=1019,30,1040` names the writer. They are **not** a
    `disk_gravel` and have nothing to do with the `probe_disk_origin` thread,
    which is a different feature at seed 20260722 chunk (63,68). This file
    called them that for days.
  * The 2 diorite are `ore_diorite` from the same chunk, under the same lake —
    not "stone-variant drift below the noise floor", which is what they were
    written off as.
  * All 13 are positions where a lake's stone shell and an ore blob **overlap**.
    Intersecting this port's own writes:

    ```text
      lake_lava_underground (63,64) stone  ∩  all ore writes
          over the whole window   35 positions
          inside the diff bbox    19
          that we get "wrong"     13     <- exactly the 11 gravel + 2 diorite
    ```

    The 6 that agree with every vanilla world are the ones where the lake and
    the ore belong to the **same chunk** — there the step order decides (lake
    at step 1, ore at step 6, ore wins) and nothing can vary. Plus a
    cross-chunk control in the other direction: `ore_lapis` from (63,63) under
    a lake from (64,63), where the lake lands last in every world.

  * No third writer exists. Every chunk that could reach those positions —
    (62..64, 63..65), eleven of them — was dumped with `DecorateGolden` and
    only `ore_gravel`/`ore_diorite` from (63,65) and the lake from (63,64)
    touch them.

  * `ore_gravel` has `discard_chance_on_air_exposure: 0.0`, so
    `shouldSkipAirCheck` returns true without drawing and the blob's shape
    cannot depend on the world. The lakes match block for block and the ore
    blobs match block for block in every world. **Only the winner differs.**

So the whole disagreement is *which of two chunks decorated first*, and vanilla
does it both ways run to run. Nine global orders were swept before the second
reference existed, and none of them reproduces `van-s2-c62`:

```text
  raster 14   diag 14   spawn 232   zx 234   spiral_in 729
  zx_rev 1120   spiral 1199   zx_zrev 1901   reverse 3016
```

`zx_zrev` (z descending, x ascending) is the only simple scan satisfying the
pairwise constraints, and it costs 1887 blocks to buy 13. That was the clue
that no scan is the answer: **vanilla's own order is not a scan and not stable
between runs**, which is what a ticket-driven chunk system looks like from
outside. Chasing it further would have been chasing a coin flip.

**Rule 1's "order-invariant" wording is therefore not a formality — it is the
only kind of number this window can carry.** A single-reference figure here is
73% noise.

### What this owes the rest of the file

Every "genuine" residual in this document that was established against **one**
vanilla world needs re-checking against a second. The technique is cheap and
mechanical:

```text
  region-differ diff <vanillaA> <vanillaB> --bbox <same> --positions
```

Any block on which two vanilla worlds of one seed disagree is not evidence
about this port at all. The claim recorded earlier that "both
server-generated vanilla worlds agree with each other" was true of the pair
it was measured on and is **not** a general property; here two of three agree
and the third does not.

**Started, on the r7 window (seed 20260722, chunks 58..70 x 62..74, 156
chunks, 15,335,424 blocks):**

```text
  vanilla-r7  vs  vanilla-r7-b    mismatches=3006    99.980398%
  vanilla-r7  vs  van-rows-c64    mismatches=15917   99.896208%
```

3006 blocks between two vanilla worlds generated *the same way*. That is
**~19 blocks per chunk**, against the "~109 per 25-chunk window" (~4.4 per
chunk) this file has been quoting as the oracle noise floor. And the families
are not incidental — they are the ones under investigation, in **both**
directions:

```text
  324  cave_air -> sulfur        249  sulfur -> cave_air
  236  sulfur   -> cinnabar      125  cinnabar -> sulfur
  279  andesite -> diorite       231  sulfur -> water[level=0]
   90  water    -> seagrass       83  seagrass -> water
```

So on that window the sulfur/cinnabar swaps, the stone-variant swaps and the
water/vegetation families are **all** things vanilla does differently to
itself, by hundreds of blocks.

**What it does not do is excuse the three positions under investigation.**
Checked individually, and this is why the test is worth running rather than
assuming: `(1013,1,1079)`, `(1016,2,1077)`, `(1017,2,1077)` — the sulfur
`tip_merge` blocks — and the other eight dumper-versus-server positions are
**not** in the vanilla-vs-vanilla diff. Those two worlds agree there. The
sulfur thread survives the test; what dies is reading any *aggregate* on that
window as a port measurement.

### DONE 2026-07-28: the r7 window's genuine set, and the margin sweep

`worldgen-dump full 20260722 6 oracle-work/rustmc-20260722-r7 64 68` (53 s on
the Threadripper), then all three diffs at `--bbox 58 62 70 74 --positions`,
vanilla first every time. Working files kept at
`oracle-work/r7-genuine/` on the Threadripper (`a_ours_vs_r7.txt`,
`b_ours_vs_r7b.txt`, `c_r7_vs_r7b.txt`, `genuine_a.txt`).

```text
  vanilla-r7   vs ours      mismatches=1470    99.990414%   single-reference
  vanilla-r7-b vs ours      mismatches=3624    99.976368%   single-reference
  vanilla-r7   vs r7-b      mismatches=3006    99.980398%   the noise
  GENUINE = A \ C                        1043  99.993200%
```

Denominator on all four: the 156 chunks the differ actually overlapped,
15,335,424 blocks. **Cross-check passed**: `B \ C` is the *same 1043
positions*, key for key — which it must be, since `r7 == r7b` there makes
`ours != r7` and `ours != r7b` the same condition. A derivation that failed
this would have been arithmetic, not measurement.

Note how far apart the two single-reference figures are: 1470 against one
world and 3624 against the other, from the *same* dump. Either could have been
quoted as "the r7 residual". Neither is one.

**Then a shrink sweep, and its first reading was wrong.** Shrinking the bbox
ring by ring:

```text
  margin  bbox              chunks   blocks       raw    GENUINE   exactness
    0     58 62 70 74        156    15,335,424   1470     1043     99.993200%
    1     59 63 69 73        121    11,894,784   1011      707     99.994056%
    2     60 64 68 72         81     7,962,624    207       80     99.998995%
    3     61 65 67 71         49     4,816,896    136       13     99.999730%
    4     62 66 66 70         25     2,457,600    129        9     99.999634%
    5     63 67 65 69          9       884,736    128        8     99.999096%
```

(`raw` is against `vanilla-r7` alone; chunk counts and block counts are the
differ's own, taken at each bbox, not scaled from a wider one.)

963 of the 1043 — 92% — sit in the outer two rings of the dumped square, and
the obvious reading of that is "the margin rule already declares them
invalid". **That reading is wrong, and it was committed once before being
checked.** `Pipeline::new` calls `area.grown(DECORATION_MARGIN)` and every
stage, decoration included, runs over `generated()`, not `area()`. A `full`
dump of 58..70 x 62..74 therefore generates and decorates 56..72 x 60..76, so
the whole *written* square already has its two rings of context. There is no
invalid ring in this dump to discount.

The vanilla side is sound too: `region-differ scan` puts both references at
`full=362 bbox=4,3 -> 73,73` — a 19x19 forced square plus one — and a vanilla
chunk reaches `full` only after real decoration against a real dependency
cone. Chunk z = 74 is simply absent from both, which is the whole reason the
differ compares 156 chunks and not 169.

**So the r7 window's parity number is the margin-0 one: 1043 blocks over 156
chunks, 99.993200%.** The shrink sweep is not a validity correction — it is a
map. What it shows is that the residual is *spatially concentrated*, and
shrinking the box walks past one cluster at a time:

```text

  187   stone variants            diorite/andesite/granite
  139   an acacia tree we plant and vanilla does not     chunks (69,72) (69,73)
   43   an ocean ruin we build and vanilla does not      chunk  (68,70)
   33   water levels
   24   other
  ----
  1043
```

Two chunks carry 682 of it: (59,63) has 423 — 117 `cave_air -> sulfur`, 106
`diorite -> andesite`, 45 `water -> sulfur`, 29 `sulfur -> deepslate` — and
(58,63) has 149 of the same families in the other direction. That is one
sulfur cave, and it is the largest single object in the window.

**Do not quote margin 2 or 3 as the parity number.** The rate *rises* as the
box shrinks (6.8e-5 at margin 0, 1.0e-5 at 2, 2.7e-6 at 3, 3.7e-6 at 4,
9.0e-6 at 5): the small boxes have simply excluded the sulfur cave and kept

### The acacia: vanilla's own oracle plants it, and no real server does

Measured 2026-07-28, after the ruin gate. This is the second-largest family on
the r7 window at 139 genuine blocks, and it is **not** a placement bug.

**We are a strict superset of vanilla's trees.** `region-differ census
--match acacia_log --positions`, same bbox 58 62 70 74 on all three worlds,
positions compared as sets:

```text
  vanilla-r7     133 logs
  vanilla-r7-b   133 logs      identical position sets
  ours           203 logs
  ours \ vanilla  70 extra    vanilla \ ours  0 missing
```

Of the 70 extra, **59 are at cz = 74**, a chunk row that is absent from both
references (`scan` puts them at `bbox=4,3 -> 73,73`), so the differ never sees
them and they are not part of any residual. Restricted to the 156 compared
chunks: **11 extra logs, 0 missing.** Every acacia vanilla plants, we plant,
block for block — we add.

The extras, in the compared region:

```text
  1091 73 1183
  1106 65..71 x 1167..1171      one whole tree, ten logs, trunk base (1106,65,1168)
```

`RUSTMC_TRACE_WRITE=1106,66,1168` names the writer: `minecraft:trees_savanna`
from chunk (69,73). `RUSTMC_TRACE_ATTEMPT=trees_savanna` on that chunk:
`reached-feature=1 draws=12 rejected:` — nothing in the chain rejects.

**Vanilla's own dumper places the same tree.** `ci/decorate-once.sh` at seed
20260722, centre 69,73, with the fixed `GenLevel`:

```text
  feature: minecraft:trees_savanna   step 9   index 9
  placed: true   draws: 12   positions: [[1106,65,1168]]   positionDraws: [3]
  changes: 97, including [1106,68,1167 acacia_log], [1106,69,1167 acacia_log],
                         [1106,70,1167 acacia_log]
```

Byte for byte what we write. So the port matches the oracle and the oracle
does not match the server.

**And it is order-invariant on our side.** All nine `RUSTMC_DECORATE_ORDER`
values, full r7 dump each:

```text
  raster 203   reverse 203   zx 203   zx_rev 194   zx_zrev 212   diag 203
  spiral 203   spiral_in 203   spawn 203
  chunk (69,73): 6 logs in every one of the nine
```

The tree does not move and does not disappear under any order we can produce,
so cross-chunk decoration order is not the mechanism.

**The biome filter is excluded too.** `region-differ diff` reports
`biomes=239616/0` on this window: our biome containers are identical to
vanilla's, cell for cell, so `minecraft:biome` — the last modifier in
`trees_savanna`'s chain — cannot be answering differently. Nor can the
terrain: the block under the trunk is `grass_block[snowy=false]` in vanilla and
`dirt` in ours *only because our tree ran* `setDirtAt`, and the column above is
air in vanilla all the way up.

**This is the same split as the sulfur `tip_merge` trio**, which this file
already records: "six of our orders produce `tip_merge`, two independent
server orders produce `tip`, and vanilla's own isolated dumper produces
`tip_merge`". Two families now, 139 blocks and 5, plus the 104-block
dumper-versus-server disagreement already recorded in chunk (63,67). Ours and
`DecorateGolden` on one side; every real server on the other.

That makes "what does a real server do here that `DecorateGolden` does not"
the highest-value open question on the parity item, and the acacia is by far
the cheapest probe yet found for it: one feature, 12 draws, one position, no
carvers or noise involved.

### The missing tree is located: draw 827, same index, different BOUND

`trees_birch_and_oak_leaf_litter` in chunk (-59,-30), seed 20260722. Vanilla
reaches **9** origins and spends 6296 draws; we reach **7** and spend 4733. The
first two origins are identical — `(-937,71,-474)` and `(-943,72,-465)` — and
vanilla's third is `(-935,71,-479)` where ours is `(-932,72,-478)`.

Vanilla's `positionDraws`: `[3, 797, 1592, 2373, 2394, 3181, 3961, 4750, 5527]`
— so each placed tree's body costs ~790 draws and the third origin is emitted
at 1592.

The draw logs (vanilla's is the **last of four** segments: 21, 2354, 6187,
2351, 6251 lines) agree line for line for 816 logged draws, then:

```text
  logged line 817
    vanilla:  DRAW 827 nextInt(12) -> 3
    ours   :  DRAW 827 nextInt(9)  -> 3
```

**Same index, different bound.** Not a stream drift — both sides are at the
same stream position and are executing *different code*. That is the sharpest
kind of divergence this project can get, and it is inside tree #2's body.

`nextInt(12)` is `getTreeHeight` for the fancy oak: the selector's members are

```text
  trees_birch_and_oak_leaf_litter = random_selector
      0.0025  fallen_birch_tree
      0.2     birch_bees_0002_leaf_litter       straight, base 5, rand_a 2  -> nextInt(3)
      0.1     fancy_oak_bees_0002_leaf_litter   fancy,    base 3, rand_a 11 -> nextInt(12)
      0.0125  fallen_oak_tree
      default oak_bees_0002_leaf_litter         straight, base 4, rand_a 2  -> nextInt(3)
```

and `base + nextInt(a+1) + nextInt(b+1)` is what `trunk.rs` computes, which
matches. **So vanilla is placing the fancy oak at that point and we are placing
something whose `a` is 8** — and no member of this selector has `height_rand_a`
= 8, so `nextInt(9)` is not a tree height at all and the branch we are in is
something else entirely.

**Resume here.** The selector's chance rolls are `nextFloat`, which neither
side logs, so the pick itself is invisible in the logs — but both sides consume
the same values, so a different pick means a different *comparison*, not a
different stream. Two candidates, in order:

  1. **Our selector's iteration order or chance comparison.** Vanilla is
     `for entry : features { if (random.nextFloat() < entry.chance()) return
     entry.feature().place(...) }` — file order, strict `<`, and it **returns**
     on the first hit. Read `RandomSelectorFeature.place` from the bytecode and
     compare against our `configured.rs` arm.
  2. **`fallen_tree` is refused by us** and two of this selector's five members
     are fallen trees. What our selector does when the chosen member refuses —
     fall through to the default, or return — decides everything downstream,
     and vanilla has no such path because it places them.

Find what draws `nextInt(9)` on our side at draw 827:
`RUSTMC_TRACE_FEATURE=trees_birch_and_oak_leaf_litter` names every write and
its feature, and `RUSTMC_TRACE_ATTEMPT_POS=1` already shows our seven
survivors.

### The acacia is BLOCKED: the oracle read the server's world and still planted

`-Ddecorate.reads=trees_savanna` at seed 20260722 centre 69,73 gives the
complete list of world questions vanilla asked before planting — 1602 reads
over **406 distinct positions**, beginning exactly as the feature's shape
predicts:

```text
  1106,64,1168 = grass_block[snowy=false]     the block below the trunk
  1106,65,1168 ~ air                          the trunk position
  1104..1108, 66, 1166..1170 ~ air / tall_grass[half=upper]   the 5x5 free-space scan
```

Compared against `vanilla-r7`'s final world at the same 406 positions:

```text
  positions where the oracle's answer differs from the server's world:  3
      3  oracle air  ->  server short_grass
  of those, ones that could block a tree:  0
```

`short_grass` is a replaceable plant and `TreeFeature.validTreePos` accepts it,
so **none of the three is a blocker**. The oracle was reading, to 403 of 406
positions, the same world the server has — and it planted the tree while the
server did not.

**That exhausts what can be measured from here**, and the block is worth stating
precisely: every remaining hypothesis needs a real server's *mid-decoration*
state, which nothing in this project can observe. The three candidates are

  * `ChunkGenerator.applyBiomeDecoration`'s feature *selection* — the biome set
    is collected over `ChunkPos.rangeClosed(cp, 1)` from the chunks' stored
    containers and intersected with `biomeSource.possibleBiomes()`, and one of
    those chunks (cz = 74) is **absent from both references**, so it has never
    been checked against vanilla at all;
  * a neighbour whose features run before (69,73) on a server and after it in
    the harness — the mechanism that turned out to be the whole sulfur cave;
  * a `TreeFeature` branch reading something neither log captures.

**Resume point**: build a *third* vanilla reference for seed 20260722 whose
saved region covers cz = 74, and re-run the acacia census against it. If chunk
(69,74)'s biome container disagrees with ours, the first candidate is the
answer; if it agrees, the acacia is an order effect of a kind our nine orders
cannot express, and the honest move is to say so in BENCH.md rather than keep
chasing it. `ci/gen-vanilla-region.sh` is the generator.

### THE SULFUR CAVE IS ORDER, NOT A DEFECT — r7's invariant core is 176 blocks

The chase ended by falsifying itself, and the falsification is the most useful
number this window has produced.

**How it turned.** Vanilla's scan of column `(940,1010)` reads **one** block —
`sulfur` at y -19 — and stops, because `Column.scan`'s predicate is
`SpeleothemUtils.isEmptyOrWater = st.isAir() || st.is(Blocks.WATER)` (bytecode,
via the two `invokedynamic` lambdas), and `sulfur` is neither. Ours scans a
whole cave there. Our predicate is **identical** — `speleothem.rs`'s
`is_empty_or_water` is `air_at() || plain == "minecraft:water"`. So the
predicate is right and the *block* differed:

```text
  WRITE (940,-19,1010) <- stone                     noise
  WRITE (940,-19,1010) <- deepslate[axis=y]         surface
  WRITE (940,-19,1010) <- sulfur      by sulfur_pool from chunk (58, 62)
  WRITE (940,-19,1010) <- water       by sulfur_pool from chunk (58, 63)
```

**Our pipeline decorates x-outer, z-inner**, so `(58,63)` runs *before*
`(59,62)` and its lake floods the cell before the cluster scans it.
`DecorateGolden`'s region loop is `for dz … for dx …` — **z-outer** — so in the
harness `(59,62)` runs first, the cluster sees `sulfur`, stops, and grows the
spike at `(943,-19,1003)` that later makes `(58,63)`'s lake abandon. The whole
chain — lake, spike, cluster, back to lake — is a **decoration-order loop**.

**Measured, not argued.** The r7 window under `RUSTMC_DECORATE_ORDER`, same
bbox, same two references, genuine = rows absent from `r7-genuine/c.keys`:

```text
  raster      986        diag        986
  spawn      2774        zx         3161
  spiral_in 10330        spiral    28100
  zx_rev    32922        zx_zrev   33233
  reverse   48274
```

z-outer globally costs 3161 against raster's 986, so it is not "the right
order" either — vanilla's is neither, and this file has said for weeks that
vanilla's own order is not a scan and not stable between runs.

**So intersect them, which is what rule 1 has always demanded and this window
had never had done:**

```text
  ORDER-INVARIANT CORE, nine orders, two references
      176 / 15,335,424 over 156 chunks  =  99.998852%
```

and its composition is a completely different list from the single-order one:

```text
  139  an acacia we plant and vanilla does not
   16  water[level=0] -> bubble_column[drag=true]
   15  water[level=0|1|8] -> air        the fluid post-processing family
    4  sulfur_spike tip -> tip_merge
    2  obsidian -> lava[level=0]
  ---
  176
```

**The 617-block sulfur cave family is gone.** Every block of it survives some
orders and dies in others, which is the definition of an order artifact and
exactly what rule 1's order-invariance clause exists to catch. The lake
abandon, the missing spike at `(943,-19,1003)`, the 65/19/77 cluster
breakdown, the draw-363 divergence — all of it was a real, correctly traced
causal chain, and all of it was chasing which of two chunks decorated first.

Nothing in that work was wrong; the two committed fixes it produced
(`isValidBiome`, `isSolid` vs `isSolidRender`) stand and are bytecode-verified.
What was wrong was the premise that a single-order residual on this window was
a defect list. **This file now has the number that is one**, and it is the
first time the r7 window has carried an order-decomposed figure at all.

**Standing consequence:** never open an investigation off a single-order
residual again. Decompose first — nine dumps and nine diffs, about twenty
minutes — and work only the intersection.

### The cluster's arithmetic is right — with identical values, a branch split is a WORLD read

Read against the bytecode this turn, and **all of it matches our port**:

```text
  place            height  = config.height().sample(random)     IntProvider   uniform 1..4  -> nextInt(4)
                   wetness = config.wetness().sample(random)     FloatProvider constant 0.0  -> NO draw
                   density = config.density().sample(random)     FloatProvider uniform [0.3,0.7)
                   xRadius = config.radius().sample(random)      IntProvider   uniform 2..8  -> nextInt(7)
                   zRadius = config.radius().sample(random)      the same provider, again
                   placeColumn(level, random, pos, dx, dz, wetness, chance, height, density, config)
                                                                  signature IIFDIF — our argument order matches

  placeColumn      nextFloat  < wetness      drawn BEFORE the world is consulted
                   [pool branch]
                   nextDouble < chance       drawn unconditionally
                   [stalactite: thickness.sample -> nextInt(3); getSpeleothemHeight]
                   nextDouble < chance       drawn unconditionally
                   [stalagmite: thickness.sample; randomBetweenInclusive(-1,1) -> nextInt(3)
                                or getSpeleothemHeight]
                   [overlap split: randomBetweenInclusive]
                   nextBoolean               drawn FIRST in the merge conjunction and always spent

  getSpeleothemHeight   nextFloat > density -> return 0   (early, skipping the gaussian)
                        else (int) randomBetweenBiased(...)
  randomBetweenBiased   = ClampedNormalFloat.sample = Mth.clamp(Mth.normal(...), min, max)
                          ONE gaussian, no rejection loop — confirmed from bytecode
```

`speleothem_block_layer_thickness` is `uniform 2..4`, so its sample is a
`nextInt(3)` and is **logged** — which is why the logs show `nextInt(3)` from
two different sources (thickness, and the stalagmite height diff, which is
`randomBetweenInclusive(-1, 1)` because `max_stalagmite_stalactite_height_diff`
is 1). Do not read a `nextInt(3)` as one or the other without counting.

**The column the divergence is in.** `RUSTMC_TRACE_SPELEO_COLUMNS=1` already
stamps every column with the draw offset it ends at; for chunk (59,62)'s
cluster it prints 114 columns. Around the break:

```text
  SPELEO COL (940,1006) draw=356  cap=-1  stalactite=0 stalagmite=0    4 draws
  SPELEO COL (940,1007) draw=360  cap=-1  stalactite=0 stalagmite=0    4 draws
  SPELEO COL (940,1008) draw=367  cap=3   stalactite=0 stalagmite=0    7 draws
  SPELEO COL (940,1009) draw=371  cap=-1                               4 draws
```

A column that enters no branch costs exactly 4 — `nextFloat`, `nextDouble`,
`nextDouble`, `nextBoolean` — which is the structure above, confirmed. The
streams agree through draw **363**, which falls inside `(940,1008)`.

**And that is the whole point.** Both sides consumed the *same values in the
same order* up to 363. A stream cannot make two ports take different branches
while feeding them identical values — so the branch that split them was decided
by a **world read**: `Column.scan`'s ceiling/floor, `isLava`, or `canPlacePool`.
Our `(940,1008)` has `cap=3`, meaning we entered the stalactite branch; vanilla
writes nothing anywhere at x=940 and its 31 touched columns begin at
`(941,1004)` — where our trace says `cap=-1` and we build nothing.

Chasing the arithmetic further is chasing something already read and matched.

### `sulfur_spike_cluster` (59,62) measured on blocks: 65 missing, 19 wrong, 77 spurious

The draw divergence has a block-level counterpart, and it is not subtle.
`RUSTMC_TRACE_FEATURE=sulfur_spike_cluster` against the oracle's 95 changes:

```text

  shared           30      states differ 19
  vanilla-only     65      ours-only  402
```

Classifying the 402 against the pre-decoration world — the trap this file
records one section down, since `changes` is a diff and cannot see a write that
changes nothing:

```text
  ours-only 402:  no-op rewrites 325   genuinely new 77
      46  sulfur    -> sulfur_spike
      16  air       -> sulfur_spike
      10  deepslate -> sulfur
       5  deepslate -> sulfur_spike
```

So the honest shape of it is **30 right, 19 the wrong thickness, 65 missing,
77 spurious**, from a feature that reaches the *same six origins* as vanilla's.

The 19 are the thickness family this file has tracked on its own:

```text
  (948,-19,1005)  vanilla frustum(up,wet)    ours tip_merge(up,wet)
  (948,-17,1005)  vanilla tip(down,dry)      ours frustum(down,dry)
  (946,-19,1002)  vanilla tip(up,wet)        ours base(up,wet)
  (943,-12,1005)  vanilla tip(down,dry)      ours base(down,dry)
```

and the 65 missing include the cell the whole chain hangs on:

