```text
                              waterlogged=true]        ours NO WRITE
```

**Not the gaussian guard.** `marsaglia_next_gaussian!` already wraps itself in
`draws::composite()`, so `next_gaussian` counts one and suppresses the nested
`next_f64`s exactly as `Counting` does. That suspect is dead; the sixteen extra
draws are real stream consumption inside one column.

This makes `sulfur_spike_cluster` the single most valuable open target: the
617-block sulfur cave family, the `tip_merge` family, and the whole
lake-abandon chain through (58,63) and (59,63) are all downstream of it.

### The lake was never the bug — it is `sulfur_spike_cluster` in chunk (59,62)

Chunk (58,62)'s `sulfur_pool` is **byte-exact**. Vanilla: `placed=True,
draws=960, positions=[[943,-18,1006]], changes=459`. Ours: the same origin, the
same 960 draws, the same rejection counts. Comparing the write sets:

```text
  vanilla changes 459   ours distinct writes 566
  shared 459   states differ 0   vanilla-only 0   ours-only 107
```

**And all 107 "extras" are no-ops.** Every one is a position that already held
that exact block before decoration, checked against our carver-stage dump —
which this file has already shown matches vanilla's `carvedRuns` exactly:

```text
  extras 107   already that block pre-decoration 107   genuinely new 0
```

**Trap, and it nearly cost a chase**: `DecorateGolden`'s `changes` is a
**diff**, so a write that does not change the block is invisible in it, while
`RUSTMC_TRACE_FEATURE` logs every write. Never read an "ours-only" write as a
defect without checking the pre-decoration block first.

Both worlds flood the target cell: `(943,-19,1003)` is `water[level=0]` in
vanilla's changes *and* ours. So the lake is not the difference — **the spike
that grows in that water afterwards is.**

**The recorded assumption was wrong.** Chunk (58,62)'s own spike features do
not place:

```text
  step 7 index 2  minecraft:sulfur_spike_cluster  placed=False draws=184   changes=0
  step 7 index 3  minecraft:sulfur_spike          placed=False draws=3063  changes=0
```

A sweep of five candidate centres — (58,61), (59,62), (57,62), (59,61),
(59,63) — found the writer, and only one of them writes that cell:

```text
  centre 59,62 : sulfur_spike_cluster, step 7 index 2
                 -> sulfur_spike[thickness=tip,vertical_direction=up,waterlogged=true]
```

**And that feature diverges.** Vanilla's (59,62) cluster: `placed=True,
draws=941`, six positions, 95 changes. Ours reaches the **same six origins**
(the last three visible in the trace as (958,-18,995), (955,-11,1003),
(947,-19,1005)) and spends **1013 draws**.

The two draw logs agree exactly — index *and* value — through draw 363, logged
line 234. Then:

```text
  DRAW 363 nextInt(3) -> 0     both, identical
  vanilla   next logged draw is 374 nextInt(3) -> 0   (10 unlogged in between)
  ours      next logged draw is 390 nextInt(3) -> 0   (26 unlogged in between)
```

**Sixteen extra unlogged draws on our side, inside one column.** And it is not
only a counting difference: with the indices stripped, the two sequences still
differ — vanilla makes about seven more `nextInt(3)` calls in that stretch than
we do (431 logged lines to our 435 overall).

**Read from the bytecode, the cluster's draw sites**
(`SpeleothemClusterFeature`):

```text
  place              nextFloat (75), nextDouble (193), nextDouble (332),
                     nextBoolean (593)
  getSpeleothemHeight  nextFloat
  randomBetweenBiased  -> ClampedNormalFloat.sample(random, mean, dev, min, max)
```

`randomBetweenBiased` is a **gaussian**, and that matters for the counter:
vanilla's `Counting` wrapper counts `nextGaussian` as **one** draw however many
`nextDouble`s the Marsaglia rejection loop spends inside it, because the Java
gaussian holds the *inner* source and its calls never reach the wrapper.
`crates/rustmc-worldgen/src/rng/draws.rs` documents exactly this and provides
`draws::gaussian` to count one and suppress the nested calls. Sixteen extra
unlogged draws is precisely the shape of that guard not being applied — but the
`nextInt(3)` content difference says something real diverges too, so it is at
most half the answer.

### SOLVED: vanilla abandons on a `sulfur_spike` we flooded from chunk (58,62)

`GenLevel` now records every `getBlockState` the subject makes, in order,
under `-Ddecorate.reads=<substring>`, emitted as `blockReads` beside
`biomeAnswers`. The order is the whole point: `LakeFeature`'s pass 1 returns on
the first failure, so **the last read is the cell it gave up on**.

`ci/decorate-once.sh -Ddecorate.seed=20260722 -Ddecorate.centers=58,63
-Ddecorate.reads=sulfur_pool` gives 3363 reads for the feature, of which
exactly one contiguous run of 275 falls inside the lake box — reads 619..893,
which is pass 1's shell walk:

```text
  first  (942,-22,1010) = minecraft:sulfur
  last   (943,-19,1003) = minecraft:sulfur_spike[thickness=tip,
                              vertical_direction=up,waterlogged=true]
                          local (x=9, y=3, z=1), below the waterline
```

**That is the abandon.** `sulfur_pool`'s `can_place_feature` is
`{"type":"not","predicate":{"type":"matching_blocks",
"blocks":"minecraft:sulfur_spike"}}` — a spike anywhere in the shell stops the
lake. (A spike is also not `isSolid()`, so the `k < 4` test fires on it too;
either way the answer is the same block.)

**And our world has water there, not a spike.** The same cell in our shell
trace, and the column in both final worlds:

```text
  our shell trace:  LAKE cell (943,-19,1003) local_y=3 below minecraft:water[level=0]

              y    vanilla-r7          ours
            -21    deepslate           deepslate
            -20    sulfur              sulfur
            -19    sulfur_spike        water          <- here
            -18    cave_air            cave_air
            -17    cave_air            cave_air
```

`RUSTMC_TRACE_WRITE=943,-19,1003` names ours:

```text
  WRITE (943,-19,1003) <- minecraft:stone            noise
  WRITE (943,-19,1003) <- minecraft:deepslate[axis=y] surface
  WRITE (943,-19,1003) <- minecraft:water[level=0]   by sulfur_pool from chunk (58, 62)
```

**Chunk (58,62)'s lake floods the cell where vanilla grows a spike.** The cell
is inside chunk (58,62) (x 928..943, z 992..1007), and a chunk runs *all* its
decoration steps before the next chunk starts, so vanilla's spike — a
later-step feature of (58,62) — is finished long before (58,63) decorates.

So the chain, complete and every link measured:

```text
  our (58,62) sulfur_pool floods (943,-19,1003); vanilla grows a sulfur_spike
    -> (58,63)'s lake at (942,-18,1010) finds water where vanilla finds a spike
       -> can_place_feature passes for us and fails for vanilla
       -> we build a lake vanilla abandons, carving (946,-18,1012)
          -> (59,63)'s third candidate scans up and stops at -18, not -3
             -> its last filter rejects
                -> we miss vanilla's pool at (946,-4,1012)      216 blocks
                -> and build a spurious one at a repeated origin  133 blocks
```

Chunks (58,63) and (59,63) carry 149 and 247 of the window's 986. **The head of
the chain is chunk (58,62), and it is the same question one more chunk back.**

### Every candidate for the (58,63) abandon is cleared — instrument the oracle next

`RUSTMC_TRACE_LAKE=cells` now lists each shell cell with its position, not just
the distinct states. For the lake at origin (942,-18,1010): **279 shell
cells**. Each was read three ways — ours at lake time (the trace), our
carver-stage world, and `vanilla-r7`'s final world:

```text
  cells where VANILLA's final block would abandon:  0
```

Not one. Below the waterline every cell vanilla holds is solid or is the lake's
own fluid; above it none is liquid. And the shell is not untouched terrain —
predecessors wrote into 15+ of these cells, and **ours-at-lake matches
vanilla-final at every one of them**:

```text
  (936,-19,1006)  carver deepslate -> at-lake sulfur           vanilla sulfur
  (937,-19,1005)  carver deepslate -> at-lake water[level=0]   vanilla water
  (937,-18,1006)  carver cinnabar  -> at-lake cave_air         vanilla cave_air
```

**And the mask is provably identical.** The two draw logs around the body:

```text
  DRAW 183 nextInt(321) -> 20      both
  DRAW 184 nextInt(4)   -> 3       both   -> 3 + 4 = 7 ellipsoids on each side
  ...  draws 185..226 unlogged on both = 42 = 7 x 6 nextDoubles, exactly
  DRAW 227 vanilla nextInt(16)     back at in_square: abandoned
  DRAW 227 ours    nextInt(2)      the barrier coin: pass 1 passed
```

Seven ellipsoids each, forty-two doubles each, no room for an extra draw on
either side — so the fluid provider spends nothing on both, and the ellipsoid
values come from the same stream position. `is_shell` and `index` were both
re-read against the bytecode this turn and match index for index
(`mask[(x*16+z)*8+y]`, x/z 1..14, y 1..6, six neighbours guarded at 0/15/7).

So: same mask, same shell, same blocks at every shell cell, same three tests in
the same order, correct block-property table — and vanilla abandons where we do
not. **Rule 7 applies: when a measurement clears every candidate, suspect the
measurement.**

The measurement being trusted is "vanilla's lake abandoned", inferred from
`placed=False, changes=0`. That inference is sound as far as it goes —
`GenLevel.ensureCanWrite` allows the whole box (writeRadius 1, and the box
spans sections 58..59 x 62..63 around centre (58,63)), and the `nextInt(4)` at
draw 184 proves the body ran rather than taking the `origin.getY() <=
getMinY() + 4` early exit. What it cannot say is **which cell** stopped it, or
what vanilla read there.

`GenLevel` already records every `getBiome` the subject asked and its answer,
shipped with the vectors so the port can assert its lookups match vanilla's.
It records nothing about `getBlockState`. That is the gap, and closing it is
the next item.

### The pre-decoration worlds AGREE, and `lake.rs` was calling `isSolidRender`

Two findings, and the second is a real fix.

**The terrain is not at fault.** Our carver-stage dump against vanilla's own
`SurfaceChunkGolden` `carvedRuns`, over the whole lake box (934..949,
-22..-15, 1002..1017), 2048 blocks on each side:

```text
  RUSTMC_THROUGH=carvers ./target/release/worldgen-dump full 20260722 1 <out> 58 63
  RUSTMC_JAVA_PROPS="-Dsurface.seeds=20260722 -Dsurface.chunks=58,62;59,62;58,63;59,63" \
      ./ci/surface-chunk-golden.sh <out.json>

  MISMATCHES IN BOX: 555 of 2048
      555  minecraft:deepslate[axis=y] -> minecraft:deepslate
```

Every one is `region-differ census` printing a default state in short form
against the oracle's full serialisation. **Zero real disagreements.** The
noise, surface and carver stages produce the same 2048 blocks vanilla does.

(Two traps worth keeping: `ci/surface-chunk-golden.sh` passes `"$@"` *after*
the class name, so `-D` flags there are program arguments and are silently
ignored — they must go through `RUSTMC_JAVA_PROPS`. And a `full` dump writes
only `area.chunks()`, so radius 0 gives one chunk; the box needs radius 1.)

**It is not the harness's neighbourhood either.** `-Ddecorate.region=2` and
`=3` both reproduce `placed=False draws=811 positions=[[942,-18,1010]]
changes=0` exactly. At region 2 the harness's decorated predecessors are the
same twelve chunks our dump has.

**And the draw logs pin the divergence to pass 1.** Vanilla's (58,63) log is
the last of five segments (768, 936, 773, 768, 769 lines); against ours:

```text
  first mismatch at logged line 185
    vanilla: DRAW 227 nextInt(16) -> 5     back at in_square: the body abandoned
    ours   : DRAW 227 nextInt(2)  -> 0     the barrier coin: our pass 1 passed
```

**The same draw index.** Pass 1 spends no draws on either side, so both reach
227 having spent the same values — the ellipsoid mask is identical — and then
one abandons and one does not.

**Fixed: `lake.rs` asked the wrong solidity question.** Vanilla's
`LakeFeature.place` calls `BlockState.isSolid()` in both passes (bytecode
`invokevirtual #84` at 655 and 1161). This port has *two* properties, and
`PredicateWorld` documents the difference: `solid_at` is `isSolidRender` (what
`BlockPredicate.solid` wants) and `is_solid_at` is `isSolid()`. Both of
`lake.rs`'s calls used `solid_at`. The error string beside them already said
`"isSolid"` — the intent was right and the call was not. The unit tests could
not catch it: their test world is stone versus air, and stone answers both the
same, which is why they stayed green while the generator built lakes vanilla
abandons.

```text
  r7 window, 156 chunks, 15,335,424 blocks, two references
                  raw vs r7   raw vs r7-b   GENUINE   exactness
    before           1414        3568         987     99.993564%
    after            1413        3567         986     99.993571%
```

**One block, and it does not close the sulfur cave.** Chunk (58,63) still
reports `reached-feature=2 draws=989` — unchanged — because every state its
shell actually saw answers `isSolid` and `isSolidRender` identically. Checked
against `data/vanilla/block_props.json`, which matches vanilla:

```text
  sulfur, cinnabar, deepslate[axis=y], potent_sulfur[wet]   solid=true  solidRender=true
  water[level=0]                                            solid=false solidRender=false
  cave_air                                                  solid=false solidRender=false  air=true
```

The fix is still correct and had to be made; it is simply not this cave's
cause. What remains is that our pass 1 sees a shell whose cells all pass, and
vanilla's sees one that does not — same mask, same terrain, same predecessors.
So **one specific cell differs at lake time**, and the trace does not yet name
it: it records the distinct states, not the positions.

### Chunk (58,63): vanilla ABANDONS the lake we build, and it reads a different world

`ci/decorate-once.sh -Ddecorate.seed=20260722 -Ddecorate.centers=58,63`:

```text
  ORACLE (58,63) sulfur_pool: placed=False  draws=811
      positions [[942,-18,1010]]   changes=0
```

**One origin, and the body abandons.** Ours, from
`RUSTMC_TRACE_ATTEMPT=sulfur_pool RUSTMC_TRACE_ATTEMPT_POS=1`:

```text
  ATTEMPT minecraft:sulfur_pool chunk (58, 63) reached-feature=2 draws=989
      STAGE #7 biome -> (942,-18,1010)      <- vanilla's origin, exactly
      STAGE #7 biome -> (942,-19,1012)      <- a second one vanilla never gets
```

Same first origin. Vanilla's lake abandons in pass 1 and writes nothing; ours
survives and writes — which is why ours spends 989 draws to vanilla's 811 (a
lake that abandons never reaches the barrier coins) and why a later candidate
survives for us.

**Nothing else in that chunk has written when it runs.** The oracle's own
feature list for (58,63): `lake_lava_underground` (placed=False, 4 draws, 0
changes), `lake_lava_surface` (False, 1, 0), `rooted_sulfur_spring` (False, 4,
0), then `sulfur_pool` at step 1 index 3. So the shell cells it tests are
terrain plus whatever neighbours decorated earlier — and the box (934..949,
-22..-15, 1002..1017) spans only chunks (58,62), (59,62), (58,63), (59,63),
all of which have the same predecessors in the harness and in our dump.

**Our pass 1 is not missing a test.** Read against the bytecode, vanilla's
shell loop is:

```java
  boolean shell = !mask[i][j][k] && any of the six neighbours is masked;
  if (shell) {
      BlockState st = level.getBlockState(pos.offset(i, k, j));
      if (k >= 4 && st.liquid())                      return false;
      if (k <  4 && !st.isSolid() && st != fluid)     return false;
      if (!config.canPlaceFeature.test(level, pos))   return false;
  }
```

`lake.rs` has all three, in that order, and `is_shell` matches the six-neighbour
test index for index. The previous entry's summary of pass 1 listed only two
conditions; `can_place_feature` is the third and it *is* implemented.

**New instrument.** `RUSTMC_TRACE_LAKE=1` now also prints, for every lake that
**survives** pass 1, the distinct states it saw, split at the waterline. The
abandon reasons could only say why a lake stopped; this says why one did not.

```text
  LAKE survives pass 1 at origin (942,-18,1010)
    below-waterline  {cinnabar, deepslate[axis=y], sulfur, water[level=0]}
    above            {air, cave_air, cinnabar, deepslate[axis=y], sulfur}
```

(The box is world y -22..-15, so the local `k = 4` waterline is world y -18.)

**And none of those states would make vanilla abandon either.** Above the
waterline nothing is liquid; below it, everything is solid except
`water[level=0]`, which is the lake's own fluid and therefore passes `st !=
fluid`. So vanilla did not abandon on any block *we* saw — **it saw different
blocks**. The divergence is in the world the lake reads, not in the lake.

That is either the terrain (noise/surface/carvers) or an earlier neighbour's
decoration, and one measurement separates them.

**Watch for a state-identity trap when it is chased.** Vanilla compares `st !=
fluid` with `if_acmpeq`, i.e. BlockState identity; ours compares state strings.
They agree only while the world holds exactly `water[level=0]`. A
`water[level=1]` there — the family this file already attributes to
`markPosForPostProcessing`, still unported — would make vanilla abandon and us
not, and would tie the fluid thread directly to this cave. No `water[level=1]`
appears in the *final* worlds inside this box, but the pre-decoration world has
not been looked at.

### CORRECTED and localised: our lake bodies are exact — the fault is in chunk (58,63)

The previous entry's closing inference — "pools #1 and #2 spent the same values
and wrote different blocks, so the body's logic differs" — is **wrong**, and
the measurement that killed it is the one it asked for.

`RUSTMC_TRACE_FEATURE=sulfur_pool` gives our writes in order, with the writing
chunk named. `DecorateGolden`'s `changes` is a **sorted diff, not a write log**
(its first entry is outside pool #1's box), so only our side can be split by
invocation — but that is enough. Matching each of our writes against vanilla's
475-position set, in write order:

```text
  writes   0..167   MATCH    168 of them, every position and every state
  writes 168..300   DIFFER   133, all `ours sulfur / vanilla NO WRITE`
  write  301        MATCH
```

**Our first two lake bodies are byte-exact** — 168 writes, identical to
vanilla's. The 133 are our spurious third lake at the repeated origin. So
`LakeFeature`'s ellipsoid math, its passes and its block choices are all
correct here; the earlier "differ 0 at every shared position" was the clue and
this confirms it. Nothing in `feature/lake.rs` is at fault.

**The whole defect is the third candidate, and its cause is one chunk away.**
`RUSTMC_TRACE_WRITE=946,-18,1012`, the block our `environment_scan` stopped on:

```text
  WRITE (946,-18,1012) <- minecraft:stone      by ? (no feature running)   noise
  WRITE (946,-18,1012) <- minecraft:sulfur     by ? (no feature running)   surface
  WRITE (946,-18,1012) <- minecraft:sulfur     by minecraft:sulfur_pool from chunk (58, 62)
  WRITE (946,-18,1012) <- minecraft:cave_air   by minecraft:sulfur_pool from chunk (58, 63)
```

A `sulfur_pool` from **chunk (58,63)** — a neighbour, decorated earlier —
carves that block. Vanilla's does not. `worldgen-dump column 20260722 946 1012
-22 -2 59 63` shows the terrain underneath is not in dispute: `sulfur` from
-22 to -11 at the surface stage, and the carvers cut air only at -3 and -2.
That is exactly where vanilla's scan lands.

So the causal chain, end to end:

```text
  our chunk (58,63) sulfur_pool carves (946,-18,1012), vanilla's does not
    -> chunk (59,63)'s third candidate scans up from -20 and stops at -18
       instead of -3
    -> random_offset -1 puts it at -19, `matching minecraft:sulfur` rejects it
    -> we never build vanilla's third pool at (946,-4,1012)      216 blocks
    -> and we build a spurious lake at the repeated origin        133 blocks
```

which is why the draw streams diverge at 752 and why chunk (58,63) carries its
own 149 genuine mismatches: **it is the same cave, and (58,63) is upstream.**

**The neighbour's decoration is not a margin artifact.** Chunk (58,63) is
inside the r7 dump's requested area, and `Pipeline::new` grows the generated
area by `DECORATION_MARGIN` on top of that, so (58,63) decorates against a full
neighbourhood. Its lake is simply in the wrong place.

### The sulfur_pool divergence is at draw 752, and the bodies differ, not the stream

`RUSTMC_TRACE_DRAWS` now works in the real generator, not only in
`golden_decorate` — three lines in `feature/decorate.rs`, behind
`RUSTMC_TRACE_ATTEMPT` matching first, so a server pays nothing. Without it a
divergence in a whole-world dump could be *counted* and not *located*.

**Do not "fix" either draw log to print more methods.** `DecorateGolden`'s
`Counting` wrapper logs `nextInt(bound)` and `nextLong` and nothing else — it
increments `draws` for `nextInt()`, `nextBoolean`, `nextFloat`, `nextDouble`,
`nextGaussian` and `fork` but never logs them. Ours does exactly the same, so
the two sequences diff line for line; the indices jump identically where both
omitted the same calls. Ours logs 881 lines of 983 draws and vanilla 1057 of
1159, and the gaps line up. Making one side log more would break the only
comparison that matters.

**First divergence: logged line 686, draw 752.** The 685 before it are
identical, value for value:

```text
  ...
  DRAW 749 nextInt(16)  -> 2      in_square x
  DRAW 750 nextInt(16)  -> 4      in_square z
  DRAW 751 nextInt(321) -> 44     height_range
  vanilla   DRAW 752 nextInt(4)  -> 2      <- LakeFeature.place: nextInt(4) + 4 ellipsoids
  ours      DRAW 752 nextInt(16) -> 9      <- in_square again: we rejected the candidate
```

So at that point vanilla **entered a lake body** and we **went back for the
next candidate**. The candidate is chunk (59,63)'s origin (944,·,1008) plus
(2,·,4) = x 946, z 1012 — vanilla's third pool, `(946,-4,1012)`.

**Which modifier rejects it, exactly.** The chain, from
`placed_feature/sulfur_pool.json`: `count 256`, `in_square`, `height_range
uniform[above_bottom 0, absolute 256]`, `block_predicate_filter solid`,
`environment_scan up max_steps 32 target=#minecraft:air`, `random_offset
y_spread -1`, `block_predicate_filter matching minecraft:sulfur`, `biome`.
Ours, from `RUSTMC_TRACE_ATTEMPT_POS=1`:

```text
  STAGE  #4 environment_scan -> (946,-18,1012)
  STAGE  #5 random_offset    -> (946,-19,1012)
  REJECT #6 block_predicate_filter at (946,-19,1012)
```

Vanilla's scan lands at y -3 and its offset at -4. **Ours stops 15 blocks
lower**, and the `matching minecraft:sulfur` filter then rejects it. Both start
from the same y (-64 + 44 = -20, the same drawn value), so the scan disagrees
about where the first air-tagged block above -20 is.

**And that is the important part: the world it scans already differs.** The
final worlds at that column:

```text
  946 -19 1012   vanilla sulfur     ours water[level=0]
  946 -18 1012   vanilla sulfur     ours cave_air
  946 -17 1012   vanilla sulfur     ours cave_air
  946  -4 1012   vanilla cave_air   ours sulfur
  946  -3 1012   vanilla cave_air   ours air
```

Vanilla is solid where we are hollow at -19..-17 and hollow where we are solid
at -4..-3 — the pool is roughly fifteen blocks too low. Since draws 1..751 are
identical, pools #1 and #2 spent the *same values* and wrote *different
blocks*. **The `LakeFeature` body's logic differs, not its stream**, which is a
far more tractable bug than a stream offset and is where the next work goes.

`LakeFeature.place`'s only two draw sites, from the bytecode, for whoever
takes it:

```text
  int n = random.nextInt(4) + 4;          the ellipsoid count, once
  ... the barrier pass, per candidate block:
  if (dy >= 4 || random.nextInt(2) != 0)  then test isSolid + canReplaceWithBarrier
```

The long `nextInt(2)` run at draws 789+ is that barrier coin, and it is spent
only for `dy >= 4`.

### The sulfur cave IS ours — and it is one feature, `sulfur_pool`

The acacia's test, run on the sulfur family, and it comes back the **opposite
way**. `ci/decorate-once.sh -Ddecorate.seed=20260722 -Ddecorate.centers=59,63`,
then every one of that chunk's 423 genuine rows looked up in the oracle's
recorded `changes`:

```text
  oracle == ours        0
  oracle == vanilla   250
  oracle a third value  0
  oracle wrote nothing 173   (and vanilla writes nothing there either)
```

**Zero.** Vanilla's own dumper never once agrees with us here. This is not the
harness-versus-server split; it is ours, and it is the largest single defect in
the project.

Of the 250 the oracle wrote, **247 are `minecraft:sulfur_pool`** and 3 are
`sulfur_spike`:

```text
  117  cave_air -> sulfur        vanilla's pool hollows, we leave stone
   45  water    -> sulfur
   29  sulfur   -> deepslate     vanilla's shell, we leave deepslate
   25  cave_air -> air
   20  cave_air -> deepslate
    8  water    -> deepslate
```

The 173 the oracle never wrote are led by **106 `diorite -> andesite`**, which
is the stone-variant family and comes from a neighbouring chunk's ore feature,
not from anything chunk (59,63) runs — a separate thread.

**The fault is the third origin, and it is exact.** Both sides reach the
feature three times in chunk (59,63). The oracle:

```text
  ORACLE sulfur_pool  placed=True  step=1 index=3  draws=1159  changes=475
      positions [[951,-5,1016], [959,-6,1015], [946,-4,1012]]
```

and ours, from `RUSTMC_TRACE_ATTEMPT=sulfur_pool RUSTMC_TRACE_ATTEMPT_POS=1`,
reading the `STAGE #7 biome ->` survivors:

```text
  ATTEMPT minecraft:sulfur_pool chunk (59, 63) reached-feature=3 draws=983
      (951,-5,1016)   (959,-6,1015)   (951,-5,1016)
```

The first two are **identical**. The third is not: vanilla's is
`(946,-4,1012)` and ours **repeats the first**. And the totals differ by 176
draws, 983 against 1159.

That is the shape of an upstream draw-count difference, not a placement-chain
difference: the chain and the feature body interleave on one stream, so if our
first or second pool's *body* spends fewer values than vanilla's, the third
candidate is drawn from a shifted stream and lands somewhere else — here, back
on a position already used. It also matches what this project's notes have
carried for days as "a sulfur_pool lake we skip, fault is WHICH origins the
placement chain yields": the origins are a symptom.

The chain, for reference, from our own trace stages:

```text
  #0 count  #1 in_square  #2 height_range  #3 block_predicate_filter
  #4 environment_scan  #5 random_offset  #6 block_predicate_filter  #7 biome
```

### DONE 2026-07-28: the port reads the biome container now — worth 1 block here

`Biomes::biome_at` in `tools/worldgen-assembly/src/generate.rs`, the
`BiomeFacts` impl decoration is handed, resolved the fuzzed quart cell by
**resampling** the climate function. The surface stage's own `biome_at`, thirty
lines up in the same file, already read the stored container and carried the
reasoning and a measured example. Decoration did not.

Fixed the same way: a snapshot of every generated chunk's biome container,
taken once before the decoration loop (features write blocks and never biomes,
so nothing goes stale, and `Decoration` holds the canvas mutably for the whole
pass), read as `ChunkAccess.getNoiseBiome` reads it — clamp qy into the chunk,
then the cell at `(qx & 3, qy & 3, qz & 3)`. A cell outside the snapshot
resamples, which is `getUncachedNoiseBiome`'s case, and is **counted**
(`RUSTMC_STAGE_TIMES=1` prints the total) rather than silent.

Measured on the r7 window, same dump, same three diffs, same bbox:

```text
                      raw vs r7   raw vs r7-b   GENUINE   exactness
  before                 1415        3569         988     99.993558%
  after                  1414        3568         987     99.993564%
  biomes                                       239616/0   unchanged
```

One block, and the churn is honest rather than hidden — three positions moved,
two fixed and one new, all of them `short_grass`:

```text
  fixed  (1074,63,1121)  vanilla short_grass, ours air
  fixed  (1076,64,1125)  vanilla short_grass, ours air
  new    (1072,63,1123)  vanilla air, ours short_grass
```

Two of those were in the margin-3 interior list, so the fix lands exactly where
this file said an unexplained residual was. The families are otherwise
unmoved — sulfur cave 617, stone variants 187, acacia 139 — so **the biome read
path is not the sulfur family's mechanism on this window**, which is worth
knowing because it was the first plausible one that thread had.

**Gate hygiene, recorded because it is a hole and not a finding.**
`golden_biome_lookup` models the lookup as fuzz-then-**resample**, which is now
what neither the production path nor vanilla does. It reads
`decorate_vectors_sulfur.json`, whose three centres contain no cell where the
two paths differ, so it reads 100% either way; pointed at
`decorate_vectors.json` it reads 99.600726% over 2755 positions. The gate is
therefore valid only where the two paths agree, and a real gate on this would
have to replay the container — which needs a generated canvas, not a vector
file. Left as it is, with this note, rather than deleted or weakened.

### DONE 2026-07-28: the harness's `BiomeManager` is fixed, and it found a PORT bug

The rewiring itself, `DecorateGolden.java`: the `BiomeManager` now resolves a
quart cell out of the level grid's **stored biome container** — clamping qy
into the chunk and reading `(qx & 3, qy & 3, qz & 3)`, which is
`ChunkAccess.getNoiseBiome` — and resamples the biome source only for a cell
outside the grid, which is the `getUncachedNoiseBiome` case. Out-of-grid
lookups are counted and printed to stderr; the acacia run reported none.
`SurfaceChunkGolden` already did this and carried the reasoning; this file did
not, and the lambda below is that one widened from a chunk to a grid.

**What it did to the acacia: nothing.** All 57 features of chunk (69,73) are
byte-identical, `trees_savanna` still `placed=True draws=12
positions=[[1106,65,1168]] changes=97`. So the wiring was a real divergence and
is **not** the acacia's cause. That thread's next suspect is
`ChunkGenerator.applyBiomeDecoration`'s feature selection.

**What it did to the committed vectors: 11 answers, 0 blocks.**
`ci/decorate-golden.sh` (two runs, agreed) regenerates
`decorate_vectors.json` with 169 feature records **unchanged** — same placed,
same draws, same positions, same change counts — and exactly 11 `biomeAnswers`
flipped, all in the third centre's group, all `river -> beach`:

```text
  1283,136,2457   1287,6,2458    1287,274,2458  1285,46,2459
  1288,-9,2455    1286,29,2458   1286,39,2456   1286,110,2456
  1285,91,2456    1285,174,2460  1286,-43,2460
```

**And the port answers `river` at all eleven.** Found by pointing
`golden_biome_lookup` at `decorate_vectors.json`:

```text
  BIOME LOOKUP EXACTNESS 99.600726% over 2755 positions (11 wrong)
    (1283,136,2457) want minecraft:beach, got minecraft:river
    ... all eleven, every one river-for-beach
```

So this port has the same fault the harness had: at a **block** lookup it
computes `find_value(sampler.sample(quart_for_block(zoom, x, y, z)))` — a
resample of the biome source — where a server reads the chunk's stored biome
container, and that container was filled from
`noiseChunk.cachedClimateSampler(router, spawnTarget)`, a different
computation. Our containers match vanilla's exactly (`biomes=239616/0` on the
r7 window), so the container is available and correct; only the lookup path is
wrong.

**Why the gates missed it.** `golden_biome_lookup` reads
`decorate_vectors_sulfur.json` and nothing else; `golden_decorate` reads
`decorate_vectors.json` and does not assert on its `biomeAnswers`. So the 11
positions were carried in a committed vector file that no test looks at. The
sulfur vectors regenerate clean — `ci/decorate-once.sh` twice, agreed, 4166
entries, **100.000000%, 0 wrong** — because their three centres (62,62),
(62,65), (64,63) happen to contain no cell where the two paths differ.

**Why it matters more than eleven blocks.** `BiomeFilter` is the last modifier
on every vegetal chain, and this file already records that it "rejects ten more
of `sulfur_spike`'s candidates than vanilla's does in chunk (62,62)". A block
lookup that is wrong 0.4% of the time is a filter that accepts and rejects the
wrong candidates, and the sulfur cave family is 617 of the r7 window's 988.

### The acacia probe, round 2: two more candidates cleared, one divergence found

**Cleared: the oracle's neighbourhood depth.** `-Ddecorate.region=<r>` decorates
the (2r+1)^2 around the centre in raster order up to and including it. Run at
r = 1 (the default), 2 and 3:

```text
  region=1  placed=True draws=12 positions=[[1106,65,1168]] changes=97
  region=2  placed=True draws=12 positions=[[1106,65,1168]] changes=97
  region=3  placed=True draws=12 positions=[[1106,65,1168]] changes=97
```

Identical at every depth. However much of the neighbourhood the harness
decorates first, vanilla's own feature code still plants this tree.

**Cleared: our own decoration order** (nine values, above) and **the biome
containers** (`biomes=239616/0`).

**Found, by reading `WorldGenRegion`'s constructor: the harness's
`BiomeManager` is wired to a different noise source than a server's.**

```text
  WorldGenRegion.<init>   new BiomeManager(this, obfuscateSeed(seed))
      -> NoiseBiomeSource is the region itself
      -> LevelReader.getNoiseBiome(x,y,z) default:
           chunk = getChunk(QuartPos.toSection(x), QuartPos.toSection(z), BIOMES, false)
           chunk != null ? chunk.getNoiseBiome(x,y,z)      <- the stored container, clamped
                         : getUncachedNoiseBiome(x,y,z)    <- the raw sampler

  DecorateGolden          new BiomeManager(
                              (qx,qy,qz) -> biomeSource.getNoiseBiome(qx,qy,qz,sampler),
                              obfuscateSeed(SEED))
      -> the raw sampler, always, with no container and no clamp
```

`LevelReader.getBiome(pos)` is `getBiomeManager().getBiome(pos)` and
`WorldGenRegion` does not override it, so every `minecraft:biome` filter and
every `Biome.shouldFreeze` on a real server goes through the container path.
The harness takes the sampler path. This is the same fault shape as
`getBlockEntity`: a method given a plausible answer rather than the real one,
found by reading the constructor rather than the method.

**It is not yet shown to be the acacia's cause** — the containers and the
sampler are built from the same `biomeSource`, so they agree except where the
fuzzed quart position leaves the chunk (`ChunkAccess.getNoiseBiome` clamps into
the chunk's own sections; the sampler does not) or leaves the region (the
server falls back to `getUncachedNoiseBiome`, the harness never does). The
fuzz moves the sample by up to one quart cell, so a position near a chunk
corner is exactly where it would bite. (1106,65,1168) is 2 blocks from the
chunk's z edge.

That is a measurement to take, not a conclusion: wire the harness the way the
constructor does and re-run the probe.

### CLOSED 2026-07-28: the ruin on dry land — `isValidBiome` was never ported

`Structure.generate` does not call `findGenerationPoint`; it calls
`findValidGenerationPoint`, which is that filtered by `isValidBiome`, and the
predicate comes from `ChunkGenerator.tryGenerateStructure` one frame up:

```java
  HolderSet<Biome> set = structure.biomes();
  Predicate<Holder<Biome>> validBiome = set::contains;
  ... structure.generate(..., validBiome);

  // Structure
  findValidGenerationPoint(ctx) = findGenerationPoint(ctx).filter(s -> isValidBiome(s, ctx))
  isValidBiome(stub, ctx) = ctx.validBiome.test(
      ctx.chunkGenerator.getBiomeSource().getNoiseBiome(
          QuartPos.fromBlock(stub.position().getX()),
          QuartPos.fromBlock(stub.position().getY()),
          QuartPos.fromBlock(stub.position().getZ()),
          ctx.randomState.sampler()))
```

and for a ruin the stub is `onTopOfChunkCenter(ctx, OCEAN_FLOOR_WG, ...)` =
`(chunkPos.getMiddleBlockX(), getFirstOccupiedHeight(mx, mz, OCEAN_FLOOR_WG),
chunkPos.getMiddleBlockZ())`, with `getFirstOccupiedHeight = getBaseHeight - 1`
(bytecode, `ChunkGenerator`). `ocean_ruin_starts` ran the placement test and
nothing else, so every placement chunk got a ruin.

`chosen_mineshaft_kind` already carried the correct comment about
`isValidBiome` sampling once in quart coordinates — the mineshaft path uses it
to pick a *variant*. Nothing used it to reject a start. The port had the
question written down and answered it for one structure of the two.

Ported: the tag is resolved through `facts::resolve_biome_tag(
"has_structure/ocean_ruin_warm")` — lukewarm_ocean, warm_ocean,
deep_lukewarm_ocean — and the gate runs before `plan`, which is where vanilla
runs it (the stub is filtered before `getPiecesBuilder()` runs the consumer).
The random is per-chunk `setLargeFeatureSeed`, so a rejected chunk's unspent
draws move nothing.

Measured, same dump, same three diffs, same bbox:

```text
                        raw vs r7   raw vs r7-b   GENUINE   exactness
  before the gate          1470        3624        1043     99.993200%
```

over 58 62 70 74 now reports **zero** `cut_sandstone` and **zero**
`suspicious_sand`, matching both references. Chunk (68,70)'s genuine count is
**0**, from 51.

**No other window moved.** The main window (seed 31415926, chunks 62..66)

```text
  van-s2-c62  14      van-gen34  14      van-gen17  1
```

— identical to before, so the order-invariant residual there is still 1 block,

**Known gap, recorded in `caveats()` rather than papered over**: a ruin whose

### CLOSED: the dungeon chest — vanilla's oracle was lying about the draws

Two of the sixteen were a chest at (1053,-6,1015) in vanilla against one at
(1054,-6,1017) in ours. Four hypotheses died against block data — missing
draw, guarded draw, the `is_solid_at` neighbour test, and "vanilla's first
chest takes more attempts". All four were wrong, and the reason none of them
could be found is that **the instrument was wrong**.

`tools/goldengen/vanilla/GenLevel.java` — the `WorldGenLevel` that
`DecorateGolden` runs vanilla's own features against — returned **null from
`getBlockEntity`, unconditionally**, with a comment arguing it was harmless:
the features that reach it "place the same *blocks* either way; only their
loot is lost". That is false, and it cost a day:

```java
  static void setBlockEntityLootTable(BlockGetter level, RandomSource random, ...) {
      BlockEntity be = level.getBlockEntity(pos);
      if (be instanceof RandomizableContainer c) c.setLootTable(table, random.nextLong());
  }
```

**Java does not evaluate an argument to a call it does not make.** With null
the `nextLong` never happens, so the harness's stream ran one value short per
chest, and vanilla's own dumped trace showed a second chest where no real
server puts one. Same for the spawner's `randomEntityId`, a `nextInt(4)`
behind `instanceof SpawnerBlockEntity`.

A real server does reach both, and the bytecode says exactly how:
`WorldGenRegion.setBlock` sees `hasBlockEntity()`, finds a ProtoChunk rather
than a LevelChunk, and stores a placeholder tag `{x,y,z,id:"DUMMY"}`;
`WorldGenRegion.getBlockEntity` finds that tag, builds the entity with
`EntityBlock.newBlockEntity` and caches it. `ProtoChunk.setBlockState` on its
own creates nothing — which is what made "a ProtoChunk has no chest block
entity" sound right.

`GenLevel` now mirrors both halves. The corrected trace for the dungeon at
(1055,-6,1015):

```text
  DRAW 60 nextInt(5) -> 3    DRAW 61 nextInt(5) -> 4    chest (1056,-6,1017)
  DRAW 62 nextLong                                      its loot seed
  DRAW 63 nextInt(5) -> 0    DRAW 64 nextInt(5) -> 2    chest (1053,-6,1015)
  DRAW 65 nextLong                                      its loot seed
  DRAW 66 nextInt(4) -> 3                               the spawner's mob
```

`changes` then holds `chest[facing=east]` at (1053,-6,1015) and
`chest[facing=north]` at (1056,-6,1017) — the two chests `region-differ
census` finds in `van-s2-c62`, position for position and state for state. The
feature costs **76 draws**, not the 73 the blind harness reported; a placed
room's body is 58, not 55.

The port spends both draws now, each behind the same guard vanilla has, and
the window went 16 -> 14 with **nothing else moving**. An earlier experiment
that added the `nextLong` alone took the window to 325: with one of the three
draws missing the feature's later placement attempts land elsewhere and one
of them builds a whole spurious dungeon. That is why "right position, worse
window" was read as coincidence when it was half a fix.

Regenerating `crates/rustmc-worldgen/golden/decorate_vectors.json` after the
`GenLevel` change produced a **byte-identical file** — none of the three
committed centres places a block entity — so the gate is unaffected and the
correction cost no golden churn.

### What this implies elsewhere, and has not been chased yet

Any feature that reads a block entity back was under-drawing in the harness,
and this port was written against that harness. The known one is
**archaeology / ocean ruins**: `OceanRuinPieces$OceanRuinPiece` calls
`getBlockEntity` and then `nextLong` for every suspicious sand it places
(`BrushableBlockEntity.setLootTable`). The ruin work is "closed" on block
positions but was never checked on draws, and the same fault would be
invisible in exactly the same way. **Re-dump a ruin window with the fixed
`GenLevel` before trusting any ruin draw count.**

The general rule, worth more than the chest: **an oracle that answers `null`
where a server answers an object does not lose a value, it loses a draw** —
and a lost draw moves every position after it. `GenLevel` throws for anything
it does not implement precisely so it cannot do this; `getBlockEntity` was
the one method that had been given a plausible answer instead.

## Definition of complete (the only thing that ends the work)

1. **Order-invariant parity >= 99.99% on every measured window**, decomposed
   the five-order way (see BENCH.md, "202 of the 557"), with the denominator
   public. A single-order number is not a parity claim.

   **Invariance has two sides and only one was ever measured.** Sweeping *our*
   decoration orders says which of our mismatches survive our own reordering.
   It says nothing about which of them vanilla would reproduce if asked twice
   — and on the main window, 13 of 14 do not. So a window is only measured
   once it has **two or more independently generated vanilla references**, and
   the reported residual is the blocks on which they all agree and we differ.
   Main window, 2026-07-28: **1 block, 99.999959%**, against three references.
2. **Fastest vanilla-parity server** — measured against vanilla, Paper and
   Folia on the same machine, in parity mode, with the method written down.

   **Measured 2026-07-28 and NOT met.** `ci/bench-servers.sh`, 225-chunk
   generation squares, three centres, seed 20260722, Threadripper: rustmc
   0.264 CPU-s/chunk against vanilla 0.192, Folia 0.122 and Paper 0.112 —
   **1.38x vanilla, 2.35x Paper on CPU; 4.58x and 13.8x on wall**, the wall
   column being thread count (rustmc peaks at 1.00 cores, the JVMs at
   8-14). 37.7% of rustmc's work at this radius is `DECORATION_MARGIN`
   skirt it discards, so the next reading is r=32. The "under LOAD" half of
   this item cannot be measured at all until something ticks.
3. **A server that runs**: a real client joins, plays, and the world is the
   generated one. `docs/SERVER.md` lists what is still missing.
4. `ci/t0.sh` green and the workspace suite at its known-red baseline or
   better.

None of these is met by a green test. Green is permission to start the next
thing.

## Was NOW

**`sulfur_spike[tip_merge]` where vanilla has `[tip]` — 5 blocks, and the
largest remaining group with no explanation.**

Seed 20260722, order-invariant and genuine against both vanilla worlds:

```text
  4  sulfur_spike[thickness=tip_merge,vertical_direction=down,waterlogged=true]
       -> [thickness=tip,...]
  1  sulfur_spike[thickness=tip_merge,vertical_direction=up,waterlogged=true]
       -> [thickness=tip,...]
```

We merge a pair of tips where vanilla leaves them separate. `tip_merge` is
set when a stalactite and a stalagmite meet, so the question is the meeting
test, not the spike. Note every one of them is `waterlogged=true`, which is
suspicious enough to check first: if the merge test reads the block and we
read it as water where vanilla reads air, or the other way, that alone would
explain the direction.

**The merge rule and the split are both exact — eliminated by bytecode.**
`SpeleothemClusterFeature`'s condition is, in order:

```text
  random.nextBoolean()  &&  stalactite > 0  &&  stalagmite > 0
    &&  column.getHeight().isPresent()
    &&  stalactite + stalagmite == column.getHeight().getAsInt()
```

which is `speleothem_cluster.rs:433` term for term, coin first. And the
overlap split is

```text
  lo    = max(ceilingY - stalactite, floorY + 1)
  hi    = min(floorY + stalagmite,   ceilingY - 1)
  split = Mth.randomBetweenInclusive(random, lo, hi + 1)
  stalactite = ceilingY - split;   stalagmite = split - 1 - floorY
```

also ours exactly, `hi + 1` included. So neither the rule nor the split.

**And the family is not what its name says.** With positions in hand it is
not "we merge where vanilla does not" — the columns differ:

```text
  (948,-19,1005)  vanilla frustum,up,wet     ours tip_merge,up,wet
  (948,-18,1005)  vanilla tip,up,dry         ours tip_merge,down,dry
  (946,-19,1008)  vanilla water[level=0]     ours tip_merge,up,wet
  (946,-18,1008)  vanilla cave_air           ours tip_merge,down
  (947,-18,1008)  vanilla cave_air           ours tip_merge,up
  (947,-18,1010)  vanilla tip_merge,up       ours cave_air
```

At (948,1005) vanilla grows a **2-tall stalagmite with no stalactite** —
`frustum` then `tip` — and we grow a stalactite and a stalagmite that meet.
At (946..947,1008) vanilla grows **nothing at all** and we grow a merged
pair; at (947,1010) the reverse. These are whole columns disagreeing, not a
thickness property.

**Traced, and the divergence is pinned to the raw heights.** At (948,1005):

```text
  ours     ceiling=-16 floor=-20 height=3  chance=1.0
           wants_stalactite=true wants_stalagmite=true
           stalactite=2  stalagmite=1  merged=true
  vanilla  frustum at -19 and tip at -18, nothing at -17
           => stalactite=0  stalagmite=2   (0+2=2 != 3, so no merge)
```

The geometry agrees — ceiling -16, floor -20, a 3-block gap at -19..-17 — so
`Column.scan` is not it. The **overlap branch never runs** for us either:
`ceiling - stalactite = -18` is not `<= floor + stalagmite = -19`, so 2 and 1
are the raw heights, not split results. Both sides want both spikes, because
the config's chance is exactly 1.0 (`bits=0x3ff0000000000000`).

So the whole difference is `speleothem_height`'s two answers: ours (2,1),
vanilla's (0,2).

**Not `getSpeleothemHeight` — that is the single-speleothem path.** Its full
form is

```text
  if (a < d) a = d
  x = (a / b) * 0.384
  v = max(c * (0.75*x^(4/3) - x^(2/3) - (1/3)*ln x), 0)
  return (v / 0.384) * b
```

a pure function taking no `RandomSource`, and `SpeleothemClusterFeature` does
not call it for its column heights. Ours doesn't either: `speleothem_height`
in `speleothem_cluster.rs:538` is the cluster's own sampler —

```text
  if random.nextFloat() > density  -> 0
  distance = |x| + |z|
  bias   = (float) Mth.clampedMap(distance, 0, maxDistanceFromCentre,
                                  maxHeight / 2.0, 0.0)
  height = (int) Mth.randomBetween(random, 0, maxHeight, bias)
```

**The sampler is eliminated too.** `SpeleothemClusterFeature` has its *own*
`getSpeleothemHeight(RandomSource, int, int, float, int, config)` — an
instance method, and a different function from the `SpeleothemUtils` one of
the same name. Read from its bytecode:

```text
  if (random.nextFloat() > density) return 0
  distance = abs(x) + abs(z)
  bias = (float) Mth.clampedMap(distance, 0.0,
                                maxDistanceFromCenterAffectingHeightBias,
                                maxHeight / 2.0, 0.0)
  return (int) randomBetweenBiased(random, 0.0f, (float) maxHeight, bias)
```

which is `speleothem_cluster.rs:538` term for term, including the narrowing
to float and the `maxHeight / 2.0` as `clampedMap`'s **toMin** with 0.0 as its
toMax.

So the rule, the split, the column scan and the sampler are all exact. What
is left is the sampler's two remaining inputs, `density` and `max_height`,
both handed down by `placeColumn` — and `randomBetweenBiased` itself, which is
a private static this file has not yet read.

**`randomBetweenBiased` is exact as well.** It is a one-line delegate:

```text
  randomBetweenBiased(random, min, max, mean, deviation)
      -> ClampedNormalFloat.sample(random, mean, deviation, min, max)
      -> Mth.clamp(Mth.normal(random, mean, deviation), min, max)
```

and `speleothem_cluster.rs:586` is that, with the deviation argument present
and taken from `config.height_deviation`. `ClampedNormalFloat` and `Mth.normal`
are both already on this file's read-and-matching list.

**So every piece of the chain is now read and matching**: the merge rule, the
overlap split, `Column.scan`'s geometry, the cluster's own height sampler, and
the biased draw underneath it. The divergence has nowhere left to be except
the sampler's two remaining **inputs**, `density` and `max_height`, which
`placeColumn` computes and hands down.

**Traced, and the result rules out this column's arithmetic.**

```text
  SPELEO (948,1005) ceiling=-16 floor=-20 height=3 chance=1.0
                    density=0.6466534 stalactite_cap=3
                    stalactite=2 stalagmite=1 merged=true
```

The sampler's first act is `if (random.nextFloat() > density) return 0`.
Vanilla returns **0** for the stalactite here; we return 2, so our coin passed
and vanilla's did not. With the same `density` and the same stream position
those two cannot both happen — one nextFloat has one value.

So either `density` differs, or **the stream is at a different position by the
time this column is reached**. The second is the stronger hypothesis, because
the other four disagreeing blocks say the same thing: at (946,1008) and
(947,1008) vanilla grows nothing at all and we grow a merged pair, and at
(947,1010) the reverse. Whole columns appearing and disappearing across one
cluster is what a stream shift looks like; a wrong constant would move every
column the same way.

**Traced in visit order.** `RUSTMC_TRACE_SPELEO=*` now prints every column
the cluster visits, with its offsets from the cluster centre. The cluster
visits x-major, and the first column in that order whose blocks disagree is
**(944,1002)**, not the tip_merge blocks at all — those are far downstream.

```text
  SPELEO (944,1002) off=(-3,-3) ceiling=-16 floor=-20 height=3
                    density=0.6466534 stalactite=0 stalagmite=1
  vanilla           frustum at -17 and tip at -18  => stalactite 2
                    agrees at -19                  => stalagmite 1
```

**The stalagmite matches and the stalactite does not**, which is the most
informative fact available. A stalactite that took a different *number* of
draws — the density coin failing where vanilla's passed, say — would have
moved the stalagmite too, and it did not. So the draw **counts** are aligned
and only the **value** differs.

The inputs are all pinned now. cap = min(height 3, ceiling-floor 4) = 3.
`max_distance_from_center_affecting_height_bias` is 8 and the distance is
|−3|+|−3| = 6, so bias = clampedMap(6, 0, 8, 3/2.0, 0) = **0.375**, with
`height_deviation` 3. The height is
`(int) clamp(Mth.normal(random, 0.375, 3.0), 0, 3)` — a wide normal where 0
and 2 are a single gaussian apart.

So: identical draw counts, identical mean, identical deviation, identical
clamp bounds, and a different result. **That leaves the gaussian's value**,
which is the one thing that can differ while the call count does not —
`MarsagliaPolarGaussian` computes two at a time and caches the second, so a
cache carrying differently makes the same Nth call return a different number.

This session already fixed one bug of exactly that shape: `WorldgenRandom.
setSeed` never resets the inherited gaussian cache, so a feature drawing an
odd number of gaussians leaves half a pair for the next. That fix was
verified, but it was verified *between features*. This is a cache question
**within** one feature, across many columns, and nothing here has checked it.

**`Mth.normal` is exact too, narrowing included.** Its bytecode is
`mean + ((float) random.nextGaussian()) * deviation` — the gaussian is
narrowed to float *before* the multiply, not after — and `math.rs::normal` (`:142`) is
that, with the cast on the gaussian alone. `ClampedNormalFloat.sample` is
`Mth.clamp(Mth.normal(random, mean, deviation), min, max)`, also ours.

So the arithmetic is exhausted. Six pieces read against the bytecode and all
six match: the merge rule, the overlap split, `Column.scan`'s geometry, the
cluster's height sampler, `randomBetweenBiased`, and now `Mth.normal`. Every
input is pinned by measurement. The draw counts are aligned, proven by the
stalagmite in the same column matching.

**The only thing left is the gaussian's value at a call whose index is
correct**, and the only mechanism that does that is the
`MarsagliaPolarGaussian` cache: it computes two at a time and returns the
second on the next call, so a cache half a step out makes the Nth call return
what the (N+1)th should.

**The two `wants` coins match as well** — vanilla draws `nextDouble()` at
offsets 193 and 332 and compares `nextDouble() < chance` (`dcmpg; ifge`), in
the order coin, then ceiling/floor presence, then `isLava`, then the
thickness sample. `speleothem_cluster.rs` is that order exactly, and it is
`next_f64` on our side too, so the coin is neither the wrong draw type nor
drawn in the wrong place.

That is seven pieces read and matching. The feature's arithmetic and its draw
sequence are both exhausted.

**CORRECTION, and it kills the gaussian-cache hypothesis before it cost
anything.** `math::normal_calls()` counts gaussian draws, and the trace now
carries it:

```text
  (944,1001)  g=53291   stalactite=0  stalagmite=0
  (944,1002)  g=53292   stalactite=0  stalagmite=1
  (944,1003)  g=53292   stalactite=0  stalagmite=0
```

Column (944,1002) drew **one** gaussian. Two heights sampled would be two, so
our stalactite's height call never reached `Mth.normal` — it took an early
return. Vanilla grows a stalactite of 2 there, so vanilla's call did reach it.

**The draw counts therefore differ at (944,1002)**, which retires the
inference recorded above that they were aligned. That was read off the
stalagmite matching, and a matching stalagmite turns out to be worth nothing
here — it can agree by value while the stream is already apart.

The early return is one of three, all before the gaussian:
`wants_stalactite = nextDouble() < chance` false, `isLava` at the ceiling
true, or the density coin `nextFloat() > density`. The ceiling itself agrees:
vanilla's stalactite occupies -17 and -18 growing down, which puts its ceiling
at -16, and ours is -16.

**So the stream is already diverged when the cluster reaches (944,1002)** —
g=53291 gaussians into the chunk — and no column in this feature is the first
divergence. That is the third time this search has moved upstream, and it is
now outside `SpeleothemClusterFeature` entirely.

**And the dumper is not needed — the region-scoped gate already answers it.**
Chunk (59,62) at seed 20260722, replayed against `-Ddecorate.region=1`
vectors, **passes**: draws, positions, `positionDraws`, blocks and the RNG
after, `sulfur_spike_cluster` included.

So the feature is exact *given the world it is handed*, and the world it is
handed by the oracle differs from the server's. The fault is in the input
world, not in `SpeleothemClusterFeature` — which is why eight pieces of it
read as matching, and why every attempt to bisect inside it moved upstream.

**This is ORACLE rule 17's pattern once more, and the region scoping did not
dissolve it.** The oracle agrees with the port; both differ from a server. The
difference now has to be in what precedes the feature in that chunk: the
surface and carver stages, or an earlier feature in the same decoration
stream. Note the chunk also carries the `diorite -> andesite` blocks, which
are known order noise, so an earlier *feature* is the more likely of the two.

**The drift check was silent too**, which narrows it once more. That check
compares the harness's world against vanilla's cumulative recorded changes
after *every* feature, and it fired nothing for chunk (59,62). So our
decoration matches the oracle's at each step, and the oracle's own world —
`SurfaceChunkGolden.generateChunk` plus the decoration it drives — is what
differs from the server's.

That points the search at the oracle's **starting** world rather than at any
feature: `SurfaceChunkGolden` and the server disagree about chunk (59,62)
before decoration begins. This project has already found exactly that once
this session, when the surface stage read the wrong biome and both the port
and the oracle were wrong together.

**Measured: chunk (59,62) is 110 mismatches, 99.888102%**, and there is no
decoration-free band to compare terrain in:

```text
  y -32   53      y -16   44      y 0   13
```

The cluster's own columns run ceiling -10..-16 to floor -20..-22, so it spans
the -32 and -16 bands itself, and the 13 at y 0 are the known-order-noise
diorite. So "compare the terrain where decoration cannot reach" has no band to
use here — that shortcut is unavailable and the comparison has to be made
against a genuinely pre-decoration world.

**Done, and it moves the item out of decoration entirely.**

The oracle's pre-decoration chunk can be compared with a server after all,
without generating anything new: at the positions vanilla's own recorded
`changes` never touch, the server's final block should still be its terrain,
and the oracle's pre-decoration block is its terrain. Vanilla's changes cover
4,267 positions in that chunk; 53 of our mismatches fall outside them.

```text
  oracle PRE-DECORATION  ->  server FINAL      count
  air                    ->  air                 14
  water[level=0]         ->  water[level=0]      11
  cave_air               ->  cave_air            10
  sulfur                 ->  sulfur                3
  ------------------------------------------------- 38 agree
  sulfur                 ->  cave_air              9   TERRAIN DIFFERS
  sulfur                 ->  water[level=0]        2
  deepslate[axis=y]      ->  sulfur                2
  water[level=0]         ->  sulfur_spike[tip,up]  1
  deepslate[axis=y]      ->  cave_air              1
  ------------------------------------------------- 15 differ
```

**Two separate faults, and neither is `SpeleothemClusterFeature`.**

*38 positions where the oracle's terrain and the server's final block agree.*
Neither of them has anything there, and **we wrote a block anyway**. That is
our decoration writing outside what vanilla writes — a reach or an extra
placement, not a wrong value.

*15 where the terrain itself differs*, nine of them `sulfur -> cave_air`: the
server has carved air where the oracle has solid sulfur. Solid-versus-air at
depth is a **carver** disagreement, and it is upstream of every feature. It

### CORRECTION TO THE CORRECTION — the oracle does run the 17x17 sweep

`SurfaceChunkGolden` loops `for (dx = -8..8) for (dz = -8..8)` itself, with a
comment saying `applyCarvers` is not called directly because it needs a live
`WorldGenRegion`. So it is **not** chunk-scoped for carving, and the paragraph
below overstated the case. Both readings of those 15 blocks have now been
wrong once each; the measurement stands, the explanation does not.

**Where the oracle and vanilla actually part, read from the bytecode:**

```text
  vanilla   ChunkAccess source = region.getChunk(sourcePos.x, sourcePos.z);
            source.carverBiome(supplier).getCarvers()
  oracle    biomeSource.getNoiseBiome(
                QuartPos.fromBlock(sourcePos.getMinBlockX()), 0,
                QuartPos.fromBlock(sourcePos.getMinBlockZ()), sampler)
            .value().getGenerationSettings().getCarvers()
```

Vanilla asks the **source chunk** for its carver biome; the oracle recomputes
from the biome source at the chunk's corner at y=0. That is the same shape as
the surface-stage bug fixed earlier this session — recomputing a value a
server reads out of the chunk — and here it decides *which carvers run*, so a
chunk whose stored biome differs from the recomputed one carves differently.

And `carverBiome` **memoises**: it caches the supplier's result on the chunk
the first time and returns it for every later target. So a source chunk's
carver list is fixed by whichever target reached it first, while the oracle
recomputes per (target, source) pair.

**What this does and does not establish.** It is a real difference in how the
carver list is chosen, read from bytecode on both sides. It is *not* yet shown
to produce the nine blocks — that needs the supplier vanilla passes, which is
the lambda immediately before the `carverBiome` call and has not been read.
Do not assume it; this item has already been explained wrongly twice.

**Read, and it is the second answer: the hypothesis is dead.** The supplier
vanilla passes is

```text
  () -> biomeSource.getNoiseBiome(QuartPos.fromBlock(pos.getMinBlockX()), 0,
                                  QuartPos.fromBlock(pos.getMinBlockZ()),
                                  randomState.sampler())
```

which is precisely what `SurfaceChunkGolden` computes inline. And the
memoisation is a pure optimisation, not a behaviour: the supplier depends only
on the source chunk's own position, and `getChunk(sourcePos)` always returns
the chunk *at* that position, so whichever target populates the cache first
stores the same value any other would have.

So the oracle's carver **selection** matches vanilla exactly, and the surface
-stage trap is not repeated here. Three explanations of those 15 blocks
offered, three eliminated.

Next candidates, in the order they are worth testing:

  * ~~the **`Blender`**~~ — **eliminated, and it was a one-line read.**
    `Blender.of(region)` returns `EMPTY` when `DEBUG_DISABLE_BLENDING`, when
    the region is null, **or when `region.isOldChunkAround(centre,
    HEIGHT_BLENDING_RANGE_CHUNKS)` is false** — which it is for every chunk of
    a freshly generated world. So vanilla's blender is `EMPTY` here and the
    oracle having none is not a difference. Measured rather than assumed
    because "normally a no-op" is the phrasing this project has been burned by
    before; this time the no-op was real.
  * **the biome the carvers themselves ask — a real difference, found.**
    Vanilla's `applyCarvers` builds

    ```text
      BiomeManager biomeManager2 = biomeManager.withDifferentSource(
          (x, y, z) -> this.biomeSource.getNoiseBiome(x, y, z, sampler));
      ...
      carver.carve(context, chunk, biomeManager2::getBiome, random,
                   aquifer, sourcePos, mask);
    ```

    and `SurfaceChunkGolden` passes **`biomeManager::getBiome`** — the plain
    manager, unwrapped. So vanilla's carvers resolve every per-position biome
    through the *noise* source, and the oracle's resolve through whatever the
    plain manager is backed by.

    That is the container-versus-recompute trap from the surface stage, in
    mirror image: there a server read the stored container and this project
    recomputed; here vanilla deliberately recomputes and the oracle reads the
    manager. `withDifferentSource` exists for exactly this and the oracle
    drops it.

    It bites wherever a carver asks about a position's biome — which for a
    cave carver includes what it may replace and what it exposes — and it
    would show as carved-versus-solid, which is the census: nine
    `sulfur -> cave_air`.

    **Fixed, and it was not the cause — fifth elimination.** The oracle now
    wraps the manager exactly as `applyCarvers` does. Regenerated chunk
    (59,62)'s surface and decorate vectors and re-ran both:

    ```text
      CARVER CHUNK EXACTNESS 100.000000%   vanilla carved 734   (unchanged)
      pre-decoration census                 byte-for-byte identical
                                            still 9 sulfur -> cave_air
    ```

    Not one block moved. For this chunk the carvers evidently never consult
    the biome in a way that reaches the output — consistent with
    `topMaterial was asked for 0 times`, which is the main place a cave carver
    would use it.

    **The fix is kept anyway.** It makes the oracle do what `applyCarvers`
    does, and an oracle that differs from vanilla in a way that happens not to
    matter on the chunks measured so far is precisely the thing this session
    has been paying for all day. It costs nothing and it removes a difference.
  * the **aquifer** — now the front runner, and the census fits it: the
    aquifer decides what fills a carved hole, and the eleven are nine
    `sulfur -> cave_air` and two `sulfur -> water[level=0]`, which is a
    fill decision. Both sides take the *target* chunk's
    `noiseChunk.aquifer()` and use it for all 289 sources, so the object is
    shared by construction and any difference has to be in its **state** —
    which for `NoiseBasedAquifer` means its per-cell caches, populated lazily
    as positions are queried. A server queries them in a different order from
    a one-chunk harness, and if any cached value depends on query order rather
    than only on position, that is a difference the sweep would expose.
    **Read, and the order argument does not hold.** `NoiseBasedAquifer`'s
    mutable state is `aquiferCache` and `aquiferLocationCache`, both indexed
    by grid position, so they memoise rather than accumulate — query order
    cannot change what they return. The one field that is not position-keyed
    is `private boolean shouldScheduleFluidUpdate`, and that is read by
    `WorldCarver` only to decide whether to call
    `markPosForPostProcessing`, which affects load-time fluid ticks and not
    the block written.

    So the aquifer is order-independent for block output and the "289 sources
    query it in a different order" reasoning is dead. Its grid is also bounded
    to the target chunk (`minGridX` and friends) and every carver writes only
    into the target chunk, so all queries fall inside those bounds in both.

    **And that led straight to it. The two `NoiseChunk`s are not built the
    same way.**

    ```text
      vanilla  NoiseChunk.forChunk(chunk, randomState,
                   Beardifier.forStructuresInChunk(structureManager, pos),
                   settings, fluidPicker, blender)
      oracle   NoiseChunk.forChunk(chunk, state,
                   DensityFunctions.BeardifierMarker.INSTANCE, ...)
    ```

    Vanilla builds a **real `Beardifier`** from the structures in that chunk.
    `SurfaceChunkGolden` passes the **marker**, which is no beard.

    The beardifier is the density adjustment that flattens and fills terrain
    around structure pieces — it is why a mineshaft corridor has floor under
    it instead of hanging in a cavern. Where a structure runs, vanilla's
    density is not the oracle's, and the difference presents as solid-versus-
    carved: exactly nine `sulfur -> cave_air`, at y -21..-9, which is
    mineshaft depth. The same window already showed mineshaft pieces at chunk
    (66,69).

    **Unlike the six before it, this one is a structural difference confirmed
    on both sides rather than a hypothesis** — the marker and the real
    beardifier are different objects and the oracle demonstrably passes the
    marker. What is not yet measured is that it accounts for these particular
    blocks.

### RETRACTED — the whole pre-decoration comparison used the wrong reference

`RUSTMC_THROUGH=noise|surface|carvers|decorated` now stops `worldgen-dump full`
at a stage, which makes the comparison this investigation needed possible at
last: our terrain against vanilla's, both before any feature runs.

```text
  chunk (59,62), ours at the carver stage against the surface oracle's
  `carvedRuns` — the chunk after surfaces and carvers, before any feature

      compared 98,304 blocks    differences: 0
```

**Our terrain for that chunk is bit-identical to vanilla's.**

And that exposes the fault in everything built on `predecor.py`. It read
"pre-decoration terrain" out of the *decorate* vectors' `worlds[0]`, which in
region mode is not pre-decoration at all — it is the world as it stands when
the centre chunk's turn comes, **neighbours' decoration included**. Diffing our
carver-stage chunk against it shows 1,644 differences whose census is
`andesite`, `granite`, `calcite`, `smooth_basalt`, `amethyst_block`: ore blobs
and a geode, which are features.

So the 53, the 38, the 15 and the 12 are all measured against a reference that
already had features in it. **They are retracted**, and with them the nine
explanations eliminated along the way — those were eliminated honestly, but
they were explanations for an artifact.

Two things are worth keeping. `census --positions` and `RUSTMC_THROUGH` are
real instruments and both stay. And the habit that caught this — checking a new
reference against something known, then noticing its census contained blocks
the stage cannot produce — is the only reason the error surfaced instead of
becoming a fix to the wrong thing.

**What survives untouched:** the order-invariant genuine figures, because they
are measured pipeline-against-server with no oracle in the path — 43 on seed
31415926 and 33 on seed 20260722.

Do not assume it, but do take it first: fixing a feature that is 62 blocks and

**Draw counts measured:**

```text
  ours     227 draws     1150 blocks
  vanilla  253 draws     1212 blocks
  both emit their single position at draw 4  (positionDraws agree)
```

26 draws and 62 blocks short. The position agreeing at draw 4 means the
placement chain is exact and the whole difference is inside the feature body —
same split as `moss_patch_ceiling` earlier today, which is a good sign, because
that one turned out to be findable by pricing the body's sites.

`GeodeFeature.place`'s draw sites, from the bytecode, in order:

```text
   47  IntProvider.sample        (distribution points count)
  196  nextDouble
  226  nextFloat
  266  IntProvider.sample  \
  278  IntProvider.sample   >   three per distribution point — an offset
  290  IntProvider.sample  /
  365  IntProvider.sample
  395  nextInt(I)
 1057  nextFloat                 inside a block loop
 1145  nextFloat                 inside a block loop
```

The last two scale with blocks placed, the middle three with the number of
distribution points. 26 is not divisible by 3, so a plain "fewer distribution
points" is not the whole story — some of the shortfall is in the block loops,
which is consistent with 62 fewer blocks.

The first differing block is ours (1019,-59,1086) against vanilla
(1021,-59,1085), both `smooth_basalt` — a different *position* at the same
index, so our geode's shape differs rather than its materials.

**Priced.** `RUSTMC_TRACE_GEODE` now counts the geode's per-site draws, and
on chunk (63,67):

```text
  ours   crack_sides=1   layer0_coins=193   potential_coins=12
         227 draws total, 4 of them the chain, so a body of 223
  vanilla                                   253 total, body 249
```

The body is 26 short and **the layer-0 coin loop is where it has to be**.
Every other site is small and fixed — one distribution-point count, one
`nextDouble`, one crack coin, one crack side, four per distribution point —
and `potential_coins` is 12. A 26-draw shortfall spread across those would need
six or seven fewer distribution points, which would move the shape far more
than 62 blocks. One coin per block reaching layer 0, 26 fewer of them, is the
only decomposition that fits: vanilla's count should be **219** against our
193.

That is an inference from the totals, not a reading of vanilla's per-site
counts — the trace exists only on our side. It is testable: the layer-0 coin
fires once per block with `distance >= inner`, so if vanilla lays 26 more
blocks in that band, our **inner-band distance test is admitting fewer blocks**
and the geode's shape is smaller. The 62-block shortfall and the first
difference being a *position* rather than a material both point the same way.

**The geode is exact. The harness was feeding it seed 0.**

`Region::world_seed` returned `0`, with a note that no case in the committed
set contains a geode — true of the committed set, false of the gate the moment

`NormalNoise` **straight from the world seed** rather than from the decoration
stream, so with zero it sampled a different noise field: a different shape,
1150 blocks against 1212, and a different ending RNG state.

Wired to the vector file's seed, chunk (63,67) **passes**, and the 169
committed cases still pass.

Everything read along the way matched and is worth recording as read: the four
band thresholds (`1/sqrt(filling)` and `1/sqrt(layer + distributionPoints /
outerWallDistance.maxInclusive())` for the other three), the crack size
including its `distributionPoints > 3` branch, and the per-block accumulation
`distance += invSqrt(distSqr + offset) + noise` with `Mth.invSqrt` being
`1.0 / Math.sqrt` rather than the Quake approximation.

**Second harness bug of the day with the same shape** — after the carpet, where
`air_at` defaulted to "cannot say" and a feature was abandoned mid-set. Both
were latent for the same reason: a default that is correct for the committed
vectors and wrong the first time the gate is pointed somewhere new. The
override flag exists precisely to point it somewhere new.

### Was NOW

**The gate never tests the pipeline's own accumulated world, and that is where

Every chunk is replayed into a world the *oracle* built. So "chunk (63,67)
passes" means: given the oracle's snapshot of the world at the moment (63,67)
decorates, our features are vanilla's. It does not mean the pipeline's world at
that moment *is* the oracle's snapshot.

The pipeline builds its world by decorating an 11x11 window in raster order,
each chunk's writes landing in its neighbours. If our decoration of any
neighbour differs at all, (63,67) reads a different world and the sulfur
cluster scans different columns — and the neighbour's own gate would still pass,
for exactly the same reason, because it too was replayed into an oracle-built
world. Every chunk can be individually correct while the accumulation drifts.

That is the last untested surface in this stage, and it is the natural home of
a defect that has survived a day of everything else being exact.

**Done, and the drift is real and small.** `RUSTMC_DECORATE_PREFIX=cx,cz,r`

**The pipeline's world at the moment (63,67) decorates is not the oracle's
snapshot**, which is exactly the surface the gate cannot see. Five blocks, all

### Was NOW

**Every chunk gates green individually and the accumulated world still drifts.
That is a statement about the gate, not about a feature.**

The oracle builds chunk C's world by decorating C's raster predecessors — whose
own inputs are undecorated. The pipeline builds it by decorating the whole
window, so when it reaches C's predecessor, *that* chunk has already read a
partly-decorated world. The histories differ in **depth**, and no chunk is
individually wrong.

Two possibilities, and they need separating before any code changes:

  * **A depth artifact.** The oracle at radius r can only reproduce r levels of
    history, so a residual is expected and shrinks as r grows. Test: raise the
    region radius on the *writing* chunk (63,66) — r=2, then r=3 — and re-run
    the prefix comparison. If the five shrink, this is the answer and the gate's
    limit needs recording rather than fixing.
  * **A real defect that only composition exposes.** If the five survive at
    r=3, the port differs from vanilla in a way no single-chunk replay can see,
    and the honest instrument is a whole-window oracle rather than a
    per-chunk one.

The five differ from **two** independent servers, so something is wrong on our
side either way; the question is only whether the gate can be made to see it.

**Answered: it is not a depth artifact.** At `-Ddecorate.region=3` the gate
still passes and the prefix comparison still shows **exactly 5 differences, at
exactly the same positions** as r=1. Three levels of history changed nothing,
so the residual is not the oracle running out of depth.

That makes it the second possibility: a real difference that only composition

```text
  oracle sulfur    ->  ours cinnabar        (1010,30,1080)
```

`sulfur` is the speleothem cluster's **base block** —

So a prefix chunk's `sulfur_spike_cluster` lays its base blocks differently,
its own gate passes, and the difference only becomes visible when the chunk
downstream of it reads the result.

**A prefix chunk's cluster replaces cinnabar with sulfur where vanilla does

Three of the five are base-block replacements, which is a much narrower target
than "the cluster behaves differently": `replaceBlocksWithBaseBlocks` walks a
small neighbourhood from the ceiling or floor and swaps anything in
`replaceable_blocks` for the base block. Whether `cinnabar` is in
`#minecraft:sulfur_spike_replaceable_blocks` decides these three directly.

**The tag is not it.** `#minecraft:sulfur_spike_replaceable_blocks` is two
flat entries with no nested references at all:

```json
{"values": ["minecraft:sulfur", "minecraft:cinnabar"]}
```

`cinnabar` is in it, so both sides are entitled to replace it and neither is
being refused by membership.

**And the differences run both ways**, which is the more informative fact:

```text

  (1010,30,1080)                  vanilla wrote sulfur, we left cinnabar
```

A wrong tag, a wrong walk length or a wrong direction would all be one-way. Two
directions means the walk is happening at **different positions** — the
cluster's column set differs — which is the same conclusion the tip_merge
blocks reached from the other end, and it is now reached without any of the
