### FIXED — three unit tests broke this morning and no gate noticed

`ci/t0.sh` runs fmt, clippy and check. **It runs no tests.** So the
`block_column` fit-walk fix shipped with three of its own module's unit tests
failing, and every `./ci/t0-remote.sh` after it came back green.

They were failing because the fix changed their premise, not because it was
wrong: vanilla writes the origin **without testing it** and counts room from
`origin + direction`, so

  * "two blocks of room for a three-block column" is now one block of room,
    and the column truncates to a single block at the origin;
  * with the tip prioritised that single block is the **flower**, because
    `truncate` walks from layer 0 and takes the body first — which is a
    sharper demonstration of the flag than the old assertion was;
  * and a column blocked *at* the origin is no longer blocked at all, so that
    test now blocks at `origin + direction`, which is the position the walk
    actually tests.

572 lib tests green. The server-diff evidence for the fix is unchanged and was
never in doubt — the lush family vanished and the window went 584 to 369 — but
that is exactly why this is worth recording: **a change verified against a
server still broke three unit tests for two hours, because the gate that runs
before every commit does not run tests.**

That is a hole in the standing procedure, not a one-off. `./ci/t0-remote.sh`
is what this file's rule means by "gated", and it cannot see a broken test.

**Our carver-stage terrain matches the oracle on a third chunk**: (66,69),
98,304 blocks, 0 differences — after (59,62) and (63,67), both also 0. Three
chunks, three exact.

**But that is not evidence about the beard**, and the same run shows why. The
gate cannot see the beardifier gap at all: vanilla passes
`Beardifier.forStructuresInChunk`, and *both* our pipeline and

because the two unbearded worlds agree with each other. The oracle cannot
falsify a gap it shares. That is the third instance today of the same trap and

**And a separate finding fell out of it**: the server has **zero** `oak_planks`

```java
    m.move(direction);
}
```

`speleothem_cluster.rs:690` is that exactly: starts **at** `pos` with no offset,
returns on the first refusal rather than continuing, moves in `direction`. And


`speleothem_cluster.rs:542` is that exactly, including computing in `f32` and

`RandomizableContainer.setBlockEntityLootTable` is

SpawnerBlockEntity)`. **Both draws are behind a block-entity lookup**, and

```text

  169 committed cases           pass
  seed 20260722 raster          1451 / 11,894,784 = 99.987801%
```

**The prediction failed, and that is the finding.** Six orders re-run on the
fixed code, intersected, second world checked:

```text

  genuine                33      (was 33)
  GENUINE exactness      99.999723%   (unchanged)
```

**Not one block moved.** I predicted the five `tip_merge` blocks would move
with this fix and wrote that a failure to move would mean the causal chain was

The fix itself is not in doubt — chunk (60,59)'s gate went FAIL to pass, the
draw sequences now agree line for line, and 572 lib tests and 169 committed
cases hold. What is wrong is the *inference* that connected it to the sulfur
family: the drift it caused was measured in the **raster** prefix world, and
the 33 genuine blocks are order-**invariant**. A difference that only some
orders produce is exactly what the six-order intersection is built to remove,
so a fix to one could never have moved the other.

That is a real error in reasoning and it ran through several commits today:
"chunk (60,60) is the first diverging chunk" was measured under raster, and
every step after it inherited the assumption that raster drift explains
order-invariant mismatches. It does not.

**`tip_merge` is a *thickness* — check where the thickness is decided rather
than where the column is.**

Everything about *placement* is now eliminated for this family: same world,
same draws, same positions, same heights. What remains is what turns a placed
speleothem into `tip` versus `tip_merge`, which is
`buildBaseToTipColumn(direction, height, merge, consumer, block)` and the
`merge` flag handed to it — and that flag is computed from the *pair* of
heights, not from either column alone.

`SpeleothemUtils.buildBaseToTipColumn` was read early in this investigation and
matched, but it was read for its *draw* behaviour, when the question was a
stream divergence. The question now is its **output** for a given `merge`, and
those are different readings of the same method.

**Done, and it reframes the family completely.** Vanilla's own dumper writes
`tip_merge` at all three positions:

```text
  [1013, 1, 1079]  sulfur_spike[thickness=tip_merge,vertical_direction=down,waterlogged=true]
  [1016, 2, 1077]  sulfur_spike[thickness=tip_merge,...]
  [1017, 2, 1077]  sulfur_spike[thickness=tip_merge,...]
```

with full columns above them — `frustum`, `base`, then `sulfur` — exactly the
shape our pipeline produces. **The oracle writes what we write.** The *server*
has `tip`.

So this was never a divergence in the cluster, which is why twelve bytecode
reads, an identical draw sequence and bit-identical terrain all came back
clean. It is **ORACLE rule 17's pattern once more**: the oracle agrees with the
port, and both differ from a server-generated world.

Something the server does *after* `applyBiomeDecoration` turns `tip_merge` into
`tip`, and neither the isolated dumper nor this pipeline does it.

### Was NOW

**What converts `tip_merge` to `tip` on a server after decoration.**

`tip_merge` is the thickness a speleothem takes when a stalactite and a
stalagmite meet. `tip` is what one becomes when its partner is no longer there —
which is a `updateShape` outcome, not a generation-time decision.

Candidates, in order of how cheaply they can be tested:

  * **`postProcessGeneration`.** It runs `Block.updateFromNeighbourShapes` on
    every marked position at chunk load, and that is exactly where a thickness
    would be recomputed. `SHAPE_CHECK_BLOCKS` does not list speleothems, but
    the *fluid* branch does run for waterlogged blocks — and all five of these
    are `waterlogged=true`, which this file noticed on day one and never
    explained.
  * a later feature removing the opposing spike, so the survivor reshapes;
  * `safeSetBlock`'s flags triggering a shape update the port does not model.

**Read, and the post-processing route is eliminated.**
`SpeleothemBlock.updateShape` does recompute the thickness — and its first act
is `if (state.getValue(WATERLOGGED)) scheduleTick(pos, Fluids.WATER, ...)`,
which is why every one of these five is waterlogged. So the mechanism that
would turn `tip_merge` into `tip` exists and is exactly `updateShape`.

**But nothing marks a speleothem for it.** `postProcessGeneration` only visits
marked positions; `WorldGenRegion.setBlock` marks only when
`state.getPostProcessPos(...)` is non-null, and that is four blocks —
`brown_mushroom`, `magma_block`, `red_mushroom`, `soul_sand`; and
`ProtoChunk.setBlockState` contains no `markPosForPostProcessing` call at all.
A waterlogged speleothem is never marked, so `updateShape` never runs on it at
chunk load.

So the reshape happens some *other* way on a server, and the remaining
candidates are all outside the generation stage:

  * the **scheduled water tick** itself — `updateShape` schedules one, and a
    server that runs it may cascade a neighbour update onto the speleothem;
  * a **later chunk's** cluster calling `safeSetBlock` on the partner spike
    with flags that trigger neighbour updates across the boundary;
  * the chunk's transition to `FULL` doing something neither dumper models.

### Was NOW

**Establish whether the server's `tip` is a generation product at all.**

Every remaining candidate is a *server* behaviour rather than a worldgen one,
and this project has been caught by that distinction before: the flowing-water
family was called an unreachable tick artifact, corrected to reachable, and
then correctly attributed to `postProcessGeneration` — three readings of the
same blocks.

**Checked: the scheduled-tick route is out.** `ci/gen-vanilla-region.sh` issues
`tick freeze` before any chunk loads, and its own header says so — *"the
load-bearing one: it stops the game loop entirely"*, added after 27 blocks of
mid-flow fluid drift survived a 30-second settle. A frozen server never fires a
scheduled tick, so the reference world's `tip` cannot come from the water tick
`updateShape` schedules.

That leaves the reshape happening **during generation or chunk load**, with
speleothems provably not marked for post-processing. The remaining route is a
neighbour update triggered by another `setBlock` — `WorldGenRegion.setBlock`
takes update flags, and a later chunk's cluster writing across the boundary
could reshape a spike this chunk placed.

### The fourth route is out too — the writes use flag 2

`SpeleothemUtils.growSpeleothem` writes with `iconst_2` — **flag 2**, block
update only, no neighbour updates. So a spike placed by one chunk is never
reshaped by a later chunk's write, and **nothing in generation can turn
`tip_merge` into `tip`.**

All four routes eliminated by reading: post-processing marks (speleothems are
never marked), the scheduled water tick (`tick freeze`), the cluster itself
(identical draws, identical terrain, and vanilla's own dumper writes
`tip_merge`), and now neighbour updates (flag 2).

**Which forces a different conclusion.** The server's `tip` is not produced
after decoration at all — so the server's *cluster* must have decided `merge =
false`, which it can only do if its world differed when it ran. The merge flag
is `stalactite + stalagmite == column.getHeight()`, and `getHeight` reads the
world.

And that is compatible with everything measured, because a server decorates in
**ticket order**, not in any of the six orders sampled here. These five blocks
are in the order-invariant core — all six of our orders produce `tip_merge` —
which proves only that *those six* agree, not that the server's order is among
them.

### Not order noise — two independent server orders agree on `tip`

Read directly from both reference worlds, bypassing the differ's overlap:

```text
  vanilla-r7      1013 1 1079  sulfur_spike[thickness=tip,...]
                  1016 2 1077  sulfur_spike[thickness=tip,...]
                  1017 2 1077  sulfur_spike[thickness=tip,...]
  van-rows-c64    identical at all three
```

`van-rows-c64` is the same seed generated with `GEN_ORDER=rows` — a **different
server order**. Both agree on `tip`.

So the order worry raised one commit ago is answered and dismissed: six of our
orders produce `tip_merge`, two independent server orders produce `tip`, and
**vanilla's own isolated dumper produces `tip_merge`**. That is not a spread of
order noise; it is a clean split between servers on one side and both isolated
harnesses on the other.

### Was NOW

**Vanilla's dumper and this port share a world no server has, at the moment the
cluster runs.**

The merge flag is `stalactite + stalagmite == column.getHeight()`. Everything
feeding it has been checked and matches between the port and the dumper —
draws, terrain, arithmetic. Both produce `tip_merge`. Both servers produce
`tip`. So on a server, `column.getHeight()` at these columns returns something
else, which means the *world the cluster scans* differs.

This is the same shape as the two defects this project has actually caught —
`isAir` and the biome container — where the port and the oracle agreed and both
differed from a server, and the fix was in what the oracle recomputed instead
of read.

**Dumped, and the pre-decoration column is identical.** At (1016,1077):

```text
  y  -1  deepslate   both        <- the floor
  y   0  water       both
  y   1  water       both
  y   2  water   |   sulfur_spike[tip,down]      <- the server's spike
  y   3  water   |   sulfur_spike[frustum,down]
  y   4  cinnabar|   sulfur      <- base blocks replacing cinnabar
  y   5  cinnabar|   sulfur
  y   6  cinnabar|   sulfur
  y   7  cinnabar   both         <- the ceiling
```

Every block below the decoration is the same. The floor is y -1, the ceiling
y 4, and the gap is y 0..3 — four blocks.

**So the server's column is stalactite 2, stalagmite 0.** The spike hangs from
the ceiling into y 3 and 2 and nothing grows from the floor; y 0 and 1 stay
water. `2 + 0 = 2 != 4`, so `merge` is false and the tip is `tip`.

Ours sums to 4 — `merge` true, `tip_merge`.

**And a stalagmite of 0 is one our formula cannot produce.** With a ceiling
present the port draws the stalagmite *relative* to the stalactite:

```rust
stalagmite = 0.max(stalactite + random_between_inclusive(random, -diff, diff))
```

with `max_stalagmite_stalactite_height_diff` = 1. A stalactite of 2 therefore
gives 1, 2 or 3 — never 0. Vanilla got 0 with the same draws and the same
world.

### Was NOW

**Vanilla's stalagmite-with-ceiling branch is not `max(0, stalactite + diff)`.**

That is the one place the two can diverge given identical draws, an identical
world and an identical stalactite: the formula that turns them into a
stalagmite height.

The relevant bytecode is the block around offsets 490..530 in
`SpeleothemClusterFeature`, which this file read once — for the *overlap split*
that follows it, not for the relative-height branch itself. `Math.max` and
`Math.min` both appear there and only one of them was accounted for.

**Read, and the relative-height formula itself matches** —
`Math.max(stalactite + Mth.randomBetweenInclusive(random, -maxDiff, maxDiff),
0)` at offsets 431..444, which is `speleothem_cluster.rs`'s
`0.max(stalactite + random_between_inclusive(...))` exactly.

**But there is a third branch the port has no equivalent of.** The block ends:

```text
  441  Math.max(...)            -> istore 20     the relative branch
  446  goto 466
  449  getSpeleothemHeight(...) -> istore 20     the sampled branch
  466  goto 472
  469  iconst_0                 -> istore 20     <-- sets the height to ZERO
  472  ...
```

Offset 469 stores **0** into the same local, drawing nothing. The port has two
branches here — relative when a ceiling exists, sampled otherwise — and vanilla
has three.

That is exactly the shape of the measurement: a stalagmite of 0 that the port's
two branches cannot produce, reached without spending a draw, which is why the
926-draw sequences still agreed.

**Read, and the zero branch is the port's own default.** The block is

```text
  393  replaceBlocksWithBaseBlocks(level, pos.atY(floor), thickness, DOWN, config)
  414  if (!ceiling.isPresent()) goto 449
  422  stalagmite = Math.max(0, stalactite + randomBetweenInclusive(-d, d))
  446  goto 466
  449  stalagmite = getSpeleothemHeight(...)
  469  stalagmite = 0                      <- reached from *above* 393
```

Offset 469 is jumped to from before 393 — it is the value when the whole
stalagmite block is skipped, i.e. when `wants_stalagmite` is false, the floor is
absent, or the floor is lava. `speleothem_cluster.rs` initialises
`let mut stalagmite = 0;` and computes it only inside exactly that guard, so the
two are equivalent and this is **not** the difference.

Which sharpens the contradiction rather than resolving it. Vanilla reaching 469
means its guard failed — and the guard's only draw is the `wants_stalagmite`
coin, with the thickness sample at 391 *inside* the block. If vanilla skipped
the block it also skipped that sample, and our sequence would carry one draw
more than vanilla's. **It does not: all 926 agree.**

So vanilla did *not* take the zero branch, its guard passed, and it reached
either 422 or 449 — both of which are the port's formulas, on identical draws,
in an identical world. And it still got 0 where the port gets 1, 2 or 3.

### Was NOW

Unlike every other input in this investigation, that one does **not** need a

```text
  setSeed(worldSeed)
  a = nextLong() | 1
  b = nextLong() | 1
  populationSeed = (x * a + z * b) ^ worldSeed
```

so it can be computed from the world seed and the chunk origin and compared
with what the vectors carry. If they disagree, that is the defect and it
explains everything at once — same code, same world, a different stream, and
two harnesses agreeing because they share the mistake.

`legacy_random_source = false`, confirmed in
`noise_settings/overworld.json`, so features seed from
**`XoroshiroRandomSource`** and a Legacy computation answers a different
question.

Recorded rather than deleted because it is the fourth inference of mine this
investigation has had to retract, and the pattern in all four is the same:
a number computed under an assumption that was never checked, presented as a
measurement. The check here was one grep.

### Was NOW

**Compute the population seed with Xoroshiro, from the spec.**

The value of doing it is unchanged and it is still the only input checkable
without a second implementation. It needs `Xoroshiro128PlusPlus` with vanilla's
seed-mixing — `RandomSupport.upgradeSeedTo128bit`, then the same
`(x * (nextLong()|1) + z * (nextLong()|1)) ^ worldSeed` — written from the
bytecode rather than from `crates/rustmc-worldgen/src/rng/xoroshiro.rs`, since
using the port's own implementation would defeat the purpose.

**Done, and the result is not usable as evidence.** The formula is confirmed
from `WorldgenRandom.setDecorationSeed`'s bytecode —

```text
  setSeed(worldSeed)
  a = nextLong() | 1
  b = nextLong() | 1
  return (x * a + z * b) ^ worldSeed
```

— so that half is right. But my Xoroshiro, written from
`upgradeSeedTo128bit` and `mixStafford13`, gives `-2863772679376894862`
against the vectors' `-4746405627041933582`, and my earlier Legacy attempt gave
a third value. **Two independent attempts, two different answers, neither
verified against anything.**

The port's `population_seed` *is* verified — the gate compares it against the
vectors and passes — so the likeliest explanation by far is that my Python is
wrong, not that both harnesses are. Reporting "the seed differs" from an
unverified reimplementation would be the fifth retraction of this
investigation, and this one is caught before the commit rather than after.

**What that means for the approach.** "Check it against a formula rather than
another implementation" is sound, but only with an implementation trustworthy
enough to be the referee — and writing one correctly is not a five-minute job.
An unchecked referee is just a third opinion.

### The referee is verified and it disagrees with both harnesses

```text
  xoroshiro128pp_seed_20260708.json, first 8 outputs   MATCH exactly
```

The Python Xoroshiro reproduces a vanilla-produced golden sequence, so
`upgradeSeedTo128bit`, `mixStafford13` and the `128++` step are all right. And
`XoroshiroRandomSource.setSeed(long)` is
`new Xoroshiro128PlusPlus(upgradeSeedTo128bit(seed))` — **identical to
construction**, so modelling the constructor models the reseed.

With the arithmetic done in proper 64-bit two's complement (the previous
attempt used Python's arbitrary-precision `^`, which is not the JVM's `lxor`):

```text
  world seed 20260722, chunk origin (1008, 1072)
    computed populationSeed  -2863772679376894862
    both harnesses carry     -4746405627041933582
```

Every input confirmed from the vector file itself: `seed 20260722`, `origin
[1008, -64, 1072]`, `centre 63,67`.

**Held as open, not as a defect.** A verified referee disagreeing with two
independent implementations is exactly as likely to mean the referee models the
wrong *call path* — and one candidate is visible: `WorldgenRandom` may wrap a

`setDecorationSeed`'s `setSeed` goes somewhere else entirely. An earlier Legacy
attempt did not match either, but it was made before the arithmetic was fixed
and is worth redoing now that the referee is trustworthy.

### It is Xoroshiro — the referee models the right path

`ChunkGenerator.applyBiomeDecoration` builds

```java
WorldgenRandom random = new WorldgenRandom(
    new XoroshiroRandomSource(RandomSupport.generateUniqueSeed()));
random.setDecorationSeed(level.getSeed(), origin.getX(), origin.getZ());
```

so the source is Xoroshiro, `setSeed` reseeds through `upgradeSeedTo128bit`,
and the initial unique seed is discarded by the reseed. That is exactly what
the referee models, and the referee reproduces a vanilla golden sequence
exactly.

**So every input and every step is now confirmed, and the disagreement stands:**

```text
  referee   -2863772679376894862
  port      -4746405627041933582   (gated against the dumper, and passes)
  dumper    -4746405627041933582
```

### CLOSED — the referee was wrong, the population seed is correct

The port's two scales are `a = 6264548325980982265`, `b =
-3227766592155663525`; the referee's were `6264548328051964541` and
`-1126660801248313201`. Different from the **first** draw, which is what
localised it.

`WorldgenRandom` extends `LegacyRandomSource` and implements
`BitRandomSource`, so its `nextLong()` is **not** the wrapped source's
`nextLong()` — it is the bit composition, `((long) next(32) << 32) + next(32)`,
and `XoroshiroRandomSource.next(bits)` is `(int)(nextLong() >>> (64 - bits))`.
So one `WorldgenRandom.nextLong()` consumes **two** Xoroshiro draws and keeps
only the top 32 bits of each. The referee called `nextLong()` once per scale.

Modelling that composition:

```text
  referee a = 6264548325980982265   port a = 6264548325980982265
  referee b = -3227766592155663525  port b = -3227766592155663525
  referee populationSeed = -4746405627041933582 = the vectors
```

**Exact match.** The population seed is right in both harnesses, and the last
shared input is eliminated — correctly this time, by a referee that now agrees
where it should.

Why the goldens did not catch it: all five test
`XoroshiroRandomSource.nextLong()` directly, and the composition only appears
when a `WorldgenRandom` wraps it. A golden for `WorldgenRandom.nextLong()` over
a Xoroshiro source would have — and there isn't one.

### DONE — the wrapper golden exists and passes

`crates/rustmc-worldgen/tests/golden_worldgen_random_wrapper.rs` pins
`WorldgenRandom.nextLong()` over a Xoroshiro source. Its expected values are
built from `xoroshiro128pp_seed_0.json`'s **vanilla-produced** outputs,
recombined by the documented rule — `((long) next(32) << 32) + next(32)` with
`next(bits) = (int)(nextLong() >>> (64 - bits))` — rather than by running the
port. A vector taken from the thing it checks would prove nothing.

Passes on the first run, which is the point: the port was already right, and
what was missing was any vector saying so.

**The beardifier: the port generates every chunk as though no structure were in
it.**

`chunk_gen.rs:21` says so outright — *"`Beardifier` is 0 throughout, which is

replace it, and the density graph already routes it through the same `add`
vanilla does, so wiring it later changes no arithmetic anywhere else."*

Vanilla passes `Beardifier.forStructuresInChunk(structureManager, pos)` into
`NoiseChunk.forChunk`. The beard is the density adjustment that flattens and
fills terrain around structure pieces — the reason a mineshaft corridor has
floor under it instead of hanging in a cavern.

Unlike the sulfur family this is **unambiguous, unblocked and large**: wherever
a structure sits, our terrain is not a server's, and every window this file
measures contains structures. It is also invisible to both harnesses, since
`SurfaceChunkGolden` passes `BeardifierMarker.INSTANCE` and therefore shares
the gap — which is why three chunks came back bit-identical earlier today and
proved nothing about it.

**CLOSED by measurement — the beardifier is inert in 26.2.**

`NoiseChunk` stores the `BeardifierOrMarker` it is given and substitutes it
wherever `DensityFunctions.BeardifierMarker.INSTANCE` appears in the density
tree — offsets 296..303 are exactly that swap. So the beard reaches terrain
only through a **marker node in the router**.

And there is no such node:

```text
  grep -c beardifier  noise_settings/overworld.json          0
  grep -rl beardifier generated-data/.../worldgen/           0 files
```

**Not one file in the entire datapack mentions it.** With no marker in the
router the substitution matches nothing, the beard never enters the density,
and `chunk_gen.rs`'s `Beardifier = 0` is not an approximation — it is the
correct value for this version.

So the item recorded earlier today as *"our terrain differs from a server's
wherever any structure sits"* is wrong, and the three bit-identical chunk
comparisons that "proved nothing about it" in fact proved exactly what they
appeared to.

That also explains why vanilla still passes a real `Beardifier` from
`applyCarvers`' caller: the plumbing survives from versions whose routers did
carry the marker, and is dead weight here.

`chunk_gen.rs:21`'s comment should be corrected — it says structures "will
replace it", implying work outstanding, when the measurement says there is
none for 26.2.

The `chunk_gen.rs` note is corrected in the same commit — a comment describing
a gap that does not exist is worse than no comment, because it sends the next
reader to wire a term that must stay zero, and the wiring would be invisible to
both harnesses since they share the zero.

blocks on the seed-31415926 window.**

That is the sharpest possible starting point. It is the largest single family in
either window, its absence is certain rather than inferred, and the measurement
that proves it is already in this file.

**Scoped by measurement.**

```text
  ocean_ruin_warm / _cold   type ocean_ruin, step surface_structures
                            cluster_probability 0.9, large_probability 0.3
  structure set             random_spread, spacing 20, separation 8,
                            salt 14357621
  templates in the jar      1,212 total, 49 named underwater_ruin
```

**The placement half is already done** — `structure/placement.rs` implements
`random_spread`, and `golden_structure_starts` already proves layouts against
mineshaft pieces read out of a real world's chunk NBT.

**The assembly half does not exist at all.** The port has `mineshaft`, `pieces`,
`placement` and `writer`, and mineshaft is *procedural* — it computes its boxes
in code. Ocean ruins are **template-based**: 49 `.nbt` files loaded from the
jar, rotated, and run through processors. Nothing in the port loads an NBT
structure template.

That is the real shape of "19 of 20 structure sets": almost all of them are
template-based, so the missing piece is one subsystem rather than nineteen
features. Building it once unlocks the rest.

### DONE — the template loader reads all 48 ruin templates

`crates/rustmc-worldgen/src/structure/template.rs` parses a template's `size`,
`palette` and sparse `blocks` from its NBT root, canonicalising palette entries
to `name[k=v,...]` with properties sorted — the same form every golden vector
in this project uses, so a template block is directly comparable with a
generated one.

`golden_structure_template.rs` gates it against **the real files**, not a
fixture:

```text
  loaded 48 underwater_ruin templates, 74944 blocks
```

and checks per template that every block lies inside the template's own
declared `size` (one that did not would write into a neighbouring chunk), that
every `state` indexes a real palette entry, and that every palette entry is a
namespaced block with a terminated property list.

Deliberately not done: rotation, processors, loot, jigsaw, and the plural
`palettes` variant. Each is separable, none is needed to establish that a
template can be read correctly, and guessing at `palettes` before a structure
uses it would be an unexercised path — which is the exact failure this week has
been made of.

### DONE — the identity transform, gated

`Template::blocks_at(origin)` emits every block as `(world position, state)`.
With no rotation and no mirror,
`calculateRelativePosition(settings, pos).offset(origin)` reduces to a
translation, and that is all this does.

```text
  placed 294 blocks from warm_1 at (100, -12, -37)
```

The gate checks against a **real** template that every emitted position lands
inside the box the template's own `size` describes — the bug it guards is an
off-by-one in the origin convention, which only real `size`/`pos` data can
expose — and that the count equals the template's block count exactly.

**Nothing is filtered, and the test asserts that.** Vanilla removes
`structure_void` and `jigsaw` with `BlockIgnoreProcessor.STRUCTURE_BLOCK`,
which is a *processor the caller attaches*, not something the template does to
itself. Filtering in the loader would bake one caller's processor list into it
and hide which structures actually use it.

Rotation and mirroring are deferred on purpose: they change the origin
convention as well as the coordinates, and a wrong convention puts a whole
structure one block out in a way only a server diff would show.

### DONE — rotation and mirror, labelled by geometry not by switch order

`transform(pos, mirror, rotation, pivot)` in `structure/template.rs`, read from
the bytecode:

```text
  mirror LEFT_RIGHT    z = -z          applied *before* the rotation
         FRONT_BACK    x = -x
  CLOCKWISE_90         (px + pz - z, y, pz - px + x)
  COUNTERCLOCKWISE_90  (px - pz + z, y, px + pz - x)
  CLOCKWISE_180        (px + px - x, y, pz + pz - z)
  y is never touched
```

**Which formula is which rotation could not be read off the bytecode.** The
switch dispatches through a `$SwitchMap` whose table lives in a synthetic class,
so the case labels do not say which enum constant they serve. Evaluating each at
pivot `(0,0)` does: `(-z, x)` is a clockwise quarter turn seen from above,
`(z, -x)` the counter-clockwise one. Reading the labels in order would have been
a coin flip on a value that only a server diff could later contradict.

Gated by **composition rather than fixtures**, for the same reason — a wrong
labelling still produces valid-looking rotations:

```text
  +x maps to +z under clockwise
  four clockwise turns are the identity
  two clockwise turns equal the 180
  clockwise then counter-clockwise cancel
  each mirror is an involution
  y survives every combination
```

Three template gates green.

### Read — and there is a second half nobody accounted for

```text
  114  calculateRelativePosition(settings, pos)
  118  .offset(origin)                     transform first, then translate
  127  settings.getRotation()
  130  state.rotate(rotation)              <- the block STATE is rotated too
```

**Rotating a template rotates its blocks' *states*, not just their positions.**
A north-facing stair becomes east-facing under a quarter turn; a `facing`
chest, a `axis` log, a `rotation` sign — every directional property has to turn
with the structure.

That is a whole requirement this file had not named, and it is larger than the
coordinate transform: `BlockState.rotate` dispatches per block, and the
property sets differ (`facing`, `axis`, `rotation`, the multi-face booleans).
Placing a rotated ocean ruin without it puts every stair and every chest facing
the wrong way — a difference of hundreds of blocks per structure that no
coordinate test would catch.

`getRotationPivot` is a stored field on `StructurePlaceSettings`, so its
default comes from the constructor and still needs reading.

### Measured — it is one property, not a general dispatch

`probe_template_properties.rs`, using the loader already gated on all 48 files:

```text
  402 palette entries across the ruin templates
  properties present:
      48  mode          (structure_block only)
      46  facing
      34  half
      34  shape
      34  waterlogged
  blocks carrying properties:
      48  minecraft:structure_block
      30  minecraft:stone_brick_stairs
      12  minecraft:purple_glazed_terracotta
       4  minecraft:sandstone_stairs
```

**`facing` is the only rotatable property in the entire ruin set.** `half`,
`waterlogged` and `mode` do not turn; `shape` is recomputed by `updateShape`
from the neighbours rather than rotated. And the 48 `structure_block` entries
are exactly the markers `BlockIgnoreProcessor.STRUCTURE_BLOCK` strips — one per
template, which is the data-shape confirmation that the processor is real and
that the loader is right not to filter them itself.

So `BlockState.rotate` for these structures reduces to **turning one horizontal
`facing` through the quarter turns** — a four-entry table, not a per-block
dispatch. That is what the measurement was for: it turned an open-ended piece
of work into a table plus a test.

### DONE — `facing` rotates, gated by composition

`rotate_state(state, rotation)` turns `facing` through the quarter turns and
leaves every other property alone. The cycle's direction is pinned by geometry,
not by a switch: north is `-z`, east is `+x`, and the clockwise coordinate turn
sends `+x` to `+z`, so clockwise must send **north to east**.

Gated with the same composition properties as the coordinate transform, plus
the cases the census says matter:

```text
  north -> east under clockwise
  four turns are the identity; two equal the 180
  clockwise then counter-clockwise cancel
  half / shape / waterlogged survive untouched
  a stateless block is returned as-is
  a vertical `facing` does not enter the horizontal cycle
```

Four template gates green.

### DONE — `blocks_rotated` joins both halves

`Template::blocks_rotated(origin, mirror, rotation, pivot)` applies `transform`
to the position and `rotate_state` to the block, which is what `placeInWorld`
does: `calculateRelativePosition(settings, pos).offset(origin)` for the
coordinate and `state.rotate(rotation)` for the state.

The **pivot is a parameter, not an assumption**. `StructurePlaceSettings`
stores one and ocean ruins set it; rotating about the wrong point translates a
whole structure, and that is a difference only a server diff would show. The
call site can answer it from the structure's own configuration; the loader
cannot, so it does not pretend to.

```text
  warm_1: 294 blocks, span (6, 7, 7), swapped under a quarter turn
```

Gated on **extent rather than absolute position**, for the same reason: the
absolute placement depends on the unknown pivot, but the *shape* does not. The
test asserts the block count is preserved under every rotation and mirror, that
a quarter turn swaps the x and z extents, that the 180 and both mirrors
preserve them, and that the unrotated span fits the declared `size`. That
catches a wrong axis pair, a dropped mirror and a non-rigid transform without
baking in a guessed origin.

Five template gates green.

### ANSWERED — the pivot is zero, and the mirror is always NONE

```text
  StructurePlaceSettings()      rotationPivot = BlockPos.ZERO
                                mirror = NONE, rotation = NONE
  OceanRuinPieces.makeSettings(rotation, integrity, type)
                                setRotation(rotation)
                                setMirror(Mirror.NONE)
                                — no setRotationPivot call at all
```

So ocean ruins rotate about **`BlockPos.ZERO`** and never mirror.
`blocks_rotated(origin, Mirror::None, rotation, (0, 0))` is exactly their case,
and the pivot parameter — kept general because the answer was unknown — turns
out to need only its default here.

**And `makeSettings` names the next requirement: `integrity`.** It takes a
float, which is `BlockRotProcessor`'s — the processor that randomly deletes
blocks so a ruin looks ruined. That is not cosmetic for this project: it
**consumes draws**, one per block, so a template placed without it leaves the
structure's random in the wrong state for everything after it. The structure
JSON's `large_probability 0.3` and `cluster_probability 0.9` sit in the same
family of draws.

### CORRECTION — the integrity pass does *not* spend the feature's stream

`makeSettings` in full:

```text
  new StructurePlaceSettings()
    .setRotation(rotation)
    .setMirror(Mirror.NONE)
    .addProcessor(new BlockRotProcessor(integrity))
    .addProcessor(BlockIgnoreProcessor.STRUCTURE_AND_AIR)
    + a COLD/WARM suspicious-block processor
```

**No `setRandom` call.** And `BlockRotProcessor.processBlock` takes its random
from `settings.getRandom(info.pos())`, which returns the settings' random *if
one was set* and otherwise derives one from the block position. Nothing sets
one, so the integrity draws are position-derived and the feature's stream is
untouched.

So the previous commit's reasoning — "do this next because it spends the
stream" — was wrong. It does not, and the urgency it claimed was invented. The
processor still has to be implemented for the blocks to be right; it simply
does not have the ordering hazard that made it a priority.

**And a second correction from the same read:** the ignore processor is
`BlockIgnoreProcessor.STRUCTURE_AND_AIR`, not `STRUCTURE_BLOCK`. Ocean ruins
strip structure blocks **and air**, so a template's air is not written and the
existing terrain shows through. That is a visible difference — a ruin that
writes its air would carve a box out of the seabed — and it is exactly the kind
of detail the earlier decision to filter nothing in the loader was designed to
keep visible.

`processBlock` also skips the draw entirely when `rottableBlocks` is present
and the block is not in it, which is the same conditional-draw shape that made
`monster_room` two draws heavy.

### DONE — the position seed, with both of its traps gated

`getRandom(pos)` falls through to `RandomSource.create(Mth.getSeed(pos))`, and
`Mth.getSeed` is

```text
  l = (long)(x * 3129871) ^ ((long) z * 116129781L) ^ (long) y
  l = l * l * 42317861L + l * 11L
  return l >> 16                    // lshr — arithmetic
```

**Two details that a transcription drops and no hand-written test would
catch.** `x * 3129871` is an `imul` followed by `i2l`, so it wraps in 32 bits
*before* widening — computing it in 64 bits agrees with vanilla for every small
coordinate and diverges past roughly x = 686 million. And the final shift is
`lshr`, arithmetic, so a negative intermediate stays negative instead of
becoming huge and positive.

Both are gated directly: the test asserts the 32-bit wrap by constructing the
same value both ways and requiring them to differ *first* (so the test cannot
pass vacuously), and asserts that some position yields a negative seed, which a
logical shift could never produce.

That failure shape is worth naming: a port that got either wrong would agree
with vanilla across every coordinate anyone would think to test by hand, and be
wrong only in the far reaches of a real world.

Six template gates green.

### DONE — both processors, and the generator was worth checking

`RandomSource.create(long)` returns a **`LegacyRandomSource`** — the LCG, not
the xoroshiro the rest of worldgen uses. That was one read and it decides every
rotted block; guessing xoroshiro because "worldgen uses xoroshiro" would have
produced a ruin that rots plausibly and matches nothing.

```text
  ignored_by_structure_and_air   [air, structure_block], from the static init
  survives_rot(pos, integrity)   LegacyRandomSource(Mth.getSeed(pos))
                                 .nextFloat() <= integrity
```

The comparison is `<=` and not `<`: at integrity 1.0 every block must survive,
and `nextFloat` can land arbitrarily close to 1. The gate asserts exactly that
over 120 positions, that integrity 0.0 keeps at most one of 400, and that 0.5
keeps between 60 and 140 of 200 — a distribution check that fails on a wrong
seed *or* a wrong generator, which a single-value assertion would not.

Dropping air is not a detail either: a template's air cells mean "leave the
world alone", so writing them would carve the template's bounding box out of
the seabed around every ruin.

**Seven template gates green**, and every piece of template placement now
exists: load, transform, rotate the state, ignore, rot.

### READ — `addPieces`, draw for draw

```java
boolean large = random.nextFloat() <= structure.largeProbability;  // always drawn
float integrity = large ? 0.9f : 0.8f;
addPiece(manager, pos, rotation, accessor, random, structure, large, integrity);
if (large && random.nextFloat() <= structure.clusterProbability) {  // conditional
    addClusterRuins(...);
}
```

The distinction that mattered is settled: **the large coin is unconditional, the
cluster coin fires only when `large`.** A port that spent both every time — the
natural transcription — would be one draw heavy on every small ruin, which is
exactly the `monster_room` failure repeated.

And the integrity constants are concrete: **0.9 for large, 0.8 for small**, so
`survives_rot` already has its real arguments rather than a placeholder.

With `large_probability` 0.3 from the structure JSON, roughly seven ruins in ten
are small, take integrity 0.8, and spend exactly one draw here.

### READ — the choosers are one draw each, and the tables match the files exactly

```text
  getSmallWarmRuin  Util.getRandom(WARM_RUINS,     random)
  getBigWarmRuin    Util.getRandom(BIG_WARM_RUINS, random)
```

`Util.getRandom(array, random)` is the array overload of the helper already
verified for lists: `array[random.nextInt(array.length)]` — **one draw**, not
two, and not zero.

**And the tables are exactly the files:**

```text
  names in OceanRuinPieces' static tables   48
  .nbt files extracted from the jar         48
  named in a table but missing on disk       0
```

A free cross-check that the loader is looking at the same set vanilla is — the
kind of confirmation that costs one command and would have caught a stale
extract silently shrinking the gate.

So the structure's draw accounting is now: one coin for `large`, one for
`cluster` when large, one `nextInt` per template chosen. What remains unread is
`addPiece` itself — the rotation and offset it applies — and `addClusterRuins`,
which places several pieces and is where most of the class's 24 draw sites must
live.

### READ — `addPiece` branches on ruin type, and cold costs more draws

```text
  switch (type.ordinal())
    WARM   large ? getBigWarmRuin(random) : getSmallWarmRuin(random)   1 draw
           construct one OceanRuinPiece, add it
    COLD   ... nextInt(...) ...                                        1 draw
           construct up to three pieces, add each
```

The warm path is one draw and one piece. The cold path draws a `nextInt` and
constructs **three** pieces — the brick, cracked and mossy tables layered —
which is where most of the class's remaining draw sites live.

That matters for what to build first: the seed-31415926 window's absent ruin is
in a **warm** ocean, so the warm path alone would close those 33 blocks, and it
is the cheaper of the two by a wide margin.

### BLOCKED — the Threadripper is unreachable

```text
  ping threadripper   Temporary failure in name resolution
  ssh 192.168.1.122   No route to host
```

Every build, test, gate and `javap` read runs there; the laptop is the user's
machine and does not compile this project. So **no code can be gated, and
therefore none should be committed** — the standing rule is
`./ci/t0-remote.sh` before every commit, and a commit that skips it because the
gate is unavailable is exactly the habit that let three broken unit tests ship
this morning.

`crates/rustmc-worldgen/tests/probe_ocean_ruin_placement.rs` is written and
**left uncommitted in the working tree**, unbuilt and unverified. It asks the
existing `random_spread` placement which chunks in the 59..69 window hold an
ocean ruin at seed 31415926, to compare against the census's (63,68) and
(63,67). One command answers it when the machine returns.

### Measured locally while blocked

The datapack extract is on this machine, so biome membership is answerable
without a build:

```text
  has_structure/ocean_ruin_warm   lukewarm_ocean, warm_ocean, deep_lukewarm_ocean
  has_structure/ocean_ruin_cold   frozen, cold, ocean, deep_frozen, deep_cold, deep_ocean
```

Chunk (63,67)'s recorded biome set is `sulfur_caves, lukewarm_ocean, savanna,
beach` — so the absent ruin is a **warm** one, confirming from local data that
the warm path is the one worth building first. That was an inference from the
census a moment ago; it is now a fact from the tags.

### Also readable locally: the set carries both ruin types

```text
  ocean_ruins structures   ocean_ruin_cold weight 1, ocean_ruin_warm weight 1
  placement                random_spread, salt 14357621, spacing 20, separation 8
```

Both types sit in the same set at equal weight, so a placement chunk picks
between them — and the `has_structure` biome tags then decide whether the
chosen one can actually generate there. That is a draw this file had not
accounted for: the structure-set weighted pick happens *before*
`OceanRuinPieces.addPieces` and its `large` coin.

For chunk (63,67) the biome is `lukewarm_ocean`, which is in the warm tag and
not the cold one, so only the warm structure can succeed there — but the pick
still happens, and a port that skipped it would be a draw short.

### FOUND WHILE BLOCKED — the port ignores a structure set's `structures` list

`StructurePlacement::parse` reads a set's **`placement`** and nothing else.
Nothing in the port reads the `structures` array or its weights. And that is
not a future-work gap — it touches the one structure already shipped:

```text
  structure sets by entry count   1: 14,  2: 4,  5: 1,  7: 1
  sets with more than one         mineshafts 2, nether_complexes 2,
                                  ocean_ruins 2, shipwrecks 2,
                                  villages 5, ruined_portals 7
```

```text
  mineshafts.json   [mineshaft weight 1, mineshaft_mesa weight 1]
  mineshaft         biomes #has_structure/mineshaft
  mineshaft_mesa    biomes #has_structure/mineshaft_mesa
```

**Both mineshaft variants share one set at equal weight, with disjoint biome
tags.** So at a placement chunk vanilla chooses between them and the chosen one
may then be refused by its biome — meaning the choice decides whether a
mineshaft exists at all, not merely which kind.

The port implements `mineshaft` and performs no choice. `golden_structure_starts`
passes because it reads 659 real pieces out of a world whose chunks are all in
plain-mineshaft biomes, where the outcome is unambiguous — the same
"correct for what was measured, absent for what wasn't" shape as `isAir`, the
biome container, the world seed and the beardifier note.

**Not yet claimed: the exact semantics.** Vanilla may pick once, or pick with
retry after a biome refusal, and those differ both in blocks and in draws. That
needs `tryGenerateStructure`'s bytecode, which needs the machine.

### RESOLVED — the ocean-ruin placement was already correct

And the reason it looked wrong is worth more than the result.

**The saved oracle worlds' directory names lie about their seeds.** There is no
`level.dat` beside the region files, so a world's seed is recorded nowhere but
its name. Refereed by terrain — bit-exact-gated, and owing nothing to placement:

```text
  worldgen-dump full 31415926 3 /tmp/ref-s1 60 64
  region-differ diff /tmp/ref-s1/region oracle-work/<dir> --bbox 58 62 62 66

    van-s2-c62      99.995646%   biomes 38400/0        <- IS seed 31415926
    vanilla-r7      76.354451%   biomes 38400/38400
    van-rows-c64    76.350952%   biomes 38400/38400
```

Every biome differing is the signature of a different seed; 76% is what two
unrelated worlds of the same generator score by coincidence.

With the pairing fixed, vanilla's **own saved structure start** says:

```text
  minecraft:ocean_ruin_warm start (67, 65) 1 pieces,
                                  union 1066,48,1040..1072,54,1045
```

and the port's placement selects exactly `[(67,65)]` in that window — not a
superset, exactly that. The shipwreck set is the control and matches too, at
both seeds, in both directions:

```text
                       port           servers
  seed 31415926        (54,59)        van-s2-c62      (54,59)   ok
  seed 20260722        (57,65)        vanilla-r7      (57,65)   ok
                                      van-rows-c64    (57,65)   ok
```

Four independent agreements. `random_spread` is sound. Gated in
`golden_ocean_ruin_placement.rs`, which also pins that the union reaches out of
its own placement chunk — reading the *visible blocks* as the placement chunk is
what produced the wrong verdict in the first place.

**A standing hazard, now written down:** any diff whose two sides were not
refereed for seed is not a parity measurement. It is noise that happens to be
formatted like a percentage.

### The server's union already decides the first coin

`addPieces` reads, from bytecode:

```text
  large     = nextFloat() <= largeProbability      (unconditional)
  integrity = large ? 0.9 : 0.8
  addPiece(..., large, integrity)
  if (large && nextFloat() <= clusterProbability)  addClusterRuins(...)
```

and `addPiece`'s warm branch is a single draw — `Util.getRandom(array, random)`
is exactly `array[random.nextInt(array.length)]`, confirmed by javap — over

```text
  WARM_RUINS       warm_1 .. warm_8        (8)
  BIG_WARM_RUINS   big_warm_4 .. big_warm_7 (4)
```

Measured before implementing anything, every warm template's declared size:

```text
  warm_1 .. warm_8        6x7x7    294 blocks each
  big_warm_4 .. big_warm_7   16x16x16  4096 blocks each
```

The server's union is 7x7x6 inclusive. That is a **small** ruin — so
`large == false`, `integrity == 0.8`, and the second `nextFloat` is never
spent — and it is turned, rotation 90 or 270, since 6x7x7 only reaches 7x7x6
with x and z swapped.

What the union does **not** decide is which of the 8: they are all the same
size. The discriminator is the 5 suspicious_sand at (1067..1071, 48,
1041..1044), which come from `WARM_SUSPICIOUS_BLOCK_PROCESSOR` rewriting sand
by rule, so their arrangement fingerprints both the template and the rotation.

### The ruin's choice is DONE and gated against the server, exactly

`structure/ocean_ruin.rs` — `plan()` in vanilla's draw order, plus
`settle_height()`, the `getHeight` column walk.

Predictions were fixed from bytecode and from the server's union **before**
running it. All of them held first time:

```text
  plan at (67,65), seed 31415926:
    template  warm_7        rotation Clockwise90
    integrity 0.8           large    false
    origin    (1072,90,1040)
    cluster_coin_spent false

  warm_7 rotated Clockwise90 from (1072,90,1040)
    spans x 1066..1072, z 1040..1045
  server union
          x 1066..1072, z 1040..1045
```

The footprint is the server's union **by coordinate**, not by extent — which
ties together, against one number vanilla wrote to disk: the placement chunk,
the rotation draw, the template-index draw, the template's own size, and
`transform`'s handedness. That last one could not be read off the bytecode
switch (it dispatches through a synthetic `$SwitchMap`) and was fixed
geometrically; this is the first evidence from vanilla that it was fixed the
right way round.

Draw accounting is counted with the real `draws` counter, not inferred:
small = 3 draws (rotation, large coin, template index), large = 4 (cluster
coin). The cluster coin is guarded by `large`, so getting it wrong shifts every
later structure in the chunk rather than only this one.

### The suspicious-sand processor, fully specified from bytecode

`WARM_SUSPICIOUS_BLOCK_PROCESSOR` is

```java
CappedProcessor(
    RuleProcessor([ ProcessorRule(BlockMatchTest(SAND),
                                  AlwaysTrueTest.INSTANCE,
                                  PosAlwaysTrueTest.INSTANCE,
                                  SUSPICIOUS_SAND.defaultBlockState(),
                                  AppendLoot(OCEAN_RUIN_WARM_ARCHAEOLOGY)) ]),
    ConstantInt.of(5))          // <- iconst_5
```

The cap is **5**, and the server's world holds **exactly 5** suspicious_sand.
That is an independent confirmation of the whole chain arriving from a
direction none of the placement work could reach.

`CappedProcessor.finalizeProcessing`, decoded:

```java
if (limit.maxInclusive() == 0 || list.isEmpty()) return list;
if (a.size() != b.size()) Util.logAndPauseIfInIde(...);   // warning only
RandomSource random = RandomSource.createThreadLocalInstance(level.getLevel().getSeed())
                                  .forkPositional()
                                  .at(pos);               // aload_2 = the piece origin
int n = Math.min(limit.sample(random), list.size());
if (n < 1) return list;
IntArrayList order = Util.toShuffledList(IntStream.range(0, list.size()), random);
int done = 0;
for (int i : order) { if (done >= n) break; ... processBlock(...) ... }
```

Two properties matter more than the rest:

  * **It spends nothing from the structure's stream.** The source is
    positional, forked from the *world seed* at the piece's origin — the same
    shape as `BlockRotProcessor`. A port that drew from the feature stream here
    would corrupt every later structure in the chunk while still producing
    plausible-looking sand.
  * `ConstantInt.sample` ignores its argument, so the only draws are inside
    `Util.toShuffledList` — a descending Fisher-Yates, `for (i = size; i > 1;
    i--) swap(i-1, random.nextInt(i))`, bound `i` and **not** `i + 1`.

### The ruin's blocks agree with the server, to the block

`place_blocks` mirrors `processBlockInfos`' two passes: the per-block chain
(`BlockRotProcessor(0.8)`, then `BlockIgnoreProcessor.STRUCTURE_AND_AIR`),
then `finalizeProcessing` (the capped sand rule) over the **survivors**.

```text
  survivors 32 blocks          (of the template's 294 cells, mostly air)
  ours   (1067,48,1044) (1068,48,1041) (1068,48,1042)
         (1071,48,1042) (1071,48,1043)
  server (1067,48,1044) (1068,48,1041) (1068,48,1042)
         (1071,48,1042) (1071,48,1043)
```

Five exact positions in a 7x7x6 volume, from a server. One assertion, and it
holds all of this at once: the template choice, the rotation, the origin,
`Mth.getSeed`'s 32-bit wrap inside the rot processor, the ignore processor,
the survivor count that sets the shuffle's length, Fisher-Yates with bound `i`,
the positional fork off the world seed at the piece origin, and counting
changes rather than visits. Get any one wrong and there would still be five —
just five of the wrong ones, which is exactly why this asserts the set.

`y` came from the server, not from `settle_height`, so the two stay
independently falsifiable.

### settle_height is a NO-OP at this ruin — the block gate does not cover it

Measured rather than assumed. From our own generated world at (67,65), the
column the piece is placed from:

```text
  origin (1072,1040) chunk (67,65):
      OCEAN_FLOOR=48   MOTION_BLOCKING=63   WORLD_SURFACE=63
```

(Stored heightmaps are `y - min_y`; the reader returns the stored form, so the
raw 112 needed -64 adding back. Reading it raw shows a seafloor at 112 and
would have made this whole check meaningless.)

`postProcess` sets y from `OCEAN_FLOOR_WG` **first**, and that is already 48 —
the y the server used. `getHeight` only ever lowers a piece, so here it
lowered nothing. **The block-exact suspicious-sand gate therefore says nothing
about `settle_height`**: it is still tested only against hand-built columns.

This is the same shape as the beardifier and the biome container — a thing
that looks covered because something next to it is. Recorded as a gap rather
than banked as a pass.

### The chest is in, from a data marker the loader was silently dropping

`Template` parsed `pos` and `state` and threw the block's `nbt` away. Every
ocean-ruin template carries exactly one `structure_block` entry whose
`nbt.metadata` is the marker string, and
`BlockIgnoreProcessor.STRUCTURE_AND_AIR` strips that block before it reaches
the world — so the loss was invisible: no error, no missing block in the
template, just no chest, ever.

```text
  warm_7      1 marker  [((3,0,3), "chest")]
  warm_1      1 marker  [((3,1,1), "chest")]
  big_warm_4  3 markers [((11,0,8),"chest"), ((3,1,5),"drowned"),
                         ((4,2,6),"drowned")]
```

`marker_blocks` now places it, and it matches the server exactly:

```text
  ours    (1069,48,1043) minecraft:chest[facing=north,type=single,waterlogged=true]
  server  1069 48 1043   minecraft:chest[facing=north,type=single,waterlogged=true]
```

**`facing=north` had to come from the server.** The piece is rotated CW90, so a
chest inheriting the piece's rotation would read `facing=east`.
`handleDataMarker` uses `defaultBlockState()` and does not rotate — reading
that off bytecode alone would have been a judgement call.

The `nextLong` behind the chest's loot table sits inside
`getBlockEntity(pos) instanceof ChestBlockEntity`, the same guard as the two
draws removed from `monster_room`. Treated as unspent, and flagged in the code
rather than assumed, because if a ProtoChunk does carry one the ruin costs the
decoration stream a draw.

### The whole ruin is block-exact: 33 of 33 against the server

`golden_ruin_full_blocks` compares **every** block the ruin writes — the 32
template survivors plus the chest — state for state against `van-s2-c62`.

```text
  ruin writes 33 blocks; 33 agree with the server
```

It was written as a probe, expecting to have to separate genuine errors from
blocks a later feature legitimately overwrote. There were none of either.

**It caught a real defect on its first run**, which is why the subset gates
were not enough. The five suspicious sand were written as bare
`minecraft:suspicious_sand`; the server has `minecraft:suspicious_sand[dusted=0]`,
because the rule replaces with `SUSPICIOUS_SAND.defaultBlockState()` and that
default carries `dusted`. The dedicated suspicious-sand gate compared with
`starts_with` and passed. A block that reads right to a human and wrong to a
diff is the failure this project keeps finding; the fix is always the same,
compare canonical states over the whole set against a server.

The subset gate now matches on `suspicious_sand[` so it cannot pass on a
propertyless state again.

### The ruin is IN THE PIPELINE and the window is bit-exact where it lands

Wired at decoration step 4 (`surface_structures`), alongside the mineshaft's
step-3 hook. `ocean_ruin_starts` finds the placement chunks and loads each
chosen template once; `place_ocean_ruin_in_chunk` recomputes the y from the
origin column each chunk pass, which is what `postProcess` does.

```text
                      the ruin's two chunks        the whole 25-chunk window
  before   33 mismatches   99.983215%      35 mismatches   99.998576%
  after     0 mismatches  100.000000%       2 mismatches   99.999919%
```

**100.000000% on the two chunks the ruin occupies.** The 2 left on the wider
window are at y -6 — mineshaft chests, a separate question, untouched by this
and present before it.

No structure index was needed. The ruin spends nothing from the decoration
stream: its processors are positional or world-seed derived, and the one
`nextLong` sits behind a block-entity guard a ProtoChunk does not satisfy.
That is why placing it moved no other feature — and the unchanged 2 on the
rest of the window is the evidence, not the argument.

### The structure-set pick, decoded — and a single-entry set spends NO draw

The item that was blocked on the machine. `ChunkGenerator.createStructures`:

```java
  if (entries.size() == 1) {            // <- fast path, NO RANDOM AT ALL
      tryGenerateStructure(entries.get(0), ...);
      return;
  }
  remaining = new ArrayList<>(entries);
  random = new WorldgenRandom(new LegacyRandomSource(0));
  random.setLargeFeatureSeed(levelSeed, chunkPos.x(), chunkPos.z());
  total = sum of weights;
  while (!remaining.isEmpty()) {
      roll = random.nextInt(total);
      index = bucket walk over remaining;
      if (tryGenerateStructure(remaining.get(index), ...)) return;
      remaining.remove(index);  total -= weight;
  }
```

Three consequences, in order of how much they matter:

  * **The single-entry fast path.** Fourteen of the twenty sets hold one
    structure and vanilla never touches the random for them. A port that
    "correctly" drew once per set would diverge on all fourteen. The draw
    exists only where there is a choice.
  * **It is pick-with-retry, not one pick.** A refusal removes the entry and
    rolls again over the reduced total, so the list is exhausted rather than
    abandoned. In a non-mesa biome `mineshaft_mesa` always refuses and the
    retry lands on `mineshaft` — **which is why this port's unconditional
    mineshaft has been right all along in every window measured**, and why
    the earlier worry that shipped parity numbers were contaminated was
    wrong. They were not.
  * The random is its own `LegacyRandomSource(0)`, reseeded per chunk, so
    these draws cannot shift a feature or another structure.

`weighted_attempt_order` implements it, with tests for the no-draw fast path,
that the order is a permutation (the retry loop exhausts), and that a 9:1
weight actually leads.

The remaining half is the biome test that decides which attempt succeeds. Only
then does a mesa mineshaft appear where vanilla has one.

### The mineshaft defect is scoped exactly: badlands only

`isValidBiome` is one sample, at the generation stub's position, in quart
coordinates, tested against the structure's biome set:

```java
  biome = chunkGenerator.getBiomeSource().getNoiseBiome(
              QuartPos.fromBlock(pos.getX()),
              QuartPos.fromBlock(pos.getY()),
              QuartPos.fromBlock(pos.getZ()),
              randomState.sampler());
  return predicate.test(biome);
```

Those sets are biome tags and vanilla's biome tags **nest** —
`has_structure/mineshaft_mesa` is literally `["#minecraft:is_badlands"]`.
`resolve_biome_tag` follows them (a resolver that kept the `#` would return an
empty set, which reads as "no biome qualifies" and is indistinguishable from a
correct refusal). Gated in `golden_biome_tags`:

```text
  mineshaft 51 biomes, mineshaft_mesa 3 biomes, shared 0
```

**Disjoint.** Combined with pick-with-retry that settles the whole question:

  * outside the badlands only `mineshaft` can succeed, and the retry loop
    guarantees it is reached — so this port's unconditional mineshaft is
    **correct**, not merely lucky, everywhere except badlands;
  * inside the badlands only `mineshaft_mesa` can succeed — so the port
    currently builds a *normal* mineshaft where vanilla builds a mesa one.

A precisely bounded defect rather than a vague one, and it explains why no
measured window ever saw it: none of them are badlands.

### A real mesa mineshaft exists now, and our layout already matches it 100%

The defect was scoped to badlands but there was no badlands world to gate a
fix against — the same bind that keeps `settle_height` unwired. So the target
was searched for rather than assumed.

`probe_find_badlands_mineshaft` sweeps mineshaft placement chunks (pure
arithmetic, cheap) and samples the biome only on the survivors, at the stub
position `BlockPos(chunkPos.getMiddleBlockX(), 50, chunkPos.getMinBlockZ())` in
quart coordinates, through the multi-noise source that is already gated
bit-exact:

```text
  seed 31415926: 151 placement chunks in +-96, 3 of them badlands
    (-56,83) wooded_badlands    (-54,93)    (-69,94)
  seed 20260722: 143 placement chunks, 0 badlands
```

A vanilla server was then driven at (-56,83), and it agrees:

```text
  vanilla mesa mineshafts in oracle-work/van-badlands: 1
    start (-56, 83) 104 pieces, vanilla dy Some(35) -> 10 surfaces fit,
                    90..328  (every piece box exact)
  MESA LAYOUT 1 of 1 starts reproduced exactly
  MESA 100.000000%
```

Two things at once. The prediction was right — that chunk is a mesa mineshaft
in a real server. And **the port's mesa layout was already correct**: 104
pieces, every bounding box exact, 100.000000%. `worldgen-dump mineshaft-mesa`
was written for exactly this and had never had a world with a mesa mineshaft
in it; until today it only ever printed "MESA nothing to compare".

So the missing piece is not the mesa mineshaft. It is only the **choice** —
picking Mesa at (-56,83) instead of Normal.

### The mesa selection is WIRED, and the mesa woods now match

`chosen_mineshaft_kind` runs `weighted_attempt_order` over the set's two
entries and takes the first whose biome tag contains the biome at the stub
position — `BlockPos(getMiddleBlockX(), 50, getMinBlockZ())`, quart
coordinates, exactly where `isValidBiome` samples. The roll is performed
rather than short-circuited: with disjoint tags it cannot change the outcome,
but a set with overlapping tags would depend on it, and skipping it would be a
silent behaviour change rather than an omission.

Two things had to be threaded through to make it work, and the second was only
discovered by running it:

  * the biome sampler, from the same `ClimateSampler` + parameter list the
    pipeline already uses;
  * a **`WORLD_SURFACE_WG` source**. A mesa mine hangs off the surface instead
    of the sea level, so `generate_with_kinds` — which has no surface callback
    and refuses — was never enough. It had simply never been asked, because no
    start was ever Mesa.

Measured on the shared 49-chunk window at (-56,83):

```text
                      dark_oak_fence   dark_oak_planks
  rustmc                    360              343
  vanilla                   360              337
```

Before this, both were **zero** — the mine was built in oak. The fences are
now exact. The planks are 6 over, which is the open thread.

Whole-window exactness there is 99.853350%, dominated by badlands vegetation
this port does not place at all (`short_dry_grass`, `tall_dry_grass` refusals,
359 and 343 of them) — not by the mineshaft.

### The 6 planks are noise; the badlands window is three KNOWN threads

Chased before assuming. The plank difference is 17 missing and 12 extra of
`cave_air <-> dark_oak_planks`, plus 6 involving stone and dirt — i.e. the
corridor floor following terrain that itself differs, not a wrong piece. The
fences, which do not depend on the ground, are exact at 360.

And the window's real content is not the mineshaft at all:

```text
   1506  sculk                  -> deepslate[axis=y]
    741  stone                  -> coal_ore
    621  coal_ore               -> stone
    369  dead_bush              -> air
    206  air                    -> cave_air
    182  air                    -> oak_leaves[...]
```

Every one of the top items is an **already-open thread**: the intrinsic VSculk
RNG (top target on the standing list), the ore placement-origin drift, and
vegetation this port does not place. Attributing any of it to the mesa work
would be wrong, and attributing the mesa work's success to a 99.85% would be
equally wrong — the two are independent.

### Three more warm ruins measured — and CLUSTERS are the real next gap

Vanilla reference worlds generated at the three nearest warm ruins. Their own
saved starts:

```text
  (-57,42)   ocean_ruin_warm  7 pieces  union -942,37,657..-898,56,692
  (-58,28)   ocean_ruin_warm  6 pieces  union -960,43,417..-923,58,462
  ( 64,47)   ocean_ruin_warm  1 piece   union 1018,49,752..1024,55,757
```

**Two of the three are clusters.** `addClusterRuins` is reached whenever the
ruin is large *and* the second coin passes at 0.9 — so it is not a rare path,
it is the common one, and this port does not implement it at all. The (67,65)
ruin that everything was built on is the unusual case, not the typical one.

Whole-window diffs:

```text
  (-57,42)   9574 mismatches   99.610433%    <- cluster, 7 pieces
  (-58,28)   1715 mismatches   99.930216%    <- cluster, 6 pieces
  ( 64,47)    320 mismatches   99.986979%    <- single piece
```

And at the single-piece one the ruin is **not in the top mismatches at all**:


### `addClusterRuins` is in, and all three piece counts match on the first run

```text
  (-57,42) large=true  clustered=true  big_warm_7  CW90   8 candidates, 6 placed
                                                          -> 7 pieces, server 7
  (-58,28) large=true  clustered=true  big_warm_5  CW180  5 candidates, 5 placed
                                                          -> 6 pieces, server 6
  ( 64,47) large=false clustered=false warm_6      CW90   0 candidates
                                                          -> 1 piece,  server 1
```

The piece count is a strict joint check: it is the outcome of the large coin,
the cluster coin, `allPositions`' sixteen draws, `Mth.nextInt(4,8)`, one
removal draw and one rotation draw per candidate, and the overlap test that
decides whether the template draw happens at all. A single wrong bound
anywhere changes it.

Two details that had to come from the bytecode rather than from sense:

  * `allPositions`' eight cells use **different** spans — `n(1,8)` on the west
    column but `n(1,7)` elsewhere, and `n(4,6)`, `n(3,8)`, `n(4,8)` scattered
    through the rows. They look like they should be uniform and are not;
  * a **skipped** satellite still spends the removal and rotation draws but
    not the template draw, because `addPiece` is inside the intersection test.
    (-57,42) skips 2 of its 8 candidates, so this is exercised.

The satellite's overlap probe is `BlockPos(5, 0, 6)` — a fixed box, not the
chosen template's real size.
