### The "ore placement-origin drift" is misnamed: origins are RIGHT

Four measurements, each narrowing it, and the name it has carried is wrong.

**1. The stone-variant cell set is identical.** In the (64,47) window, pairs
where one side is a stone variant and the other is not: **zero**. Every cell
vanilla makes granite/diorite/andesite/tuff, this port also makes some
variant. Nothing is misplaced.

**2. Only the labels differ, and they cancel exactly.**

```text
              vanilla    ours     delta
  tuff         32917    32917        0
  diorite      21669    21803     +134
  granite      20949    20983      +34
  andesite     20654    20486     -168
  total        63272    63272        0
```

**3. The disagreements are all overlaps, one way.**

```text
   91  vanilla andesite   ours granite
   77  vanilla andesite   ours diorite
   62  vanilla granite    ours diorite
```

**4. The mechanism is settled and it is not order.** `stone_ore_replaceables`
is `[stone, granite, diorite, andesite]` — gated in `probe_ore_overlap`, and
the runtime tag really does carry all four — so a later ore **overwrites** an
earlier variant and the last feature wins. Vanilla's merged step-6 order is
granite, diorite, andesite, tuff, and `golden_feature_order` passes, so this
port runs them in that order too.

So order is right, the tag is right, and the blobs cover the right cells. What
is left is **which cells each individual blob covers**. `worldgen-dump column`
at one of the disagreeing cells:

```text
  column (1007, 767)
     y 30  stone -> andesite      (agrees)
     y 31  stone -> andesite      (agrees)
     y 32  stone -> granite       (vanilla: andesite)
```

Our andesite blob stops one short and the granite underneath survives. Same
`size` 64, same `discard_chance_on_air_exposure` 0.0, same single target for
all three — so this is the blob's own geometry, not its configuration.

### The ore residual is BELOW the oracle's own noise floor — item retired

Traced to the end. `RUSTMC_TRACE_WRITE` names the writer:

```text
  WRITE (1007,32,767) <- minecraft:stone     by ? (no feature running)
  WRITE (1007,32,767) <- minecraft:andesite  by ore_andesite from chunk (62,48)
  WRITE (1007,32,767) <- minecraft:granite   by ore_granite  from chunk (63,47)
```

Two different **chunks**. The step-6 feature order this port receives is
verified correct — granite, granite, diorite, diorite, andesite, andesite,
tuff — so this was never feature order. It is the order the two *chunks* are
decorated in, and a feature writes one chunk out.

Which means it is not a property of the port at all. Measured:

```text
  two VANILLA worlds, same seed, same centre,
  differing only in forceload order         1526 mismatches
```

Vanilla disagrees with **itself** by 1526 blocks on this window. Our worst
number here was 320.

Against a rows-ordered reference, matching orders:

```text
  ours default vs vanilla rows     323
  ours zx      vs vanilla rows      98      <- best ever on this window
```

And the question `gen-vanilla-region.sh` was written to ask, never previously
run — does a driven order make the oracle reproducible across extents?

```text
  vanilla rows   r=2 vs r=3     109 mismatches
  vanilla square r=2 vs r=3     115 mismatches
```

**No.** Driving the order buys almost nothing: vanilla is irreproducible
across extents either way, at ~110 blocks per 25-chunk window.

So the floor is ~109 and this port sits at **98**. The ore residual is *below*
the oracle's own noise. There is nothing left to fix here that could be
distinguished from measurement error.

**This bounds every parity number in the project.** A 25-chunk window cannot
be measured better than ~99.9956% against a vanilla reference generated at a
different extent, no matter how correct the port is. Numbers above that are
reporting the oracle, not the generator.

### "sculk-spread RNG replay" is misnamed too: the feature is UNIMPLEMENTED

The item was inherited from another project's notes and never checked here.
It is not an RNG divergence. The port declines the feature outright:

```text
  REFUSED (features the port declined, and how often):
     1658x minecraft:sculk_patch
```

1658 refusals, and 1506 missing sculk blocks in that window. `sculk_vein` —
the multiface growth — *is* implemented; `sculk_patch`, which places the sculk
itself, is not.

That also makes it the largest single block-count gap now known, and unlike
the ore residual it is an order of magnitude above the ~109 oracle noise
floor, so it is worth real work.

**Scope, from `SculkPatchFeature.place`:**

```java
  if (!canSpreadFrom(level, origin)) return false;
  SculkSpreader spreader = SculkSpreader.createWorldGenSpreader();
  int rounds = config.spreadRounds() + config.growthRounds();
  for (int i = 0; i < rounds; i++) {
      for (int j = 0; j < config.chargeCount(); j++)
          spreader.addCursors(origin, config.amountPerCharge());
      boolean convert = i < config.spreadRounds();
      for (int k = 0; k < config.spreadAttempts(); k++)
          spreader.updateCursors(level, origin, random, convert);
      spreader.clear();
  }
  ... origin.below(), catalyst placement
```

with `sculk_patch_deep_dark` = charge_count 10, amount_per_charge 32,
spread_attempts 64, spread_rounds 1, growth_rounds 0, catalyst_chance 0.5.

So one round, 10 cursors of 32 charge each, 64 update passes. The work is
`SculkSpreader` itself — cursors, charge decay, the spread search and
`SculkBehaviour` — which is the same machinery the sculk catalyst uses at
runtime, so porting it is not only worldgen work.

### `SculkSpreader` step 1: the container and `addCursors`, gated

`feature/sculk_spreader.rs`. Constants read off the class file, not the wiki:

```text
  MAX_GROWTH_RATE_RADIUS 24    MAX_CHARGE          1000
  MAX_DECAY_FACTOR      0.5f   MAX_CURSORS           32
  SHRIEKER_PLACEMENT_RATE 11   MAX_CURSOR_DISTANCE 1024
```

`createWorldGenSpreader()` is `new SculkSpreader(true,
SCULK_REPLACEABLE_WORLD_GEN, 50, 1, 5, 10)` — worldgen true, growthSpawnCost
50, noGrowthRadius 1, chargeDecayRate 5, additionalDecayRate 10. The level
spreader differs in every one of those, which is why they are constructor
arguments rather than constants.

Two behaviours worth having tests for now rather than later, because both
*lose* charge and both would otherwise look like a shortfall in the wrong
place:

  * `addCursor` **silently drops** a cursor once 32 exist. A port that grew
    the list would keep charge vanilla throws away and produce *more* sculk;
  * `addCursors` splits at `MAX_CHARGE` 1000 rather than clamping, so a large
    charge becomes several cursors — invisible on the worldgen path, where
    `amount_per_charge` is 32, and load-bearing on the catalyst path.

7 unit tests. `is_pos_unreasonable` is x/z only, not y.

### `SculkSpreader` step 2: the 18 neighbour offsets, and their order

`NON_CORNER_NEIGHBOURS` is the 3x3x3 block minus the centre minus the eight
corners — a corner being exactly the case where all three coordinates are
non-zero, which is what vanilla's filter says:

```java
  betweenClosedStream((-1,-1,-1), (1,1,1))
      .filter(p -> (p.getX() == 0 || p.getY() == 0 || p.getZ() == 0)
                   && !p.equals(BlockPos.ZERO))
```

**The base order matters even though every caller shuffles it**, because the
shuffle permutes *indices*: a different base order gives a different answer
from identical draws. `betweenClosedStream` runs through `Cursor3D`, whose
arithmetic is `x = i % width`, `y = (i / width) % height`,
`z = i / width / height` — x fastest, then y, then z. Taken off the bytecode
rather than recalled, because the plausible alternatives differ only in
results and never in shape.

`getRandomizedNonCornerNeighbourOffsets` is `Util.shuffledCopy`, which is
`Util.shuffle` — the same descending Fisher-Yates with bound `i` the capped
processor uses, so it shares
`structure::processor::shuffled_order` rather than owning a second copy that
could drift.

10 unit tests on the module now.

### NOW — `ChargeCursor::update` and `SculkBehaviour`

The remaining bulk, in dependency order:

  1. ~~`isMovementUnobstructed` / `isUnobstructed`~~ **DONE**, 14 tests on the
     module. Two details each worth a test:
     * `isUnobstructed` reads the **neighbour's opposite** face — the one
       pointing back at the cursor — not the cursor's own face. Both choices
       agree in most worlds;
     * a diagonal needs only **one** of its two component faces free (`||`),
       and `Direction.fromAxisAndDirection` is asked `< 0`, so a **zero
       component counts as POSITIVE**. `isMovementUnobstructed` builds a
       direction per axis *before* testing which axis is zero, so treating
       zero as negative picks the opposite face on exactly the axes that
       decide the branch.
     `getValidMovementPos` and `hasSubstrateAccess` are **also done** now, 19
     tests on the module. Two behaviours that are easy to get backwards:
     * it returns the **last** valid neighbour, not the first — `best` is
       overwritten each time and only a vein *with substrate access* breaks
       the loop early;
     * `instanceof SculkBehaviour` is a **class** test, not a tag. Only
       `sculk`, `sculk_vein` and `sculk_catalyst` qualify; deepslate is
       sculk-*replaceable* but is not a step target, and `sculk_shrieker` and
       `sculk_sensor` are not either.
  2. `getDecayPenalty` **DONE** (23 tests). Three details that read
     differently from the usual description:
     * the clamp is at **1.0**, not at `MAX_DECAY_FACTOR`; the 0.5 is a
       separate final multiply, so clamping at 0.5 *and* multiplying would
       halve it twice;
     * `(int)` is `f2i` — **truncation**, no `+ 0.5f` rounding;
     * the arithmetic is `f32` after `d2f`, so computing in `f64` and
       narrowing at the end differs at the boundaries.

     `SculkBehaviour` defaults are read: `getSculkSpreadDelay` 1,
     `depositCharge` false, `canChangeBlockStateOnSpread` true,
     `updateDecayDelay` 1, `attemptUseCharge` abstract.
  3. `canPlaceGrowth` **DONE** (27 tests). The space above must be air **or
     source water** — two conditions, block *and* fluid state, so flowing
     water does not qualify — and the crowding box is 9x3x9, asymmetric in y:
     two blocks up, none down, so a sensor directly below does not count.

     A test caught a real precedence bug while writing it: `bare == water &&
     !contains("level=") || contains("level=0")` binds the `||` loosely, so
     *any* block carrying `level=0` read as water — a composter, a cauldron.
     Only the composter case failed; the water cases all passed.
  4. `attemptUseCharge` **DONE** for `SculkBlock`, plus `getRandomGrowthState`
     (31 tests). The draw accounting is what had to be exact, because a
     spurious or missing draw moves every later cursor:
     * the decay roll is **skipped entirely** at zero charge, so a spent
       cursor cannot disturb the stream — asserted by checking a fresh source
       still agrees afterwards;
     * `nextInt(cost)` is spent whether or not the growth spawns; only the
       *comparison* is conditional;
     * `Math.max(0, charge - cost)` is returned on the growth branch **even
       when nothing spawned**, so reaching it always costs the full cost;
     * a worldgen shrieker has `can_summon=true` — it is the worldgen flag,
       not a constant, so catalyst-grown shriekers differ.
  5. remaining `SculkBehaviour` — `attemptSpreadVein`,
     `canChangeBlockStateOnSpread`, `updateDecayDelay`, `getSculkSpreadDelay`,
     with implementations on `SculkBlock`, `SculkVeinBlock` and the default;
  6. `updateCursors` **DONE for worldgen** (35 tests). The finding that made
     it small: **`isWorldGeneration()` branches straight past the merge**, so a
     sculk patch never combines two cursors landing on one block — they both
     survive. The per-position charge map and `mergeWith` exist only for the
     catalyst path, and are deliberately left unimplemented and named rather
     than written untestable.

     Also pinned: an *unreasonable* cursor is dropped **without** being
     updated, so it cannot spend a draw on its way out; a spent cursor is
     dropped rather than kept at zero; and surviving order is preserved.
  7. `shouldUpdate` **DONE** (37 tests): charge is checked *before* the
     worldgen shortcut, so a spent cursor refuses even during generation, and
     outside worldgen the answer is `ServerLevel.shouldTickBlocksAt` — which
     this port has no model for and therefore refuses rather than guessing.
     That asymmetry is why a patch spreads through chunks nowhere near a
     player: the same code would decline at runtime.
  8. `ChargeCursor::update` **DONE for worldgen** (42 tests). Three details
     that decide the stream rather than the appearance:
     * `updateDelay` is decremented **and the update returns** — a delayed
       cursor draws nothing that pass, asserted by checking a fresh source
       still agrees afterwards;
     * a *spent* cursor returns before even the decrement, because
       `shouldUpdate` is checked first;
     * the 15-block leash applies **only during worldgen**, and it zeroes the
       charge **after** the move — so a killed cursor has already left its old
       block, which a port that checked before moving would get wrong.

     `attemptSpreadVein` is injected as a closure. Passing "never converts" is
     exactly the `growthRounds` case, so everything around it is gated now.
  9. **RETRACTED — the spread geometry was already ported.** I wrote a second
     copy of `SpreadType`, `getSpreadPos` and
     `getSpreadFromFaceTowardDirection`'s guards into `sculk_spreader.rs`
     before searching. `feature/multiface_growth.rs` has had all of it, gated,
     since glow lichen — `SpreadType`, `DEFAULT_SPREAD_ORDER`, `spread_types`,
     `is_other_block_valid_as_source`, `can_spread_into`,
     `state_can_be_replaced` (including sculk vein's sculk / sculk_catalyst /
     moving_piston refusals and the sturdy-backing test at Manhattan distance
     2) and `spread_from_face_toward_direction`.

     Removed and re-exported instead. Two copies of a spread rule agree on the
     day they are written and drift the first time either is corrected.

     **The lesson is the search, not the deletion.** The module doc of
     `multiface_growth.rs` describes sculk vein's spreading rules in prose, in
     the file, and I had read that file earlier in this same session to check
     whether `spread_all` existed. Finding "no `spread_all`" and concluding
     "nothing here" was the error: the method names differ from vanilla's
     because the port names them after what they do.

     **`spread_all` is now DONE**, in `multiface_growth.rs` where the rest of
     the spreader lives, built on the existing
     `spread_from_face_toward_direction`:

     ```java
       spreadAll = Direction.stream()
           .filter(d -> config.canSpreadFrom(state, d))
           .map(d -> spreadFromFaceTowardAllDirections(...))   // 6 directions
           .reduce(0L, Long::sum);
     ```

     Every face crossed with every direction — up to **36** attempts — and the
     result is a *count of successes*, not stop-at-first. Vanilla's callers
     only compare it against zero, but short-circuiting would place fewer
     blocks rather than merely report a different number.

     `canSpreadFrom` is `isOtherBlockValidAsSource || hasFace`, and for a vein
     the first is true of any non-vein block — so **deepslate can spread from
     every face**, which is how a patch starts at all. Glow lichen has no such
     escape. Both directions tested.

     No random is taken anywhere on this path.
 10. **`feature/sculk_patch.rs` is written** — the whole feature, 5 tests, on
     top of the spreader. Two draw-order details:
     * the catalyst's `nextFloat` is **unconditional**: drawn *before* the
       full-block test, so a patch on soft ground still spends it;
     * `extraRareGrowths` is `ConstantInt(0)` for both shipped patches and a
       constant provider spends nothing.

     `canSpreadFrom` is stricter than it looks: a patch starts on existing
     sculk, **or** in air/source water that touches at least one solid face.
     Open air alone refuses — and a refusal spends no draws at all, so it
     returns `None` rather than an empty patch.

     Still injected: `attemptSpreadVein`, which routes into
     `multiface_growth::spread_all` and needs a `MultifaceWorld` plus the
     block tags that the `SculkWorld` trait does not carry.

 11. **Wired into the dispatcher — and the measurement says the stub is the
     whole feature, not a harmless default.**

     The refusals are gone and the feature runs. But:

     ```text
       vanilla   5509 sculk   1794 sculk_vein   20 sensor   3 catalyst   2 shrieker
       ours         0 sculk     17 sculk_vein    0 sensor   1 catalyst   0 shrieker
       window exactness unchanged at 99.854492%
     ```

     **Zero sculk.** I described the injected `|_, _| false` as "exactly the
     `growthRounds` case vanilla itself runs", and that is true of the
     *configuration* but false of this feature: `sculk_patch_deep_dark` has
     `spread_rounds: 1`, so conversion is not an optional extra, it is where
     the sculk comes from.

     The sculk block itself is placed by `SculkVeinSpreaderConfig.placeBlock`
     on the `spreadToFace` path — a vein with substrate converts to
     `minecraft:sculk`. Stubbing `attemptSpreadVein` therefore removes the
     entire output, and the 17 veins and 1 catalyst that do appear come from
     the charge/catalyst paths alone.

     Retracting that claim: the stub was a hole, not a configuration.

 12. **The vein behaviour is in; the vein *spread* is measured not viable.**

     Two real gaps were found and one was fixed:

     * **`getBlockBehaviour` dispatch was missing.** The behaviour is chosen
       by the block *at the cursor*, and the two differ completely:
       `SculkBlock` grows a sensor or shrieker for the full `growthSpawnCost`,
       `SculkVeinBlock` **converts its substrate to `minecraft:sculk` for one
       charge** via `attemptPlaceSculk`. Running the sculk version on a vein
       places no sculk at all. Implemented and gated (52 tests), including
       that the sculk lands on the block *behind an occupied vein face* rather
       than at the cursor, and that `Direction.allShuffled` draws even when
       nothing converts.

     * **But the cursors never sit on veins**, because veins come from
       `attemptSpreadVein`. Wiring that to `multiface_growth::spread_all`
       does **not terminate usefully**:

       ```text
         single chunk, r=0      timeout at 120 s
         25-chunk window        timeout at 590 s
         (both took seconds before)
       ```

       That is unbounded work rather than expensive work, so the call shape is
       wrong somewhere — most likely `spread_all` is being invoked per cursor
       per attempt (10 x 64 per patch) when vanilla's cost is nothing like
       that, or the port's spread path carries the feature's `search_range`
       into what should be a fixed 6x6 fold.

       **Reverted to the stub**, with the numbers recorded. Shipping a hang so
       a census looks better is not a trade this project makes, and a window
       that never finishes cannot be diffed against anything.

 13. **`spread_all` is NOT the cause — measured, one hypothesis eliminated.**

     A patch's whole budget is 10 cursors x 64 attempts = 640 calls. Timed in
     a **debug** build:

     ```text
       640 spread_all calls in 70.4 ms
     ```

     So one patch costs ~70 ms debug, far less in release, and a chunk's ~60
     patches cannot reach 120 s that way. Reading the function agreed — 6
     faces x 6 directions x 3 spread types of bounded work, **no search** —
     but it is measured now rather than argued.

     That kills the `search_range` hypothesis outright. What remains is
     **feedback**: `spread_all` writes veins; a written vein is a
     `SculkBehaviour` block, so `get_valid_movement_pos` starts finding
     targets, cursors stop dying, and each surviving cursor spreads again.
     `isOtherBlockValidAsSource` is true of *any non-vein block* for a vein,
     so every cursor position spreads from all six faces on every attempt.

     **Measured: one whole patch, `attemptSpreadVein` live, is bounded.**

     ```text
       one patch: 320 spread calls, 6 block writes, 320 growths, 49.1 ms (debug)
     ```

     320 calls against a 640 budget — cursors die partway, as they should —
     and **6** writes. Bounded, fast, and nothing like a runaway. So the
     feedback hypothesis is wrong too, at least in isolation.

     That leaves the **pipeline wiring specifically**, not the algorithm. The
     fixture and the real decoration world differ in what `is_full_block` and
     `is_sculk_replaceable` cost, in how many blocks are genuinely replaceable
     (so how many writes succeed), and in what a canvas write triggers —
     heightmaps, post-processing marks, writes escaping the chunk clip.

     **Found: a constant hoisted into a loop, not an unbounded algorithm.**

     Instrumented the dispatcher's own closure behind `RUSTMC_SCULK_VEIN=1`
     and timed one chunk:

     ```text
       vein spread OFF     4.29 s
       vein spread ON    162.95 s      (< 100k calls, so ~1.6 ms each)
     ```

     A per-call cost that high for 108 bounded operations named the cause:
     `vein_config()` was called **inside** the closure, and it runs
     `state_spec::extract_or_skip()`, which loads and parses the whole
     block-state extract. Hundreds of calls per patch, thousands per chunk.

     Hoisted into a `OnceLock`:

     ```text
       vein spread ON     23.22 s      (7x faster; 5x the baseline, not 38x)
     ```

     Both earlier hypotheses were about vanilla's algorithm. The fault was in
     my wiring, and the only reason it looked algorithmic is that I measured
     the algorithm — twice — instead of the thing that was slow.

     With the spread live over the full window:

     ```text
                  vanilla   ours(before)   ours(now)
       sculk         5509             0         198
       sculk_vein    1794            17         254
       mismatches    3576  ->  3511    (99.854492% -> 99.857137%)
     ```

     Sculk generates. The volume is ~4% of vanilla's — and that has now been
     narrowed to a single number.

     **98.7% of patches refuse:**

     ```text
       SCULK_PATCH started=20 refused=1480
     ```

     And every refused origin is solid rock:

     ```text
       SCULK_REFUSE (-943,-18,1290) tuff
       SCULK_REFUSE (-937,-62,1288) bedrock
       SCULK_REFUSE (-939,-59,1289) deepslate[axis=y]
       SCULK_REFUSE (-940,-23,1283) gravel
     ```

     That is **correct behaviour**: `canSpreadFrom` wants air or source water
     touching a solid face, and vanilla refuses solid rock identically. Nor is
     the placement chain filtering for air — `sculk_patch_deep_dark` is

     ```text
       count 256, in_square, height_range uniform(above_bottom 0 .. absolute 256), biome
     ```

     with no air predicate at all. So vanilla aims at solid rock just as often
     and refuses just as often.

     Which means the gap is **not in the patch code and not in the placement
     chain**. It is in how often an origin lands in air — i.e. in the cave
     volume of our world at these depths versus vanilla's. 20 starts against
     the ~1650 attempts implies vanilla starts far more, since a patch writes
     only about six blocks and vanilla has 5509.

     extents.** `van-badlands` is a radius-3 world (122 chunks); the port's

     Two blocks apart. Our caves are vanilla's, so the origins land in air as

       sculk_vein        253    254     exact
       sculk_catalyst      1      1     exact

       sculk_sensor        4      0     absent

     **Two missing steps found and fixed, both inside `attemptPlaceSculk`.**
     It does not stop at the `setBlock`:

     ```java
       level.setBlock(target, SCULK.defaultBlockState(), 3);
       this.veinSpreader.spreadAll(sculkState, level, target,
                                   spreader.isWorldGeneration());     // (1)
       for (Direction d : DIRECTIONS) {                               // (2)
           if (d == direction.getOpposite()) continue;
           if (level.getBlockState(target.relative(d)).is(this))
               this.onDischarged(level, ns, target.relative(d), random);
       }
     ```

     **(1) every new sculk block seeds veins around itself.** Adding it took
     sculk 198 -> 395 and veins 254 -> 508.

     **(2) neighbouring veins are then discharged** — `onDischarged` drops any
     face whose backing has just become sculk, and deletes the vein if that
     leaves none. Adding it took veins 508 -> 221.

     On the identical 25-chunk window:

       sculk             475      198     395    (83%)
       sculk_vein        253      254     221    (87%)
       sculk_catalyst      1        1       1    exact
       sculk_sensor        4        0       0
       sculk_shrieker      1        0       0
     ```

     Neither omission broke anything visibly — the sculk still appeared, the
     veins still appeared. They just produced the wrong *amount*, which reads
     as a tuning problem and is in fact two absent calls.

     **Deferred writes were the next fault, and the biggest.** The dispatcher
     collected `patch.growths` and applied them *after* the patch finished, so
     every conversion read a world that never contained the sculk already
     placed. Measured: **4076 conversions producing 395 distinct blocks**, ~10x
     redundancy — the same substrate converting over and over, charge spent on
     nothing, and no cascade at all.

     Vanilla's `attemptPlaceSculk` calls `level.setBlock` inline. `SculkWorld`
     now carries a `set_block` and the conversion writes immediately.

                     vanilla   deferred   immediate

       sculk_vein        253        221         254   <- essentially exact
       sculk_sensor        4          0           1   <- growths now happen
       sculk_catalyst      1          1           0   <- regressed
     ```

     Collecting writes and applying them later *looks* equivalent and is not.
     That is the third omission in this feature whose symptom was a wrong
     amount rather than a wrong shape.

     `SculkAdapter::set_block` goes through `MultifaceWorld::set_block` on the
     decoration world, which clips to the chunk being decorated. A conversion
     landing outside that clip is dropped, but `is_sculk_replaceable` reads
     through and still answers "deepslate" — so the same block converts on
     every attempt, forever, and the ones that *do* land inside the clip are
     the 349 extras.

     That single mechanism would explain the redundancy, the overshoot, and
     why immediate writes helped but did not fix it.

     ```text
       SCULK_BRANCH sculk_updates=1579 growths=2578 landed=2565 dropped=0
     ```

     Not one write is dropped. And the tag is right too — resolved,
     `sculk_replaceable_world_gen` has 58 members, contains `deepslate`, does
     **not** contain `sculk`. So a converted block genuinely cannot reconvert.

     Those three facts cannot all hold for one persistent world, so the world
     is not persistent: either the canvas a patch writes to is discarded
     between placement attempts, or each of the ~24 started patches is being
     run against a fresh copy.

     Note 24 patches x ~107 conversions = ~2568, which matches 2565 almost
     exactly — so every patch really does convert ~107 blocks, and only ~80
     survive in total. The survivors are roughly one patch's worth.

     **Sentinel test: writes DO persist.**

       SENTINEL written at (-944, -54, 1287)
       SENTINEL patch#2 reads minecraft:bone_block[axis=y] at (-944,-54,1287)
       SENTINEL patch#3 reads minecraft:bone_block[axis=y] ...

     So the world is persistent, every write lands, and no block is eligible

     conversions are counted over everything the run decorates, which includes

     Both are far below the charge ceiling, so charge is **not** what stops

     **The one story that links both discrepancies:** we place 61 veins in air
     vanilla leaves empty. A vein is a `SculkBehaviour` block, so it is a valid
     `getValidMovementPos` target — every spurious vein is another place a
     cursor can walk to and convert from. Over-placing veins would produce
     exactly this: more reachable substrate, cursors that live longer, uniform

     **Dumped one. The two worlds do opposite things in the same column:**

     ```text
       column (-920, ., 1299)
         vanilla   y-56 deepslate   y-55 sculk       y-54 air         y-52 air
         ours      y-56 deepslate   y-55 deepslate   y-54 sculk_vein  y-52 sculk_vein
     ```

     Vanilla **converted the substrate** at y-55 and left the air above empty.
     This port **hung a vein in the air** at y-54 and left the deepslate below
     unconverted.

     So it is not "extra veins" at all — it is a vein placed *instead of* a
     conversion. That reframes both residuals as one:

     ```text
       61  vanilla air        ours sculk_vein   } the same event,
       33  vanilla sculk      ours deepslate    } seen from two sides
      349  vanilla deepslate  ours sculk        (over-conversion elsewhere)
     ```

     The 61 and the 33 are comparable in size because they are largely the
     same positions: where vanilla converts, we vein.

     **Traced. The cursor logic is correct; the vein's FACES are the fault.**

     ```text
       CUR at (-944,-54,1287) on sculk_vein[up=true,...] charge=32
           vein-branch converted=Some(((-944,-53,1287), Up))
       CUR at (-944,-54,1287) on sculk_vein[up=true,...] charge=32
           vein-branch converted=None            (x9)
     ```

     Ten cursors start at the same origin with 32 charge each — that is
     `addCursors(origin, 32)` called ten times, exactly as configured. The
     first converts; the other nine find the block already sculk and decline.
     Charge, movement and the branch are all behaving.

     But the vein at the cursor has **`up=true`**, so it converts **upward**.
     The column that started this hunt had vanilla converting **downward**,
     from a vein with `down=true`:

     ```text
       vanilla   y-55 sculk       (converted down from a vein above)
       ours      y-54 sculk_vein  (up=true, converts up instead)
     ```

     `attempt_place_sculk` walks the vein's occupied faces and converts behind
     one of them, so **which faces a vein has decides which block becomes
     sculk**. A vein with the wrong face set converts the wrong block — and
     also survives where vanilla's would have been discharged.

     So the fault is upstream of the spreader entirely: it is in
     `multiface_growth`'s choice of *which face* a spreading vein occupies.
     **Checked glow lichen — it CLEARS the shared code.** Same window:

     ```text
       vanilla 41 glow_lichen   ours 38
       mismatches: 3, all "vanilla lichen, ours cave_air"
       wrong face-states: ZERO
     ```

     Three missing patches and not one wrong face. The shared geometry
     places faces correctly, so the conclusion above is **retracted**.

     What glow lichen never exercises is `isOtherBlockValidAsSource` —
     true for a sculk vein against *any non-vein block*, always false for
     lichen. That is the one branch the two do not share, and it is the
     branch deciding whether a spread may start from a face the source
     does not occupy. So the fault is sculk-specific after all.

     **Checked that predicate path too — it matches.** Vanilla's
     `DefaultSpreaderConfig.canSpreadInto` is
     `stateCanBeReplaced(...) && isValidStateForPlacement(...)`, and this
     port's `can_spread_into` is the same two calls in the same order.

     **And re-reading the column shows the vein is a SYMPTOM, not a cause:**

     ```text
       vanilla   y-55 sculk       y-54 air
       ours      y-55 deepslate   y-54 sculk_vein[down=true]
     ```

     A `down=true` vein at y-54 rests on y-55. Vanilla **converted** y-55
     to sculk, which discharged the vein above it — its down face now
     backs onto sculk, so the face is dropped and the vein dies. We never
     converted y-55, so our vein survives *legitimately*.

     So the 61 "spurious veins" are not a vein bug at all. They are the
     33 missing conversions, seen from one block higher. Both residuals
     collapse into one: **we convert the wrong blocks** — 349 vanilla does
     not, and miss 33 it does.

     Six hypotheses have now died: search range, feedback, clipping,
     persistence, shared geometry, and the spread predicate. Every one of
     the mechanisms is correct; the *choice of which block to convert* is
     what differs, and that is `attempt_place_sculk`'s shuffled face walk.

### Swept for the same pattern elsewhere — clean

A draw that vanilla spends only when a block entity exists is invisible in the
feature's own code, so it is worth asking where else the port could make the
same mistake. Every other `next_i64` in `feature/` and `structure/` is test
code — probes, references and assertions — and no feature body spends one.
Mineshaft places chests and spends nothing for them either.

So `monster_room` was the only instance, and the sweep is recorded rather than
repeated.

### Method note, since it cost the day

Twelve pieces of `SpeleothemClusterFeature` and six of `MonsterRoomFeature`
were read against the bytecode and every one matched, because the fault was
never in a branch — it was in *two draws that a branch guards*. Reading finds
wrong logic; it cannot find a draw that vanilla skips for a reason invisible in
the feature's own code.

Two inferences of mine died here, both built on aggregate counters that
silently summed across rooms. What ended it was making **vanilla's** side
observable rather than inferring it from totals — after which the answer was a
`diff` with no arithmetic in it at all.

That was the entire difficulty for hours: only the port's half of the body
could be seen, so every comparison went through totals, and the totals were
built on counters that silently aggregated.

First action: log the port's draws the same way — a `DRAW n method(bound) ->
value` line from `rng::draws` when armed — and diff the two sequences for
`monster_room_deep` on chunk (60,59). The first line that differs is the
defect, exactly located, with no arithmetic in between.

Fix the counters while there: `take_room_counts` must be per room, not per
chunk, or it will mislead the next reader the way it misled me.

The room is at (962,-15,954) with radii (3,2), so the floor ring is 63 known
positions and two of them differ. That is a small, fully-determined search.

First action: dump the block at each of the 63 floor positions from the
harness's world, and check each against the block-props table's `solid` column
— the same table `is_solid_at` reads. Two of them will be a block whose
`isSolid` this port answers wrongly, and that is a table or a lookup bug rather
than anything in `monster_room` at all.

Note what this predicts: the same wrong answer will affect **every** feature
that asks `isSolid` about that block, so fixing it may move far more than the
two draws. That is a claim to check after the fix, not to assume.

Every branch of `monster_room` now reads as matching, and it still spends two
draws too many, which is the same position this investigation reached with the
sulfur cluster after twelve matching reads. The lesson from that one applies
directly: stop reading and count.

Add a coin counter to the wall loop — the `RUSTMC_TRACE_PATCH` treatment — and
report it with the room's radii and the number of wall positions visited. Ours
is measurable immediately; vanilla's is not directly, but the *totals* pin it:
if our coin count is two above what the radii imply, the fault is `isSolid`; if
it matches the radii, the loop is visiting positions vanilla does not and the
bounds are wrong.

That distinction is exactly what the trace can settle and reading cannot, and
it is one instrument away.

This is the last unread branch in the feature and it is the right shape: two
extra draws is two wall positions where vanilla skipped the coin and we spent
it. The `CHEST` guard is the more interesting of the two, because the chest
loop runs *after* the wall loop, so it can only fire on a chest that was
already in the world — from a neighbouring room, or a previously decorated
chunk — which is exactly the kind of world-dependent branch a single-chunk
harness would never exercise.

Then: fix, re-run chunk (60,59)'s gate, and re-measure both windows. The five
`tip_merge` blocks and the 41 in (66,62) are downstream of this one feature and
should move together — that is the prediction to check, and if they do not move
the causal chain recorded here is wrong.

This is the end of the chain that started with five `tip_merge` blocks: a
monster room two draws wrong shifts its own chunk's later features, those
features write different blocks into the neighbouring chunk, and the sulfur
cluster there — twelve pieces of which are read and matching — scans columns
that vanilla never had.

Gates for all four are running. Two outcomes and both are decisive:

  * **A gate fails.** That is the defect, with an exact input, and twelve
    matching bytecode reads say it will not be in the cluster's arithmetic —
    so it will be in what the gate has never checked about these features.
  * **All four pass.** Then the gate is green on a chunk whose real output is
    wrong by 9 blocks against a world it agrees with, which localises the fault
    to something the gate does not compare at all — and the gate compares
    positions, positionDraws, blocks, and the RNG after. The only thing left
    outside that set is **writes into neighbouring chunks**, which the vectors
    record in `changes` but the replay only checks inside the centre.

**One of those two branches is already narrowed: the gate is *not*
centre-scoped.** `Region::changes` drains every write in the 3x3 with no filter
and sorts by `chunk_index`, so cross-chunk writes are compared like any other.
The "writes into neighbours are unchecked" reading was wrong, and it was cheap
to check.

So if all four gates pass, the fault is outside a comparison that covers
positions, `positionDraws`, blocks *including neighbours*, and the RNG after —
which is a much stronger statement, and the remaining candidates become the
things the vectors do not record at all: the order features run *between*
chunks, and anything a feature reads that the snapshot does not capture.

Every piece of the cluster matches, so cluster B's shifted output is explained
by the world it read; but that world differs because cluster A's output was
shifted, and A matches too. The regress only terminates at the window's raster
start, where a chunk has no decorated predecessors and its world *must* be
vanilla's.

The control run over (59,59)..(60,60) is in flight and is the thing that
settles it. (59,59) has an empty prefix, so its drift must be 0. If it is not
0, the comparison itself is faulty — the prefix set, the snapshot alignment, or
`RUSTMC_DECORATE_PREFIX`'s exclusivity — and every number taken from it today
is suspect, which would be worth knowing before another hypothesis is built on
one.

If it *is* 0, walk forward from there chunk by chunk in raster order. The first
non-zero is a chunk whose predecessors are all clean, and its divergence cannot
be blamed on its input world. That is the only place in this whole structure
where the cluster can be caught with an exact input and a wrong output.

The drift is a chain — each chunk reads its predecessors — so only the *first*
link is evidence. `RUSTMC_DECORATE_PREFIX` makes each link testable: decorate
the prefix up to chunk C, compare against `-Ddecorate.region` vectors for C,
and the first C that differs is where it starts.

The window's raster order begins at (59,59). Bisect: test the prefix at the
middle of the window first, and halve. Each test is one pipeline run and one
oracle run, so the whole search is about seven pairs.

**Do not start from (63,66).** Its differing columns are in (62,66), which is
its predecessor, and that chunk's own inputs are earlier still — the first link
could be many chunks back, and every chunk tested so far has gated green
individually precisely because the fault is not local to any of them.

### CLOSED — chunk (67,62) is green, and it was two faults not one

Five gate disagreements to **zero**, against region-scoped vectors, across
positions, `positionDraws`, blocks and the RNG after. The 169 committed cases
pass alongside. They were not the same kind of fault and separating them
matters:

**A port bug — `block_column` tested the origin its fit walk should skip.**
Covered below. Worth exactly one draw, and that one draw moved every later
candidate in the chunk onto a different stream.

**A harness gap — the decorate gate could not answer a carpet.**
`CarpetBlock#canSurvive` is `!level.isEmptyBlock(pos.below())`;
`Family::Carpet` implements precisely that and `moss_carpet` was already
mapped to it, so the *rule was never missing*. The harness's `SurvivalWorld`
adapter did not implement `air_at`, whose trait default is `None` meaning
"this world cannot say", and an unanswerable survival check is an `Err` that
the `?` in `distribute_vegetation` turns into abandoning the rest of the set.
Three of fifty-seven columns ran. That is the whole of the 51-blocks-against-
101, and the real pipeline never had it — it supplies `air_at` through
`SurvivalView`.

**Neither was the "vegetation_patch column search"** this file spent a long
time inside. The column search was correct throughout.

### CLOSED — `moss_patch_ceiling`'s extra draw was `block_column`'s fit walk

`BlockColumnFeature.place` keeps two cursors: `pos` at the origin, which the
write loop uses, and a copy moved one step in `direction` **before** the fit
loop (`pos.mutable().move(direction)`, offsets 110..122). The copy is what
`allowedPlacement` is tested against, so the origin block is written without
ever being tested and `room` counts the blocks after it.

This port started its fit walk at the origin, making `room` one larger
whenever the origin was allowed. Invisible while the column fits — `truncate`
removes `total - room` and removes nothing when `room >= total` — and biting
only when truncation binds, where it kept one block too many and spent one
extra `getState` draw.

```text
  ceiling body                219 draws -> 218, vanilla's 218
  third cave_vine column        6 draws ->   5
  positions                          1 -> 2, vanilla's 2
  gate disagreements                 5 -> 2
```

Green on every field the gate checks. The 169 committed cases still pass.
`truncate` itself was already exact, as were the edge coin's three gates, the
`depth`-after-`isFaceSturdy` order and the `extra_bottom_block_chance`
short-circuit — all read from the bytecode and eliminated.

**Method note worth keeping.** The defect was found by splitting the body's
draw total into its sites rather than comparing it as one number: two radii,
one coin per edge-not-corner column, one depth per accepted column, one coin
per placed column, and the rest inside the vegetation feature. Four of those
are arithmetic — 40 edge coins for an 11x13 patch is exactly its perimeter
less its corners — so the residual was forced into one feature.

**And a trap that cost real time.** Those site counters are only *taken* when
a trace name matches, so a chunk running three patches invites attributing a
line to the wrong feature. Doing exactly that produced a draw budget no
arrangement of sites could satisfy — which is how the misattribution was
noticed. `PATCHSITES` now names its feature, and `ground_draws` is *priced*
with the draw counter rather than inferred by subtraction.

### The immediate next action

Vanilla's draw sites, from the bytecode, are exactly five:

```text
  place                 xzRadius.sample x2
  placeGroundPatch      nextFloat  (edge coin)   @178
                        depth.sample             @353
                        nextFloat  (extra bottom) @368
  distributeVegetation  nextFloat  (vegetation coin) @42
```

**Two are eliminated, both by reading the branch structure rather than the
source.** `depth.sample` sits at 353, *after* `isFaceSturdy` at 342 whose
`ifeq 426` skips the whole column — so a non-sturdy column costs vanilla no
draw, and `vegetation_patch.rs:269-275` has the sturdy test before the sample
in the same order. The `extra_bottom_block_chance` coin at 368 is guarded by
`fcmpl; ifle 385` on `chance > 0.0` and keeps the block when
`nextFloat < chance` (`fcmpg; ifge`), which is the port's
`chance > 0.0 && next_f32() < chance` exactly.

That leaves **the edge coin, the two `xzRadius` samples, and
`distributeVegetation`'s vegetation coin**. The edge coin's guard is worth the
same treatment: `iload 19; ifeq 194` tests the corner flag *first*, then
`extraEdgeColumnChance == 0.0` short-circuits to 426, and only then is
`nextFloat` taken — three gates before one draw, and an extra draw would come
from any of them being ordered differently here.

`RUSTMC_TRACE_PATCH=1` already reports `wrote`/`no_move`/`veg_tried`/
`columns`/`depth_sum` per feature, which localises the extra draw to a phase
before the bytecode read narrows it to a line.

### Done this turn

`positionDraws` has been in every vector file since the dumper was written and
**nothing has ever compared it**. That is the blind spot this defect lived in:
a body spending the wrong draws is invisible while the chain still yields the
same first position, because the damage lands on the *next* candidate.

`AttemptTrace.emitted_at` already records `(position, draw count)` on the port
side. `decorate::Attempt` has no field to carry it to the gate — add
`position_draws`, fill it where `positions` is filled, and compare it in
`golden_decorate.rs` beside the position list. Guard on both sides being
non-empty so an unarmed trace cannot fail the gate. Then read our 218-vs-N
directly instead of inferring it.

After that: find the draw that differs inside `VegetationPatchFeature`'s
ceiling path, against the bytecode.

### The decoration oracle is region-scoped now — this changed the numbers

`DecorateGolden` built a fresh 3x3 per centre and decorated only the middle
chunk. Neighbours were present for reads and never decorated, which is a world
no server produces. `-Ddecorate.region=<r>` now gives each centre its own grid
of radius r+1 and decorates the inner square in raster order **up to and
including the centre**, recording only the centre.

Measured at seed 31415926 centre (67,62): **11 of that chunk's 59 features
behave differently** once the neighbourhood decorates —
`lush_caves_ceiling_vegetation` 595 draws/131 changes/1 position becomes
898/288/**2**, `ore_tuff` moves 200 blocks. And **20 of the 169 committed
vectors were wrong**, including `patch_bush` at 4 positions where vanilla has
18. The port passes the corrected vectors with **no code change**, so it was
reading the world it was given and answering correctly for it; the harness was
supplying a world in which no neighbour had decorated.

This retires the claim, recorded below and reasoned from all session, that our
draws and positions for chunk (67,62) "match vanilla exactly (595/186/549)".
They matched an oracle. Vanilla's figures are 898/186/525.

**Raster is an assumption and is named in the dumper.** A cross-chunk feature
depends on which neighbour decorated first, which on a server is ticket order.
Strictly better than assuming no neighbour ever decorates; still an assumption.

Three phantom defects this session came from the old scope — a geode, a
"stray clay" and a short ceiling patch. The pattern is now three deep: `isAir`,
the biome container, decoration scope. Each time an oracle agreed with the port
and both differed from a server.

### What was resolved, and must not be re-opened

The whole speleothem/sulfur investigation that occupied this file is **closed**
and its cause was in none of the layers it dug through. See BENCH.md for the
full narrative; the short version is that
`ChunkGenerator.applyBiomeDecoration` allocates **one** `WorldgenRandom` per
chunk and calls `setFeatureSeed` on it per feature, while this port allocated
a fresh one per feature. That reproduces every *integer* draw — which is why
it survived every gate — but not the **gaussian cache**, which
`WorldgenRandom.setSeed` never resets because its override never calls
`super`. A feature drawing an odd number of gaussians leaves half a pair for
the next feature to consume as its first gaussian.

Both halves were needed and neither alone moved anything. Fixed and gated
(`worldgen_reseeded` in `gaussian_vectors.json`, verified load-bearing).

That took the window from **498 mismatches / 99.979736%** to **18 /
99.999268%**, removing the entire cinnabar/sulfur family — the 114
`cinnabar <-> sulfur` base columns, the 80 `sulfur_spike` present/absent tips,
and the +2.4% speleothem census surplus. `sulfur_spike` in chunk (62,62) now
reports vanilla's exact 97 positions and 3169 draws.

**Do not re-check these** — all read against the jar and matching, across that
investigation: `SpeleothemClusterFeature.place`/`placeColumn`,
`Column.scan`/`scanDirection`, `SpeleothemUtils.isEmptyOrWater`,
`replaceBlocksWithBaseBlocks`, `getChanceOfStalagmiteOrStalactite`,
`getSpeleothemHeight`, `ClampedNormalInt`/`ClampedNormalFloat`, `Mth.normal`,
`MarsagliaPolarGaussian` caching, `UniformFloat`/`Mth.randomBetween`,
`SimpleRandomSelectorFeature`, `EnvironmentScanPlacement`,
`RandomOffsetPlacement`, `LakeFeature.place`, `SpeleothemFeature.place`,
`createPatchOfBaseBlocks`, and `Direction.Plane.HORIZONTAL` order = N, E, S, W.

Also settled and not to be re-run: `nextGaussian` is exact over **10,000,000**
sampled draws (`long_run`), and a seventh decoration order does not shrink the
order-invariant core — `diag` yields a world byte-identical to raster, so
enumerating orders is not enumerating worlds.

### CLOSED: the deepslate ore family — `isAir` is three blocks, not one

`Feature#isAdjacentToAir` uses `BlockState::isAir`, which answers true for
`minecraft:air`, **`minecraft:cave_air`** and `minecraft:void_air`. This port
compared against `"minecraft:air"` alone, and `cave_air` is what every carver
writes — the only air that exists at those depths. So the buried ore variants
(`ore_diamond_buried` and `ore_lapis_buried`, both
`discard_chance_on_air_exposure` **1.0**, plus `ore_diamond_large` at 0.7)
never saw the cave beside them and were placed anyway.

Found by measurement: chunk (67,61) held exactly six blocks a vanilla server
does not — three gold, two lapis, one diamond — always ours-has-ore and never
the reverse, which is what a discard that never fires looks like.
`worldgen-dump column` then put `cave_air` immediately above or below all six.
**That chunk now diffs at 0 over 98,304 blocks: 100.000000%.**

25-chunk window: 15 -> **14** mismatches, 99.999390% -> **99.999430%**.

**The lesson matters more than the blocks.** This family replayed **exact**
against its isolated `DecorateGolden` oracle while differing from two servers
— the same signature as the parked sand/gravel item, which was being read as
evidence that the harness is unfaithful. It was not. The port was wrong and
the oracle could not see it. Do not treat "isolated oracle agrees with us" as
exoneration again.

A sweep for the same mistake elsewhere came back clean: every other
`== "minecraft:air"` in the crate is a test mock, except a `lake` config check
on a configured state rather than a world block. `spring.rs` already documents

### The water family is partly NOT A PARITY TARGET

The y-16 `air -> water` blocks include **flowing** water. Chunk (60,66)
against the full server world is 4 mismatches, three of them
`water[level=1]`. Across the 121-chunk window:

```text
  vanilla-r7   10 x water[level=1]   4 x water[level=8]
  ours          0                    0
```

Worldgen emits **sources**; `level=1` and `level=8` are what a *ticking* fluid
produces. `ci/gen-vanilla-region.sh` says so in its own header — forceloaded
chunks tick, and it hardens determinism with a fixed settle window rather than
preventing the ticking. So **14 blocks in the window are server fluid-tick
artifacts that a worldgen port cannot produce**, and they are not reachable
without simulating fluid ticks.

The `level=0` members of the family are a separate question and are not
covered by this: a source block we lack is a real worldgen difference.

### CLOSED: sand/gravel — the surface stage read the wrong biome

**Both the port and the oracle were wrong, in the same way.**

A server's `BiomeManager` resolves quart cells out of the chunk's **stored
biome container**, filled by `fillBiomesFromNoise` from
`noiseChunk.cachedClimateSampler(...)`. Sampling the climate function again at
the same cell is a *different computation*:

```text
  1013,45,1098   resampled = lukewarm_ocean   STORED = savanna
```

`savanna` is not in the rule's `[warm_ocean, lukewarm_ocean,
deep_lukewarm_ocean]`, so a server falls through to **gravel** where this port
took the ocean branch to **sand**.

Fixed on both sides:

* the surface pass now reads the container, snapshotting the 3x3 chunk
  neighbourhood first because it writes to the same canvas it reads from, and
  falling back to a resample only at the edge of the generated area;
* `SurfaceChunkGolden` now resolves out of the container too, so the oracle
  stops reproducing the port's mistake.

```text
  chunk (63,68) vs a fresh vanilla server   16 mismatches -> 0   100.000000%
  the oracle                                177/79 -> 161/95 = the server
  25-chunk window                           15 -> 14 mismatches, 99.999430%
```

That is the whole 51-block family — **51 of the 67 reachable genuine
mismatches** on the 121-chunk window.

**Why nine hypotheses missed it.** Every isolated oracle *also* recomputed, so
"our surface matches `SurfaceChunkGolden` bit-for-bit" was true and useless.
The two survivors of that trap — this and the `cave_air` ore bug — were both
found by trusting the **server** over the harness. That is now the standing
rule: a harness agreeing with the port is not evidence; only a
server-generated world is.

The surface gate stayed green throughout, because its fixed seeds and chunks
contain almost no disagreeing cell — regenerating the committed vectors with
the corrected oracle changes exactly **one case**, seed 0 chunk (80,153).

### CORRECTION: flowing water is generated, not a tick artifact

An earlier commit classified the 9 `water[level=1]` / `[level=8]` blocks as
unreachable fluid-tick products. **That was wrong.**
`ci/gen-vanilla-region.sh` issues **`tick freeze`** before any chunk loads —
its own comment says so: it "stops the game loop entirely (fluids, random
ticks — everything except chunk gen), so the harvest is the PURE generator
output", added after 27 blocks of mid-flow drift survived a 30s settle.

Verified rather than re-read: two regions generated **today** under that
freeze still contain `water[level=1]` and `water[level=8]`. So vanilla's
*generator* writes flowing water, and this port writes **none** — zero across
the 25-chunk window.

They are therefore real misses, and the reachable count is **25, not 16**.

placing it wrongly.

**Eliminated this turn:** the 2 `sulfur_spike[tip] -> water` and 10
`diorite -> andesite` on the 25-chunk window are not in the order-invariant
core and are order noise. `placeSupport` is not the fence bug — vanilla's
bytecode sets `FenceBlock.WEST` and `EAST` exactly as this port does. The
water family is not `LakeFeature` — its air is `cave_air` and the mismatched
blocks are plain `air`. It is not the `amethyst_geode` at (1008,4,1062)
either: that is 15 blocks from (1020,5,1071), well outside its radius.

Seed **31415926**, chunks 59..69 (centre 64,64), six decoration orders against

  raster    584 / 11,894,784   99.995090%    biomes 185,856 / 0
  zx      1,683    zx_rev  8,624    spiral  5,757
  spiral_in 5,601  reverse 17,278

(The two-world subtraction removed nothing here: `van-s2-c62` overlaps at 4,473
